uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry/26 - Te.searchText: RATES OF REACTION Investigating the Effect of Temperature on Reaction Rate At a higher temperature, the number of collisions occurring between reactant particles is greater because the particles are moving more quickly. When a collision occurs, there is more chance of a reaction taking place because the kinetic energy in the particles is greater. At a lower temperature, the number of collisions is lower because the particles are moving more slowly. Also when a collision occurs, there is less chance of a reaction taking place because the kinetic energy in the particles is less. Changing the temperature of a reactant changes how quickly the particles are moving (i.e. it will increase the amount of energy they have, if the temperature is increased). uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry/20 - El.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY A Closer Look at Electrons Chemical reactions are occurring all around us. Metals are corroding, food is cooking, plants are photosynthesising, etc. But how can we tell if two chemicals are going to react? The answer depends on their electrons. Electrons surround the nucleus of an atom in various energy levels (often referred to as ‘shells’ or ‘layers’). Each energy level can only contain a certain number of electrons. The first level (closest to the nucleus) can hold 2 electrons. The second level can hold 8 electrons. The third level can hold 8 electrons. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry/21 - Io.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Naming Ions When naming ions, you must adhere to the following rules: • Positive ions (i.e. the metals and hydrogen) are usually named after the element they are formed from. For example, the ion formed when calcium loses two electrons is also called the calcium ion (Ca2+). • Negative monatomic ions (‘mono’ means one, so monatomic means ‘ions made of only one atom’) are usually named using the suffix - ide. For example, chlorine (Cl) forms the negative ion chloride (Cl-), and oxygen (O) forms the oxide ion (O2-) • Polyatomic ions (‘poly’ means many, so polyatomic means ‘ions made of many atoms’) are usually named using the suffix -ate. For example, SO42- is the sulfate ion and CO32- is called the carbonate ion. Exceptions to this rule include the hydroxide ion (OH-) and the ammonium ion ( NH4+). • Some ions can have more than one charge. For example, iron can be Fe2+ or Fe3+. Chemists use roman numerals to distinguish (tell the difference) between them. Therefore, Fe2+ is written as Iron(II) and Fe3+ is written as iron(III). 1. At a lower temperature, the number of collisions is lower because the particles are moving more slowly. Also when a collision occurs, there is less chance of a reaction taking place because the kinetic energy in the particles is less. Changing the temperature of a reactant changes how quickly the particles are moving (i.e. it will increase the amount of energy they have, if the temperature is increased). uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry/21 - Io.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Naming Ions When naming ions, you must adhere to the following rules: • Positive ions (i.e. the metals and hydrogen) are usually named after the element they are formed from. For example, the ion formed when calcium loses two electrons is also called the calcium ion (Ca2+). • Negative monatomic ions (‘mono’ means one, so monatomic means ‘ions made of only one atom’) are usually named using the suffix - ide. For example, chlorine (Cl) forms the negative ion chloride (Cl-), and oxygen (O) forms the oxide ion (O2-) • Polyatomic ions (‘poly’ means many, so polyatomic means ‘ions made of many atoms’) are usually named using the suffix -ate. For example, SO42- is the sulfate ion and CO32- is called the carbonate ion. Exceptions to this rule include the hydroxide ion (OH-) and the ammonium ion ( NH4+). • Some ions can have more than one charge. For example, iron can be Fe2+ or Fe3+. Chemists use roman numerals to distinguish (tell the difference) between them. Therefore, Fe2+ is written as Iron(II) and Fe3+ is written as iron(III). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Atoms Each element on the Periodic Table is made up of unique types of atoms. The atomic number of the atom defines how many protons are in each atom, and this determines the number of electrons that occur in a neutral atom. Almost all of chemistry is the study of how these electrons behave when in the elemental substance, or during chemical reactions. Atoms are made up of 3 main types of particles: electrons, protons and neutrons. These particles have different properties. Electrons have a negative electrical charge (-). They surround the nucleus, and are arranged in layers called shells. Protons are much larger and heavier than electrons and have a positive charge (+). The number of protons in an atom is the same as the atomic number of that element. Neutrons have a similar mass to protons. They have no electrical charge (0). Neutrons help hold the nucleus together, and can vary in number between atoms of the same element. The nucleus is at the centre of the atom and contains the protons and neutrons. Virtually all the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus, because the electrons have very little mass. Relative mass Relative charge Proton 1 +1 Neutron 1 0 Electron 1/1840 -1 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Isotopes The atoms of a chemical element can exist in different forms. These are called isotopes. Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but a different mass number. This means they have the same number of protons (and electrons), but different numbers of neutrons. The word isotope comes from a Greek word meaning “the same place”, and is used because isotopes of an atom are located at the same place on the Periodic Table. The Isotopes of Chlorine Atomic number 17 Cl Chlorine 35 Atomic mass 17 Both of the isotopes of chlorine have the same atomic number. This means they both have 17 protons and 17 electrons - both atoms are neutral. Chlorine However, 35Cl and 37Cl have a different number of neutrons. 35Cl has 18 neutrons (35-17=18), whereas 37Cl has 20 neutrons (37-17=20). Cl 37 Note that it is standard practice to show isotopes with the atomic number below the mass number. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Reading the Elements If you look at the NCEA Periodic Table, you will notice that each element has a number associated with it. The number is called the atomic number and represents the number of protons found in the nucleus of a single atom of that element. Since the number of protons is equal to the number of electrons, the atomic number also tells you how many electrons there are in the energy levels around the nucleus. Another important number you will not find on the NCEA Periodic Table is called the mass number. This tells you the total number of particles, protons plus neutrons, found in the nucleus of an atom. So, if you know the mass number and the atomic number of an element, it is possible to work out the number of neutrons in the nucleus. By subtracting the number of protons from the mass number, you can calculate the total number of neutrons. Worked Example 1. A lithium atom has a mass number of 7. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Naming Ions When naming ions, you must adhere to the following rules: • Positive ions (i.e. the metals and hydrogen) are usually named after the element they are formed from. For example, the ion formed when calcium loses two electrons is also called the calcium ion (Ca2+). • Negative monatomic (‘mono’ means one, so monatomic means ‘ions made of only one atom’) ions are usually named using the suffix - ide. For example, chlorine (Cl) forms the negative ion chloride (Cl-), and oxygen (O) forms the oxide ion (O2-) • Polyatomic ions (‘poly’ means many, so polyatomic means ‘ions made of many atoms’) are usually named using the suffix -ate. For example, SO42- is the sulfate ion and CO32- is called the carbonate ion. Exceptions to this rule include the hydroxide ion (OH-) and the ammonium ion ( NH4+). • Some ions can have more than one charge. For example, iron can be Fe2+ or Fe3+. Chemists use Roman numerals to distinguish (tell the difference) between them. Therefore, Fe2+ is written as iron(II) and Fe3+ is written as iron(III). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY A Closer Look at Electrons Electrons surround the nucleus of an atom. The electrons are arranged in various energy levels (often referred to as ‘shells’ or ‘layers’). Each energy level can only contain a certain number of electrons. Usually it is only the outermost electrons that are involved in chemical reactions, and it is important to learn how to calculate how many electrons are in the outermost energy level or valence shell. The first energy level (closest to the nucleus) can hold 2 electrons. The second energy Level can hold 8 electrons. The third energy level can hold 8 electrons. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Writing Chemical Formulae A chemical formula is a combination of chemical symbols (such as Na, Cl, or Mg) and subscript numbers, that are used to show the composition of a compound. For example, the chemical formula for water is H2O. This shows that a water molecule is made up of two hydrogen atoms bonded to a single oxygen atom. Notice that if no number is given, as in the ‘O’ in H2O, then only one of that atom/ion is present. Ions with different charges combine during a chemical reaction to form compounds that have equal amounts of positive and negative charge. This means the resulting compound has no electrical charge. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: MOLECULAR SUBSTANCES Drawing Lewis Diagrams of Molecules The Lewis diagram of a molecule shows where covalent bonds are located, and the location of any lone pairs of electrons. Hydrogen and helium require two electrons in their valence shell. All other atoms in molecules require eight electrons (called the ‘octet rule’) in their valence shell. It is a common exam mistake to forget to fill up all valence shells once the basic structure of the molecule’s Lewis diagram has been determined. Method 1. Determine the number of valence electrons from all atoms in the formula A . 2. Calculate the total if all the elements were to have 8 valence electrons B . 3. Subtract B from A . This is the number of electrons that need to be shared C . 4. Divide C by 2. This is the number of shared pairs (covalent bonds) D . 5. Begin the Lewis diagram by drawing the central atom and placing other atoms around it systematically. 6. Draw in the number of bonds calculated( D ). 7. Complete an ‘octet’ of electrons for each atom you have drawn. Remember that hydrogen needs only two electrons so it will be ‘satisfied’ if it has a single bond to the central atom. Example - An ammonia molecule (NH3) A = Valence electrons: 1 x N = 5 and 3 x H = 3 B = Nitrogen: 8 valence electrons. Hydrogen: 2 valence electrons x 3 = 6 C = B - A = 14 - 8 = 6 Number of shared electrons = 6 D = C / 2 = 3 Number of covalent bond

uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: IONIC SUBSTANCES Explaining the Solubility of Ionic Substances When an ionic substance dissolves, the ionic bonds holding the ions in place must be broken. Polar solvents are attracted to the ions. The negatively charged region of a solvent molecule is attracted to the positively charged cations. Similarly, the positively charged region of the solvent molecule is attracted to the negatively charged anions. If the force of attraction between an ion and the solvent molecule is greater than the force of attraction between the ions themselves, the solid will dissolve. The ions are then held in solution by being surrounded by solvent molecules. H+ H+ H+ 0 2- H+ H+ 0 H+ 2- H+ 2- H+ 0 0 2- Model of Sodium Chloride Dissolving in Water A hydrated chloride ion Water molecules are attracted to the electrostatically charged ions of the ionic solid. Sodium chloride is highly soluble in water, meaning the ions are readily removed (dissociated) from the crystal lattice by water molecules. The ions become surrounded by water molecules. In this case, the positively charged (hydrogen) ends of the water molecule is attracted to the chloride anion. The ions will stay in solution unless the amount of water is reduced. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: MOLECULAR SUBSTANCES Shapes of Molecules Lone pairs and covalent bonds are made up of electrons. They occupy areas of space and are negatively charged. These negatively charged areas repel each other, and will move around until they find an orientation with equally repulsive forces from adjacent electrons. Therefore, the shape of a molecule is governed by the arrangement of the electron pairs around the central atom. You must consider both the bonded and unbonded pairs of electrons. There are six basic shapes. 180 ° 109 ° 120 ° Tetrahedral Four regions of negative charge around the central atom. All regions bonded. Bond angle between electron clouds ~ 109 °. Trigonal planar Three regions of negative charge around the central atom. All regions bonded. Bond angle between electron clouds ~ 120 °. Linear Two regions of negative charge around the central atom. All regions bonded. Bond angle between electron clouds ~ 180 °. 109 ° 120 ° 109 ° Bent (3 regions) Three regions of negative charge around the central atom. Two bonded, one unbonded. Bond angle between electron clouds ~ 120 °. Bent (4 regions) Four regions of negative charge around the central atom. Two bonded, two unbonded. Bond angle between electron clouds ~ 109 °. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: MOLECULAR SUBSTANCES Electronegativity Elements on the Periodic Table have a property called ‘electronegativity’. Electronegativity is a measure of an atom’s tendency to attract electrons to itself. Metal atoms have low electronegativity because they only weakly attract their valence electrons. Elements in Group 17 have high electronegativity, and strongly attract their valence and bonding electrons. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: MOLECULAR SUBSTANCES Solubility - “Like Dissolves Like” Investigating the Miscibility of Various Solutions Equipment: Samples of methanol, ethanol, ethanoic acid (2.0 mol L-1), cyclohexane, turpentine, beaker of water, 5 x test tubes, 6 x plastic pipettes (one for each sample and one for the water), test tube rack. Method: 1. Place the 5 test tubes into the test tube rack. Label each test tube with the name of the substance to be tested 2. Half fill each test tube with water. 3. Use the plastic pipette to add a few drops of methanol to the appropriately labelled test tube. Shake well to mix the two liquids. 4. Record your observations on the diagram by indicating whether the substance appears soluble or insoluble in water. 5. Repeat steps 3-4 for the remaining solutions. Don’t use “like dissolves like” as an explanation in your exam answers. The rule ‘like dissolves like’ describes the fact that polar molecules will dissolve in polar solvents, and non-polar molecules will dissolve in non-polar solvents. If two liquids dissolve in each other they form a single continuous layer and are said to be miscible. Insoluble molecules are immiscible. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: METALLIC SUBSTANCES Hardness of Metals Hardness is the property of a metal that gives it the ability to resist being permanently deformed (bent, broken or having its shape changed) when a force is applied. The greater the hardness of a metal, the greater resistance it has to deformation. The range in hardness between different metals is large. Mercury is a liquid at room temperature, sodium may be cut into pieces with a blunt knife, lead can be scratched with a fingernail, and tungsten is used to make the very hard teeth on a saw blade. Generally however, scientists say that metals are hard, firstly because most metals on the Periodic Table are relatively ‘hard’ in comparison to other substances, and secondly the metallic bond is a strong bond. Hardness is directly related to the strength of bonds holding substances together. 1. Describe in scientific terms what it means when someone says “metals are hard”. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ENERGY CHANGES Energy Changes Exothermic reactions are those reactions that release heat. The energy required to break the bonds in the reactants is exceeded by the energy released when chemical bonds are formed in the product(s). The reaction between hydrogen gas and oxygen gas is exothermic. Graphically we can represent the reaction by the following diagram: H H H H + O O O H H + O H H Energy is absorbed to break the two covalent bonds linking hydrogen atoms, and the two covalent bonds linking the oxygen atoms. Energy is released when the water molecules form. Four covalent bonds forming between hydrogen and oxygen atoms release more energy than is required to break the bonds in the reactants. The excess energy is released to the environment. Bond breaking = Endothermic Bond forming = Exothermic Chemical reactions involve the breaking and formation of chemical bonds. The general rule is that energy is absorbed in the breaking of chemical bonds, and energy is released when bonds are formed. Exothermic Reactions Endothermic Reactions Endothermic reactions can be considered the opposite of exothermic reactions. They absorb energy from the environment in which they happen. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ENERGY CHANGES The Law of Multiple Proportions When ions, atoms or molecules react, they do so in ratios of whole numbers. However, rather than say that three molecules of hydrogen react with one molecule of nitrogen to make two molecules of ammonia, scientists use moles rather than small numbers of molecules. The numbers used in chemical equations to balance the reactants and products should be thought of as signifying the number of moles of reactants and products. 3H2(g) + N2 (g) 2NH3(g) Chemists read the equation above as three moles of hydrogen molecules react with one mole of nitrogen molecules to make two moles of ammonia molecules. The enthalpy changes associated with just a few molecules reacting is tiny, however, because chemists use moles we can attach more meaningful numbers to chemical equations. The ∆rH for a reaction is the enthalpy change associated with that reaction based on mole values. 3H2(g) + N2(g) 2NH3(g) ∆rH° = -92 kJ mol-1 The equation shows that 92 kJ is released to the environment (exothermic) when two moles of ammonia are made from three moles of hydrogen and one mole of nitrogen. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ALKANES AND HALOALKANES Introduction to Organic Chemistry Organic chemistry is the study of compounds containing carbon. Carbon is able to form an enormous range of compounds because it forms stable bonds with a wide range of elements, including hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur and the halogens. The term ‘hydrocarbon’ is used to describe organic compounds consisting primarily of hydrogen and carbon. Hydrocarbons with a similar general formula are called a ‘homologous series’ (‘homo-’ the same, ‘-logous’ - relationship). During this achievement standard you will study the seven homologous series shown on the right. Compounds within a homologous series typically have a fixed set of functional groups. Functional groups influence the reactivity of the compound and gives the homologous series similar chemical and physical properties. The functional groups of seven homologous series are shown on the right. Note that the ‘R’ represents the rest of the compound. Chemists have developed a method of naming carbon compounds in such a way that the name reveals the structure of the compound. Understanding ‘structure’ and learning how to name and draw carbon compounds are very closely linked. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ALKANES AND HALOALKANES Determining the Solubility of Alkanes Aim: To test whether alkanes are soluble in water. Equipment: Cyclohexane, heptane, 2 x plastic pipettes, 2 x test tubes, test tube rack, water, organic waste disposal container. Method: 1. Add approximately 5 mL of water to each test tube. 2. Place the test tubes in a test tube rack. 3. Using a plastic pipette, add 1 mL of each of the alkanes to the test tubes. 4. Record your observations by drawing the liquids on the test tube below. Label each tube with the alkane that was added. For insoluble liquids make sure you record whether the hydrocarbon floats on top or lies at the bottom of the tube. 5. Dispose of all organic wastes as directed by your teacher. Do not pour them into the sink. 1. Describe the relative density of the two alkanes used when compared to water. Use your answers from question 2 to explain your observations.  Polar liquids will dissolve in other polar liquids. Water is a polar substance  so if a liquid dissolves in water it must also be polar. Cyclohexane and  heptane did not dissolve in water so they must be non-polar. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ENERGY CHANGES This formula is not examinable but will help with your understanding of heat and energy changes. Specific Heat Capacity The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy needed to change the temperature of 1 g of the substance by 1 °C. A small specific heat capacity means less energy is required to increase the temperature. Water has a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J g-1 °C-1. Mathematically, the relationship between temperature change and energy added is given by the following equation. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: METALLIC SUBSTANCES Structure and Bonding of Metallic Substances All metals share a similar structure. Positively charged metal nuclei are arranged into a lattice. The nuclei form a regular pattern in three dimensions. Each metal atom provides one or more valence electrons that are delocalised (i.e. they are free to move through the lattice). The delocalised electrons are attracted to the positively charged nuclei, but are not associated with any particular nucleus. 3-D Representation of a Metal Lattice Delocalised electron 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ALKENES, POLYMERS AND ALKYNES Geometric (cis-trans) Isomers The single C-C bond found in alkanes allows for the rotation of the groups of atoms attached to carbon atoms. The double C=C bond associated with alkenes prevents rotation. Any atoms or groups of atoms attached either side of a double bond are fixed in space and always have the same orientation to each other. It is therefore possible for alkenes with the same molecular formula, and the same name, to have geometric (cis-trans) isomers, where groups occupy different positions in space. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ALKENES, POLYMERS AND ALKYNES The Alkenes The alkenes are a homologous series of hydrocarbons where the molecule contains one or more double bonds between two adjacent carbon atoms. This affects their reactivity, so the C=C double bond is the functional group. The prefixes of alkenes are the same for all hydrocarbons (i.e. meth, eth, prop, but, etc.). The suffix is ‘-ene’. Alkenes contain at least one double covalent bond. This means two pairs of electrons are being shared between the two carbon atoms. If this bond was to be broken, further atoms could be bonded to the carbon atoms. Therefore, alkenes are described as being unsaturated. Test tubes are shaken from side to side - not up and down! Care should be taken not to spill the contents and eye protection should always be worn. 4. Record your observations. 5. Dispose of all organic waste as directed by your teacher. Observations: Cyclohexane:  No reaction was observed initially. The cyclohexane formed  a layer above the bromine water and turned brown. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ALKENES, POLYMERS AND ALKYNES Addition Reactions Using Hydrogen Halides Hydrogen halides include the molecules HF, HCl, HBr, and HI. They are relatively reactive species and will react with alkenes without the need for a catalyst. The reaction takes a similar form to that of reactions with the halogens (Cl2, Br2, etc), but with the halogen atom AND a hydrogen atom being added to the alkene to form a haloalkane. Alkene + Hydrogen halide For example: C2H4 + HCl Haloalkane C2H5Cl For symmetrical alkenes (those with an even number of carbon atoms and a double bond in the ‘centre’ of the molecule) only one type of product is possible. Asymmetric alkenes will produce two possible products. The most common product is called the major product and the least common product is called the minor product. Markovnikov’s Rule Sometimes known as “the rich get richer” rule, Markovnikov’s rule states that “the carbon atom in the double bond with the most hydrogen atoms already attached will get another hydrogen atom and the carbon atom with the least hydrogen atoms will get the halogen atom attached”. The molecule that obeys this rule will be the major product. 1. Use Markovnikov’s rule to complete the diagrams below showing the reaction between: (a) Propene and hydrogen bromide. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ALKENES, POLYMERS AND ALKYNES Cracking Crude oil contains a mixture of hydrocarbons of various carbon-chain lengths. Long chain alkanes do not make good fuels. They do not flow easily and are difficult to ignite. In order to produce more efficient and easier-to-use fuels, the long chain alkanes are ‘cracked’ into small molecules. Cracking is the name for the process of producing smaller chain alkanes and alkenes from longer chain alkanes. It is carried out at high temperatures and in the presence of a catalyst (a catalyst is a substance that speeds up the chemical reaction without being used in the reaction). Cracking of Hexane H H H H H H H C C C C C C H H H H H H H Heat Catalyst H H H H H C C C C H H H H Hexane H H H C C H Butane H Ethene Some of the smaller molecules formed by cracking are used as fuels, and some of them are used to make polymers in plastics manufacture. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: RATES OF REACTION Catalysts and the Rate of a Reaction Catalysts can speed up chemical reactions. In biology, chemistry and industry the study of catalysts is very important. Large sums of money are available to anyone who can increase the rate or efficiency of large-scale industrial chemical processes. Catalysts increase the rate of chemical reactions by providing an alternative pathway for the reaction to occur. This ‘new’ pathway has a lower activation energy than the reaction that occurs without the catalyst present, so many more collisions happen at or above the activation energy. Catalysts are not consumed in the reaction, and one ‘particle’ of catalyst can be involved in many thousands of reactions. It is estimated that one atom of chlorine in the upper atmosphere can convert around a million molecules of ozone to oxygen every second - a rate approximately 200 x faster than uncatalysed ozone decomposition. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: RATES OF REACTION Concentration and the Rate of a Reaction The concentration of a solution tells us the number of solute particles in a given volume of solvent. The concentration of a solution can be calculated using the following formula: c=n/V c = concentration (mol L-1) n = no. of moles (mol) V = volume (L) This formula can then be arranged into a formula triangle. x Increasing concentration means more particles must occupy the same amount of space. Therefore, the particles must be closer together. In a chemical reaction, if the reactant particles are close together they will collide more often. All other factors being equal, if the reactants increase in concentration then the resulting reaction rate will also increase. When reactants are at high concentrations the distance between particles is small, and collisions will happen more frequently. 1. When reactants are at low concentration, the distance between particles is large, and collisions will happen less frequently. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM Reversible Reactions Physical changes are by definition reversible. It is relatively easy to refreeze a melted ice-block, or to melt gold and have it resolidify in a mould to make a gold bar. Many familiar chemical reactions are irreversible, particularly if they occur in open systems. You cannot turn smoke and ash back into an unlit match! Some chemical reactions are reversible. This means that not only are the reactants forming products, but the products are breaking down back into the reactants. Reversible reactions only occur in closed systems. To indicate that a reaction is reversible, chemists use double arrows. For example H2O(l) H2O(g). In an open system reactions and physical changes are rarely reversible. Particles are free to enter or leave the system. For example, evaporating water in an open system (i.e. H2O(l) H2O(g)) will go to completion as water vapour is able to leave the system. The container will eventually contain the same gases as the environment in which it is placed. With the lid on, the system is closed. Nothing can enter or leave the pot. The reaction H2O(l) H2O(g) will not go to completion as water vapour is unable to leave the system. The pot will contain liquid water as well as water vapour. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM Equilibrium - A State of Balance When a chemical reaction occurs in a closed system, chemical equilibrium can occur during which both reactants and products are present at concentrations which have no further tendency to change with time. Note that concentration of the reactants and the products is not necessarily the same, it just means the concentrations tend not to change over time. Equilibrium occurs when the forward reaction proceeds at the same rate as the reverse reaction. This does not mean that the rate of the forward reaction (i.e. reactants to products) or the rate of the reverse reaction (i.e. products to reactants) is zero. It just means the rate of both reactions is equal. Therefore, there are no net changes in the concentrations of the reactants and products. Such a state is known as dynamic equilibrium. Describe the effect of a catalyst on the activation energy of a particular reaction.   A  catalyst provides an alternative pathway for the reaction to occur. The  new pathway has a lower activation energy. For a collision between two reactant particles to be effective particles must have energy greater than the activation energy. Chemical reactions occur as a result of collisions between reacting particles. In order for collisions to be effective, there must be considerable force in the collisions. The activation energy of a chemical reaction is the minimum energy that is needed to make the reaction happen. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: RATES OF REACTION Temperature and the Rate of a Reaction Temperature affects the rate of a chemical reaction in two ways. If the kinetic energy of the reactants is increased there will be more energetic collisions between particles. Recall that there is a range of energies at which particles collide and it is only collisions above the activation energy that may lead to the formation of products. By increasing the number of collisions occurring above the activation energy in a given amount of time, the faster the rate of reaction will become. Lowering the temperature decreases the number of collisions occurring above the activation energy and thus lowers the reaction rate. Secondly, an increase in temperature means that reactant particles will be moving through space faster. They will collide more often and increase the rate of reaction. Slowing the movement of the reactants by lowering the temperature decreases the rate of collisions and thus lowers the reaction rate. 1. 2. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM Shifting Equilibrium - Temperature Chemists use a rule known as “Le Châtelier’s principle” to predict whether a change to equilibrium conditions will cause the equilibrium to change the concentrations of the reactants and/or products. It states "If a chemical system at equilibrium experiences a change in temperature, concentration, volume, or pressure, then the equilibrium shifts its position to counteract the imposed change and a new equilibrium will be established". In simple terms Le Châtelier’s principle says if you make a change to an equilibrium system, the equilibrium will ‘shift’ its position to minimise the change. Consider the following thermochemical equation: NH3(g) + HCl(g) NH4Cl(s) ΔH = -176 kJ mol-1 The reaction is exothermic, and for equilibrium changes the amount of heat is unimportant, but its production by the reaction is. It is not conventional, but you could rewrite the equation: NH3(g) + HCl(g) NH4Cl(s) + Heat If we cooled an equilibrium mixture of the above reactants and products, the equilibrium will shift to raise the temperature of the mixture. The concentrations of NH3 and HCl will fall to create more NH4Cl and more heat. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM Shifting Equilibrium - Pressure Many reactions involve reactants and products that are gases. Changing the pressure of the reaction vessel will often shift the position of the equilibrium. With a change in pressure, either the forward or reverse reaction becomes favoured, and will continue to be until a new equilibrium is established. Le Châtelier’s principle can be used to predict which of the reactions (if any) will become favoured. Remember that Le Châtelier’s principle states that a change will be minimised by the shifting equilibrium. If the equilibrium can shift to minimise the increased pressure it will do so. This can be achieved if there are more gas particles on one side of the equation than the other. Consider the following reaction: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) 2SO3(g) Note how three moles of reactants (two moles of SO2 and one mole of O2) produce two moles of product (two moles of SO3). If the system was in equilibrium and the pressure was then increased, equilibrium will shift to remove three particles by favouring the forward reaction and turning them into two particles. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES What is an Acid? Acids are compounds that dissociate into a hydrogen ion (H+) and one of several different types of anion. Hydrogen ions are basically protons since they have lost their only electron during ion formation. Acids can be defined as ‘proton donors’ and all acids must therefore contain one or more atoms of hydrogen in their formula. Acid dissociation can happen in solvents other than water. However, we will use the dissociation of acids in water to discuss acid chemistry because it is the most commonly used (and examined!) solvent for acids. Dissociated protons/ hydrogen ions will immediately bind to a water molecule to form hydronium ions (H3O+). For example, hydrochloric acid (HCl(aq)) is a solution of hydrogen chloride in water. The HCl molecule dissociates into hydrogen cations (H+) and chloride anions (Cl-) when dissolved in water. The proton (i.e the H+) bonds to a water molecule to form a hydronium ion (H3O+). HCl(g) 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES Strong and Weak Bases Bases are proton acceptors. Bases that dissociate fully into species that will accept protons are termed strong bases. Consider the following reaction: HO 2 NaOH(s) Na+(aq) + OH-(aq) Provided there is sufficient water, all the sodium hydroxide will fully dissociate into sodium ions and hydroxide ions. Hydroxide ions in solution will bond to protons, forming water molecules: OH-(aq) + H+ (aq) H2O(l) The group 1 hydroxides are all soluble in water and form strong basic solutions. Bases that are soluble in water are called ‘alkalis’, hence the frequently used term ‘alkaline solution’. However, not all bases are soluble in water (or only sparingly so). Hydroxides of group 2 metals are slightly soluble, while most other hydroxides are insoluble. Note that even insoluble metal hydroxides will react with acids in a neutralisation reaction to form a metal salt and water. Weak bases do not fully dissociate in water (i.e. some of the base does not react with water). They include ammonia and the amines. Weak bases are able to accept a proton from a water molecule in solution, for example: NH3(aq) + H2O(l) NH4+ (aq) + OH-(aq) NH4+ (aq) + Cl-(aq) Weak bases will also react with acids to produce salts. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES KW - The Ionic Product of Water In a sample of pure water, the majority of particles present will be H2O. However, some of the water molecules will have ionised (or dissociated) into H+ (and therefore H3O+) and OH-. 2H2O(l) H3O+ (aq) + OH-(aq) We know that pure water is neutral. Chemists have calculated that the product of the concentrations of [H3O+] and [OH-] at 25 °C is 1 x 10-14 mol L-1 and is a constant. This constant is called the ‘ionic product of water’ (sometimes referred to as the ‘dissociation constant’). KW = [H3O+] [OH-] = 1 x 10-14 at 25°C KW can be used to calculate the concentration of hydronium ions in a solution if the concentration of hydroxide ions is given, and vice versa. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES Strong and Weak Acids The strength of an acid is related to whether or not the acid fully dissociates or not. The terms ‘HA’, ‘HB’, etc. are generally accepted abbreviations for acids. For ‘HA’ the ‘H’ represents the hydrogen atom and ‘A’ represents the anion. When ‘HA’ dissociates the ions are abbreviated to ‘H+ and ‘A-. HA HB H+ H+ A- B- A Strong Acid A Weak Acid The term ‘strong acid’ describes an acid that fully dissociates in water. For example, if one mole of HCl molecules is added to 1.0 litre of water, there will be a solution of hydronium ions equal to 1.0 mol L-1. There will essentially be no molecules of HCl in the solution. The term ‘weak acid’ describes an acid that only partially dissociates in water. Carboxylic (organic) acids are weak acids. In solution only a fraction of the acid molecules dissociate to form hydronium ions. There will still be undissociated molecules of the acid present in the solution. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES Neutralisation - Strong Acid/Strong Base When an acid reacts with a base, a neutralisation reaction occurs. Unless exact amounts of both acid and base are mixed, there will be an excess of one or the other left over once the reaction has completed. Consider the reaction: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) The H of the hydrochloric acid has been neutralised by the OH of the sodium hydroxide to form a molecule of water. If 50 mL of 0.1 mol L-1 HCl solution is added to 50 mL of 0.05 mol L-1 NaOH solution, not all of the acid will be neutralised by the more dilute base. In order to calculate how much acid remains in the mixture we need to know how much acid was in the original solution, and how much was neutralised by the base. + - 1 n(HCl) = c(HCl) x V(HCl) = 0.1 x 0.050 = 0.005 moles 2 n(NaOH) = c(NaOH) x V(NaOH) = 0.05 x 0.050 = 0.0025 moles The reaction shows that one mole of HCl is neutralised by one mole of NaOH. From the calculations above, we see that only 0.0025 moles of HCl will be neutralised. Another 0.0025 moles of H+ ions will remain in the solution. The solution will still be acidic. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Reading the Elements If you look at the NCEA Periodic Table, you will notice that each element has a number associated with it. The number is called the atomic number and represents the number of protons found in the nucleus of a single atom of that element. Since the number of protons is equal to the number of electrons, the atomic number also tells you how many electrons there are in the energy levels around the nucleus. Another important number you will not find on the NCEA Periodic Table is called the mass number. This tells you the total number of particles, protons plus neutrons, found in the nucleus of an atom. So, if you know the mass number and the atomic number of an element, it is possible to work out the number of neutrons in the nucleus. By subtracting the number of protons from the mass number, you can calculate the total number of neutrons. Worked Example 1. A lithium atom has a mass number of 7. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons found in this atom. 3 Li Number of protons or electrons = The atomic number. Therefore, the lithium atom has 3 protons and 3 electrons. Lithium 1. Number of neutrons = Mass number - Atomic number. Therefore, the lithium atom has 7 - 3 = 4 neutrons. Use the Periodic Table to complete the table below. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Atoms Each element on the Periodic Table is made up of unique types of atoms. The atomic number of the atom defines how many protons are in each atom, and this determines the number of electrons that occur in a neutral atom. Almost all of chemistry is the study of how these electrons behave when in the elemental substance, or during chemical reactions. Atoms are made up of 3 main types of particles: electrons, protons and neutrons. These particles have different properties. Electrons have a negative electrical charge (-). They surround the nucleus, and are arranged in layers called shells. Protons are much larger and heavier than electrons and have a positive charge (+). The number of protons in an atom is the same as the atomic number of that element. Neutrons have a similar mass to protons. They have no electrical charge (0). Neutrons help hold the nucleus together, and can vary in number between atoms of the same element. The nucleus is at the centre of the atom and contains the protons and neutrons. Virtually all the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus, because the electrons have very little mass. Relative mass Relative charge Proton 1 +1 Neutron 1 0 Electron 1/1840 -1 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Isotopes The atoms of a chemical element can exist in different forms. These are called isotopes. Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but a different mass number. This means they have the same number of protons (and electrons), but different numbers of neutrons. The word isotope comes from a Greek word meaning “the same place”, and is used because isotopes of an atom are located at the same place on the Periodic Table. The Isotopes of Chlorine Atomic number 17 Cl Chlorine 35 Atomic mass 17 Both of the isotopes of chlorine have the same atomic number. This means they both have 17 protons and 17 electrons - both atoms are neutral. Chlorine However, 35Cl and 37Cl have a different number of neutrons. 35Cl has 18 neutrons (35-17=18), whereas 37Cl has 20 neutrons (37-17=20). uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES Concentrated and Dilute Acids The strength of an acid does not change depending on concentration, unless the acid solution is extremely dilute. Concentration is a measure of how many acid particles there are per unit volume of water. Students often confuse the terms concentrated with strong and dilute with weak when discussing acids. The terms ‘concentrated’ and ‘dilute’ refer to how much of an acid has been added to water. In the laboratory, acids below 1.0 mol L-1 are considered dilute. The reactivity and conductivity of acids is determined by the concentration of ions in the solution. Therefore, concentrated acids are more reactive and conductive than dilute acids of the same type. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY A Closer Look at Electrons Electrons surround the nucleus of an atom. The electrons are arranged in various energy levels (often referred to as ‘shells’ or ‘layers’). Each energy level can only contain a certain number of electrons. Usually it is only the outermost electrons that are involved in chemical reactions, and it is important to learn how to calculate how many electrons are in the outermost energy level or valence shell. The first energy level (closest to the nucleus) can hold 2 electrons. The second energy Level can hold 8 electrons. The third energy level can hold 8 electrons. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Naming Ions When naming ions, you must adhere to the following rules: • Positive ions (i.e. the metals and hydrogen) are usually named after the element they are formed from. For example, the ion formed when calcium loses two electrons is also called the calcium ion (Ca2+). • Negative monatomic (‘mono’ means one, so monatomic means ‘ions made of only one atom’) ions are usually named using the suffix - ide. For example, chlorine (Cl) forms the negative ion chloride (Cl-), and oxygen (O) forms the oxide ion (O2-) • Polyatomic ions (‘poly’ means many, so polyatomic means ‘ions made of many atoms’) are usually named using the suffix -ate. For example, SO42- is the sulfate ion and CO32- is called the carbonate ion. Exceptions to this rule include the hydroxide ion (OH-) and the ammonium ion ( NH4+). • Some ions can have more than one charge. For example, iron can be Fe2+ or Fe3+. Chemists use Roman numerals to distinguish (tell the difference) between them. Therefore, Fe2+ is written as iron(II) and Fe3+ is written as iron(III). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES The pH Scale The pH scale is used to represent the concentration of acids and bases. pH values have no units and generally range from 0 to 14. A pH of 7 is given to neutral solutions. Values below 7 are acidic solutions and values above 7 are basic solutions. pH is a measure of the concentration of hydronium ions in a solution. The more hydronium ions present, the more acidic is the solution. The pH scale is logarithmic. Each unit on the pH scale represents a tenfold change in acidity. For example, a solution with a pH of 4 is ten times more acidic than a solution with a pH of 5, and 100 times more acidic than a solution with a pH of 6. Chemists use indicators to show visually whether a solution is acidic, neutral or basic. A number of natural dyes change colour depending on whether they are placed in an acid or base. For example, the chemical formula for water is H2O. This shows that a water molecule is made up of two hydrogen atoms bonded to a single oxygen atom. Notice that if no number is given, as in the ‘O’ in H2O, then only one of that atom/ion is present. Ions with different charges combine during a chemical reaction to form compounds that have equal amounts of positive and negative charge. This means the resulting compound has no electrical charge. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: MOLECULAR SUBSTANCES Drawing Lewis Diagrams of Molecules The Lewis diagram of a molecule shows where covalent bonds are located, and the location of any lone pairs of electrons. Hydrogen and helium require two electrons in their valence shell. All other atoms in molecules require eight electrons (called the ‘octet rule’) in their valence shell. It is a common exam mistake to forget to fill up all valence shells once the basic structure of the molecule’s Lewis diagram has been determined. Method 1. Determine the number of valence electrons from all atoms in the formula A . 2. Calculate the total if all the elements were to have 8 valence electrons B . 3. Subtract B from A . This is the number of electrons that need to be shared C . 4. Divide C by 2. This is the number of shared pairs (covalent bonds) D . 5. Begin the Lewis diagram by drawing the central atom and placing other atoms around it systematically. 6. Draw in the number of bonds calculated( D ). 7. Complete an ‘octet’ of electrons for each atom you have drawn. Remember that hydrogen needs only two electrons so it will be ‘satisfied’ if it has a single bond to the central atom. Example - An ammonia molecule (NH3) A = Valence electrons: 1 x N = 5 and 3 x H = 3 B = Nitrogen: 8 valence electrons. Therefore, the shape of a molecule is governed by the arrangement of the electron pairs around the central atom. You must consider both the bonded and unbonded pairs of electrons. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: IONIC SUBSTANCES Explaining the Solubility of Ionic Substances When an ionic substance dissolves, the ionic bonds holding the ions in place must be broken. Polar solvents are attracted to the ions. The negatively charged region of a solvent molecule is attracted to the positively charged cations. Similarly, the positively charged region of the solvent molecule is attracted to the negatively charged anions. If the force of attraction between an ion and the solvent molecule is greater than the force of attraction between the ions themselves, the solid will dissolve. The ions are then held in solution by being surrounded by solvent molecules. H+ H+ H+ 0 2- H+ H+ 0 H+ 2- H+ 2- H+ 0 0 2- Model of Sodium Chloride Dissolving in Water A hydrated chloride ion Water molecules are attracted to the electrostatically charged ions of the ionic solid. Sodium chloride is highly soluble in water, meaning the ions are readily removed (dissociated) from the crystal lattice by water molecules. The ions become surrounded by water molecules. In this case, the positively charged (hydrogen) ends of the water molecule is attracted to the chloride anion. The ions will stay in solution unless the amount of water is reduced. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: MOLECULAR SUBSTANCES Electronegativity Elements on the Periodic Table have a property called ‘electronegativity’. Electronegativity is a measure of an atom’s tendency to attract electrons to itself. Metal atoms have low electronegativity because they only weakly attract their valence electrons. Elements in Group 17 have high electronegativity, and strongly attract their valence and bonding electrons. If the atoms are identical (e.g. H2, O2 etc.) then the bonding electrons will spend an equal amount of time orbiting each atom. Chemists describe these bonds as ‘nonpolar covalent bonds’. If the atoms either side of the bond are composed of different elements, then the bonding electrons will not be shared equally, spending more time orbiting one nuclei than the other. They are ‘intramolecular’. However, forces of attraction exist between molecules as well. The attractive forces between neighbouring molecules are called ‘intermolecular forces’. From particle theory we know that with the input of heat energy, particles will begin to vibrate faster. Only a small amount of heat input is necessary to break the weak bonds holding molecules together. For this reason, molecular substances have relatively low melting and boiling points. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ENERGY CHANGES Energy Changes Exothermic reactions are those reactions that release heat. The energy required to break the bonds in the reactants is exceeded by the energy released when chemical bonds are formed in the product(s). The reaction between hydrogen gas and oxygen gas is exothermic. Graphically we can represent the reaction by the following diagram: H H H H + O O O H H + O H H Energy is absorbed to break the two covalent bonds linking hydrogen atoms, and the two covalent bonds linking the oxygen atoms. Energy is released when the water molecules form. Four covalent bonds forming between hydrogen and oxygen atoms release more energy than is required to break the bonds in the reactants. The excess energy is released to the environment. Bond breaking = Endothermic Bond forming = Exothermic Chemical reactions involve the breaking and formation of chemical bonds. The general rule is that energy is absorbed in the breaking of chemical bonds, and energy is released when bonds are formed. Exothermic Reactions Endothermic Reactions Endothermic reactions can be considered the opposite of exothermic reactions. They absorb energy from the environment in which they happen. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ENERGY CHANGES The Law of Multiple Proportions When ions, atoms or molecules react, they do so in ratios of whole numbers. However, rather than say that three molecules of hydrogen react with one molecule of nitrogen to make two molecules of ammonia, scientists use moles rather than small numbers of molecules. The numbers used in chemical equations to balance the reactants and products should be thought of as signifying the number of moles of reactants and products. 3H2(g) + N2 (g) 2NH3(g) Chemists read the equation above as three moles of hydrogen molecules react with one mole of nitrogen molecules to make two moles of ammonia molecules. The enthalpy changes associated with just a few molecules reacting is tiny, however, because chemists use moles we can attach more meaningful numbers to chemical equations. The ∆rH for a reaction is the enthalpy change associated with that reaction based on mole values. 3H2(g) + N2(g) 2NH3(g) ∆rH° = -92 kJ mol-1 The equation shows that 92 kJ is released to the environment (exothermic) when two moles of ammonia are made from three moles of hydrogen and one mole of nitrogen. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: METALLIC SUBSTANCES Structure and Bonding of Metallic Substances All metals share a similar structure. Positively charged metal nuclei are arranged into a lattice. The nuclei form a regular pattern in three dimensions. Each metal atom provides one or more valence electrons that are delocalised (i.e. they are free to move through the lattice). The delocalised electrons are attracted to the positively charged nuclei, but are not associated with any particular nucleus. 3-D Representation of a Metal Lattice Delocalised electron 1. Similarly, the negatively charged electrons experience an attractive force in all directions to the positively charged metal nuclei. This is called ‘non-directional bonding’. 4. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ENERGY CHANGES This formula is not examinable but will help with your understanding of heat and energy changes. Specific Heat Capacity The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy needed to change the temperature of 1 g of the substance by 1 °C. A small specific heat capacity means less energy is required to increase the temperature. Water has a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J g-1 °C-1. Mathematically, the relationship between temperature change and energy added is given by the following equation. The double C=C bond associated with alkenes prevents rotation. Any atoms or groups of atoms attached either side of a double bond are fixed in space and always have the same orientation to each other. It is therefore possible for alkenes with the same molecular formula, and the same name, to have geometric (cis-trans) isomers, where groups occupy different positions in space. This affects their reactivity, so the C=C double bond is the functional group. The prefixes of alkenes are the same for all hydrocarbons (i.e. meth, eth, prop, but, etc.). The suffix is ‘-ene’. Alkenes contain at least one double covalent bond. This means two pairs of electrons are being shared between the two carbon atoms. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ALKENES, POLYMERS AND ALKYNES Addition Reactions Using Hydrogen Halides Hydrogen halides include the molecules HF, HCl, HBr, and HI. They are relatively reactive species and will react with alkenes without the need for a catalyst. The reaction takes a similar form to that of reactions with the halogens (Cl2, Br2, etc), but with the halogen atom AND a hydrogen atom being added to the alkene to form a haloalkane. Alkene + Hydrogen halide For example: C2H4 + HCl Haloalkane C2H5Cl For symmetrical alkenes (those with an even number of carbon atoms and a double bond in the ‘centre’ of the molecule) only one type of product is possible. Asymmetric alkenes will produce two possible products. The most common product is called the major product and the least common product is called the minor product. Markovnikov’s Rule Sometimes known as “the rich get richer” rule, Markovnikov’s rule states that “the carbon atom in the double bond with the most hydrogen atoms already attached will get another hydrogen atom and the carbon atom with the least hydrogen atoms will get the halogen atom attached”. The molecule that obeys this rule will be the major product. 1. Use Markovnikov’s rule to complete the diagrams below showing the reaction between: (a) Propene and hydrogen bromide. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ALKENES, POLYMERS AND ALKYNES Cracking Crude oil contains a mixture of hydrocarbons of various carbon-chain lengths. Long chain alkanes do not make good fuels. They do not flow easily and are difficult to ignite. In order to produce more efficient and easier-to-use fuels, the long chain alkanes are ‘cracked’ into small molecules. Cracking is the name for the process of producing smaller chain alkanes and alkenes from longer chain alkanes. It is carried out at high temperatures and in the presence of a catalyst (a catalyst is a substance that speeds up the chemical reaction without being used in the reaction). Cracking of Hexane H H H H H H H C C C C C C H H H H H H H Heat Catalyst H H H H H C C C C H H H H Hexane H H H C C H Butane H Ethene Some of the smaller molecules formed by cracking are used as fuels, and some of them are used to make polymers in plastics manufacture. For example, after the cracking of hexane, butane can be used as a fuel and ethene is used in the production of plastic polymers. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ALCOHOLS Reaction of Alcohols with Hydrogen Halides Hydrogen halides include HF, HCl, HBr and HI. They are relatively reactive compounds, and will react with alcohols to make the corresponding haloalkane. Only tertiary alcohols react relatively quickly with hydrogen halides. Primary and secondary alcohols react very slowly. The reactions take the general form (X represents a halogen atom): Alcohol + HX Water + Haloalkane For example: C2H5OH + HCl(aq) H2O + C2H5Cl Essentially, the hydroxyl group on the alcohol bonds with the hydrogen atom of the hydrogen halide to form water, and the halide atom bonds in place of the hydroxyl group. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ALCOHOLS Properties of Alcohols - Solubility in Water The trend in solubility for primary alcohols is opposite to that of melting and boiling. As the molecules get larger their solubility decreases. Think of alcohol molecules as having a hydrophilic (water liking) end and a hydrophobic (water hating) end. The hydroxyl (-OH) group links strongly to surrounding water molecules, while the ‘chain’ of carbon and hydrogen atoms does not. Short chain alcohols will dissolve in all proportions with water. From butan-1-ol onwards, the alcohols show rapidly decreasing solubility. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: RATES OF REACTION Catalysts and the Rate of a Reaction Catalysts can speed up chemical reactions. In biology, chemistry and industry the study of catalysts is very important. Large sums of money are available to anyone who can increase the rate or efficiency of large-scale industrial chemical processes. Catalysts increase the rate of chemical reactions by providing an alternative pathway for the reaction to occur. This ‘new’ pathway has a lower activation energy than the reaction that occurs without the catalyst present, so many more collisions happen at or above the activation energy. Catalysts are not consumed in the reaction, and one ‘particle’ of catalyst can be involved in many thousands of reactions. It is estimated that one atom of chlorine in the upper atmosphere can convert around a million molecules of ozone to oxygen every second - a rate approximately 200 x faster than uncatalysed ozone decomposition. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: RATES OF REACTION Concentration and the Rate of a Reaction The concentration of a solution tells us the number of solute particles in a given volume of solvent. Therefore, the particles must be closer together. In a chemical reaction, if the reactant particles are close together they will collide more often. All other factors being equal, if the reactants increase in concentration then the resulting reaction rate will also increase. When reactants are at high concentrations the distance between particles is small, and collisions will happen more frequently. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: RATES OF REACTION Temperature and the Rate of a Reaction Temperature affects the rate of a chemical reaction in two ways. If the kinetic energy of the reactants is increased there will be more energetic collisions between particles. Recall that there is a range of energies at which particles collide and it is only collisions above the activation energy that may lead to the formation of products. By increasing the number of collisions occurring above the activation energy in a given amount of time, the faster the rate of reaction will become. Lowering the temperature decreases the number of collisions occurring above the activation energy and thus lowers the reaction rate. Secondly, an increase in temperature means that reactant particles will be moving through space faster. They will collide more often and increase the rate of reaction. Slowing the movement of the reactants by lowering the temperature decreases the rate of collisions and thus lowers the reaction rate. 1. Define the term ‘reaction rate’.     2. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: RATES OF REACTION Activation Energy Activation Energy (Ea) Energy Energy in reactants Catalysts lower the activation energy by providing an alternative Energy Change reaction pathway (think of a tunnel through the hill). Energy in products Reaction progress 1. Define the term ‘activation energy’.       2. Describe the effect of a catalyst on the activation energy of a particular reaction.       For a collision between two reactant particles to be effective particles must have energy greater than the activation energy. Chemical reactions occur as a result of collisions between reacting particles. In order for collisions to be effective, there must be considerable force in the collisions. The slower-moving molecules do not have enough kinetic energy to react when they collide. Only those molecules moving at high speed have enough energy for collisions to result in a reaction. The activation energy of a chemical reaction is the minimum energy that is needed to make the reaction happen. A good analogy for a reaction pathway and its activation energy is to think about pushing a boulder over a hill. A defined amount of energy is needed to get the boulder to the top of the hill. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM Equilibrium - A State of Balance When a chemical reaction occurs in a closed system, chemical equilibrium can occur during which both reactants and products are present at concentrations which have no further tendency to change with time. Note that concentration of the reactants and the products is not necessarily the same, it just means the concentrations tend not to change over time. Equilibrium occurs when the forward reaction proceeds at the same rate as the reverse reaction. This does not mean that the rate of the forward reaction (i.e. reactants to products) or the rate of the reverse reaction (i.e. products to reactants) is zero. It just means the rate of both reactions is equal. Therefore, there are no net changes in the concentrations of the reactants and products. Such a state is known as dynamic equilibrium. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM Reversible Reactions Physical changes are by definition reversible. It is relatively easy to refreeze a melted ice-block, or to melt gold and have it resolidify in a mould to make a gold bar. Many familiar chemical reactions are irreversible, particularly if they occur in open systems. You cannot turn smoke and ash back into an unlit match! Some chemical reactions are reversible. This means that not only are the reactants forming products, but the products are breaking down back into the reactants. Reversible reactions only occur in closed systems. To indicate that a reaction is reversible, chemists use double arrows. For example H2O(l) H2O(g). In an open system reactions and physical changes are rarely reversible. Particles are free to enter or leave the system. For example, evaporating water in an open system (i.e. H2O(l) H2O(g)) will go to completion as water vapour is able to leave the system. The container will eventually contain the same gases as the environment in which it is placed. 1. With the lid on, the system is closed. Nothing can enter or leave the pot. The reaction H2O(l) H2O(g) will not go to completion as water vapour is unable to leave the system. The pot will contain liquid water as well as water vapour. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM Shifting Equilibrium - Temperature Chemists use a rule known as “Le Châtelier’s principle” to predict whether a change to equilibrium conditions will cause the equilibrium to change the concentrations of the reactants and/or products. It states "If a chemical system at equilibrium experiences a change in temperature, concentration, volume, or pressure, then the equilibrium shifts its position to counteract the imposed change and a new equilibrium will be established". In simple terms Le Châtelier’s principle says if you make a change to an equilibrium system, the equilibrium will ‘shift’ its position to minimise the change. Consider the following thermochemical equation: NH3(g) + HCl(g) NH4Cl(s) ΔH = -176 kJ mol-1 The reaction is exothermic, and for equilibrium changes the amount of heat is unimportant, but its production by the reaction is. It is not conventional, but you could rewrite the equation: NH3(g) + HCl(g) NH4Cl(s) + Heat If we cooled an equilibrium mixture of the above reactants and products, the equilibrium will shift to raise the temperature of the mixture. The concentrations of NH3 and HCl will fall to create more NH4Cl and more heat. As the concentrations of the reactants has decreased, the Kc of the new equilibrium will be higher (products increase and products are the numerator of the equilibrium expression). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM Shifting Equilibrium - Pressure Many reactions involve reactants and products that are gases. Changing the pressure of the reaction vessel will often shift the position of the equilibrium. With a change in pressure, either the forward or reverse reaction becomes favoured, and will continue to be until a new equilibrium is established. Le Châtelier’s principle can be used to predict which of the reactions (if any) will become favoured. Remember that Le Châtelier’s principle states that a change will be minimised by the shifting equilibrium. If the equilibrium can shift to minimise the increased pressure it will do so. This can be achieved if there are more gas particles on one side of the equation than the other. Consider the following reaction: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) 2SO3(g) Note how three moles of reactants (two moles of SO2 and one mole of O2) produce two moles of product (two moles of SO3). If the system was in equilibrium and the pressure was then increased, equilibrium will shift to remove three particles by favouring the forward reaction and turning them into two particles. As a result, the pressure will reduce. 1. State the: (a) reaction that would be favoured by increasing the pressure.  (b) effect an increase in pressure would have on the value of Kc. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM Equilibrium and Catalysts Catalysts affect reactions by providing a reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. They allow reactions to happen faster as there are more effective collisions per unit of time. In equilibrium systems catalysts affect the speed of both the forward and reverse reactions. This means that while equilibrium is reached faster in the presence of a catalyst, the position of equilibrium is not affected by the catalyst. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES What is an Acid? Acids are compounds that dissociate into a hydrogen ion (H+) and one of several different types of anion. Hydrogen ions are basically protons since they have lost their only electron during ion formation. Acids can be defined as ‘proton donors’ and all acids must therefore contain one or more atoms of hydrogen in their formula. Acid dissociation can happen in solvents other than water. However, we will use the dissociation of acids in water to discuss acid chemistry because it is the most commonly used (and examined!) solvent for acids. Dissociated protons/ hydrogen ions will immediately bind to a water molecule to form hydronium ions (H3O+). For example, hydrochloric acid (HCl(aq)) is a solution of hydrogen chloride in water. The HCl molecule dissociates into hydrogen cations (H+) and chloride anions (Cl-) when dissolved in water. The proton (i.e the H+) bonds to a water molecule to form a hydronium ion (H3O+). uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES Monoprotic and Polyprotic Acids The term ‘monoprotic’ describes acids that donate only one proton to a water molecule. Examples include hydrochloric acid (HCl), nitric acid (HNO3), and ethanoic acid (CH3COOH). Many other acids are able to donate more than one proton to water molecules. These acids are termed ‘polyprotic’ acids. O O N S O O OH Nitric Acid Nitric acid is a monoprotic acid. Only one proton is available to be donated to a water molecule. O OH HO P OH OH OH Sulfuric Acid Sulfuric acid is a diprotic acid. Two protons are available to be donated to two water molecules. Phosphoric Acid Phosphoric acid is a triprotic acid. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES Strong and Weak Bases Bases are proton acceptors. Bases that dissociate fully into species that will accept protons are termed strong bases. Consider the following reaction: HO 2 NaOH(s) Na+(aq) + OH-(aq) Provided there is sufficient water, all the sodium hydroxide will fully dissociate into sodium ions and hydroxide ions. Hydroxide ions in solution will bond to protons, forming water molecules: OH-(aq) + H+ (aq) H2O(l) The group 1 hydroxides are all soluble in water and form strong basic solutions. Bases that are soluble in water are called ‘alkalis’, hence the frequently used term ‘alkaline solution’. However, not all bases are soluble in water (or only sparingly so). Hydroxides of group 2 metals are slightly soluble, while most other hydroxides are insoluble. Note that even insoluble metal hydroxides will react with acids in a neutralisation reaction to form a metal salt and water. Weak bases do not fully dissociate in water (i.e. some of the base does not react with water). They include ammonia and the amines. Weak bases are able to accept a proton from a water molecule in solution, for example: NH3(aq) + H2O(l) NH4+ (aq) + OH-(aq) NH4+ (aq) + Cl-(aq) Weak bases will also react with acids to produce salts. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES Reactivity of Strong and Weak Acids It is the concentration of hydronium ions that determines the rate of reaction between an acid and a metal to produce a metal salt and hydrogen gas. Because strong acids fully dissociate into ions when placed in water, they will have a higher concentration of hydronium ions in solution compared to weak acids of the same concentration. Aim: To compare the reaction rate of strong and weak acids. Equipment: 2.0 mol L-1 solutions of sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid, citric acid, methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid, 6 test tubes, test tube rack, sandpaper, stopwatch, thermometer, 12 cm of magnesium ribbon divided into 6 x 2 cm strips. Chemists have calculated that the product of the concentrations of [H3O+] and [OH-] at 25 °C is 1 x 10-14 mol L-1 and is a constant. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES Neutralisation - Strong Acid/Strong Base When an acid reacts with a base, a neutralisation reaction occurs. Unless exact amounts of both acid and base are mixed, there will be an excess of one or the other left over once the reaction has completed. Consider the reaction: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) The H of the hydrochloric acid has been neutralised by the OH of the sodium hydroxide to form a molecule of water. From the calculations above, we see that only 0.0025 moles of HCl will be neutralised. Another 0.0025 moles of H+ ions will remain in the solution. The solution will still be acidic. The terms ‘HA’, ‘HB’, etc. are generally accepted abbreviations for acids. For ‘HA’ the ‘H’ represents the hydrogen atom and ‘A’ represents the anion. When ‘HA’ dissociates the ions are abbreviated to ‘H+ and ‘A-. HA HB H+ H+ A- B- A Strong Acid A Weak Acid The term ‘strong acid’ describes an acid that fully dissociates in water. For example, if one mole of HCl molecules is added to 1.0 litre of water, there will be a solution of hydronium ions equal to 1.0 mol L-1. There will essentially be no molecules of HCl in the solution. The term ‘weak acid’ describes an acid that only partially dissociates in water. Carboxylic (organic) acids are weak acids. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS What is a Titration? A titration is a laboratory technique which reacts precise amounts of two solutions. The concentration of one solution is known and by carefully measuring the required volume of the second solution, its concentration can be calculated. Consider the following equation: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) When some amount (no. of moles) of HCl has been added to the exact same amount of NaOH, all of the NaOH will have reacted and the resulting solution will be neither acidic or basic. In an acid/base titration, an indicator is used to find the point in the titration when the acid and base have neutralised each other and the solution has become neutral. Titrations use a standard solution to find the concentration of the unknown solution. A standard solution is prepared by weighing a mass of either an acid or base and dissolving it in a known volume. The concentration of a standard solution can be calculated to a high degree of accuracy. Not all chemicals can be used to prepare a standard solution. If the chemical contains impurities (often water) then the actual amount (in moles) cannot be determined by weighing. Chemicals that can be used are called primary standards. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Externa.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES The pH Scale The pH scale is used to represent the concentration of acids and bases. pH values have no units and generally range from 0 to 14. A pH of 7 is given to neutral solutions. Values below 7 are acidic solutions and values above 7 are basic solutions. pH is a measure of the concentration of hydronium ions in a solution. The more hydronium ions present, the more acidic is the solution. The pH scale is logarithmic. Each unit on the pH scale represents a tenfold change in acidity. For example, a solution with a pH of 4 is ten times more acidic than a solution with a pH of 5, and 100 times more acidic than a solution with a pH of 6. Chemists use indicators to show visually whether a solution is acidic, neutral or basic. A number of natural dyes change colour depending on whether they are placed in an acid or base. You should recall the use of Universal Indicator and Litmus indicator from NCEA Level 1 Science. Colour in U.I. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS A Titration Setting up the burette correctly will lead to better accuracy from a titration. The apparatus should look like the diagram below. Clamp the burette vertically. It may help to align it visually with the straight edges of the white board or window frames. Make sure the funnel is removed after filling the burette. Holding white paper behind the burette makes it easier to see the meniscus. Clamps should be firm and in the correct position to hold the burette. Do not over-tighten the clamp holding the burette. You may shatter the tube by applying too much pressure. Rinsing Check that the tap turns freely before filling the burette. Ensure there is enough room between the burette and the base to fit and move conical flask. The burette should be as low as possible to prevent too much splashing as the titrant runs into the flask. Rinse the pipette, burette and flask with distilled water. This is to remove any contaminants. Then, rinse the pipette with a small amount of the sample being investigated. Rinse the burette with a small amount of the standard solution. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: IDENTIFYING IONS IN SOLUTION Writing Ionic Equations Chemists use subscripts to give information about the state of a chemical species. In precipitation reactions the subscript ‘(s)’ is attached to any precipitates formed, and ‘(aq)’ denotes that the species is in (aqueous) solution. When writing ionic equations, chemists only write the species that are involved in the reaction. Spectator ions are not included. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: IDENTIFYING IONS IN SOLUTION Complex Ions - The Anions Complex ions are ions with a central metal ion bonded to one or more molecules or ions. The formation of complex ions must be explained when precipitates dissolve. In the flowchart for identifying anions, the test to decide whether the precipitate is silver chloride (Cl-) or iodide (I-) is to add ammonia solution. If the anion is chloride, adding ammonia solution makes the precipitate dissolve. The silver chloride precipitate is composed of silver cations and chloride anions ionically bonded together. Ammonia is able to overcome the lattice energy and pull the silver ions out of the lattice. The chloride ions go back into solution. The complex ion, diammine silver [Ag(NH3)2]+(aq) is composed of two ammonia molecules bonded to a silver ion. Dissolving this precipitate can be represented by the equation: AgCl(s) + 2NH3(aq) [Ag(NH3)2]+(aq) + Cl-(aq) Square brackets surround the ‘complex’ and the charge is shown outside the right-hand bracket. Because the complex is charged it will dissolve in water, as does the chloride ion (Cl-). The subscript ‘(aq)’ shows that the complex ion is in solution. 1. 2.
