The unknown sample may have one or more functional groups. A functional group may be identified by not reacting with any of the reagents given (identification by the process of elimination). In some cases, once identified, a further test may be carried out to confirm the identity of the functional group. You will be supplied with flowcharts that outline the procedures to follow, and which links an observation to a specific functional group. Names of possible organic compounds and their structural formulae will also be provided. This may include writing chemical equations and using chemical vocabulary, symbols and conventions. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: IDENTIFYING IONS IN SOLUTION Precipitation Reactions APPROXIMATE VOLUMES Some ionic solutions can be mixed, and the different types of ions do not interact. All the ions remain dissolved in the mixture. APPROXIMATE VOLUMES Many types of ions can exist together in solution without reacting. However, some ions, upon being mixed together, will bond to form insoluble substances. When mixing some solutions however, the ions will interact forming a solid. An ion from one solution binds to an ion from the second solution forming an insoluble product. When two solutions are mixed, and a solid forms in the mixture, chemists call the solid product a precipitate. The following rules can be used to predict whether two solutions will form a precipitate: Solubility Rules 1 Group 1 metal cations All soluble. 2 Nitrates (NO3-) All soluble. 3 Chlorides (Cl-) All soluble except AgCl, PbCl2. 4 Sulfates (SO42-) All soluble except BaSO4, PbSO4, CaSO4. 5 Hydroxides (OH-) All insoluble except KOH, NaOH. 6 Carbonates (CO32-) All insoluble except K2CO3, Na2CO3, (NH4)2CO3. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: OXIDATION - REDUCTION REACTIONS Introduction to Redox Reactions OIL-RIG Oxidation - reduction reactions are a type of chemical reaction where electrons are transferred from one species to another. Oxidation - reduction reactions are often referred to as ‘redox‘ reactions. The acronym ‘OIL-RIG’ may help you remember how to classify redox reactions. It stands for ‘Oxidation Is Loss - Reduction Is Gain’ and refers to electron transfer. Historically, redox reactions were defined as the loss or gain of oxygen. Reactions involving the gain of oxygen were called ‘oxidation’ and reactions involving the loss of oxygen were called ‘reduction’ reactions. We now use the transfer of electrons to classify redox reactions as many redox reactions don’t involve oxygen. Consider the reaction between magnesium metal and chlorine gas: Mg(s) + Cl2(g) Mg2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq) Diagrammatically the reaction can be represented as: In the chlorine molecule, chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons to have a complete ‘octet’ of electrons in their outermost (valence) shell. When they become chloride ions in the reaction, each atom gains an electron and is reduced to create a complete valence shell. The electrons were provided by a magnesium atom. Oxidation numbers are assigned to individual elements within a reactant. The change in oxidation number for that element after the reaction has occurred shows whether the element was oxidised or reduced. If the oxidation number reduces, then reduction has occurred. Oxidation involves an increase in oxidation number. In MgO, H2O, CH2O oxygen has an oxidation number of -2. In peroxides (H2O2) oxygen has an oxidation number of -1. In compounds with fluorine it has an oxidation number of +2. 4 Hydrogen in compounds has an oxidation number of +1. In HCl, H2O, CH4 hydrogen has an oxidation number of +1. They require the involvement of water molecules as either reactants or products, and some require acidic conditions to occur as the species H+ is required as a reactant. Oxidants are reduced by gaining electrons, so if a redox reaction occurs with dichromate ions, the other reactant will have lost electrons and therefore has been oxidised. From the resource table we find that the most obvious species that looks like sulfite with oxygen added is sulfate - SO42-. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS The Mole The term ‘mole’ is used by chemists to describe a fixed number of particles. Just as the word ‘dozen’ describes 12 items, a mole is always 6.02 x 1023 particles. Because the particles chemists deal with are very small (atoms, ions, molecules etc.) it is easier to use number of moles to describe the enormous number of particles that occur in day-to-day chemistry. A mole is defined as the amount of any substance that contains as many particles as there are atoms in 12 grams of pure carbon-12 (12C), the isotope of carbon with 6 protons and 6 neutrons in its nucleus. The term ‘amount’ and ‘number of moles’ are interchangeable in chemistry. Both have the symbol ‘n’ and the term mole has the abbreviation ‘mol’. 1. 2. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS What is a Titration? A titration is a laboratory technique which reacts precise amounts of two solutions. The concentration of one solution is known and by carefully measuring the required volume of the second solution, its concentration can be calculated. Consider the following equation: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) When some amount (no. of moles) of HCl has been added to the exact same amount of NaOH, all of the NaOH will have reacted and the resulting solution will be neither acidic or basic. In an acid/base titration, an indicator is used to find the point in the titration when the acid and base have neutralised each other and the solution has become neutral. Titrations use a standard solution to find the concentration of the unknown solution. A standard solution is prepared by weighing a mass of either an acid or base and dissolving it in a known volume. The formulae n = m/M and c = n/V are then used to calculate the concentration of the standard solution. 1. Complete the following table. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS Preparing a Standard Solution A standard solution is a solution that can be used to determine the concentration of another solution in a titration. The concentration of a standard solution can be calculated to a high degree of accuracy. Not all chemicals can be used to prepare a standard solution. An ion from one solution binds to an ion from the second solution forming an insoluble product. APPROXIMATE VOLUMES APPROXIMATE VOLUMES Some ionic solutions can be mixed, and the different types of ions do not interact. All the ions remain dissolved in the mixture. When two solutions are mixed, and a solid forms in the mixture, chemists call the solid product a precipitate. The following rules can be used to predict whether two solutions will form a precipitate: Solubility Rules 1 Group 1 metal cations All soluble. 2 Nitrates (NO3-) All soluble. 3 Chlorides (Cl-) All soluble except AgCl, PbCl2. 4 Sulfates (SO42-) All soluble except BaSO4, PbSO4, CaSO4. 5 Hydroxides (OH-) All insoluble except KOH, NaOH. 6 Carbonates (CO32-) All insoluble except K2CO3, Na2CO3, (NH4)2CO3. 1. The unknown sample may have one or more functional groups. A functional group may be identified by not reacting with any of the reagents given (identification by the process of elimination). In some cases, once identified, a further test may be carried out to confirm the identity of the functional group. You will be supplied with flowcharts that outline the procedures to follow, and which links an observation to a specific functional group. Names of possible organic compounds and their structural formulae will also be provided. For higher levels of achievement you will be expected to justify your identification by linking observations (chemical changes) to chemical principles. This may include writing chemical equations and using chemical vocabulary, symbols and conventions. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: IDENTIFYING IONS IN SOLUTION Complex Ions - The Anions Complex ions are ions with a central metal ion bonded to one or more molecules or ions. The formation of complex ions must be explained when precipitates dissolve. In the flowchart for identifying anions, the test to decide whether the precipitate is silver chloride (Cl-) or iodide (I-) is to add ammonia solution. If the anion is chloride, adding ammonia solution makes the precipitate dissolve. The silver chloride precipitate is composed of silver cations and chloride anions ionically bonded together. Ammonia is able to overcome the lattice energy and pull the silver ions out of the lattice. The chloride ions go back into solution. The complex ion, diammine silver [Ag(NH3)2]+(aq) is composed of two ammonia molecules bonded to a silver ion. Dissolving this precipitate can be represented by the equation: AgCl(s) + 2NH3(aq) [Ag(NH3)2]+(aq) + Cl-(aq) Square brackets surround the ‘complex’ and the charge is shown outside the right-hand bracket. Because the complex is charged it will dissolve in water, as does the chloride ion (Cl-). The subscript ‘(aq)’ shows that the complex ion is in solution. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: OXIDATION - REDUCTION REACTIONS Introduction to Redox Reactions OIL-RIG Oxidation - reduction reactions are a type of chemical reaction where electrons are transferred from one species to another. Oxidation - reduction reactions are often referred to as ‘redox‘ reactions. The acronym ‘OIL-RIG’ may help you remember how to classify redox reactions. It stands for ‘Oxidation Is Loss - Reduction Is Gain’ and refers to electron transfer. Historically, redox reactions were defined as the loss or gain of oxygen. Reactions involving the gain of oxygen were called ‘oxidation’ and reactions involving the loss of oxygen were called ‘reduction’ reactions. We now use the transfer of electrons to classify redox reactions as many redox reactions don’t involve oxygen. Consider the reaction between magnesium metal and chlorine gas: Mg(s) + Cl2(g) Mg2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq) Diagrammatically the reaction can be represented as: In the chlorine molecule, chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons to have a complete ‘octet’ of electrons in their outermost (valence) shell. When they become chloride ions in the reaction, each atom gains an electron and is reduced to create a complete valence shell. The electrons were provided by a magnesium atom. Oxidation numbers are assigned to individual elements within a reactant. The change in oxidation number for that element after the reaction has occurred shows whether the element was oxidised or reduced. If the oxidation number reduces, then reduction has occurred. Oxidation involves an increase in oxidation number. uploads/science/Scipad/Chemistry Interna.searchText: OXIDATION - REDUCTION REACTIONS Complex Half Equations Some types of redox half equations are more complex than those involving simple electron transfer. They require the involvement of water molecules as either reactants or products, and some require acidic conditions to occur as the species H+ is required as a reactant. Four steps can be used to balance complex half equations: 1 Balance the atoms on either side of the equation (other than oxygen and hydrogen). 2 Add water molecules as reactants or products to balance the number of oxygen atoms. 3 Add ‘H+’ as a reactant or product to balance the number of hydrogen atoms. 4 Add electrons so that the charge on either side of the reaction is balanced. It should be easy to remember that dichromate is an oxidant - it has seven oxygen atoms in its formula! Oxidants are reduced by gaining electrons, so if a redox reaction occurs with dichromate ions, the other reactant will have lost electrons and therefore has been oxidised. This principle can be used to predict the outcome for the other reactant in a redox reaction. 1. Ignoring the spectator ions, the reactants will be: Cr2O­72-(aq) + SO32-(aq) We know that dichromate will become Cr3+ under acidic conditions and that the sulfite ions will be oxidised. From the resource table we find that the most obvious species that looks like sulfite with oxygen added is sulfate - SO42-. uploads/science/Scipad/Genetics/41 - Ped.searchText: PREDICTING INHERITANCE Pedigree Charts A pedigree chart is like a family tree that shows the genetic relationships between members of the same family. They can show many generations and are used to track genetic conditions. Horizontal lines indicate breeding pairs and mating Squares are usually used to symbolise males Circles are usually used to symbolise females Vertical lines indicate offspring Shapes with the same colour indicate they have the same phenotype Tigers’ Fur Tigers with white fur are extremely rare in the wild. However, two orange-brown tigers in captivity in the United States, called “Simba” and “Jimba”, are known to produce white offspring. Orangebrown fur is coded by the dominant allele (T). An orange-brown tiger can have the genotype ‘Tt’ or ‘TT’. A tiger with the genotype ‘tt’ will have white fur. The pedigree diagram below shows three generations of tigers. The black shapes indicate tigers with orange-brown fur. The white shapes indicate tigers with white fur. Male tigers are shown by squares, females by circles. uploads/science/Scipad/Genetics/45 - Mut.searchText: UNDERSTANDING VARIATION Mutation as a Cause of Variation Previously you have seen that meiosis and sexual reproduction bring about new combinations of genes in individuals within a population. However, neither meiosis nor sexual reproduction can create new genes or alleles. In order to create a new gene or allele the base sequence of a section of DNA needs to change. When a permanent change occurs in the base sequence of DNA, scientists call it a mutation. Despite what you may have seen on TV or in the movies, mutations do not turn turtles into ninjas, or cause blades of metal to come shooting out of your fists when you’re angry! Most organisms are ‘carrying’ mutations – including yourself. In fact it is suggested that each of us has up to 30 mutations in our bodies at any one time. Mutations can occur naturally during DNA replication. The rate of mutation can be increased by exposure to mutagens. Common mutagens include some chemicals (such as those found in cigarettes and fatty foods), ultraviolet light (from the Sun), and radiation (from x-rays, or radioactive materials, etc.). ‘Mutation’ sounds like a word that means only bad things. However, mutations can be neutral or silent (i.e. they have no observable effect on an organism). Some mutations may be harmful and may affect the survival of the organism. One of the most common harmful effects of mutations in humans is cancer

The cell uses this energy to carry out the essential life processes (MRS C GREN). Mitochondria have two membranes that can be loosely described as a large wrinkled sac (inner membrane) packed inside a smaller, unwrinkled sac (outer membrane). The outer membrane is simple and permeable to many molecules that can pass through the outer membrane with ease. The inner membrane is more complex. The wrinkles, or folds, are organized into layers, called cristae (singlular: crista). These cristae greatly increase the surface area of the inner membrane to allow a higher transport rate of reactants (e.g. H+ and O2) and products (e.g. CO2 and H2O). The matrix is the fluidfilled space enclosed by the inner membrane, containing many enzymes that can function on the large surface area created by the cristae. These enzymes catalyse (speed up) the breakdown of glucose products into carbon dioxide and water. Liquid Matrix provides a medium for reactions. Rod shaped to increase surface area for diffusion. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: CELL STRUCTURES A Closer look at Organelles - Chloroplasts Chloroplasts are found inside the cells of green plants and algae. They are abundant in cells near the top of the leaves. Chloroplasts contain the molecule chlorophyll that absorbs sunlight for photosynthesis. A chloroplast uses carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O) to form glucose, and releases oxygen (O2). Chlorophyll is what gives green plants their green colour. The chloroplast’s structure also maximises the rate at which photosynthesis can occur. Each chloroplast is surrounded by a thin semi-permeable membrane that allows light to penetrate. In the layered stacks are flat disc-shaped thylakoids that increase the surface area for the absorption of light. It is here that chlorophyll is found. The thylakoids are organised into compact piles called grana. The grana are connected to each other by tubes called lamellae. The lamellae are suspended in a watery matrix called the stroma. Osmosis is the movement of water from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration (down the concentration gradient) via a semi-permeable membrane. Larger molecules (glucose, etc.) cannot pass through the membrane. When the concentration of water is the same on both sides of the membrane, the rate of movement of water will be the same in both directions. At this point, the net exchange of water will be zero and the system is in equilibrium. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: DNA, PROTEINS AND ENZYMES Models of Enzyme Action Enzymes are able to speed up chemical reactions without being used up in the chemical reaction. They are also specific, affecting only certain types of reactions and acting on specific types of substrate. To explain how enzymes achieve this, two models have been proposed: The Lock and Key Model The chemist Emil Fischer (1852 – 1919) proposed that the substrate fits into the enzyme’s active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex. The analogy he used was that of a lock and key. The key (substrate) has a specific shape that allows it, and no other key, to fit into the lock (the enzyme). The substrate and enzyme complement each other. Only specific molecules fit the active site. Therefore, they can fit together, like a lock and key. The final product is released and the enzyme is able to catalyse another reaction. The Induced Fit Model In 1958, Daniel Koshland modified the lock-and-key model. Since enzymes are flexible structures, he proposed that binding of the substrate to the enzyme alters the configuration of both the enzymes and the substrate, providing a better fit. Enzymes achieve specificity because only substrates with the correct functional groups in the correct configurations are able to modify the active site of the enzyme. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: PREDICTING INHERITANCE The Test Cross In many cases, animal and plant breeders only want pure bred stock. This is because the pure bred organism has no hidden genetic characteristics that may be undesirable. Remember with any test cross you can never be 100% certain that a parent is homozygous dominant. Test-crosses have an element of uncertainty and need multiple breeding attempts in order to increase the certainty of the unknown parent’s genotype. If we consider the pea plants from the previous exercises (i.e. P = purple and p = white), just because a plant displays the dominant phenotype (purple flowers), it doesn’t necessarily mean it is pure bred (homozygous). Purple flowered plants could be heterozygous (Pp) or homozygous dominant (PP). In order to determine if an organism is pure bred, a breeding test is carried out, called a ‘test cross’. A test cross simply involves mating the organism in question with an individual that is homozygous recessive for that trait. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: PREDICTING INHERITANCE The Test Cross In many cases, animal and plant breeders only want pure bred stock. This is because the pure bred organism has no hidden genetic characteristics that may be undesirable. Remember with any test cross you can never be 100% certain that a parent is homozygous dominant. Test-crosses have an element of uncertainty and need multiple breeding attempts in order to increase the certainty of the unknown parent’s genotype. If we consider the pea plants from the previous exercises (i.e. P = purple and p = white), just because a plant displays the dominant phenotype (purple flowers), it doesn’t necessarily mean it is pure bred (homozygous). Purple flowered plants could be heterozygous (Pp) or homozygous dominant (PP). In order to determine if an organism is pure bred, a breeding test is carried out, called a ‘test cross’. A test cross simply involves mating the organism in question with an individual that is homozygous recessive for that trait. If the recessive phenotype appears in the offspring then the organism in question must be heterozygous. 1. Outline why an animal or plant breeder may only want stock that is pure bred? A gamete is a sex cell (sperm in males and ova in females). A human body cell contains 46 chromosomes. Gametes only contain half as many chromosomes (23). During meiosis, genes get shuffled, and this leads to variation within a population. Meiosis is the reason you look similar, but not identical, to your parents and siblings. They are unwound as single strands of DNA that are being used to make proteins (protein synthesis). They are shown here as discrete chromosomes so you can track the differences between the parent cell and the daughter cells. 2 Chromosome replicate by DNA replication. The nuclear membrane disappears and pairs of homologous chromosomes line up next to each other. 3 Homologous pairs exchange sections of DNA (and therefore alleles) by a process called crossing over which is unique to meiosis. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: PREDICTING INHERITANCE In your exam you can tell you are dealing with a question involving incomplete dominance when the offspring shows a third phenotype which is a BLEND of the parental phenotypes. Incomplete Dominance The crosses completed on the previous pages are all examples of complete dominance, i.e. where the dominant allele completely masks the effect of the recessive allele in heterozygous conditions (i.e. when describing pea flower colour, an individual with the genotype Pp would show a purple flower phenotype. The dominant ‘P’ allele completely masked the recessive ‘p’ [white] allele). However, some alleles are incompletely dominant, meaning that heterozygous individuals are a combination of both the dominant and recessive conditions. For example, in some flowers the gene, or genes, to make the protein for red pigmented flowers is incompletely dominant over the gene that results in the protein for white pigmented flowers. A heterozygous individual is producing both proteins that contribute to the final phenotype, i.e. pink flowers. 1. 2. Both sodium chloride and sucrose are soluble in water in relatively high proportions. The molecules and ions from which they are made are ‘pulled’ from the solid by attractive forces to water molecules. Because they are so small we cannot see them in solution, although many coloured ions will produce coloured solutions. Compounds have a range of solubilities, from infinitely soluble (e.g. ethanol and water), to virtually insoluble (e.g. copper(II) oxide and water). The substance being dissolved is called the solute. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: CELL TRANSPORT Active Transport - Carrier Proteins Sometimes a cell needs to transport particles (such as Na+, K+, Mg2+, glucose, etc) against the concentration gradient (i.e. from an area of low concentration to an area of high concentration). Particles do not readily move in that direction, so in order to accomplish this energy (ATP) is required to actively transport the particles. Active transport involves the movement of small particles (via carrier proteins) or large particles (via cytosis), and the expenditure of energy. Carrier proteins Energy is used to change the shape of the carrier protein channel, forcing the protein to change shape. The process is reversible so ions and molecules can enter or exit the cell. Low concentration of solutes Carrier protein Cell interior High concentration of solutes An example of active transport via carrier proteins occurs when plants pump nitrate ions into their root hair cells. Because the concentration of nitrate ions is higher within the root hair cell than in soil water, nitrate ions tend to diffuse out of the cell via specific channel proteins. To recover the nitrate ions the plant must actively transport them back into the cell. Further examples include the cells within the gills of salt-water fish. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: METABOLISM AND THE EFFECT OF THE ENVIRONMENT Metabolic Pathways Metabolism is the set of enzyme controlled, life-maintaining chemical reactions that occur in all living organisms. A metabolic pathway is a series of chemical reactions occurring within a cell that are essential for its survival. In each metabolic pathway, a principal chemical (the substrate) is modified by an enzyme-controlled reaction. The reaction modifies the substrate into a product that is then used as a substrate for another enzyme-controlled reaction. This process continues until the final product is produced. Enzymes are crucial to metabolism because they act as catalysts, allowing these normally slow reactions to proceed quickly and efficiently. Metabolic pathways are advantageous because, when the pathway is functioning, the initial substrate is continuously converted into the final product(s). When the amount of end product reaches a certain level, feedback mechanisms stop the pathway. Feedback mechanisms give greater control over the rate of reactions. Secondly, sophisticated reactions are possible, so more complex molecules can be made. Intermediate products can also be used in other pathways. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: SCIENTIFIC INVESTIGATIONS Variables Experiments are used to investigate the relationship between two quantities (variables). The basic concept behind conducting an experiment is to change one variable and measure how that affects the second variable. For this reason, only one variable can be changed per experiment, and only one variable measured. Variables have particular names depending on what role they play in the experiment. Independent Variable The variable that is changed by the person conducting the experiment. There is only one independent variable per experiment and it must have a range of appropriate values to ensure the results are valid. Dependent Variable The variable that is measured by the person conducting the experiment. This variable changes because the independent variable has been changed. There is only one dependent variable per experiment. Control Variables Any variables, other than the dependent and independent variables, that may affect the results of the experiment. There can be an unlimited number of control variables for any experiment. It is important that you spend time to identify the most important control variables (the ones that would most likely cause a significant impact on the experiment). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: SCIENTIFIC INVESTIGATIONS Writing a Conclusion, Discussion and Evaluation The purpose of a conclusion is to summarize the findings presented in the results section. It is a written description of the processed data and should refer to the purpose (aim and hypothesis) of the investigation. Typically, it is only a paragraph long and should outline whether the data supports or refutes the hypothesis. The discussion section is where you interpret your results using relevant biological concepts and knowledge. You should analyse and describe the trends, patterns and results, and compare them to your hypothesis. You should compare your results with the findings of others, either from within your class or from outside your class. You should also evaluate your investigation. During an evaluation you should analyse the accuracy of your investigation and describe what you did to ensure the validity and reliability of your results. Explain what went well and what didn’t go so well. Outline any changes you would make for future investigations by describing any anomalies and outliers. Explain what caused them and how they could be eliminated. It is important that you comment on the validity of your data (i.e. was it consistent within your trials?). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: CELL TRANSPORT Active Transport - Carrier Proteins Sometimes a cell needs to transport particles (such as Na+, K+, Mg2+, glucose, etc) against the concentration gradient (i.e. from an area of low concentration to an area of high concentration). Particles do not readily move in that direction, so in order to accomplish this energy (ATP) is required to actively transport the particles. Active transport involves the movement of small particles (via carrier proteins) or large particles (via cytosis), and the expenditure of energy. Carrier proteins Energy is used to change the shape of the carrier protein channel, forcing the protein to change shape. The process is reversible so ions and molecules can enter or exit the cell. Low concentration of solutes Carrier protein Cell interior High concentration of solutes An example of active transport via carrier proteins occurs when plants pump nitrate ions into their root hair cells. Because the concentration of nitrate ions is higher within the root hair cell than in soil water, nitrate ions tend to diffuse out of the cell via specific channel proteins. To recover the nitrate ions the plant must actively transport them back into the cell. Further examples include the cells within the gills of salt-water fish. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: SCIENTIFIC INVESTIGATIONS Variables Experiments are used to investigate the relationship between two quantities (variables). The basic concept behind conducting an experiment is to change one variable and measure how that affects the second variable. For this reason, only one variable can be changed per experiment, and only one variable measured. Variables have particular names depending on what role they play in the experiment. Independent Variable The variable that is changed by the person conducting the experiment. There is only one independent variable per experiment and it must have a range of appropriate values to ensure the results are valid. Dependent Variable The variable that is measured by the person conducting the experiment. This variable changes because the independent variable has been changed. There is only one dependent variable per experiment. Control Variables Any variables, other than the dependent and independent variables, that may affect the results of the experiment. There can be an unlimited number of control variables for any experiment. It is important that you spend time to identify the most important control variables (the ones that would most likely cause a significant impact on the experiment). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: SCIENTIFIC INVESTIGATIONS Writing a Conclusion, Discussion and Evaluation The purpose of a conclusion is to summarize the findings presented in the results section. It is a written description of the processed data and should refer to the purpose (aim and hypothesis) of the investigation. Typically, it is only a paragraph long and should outline whether the data supports or refutes the hypothesis. The discussion section is where you interpret your results using relevant biological concepts and knowledge. You should analyse and describe the trends, patterns and results, and compare them to your hypothesis. You should compare your results with the findings of others, either from within your class or from outside your class. You should also evaluate your investigation. During an evaluation you should analyse the accuracy of your investigation and describe what you did to ensure the validity and reliability of your results. Explain what went well and what didn’t go so well. Outline any changes you would make for future investigations by describing any anomalies and outliers. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: ANALYSING BIOLOGICAL INFORMATION Analysing Socioscientific Information Socioscientific issues are controversial social issues that relate to science. Examples of socioscientific issues include issues such as genetic engineering, climate change, animal testing for medical purposes, oil drilling in national parks, “fat taxes” on “unhealthy” foods, and oil extraction by fracking, etc. Articles that appear in scientific journals (such as ‘Nature’, and ‘The Lancet’) must go through a rigorous peer review process. Peer review means that the article is evaluated by one or more people of similar competence to the producers of the work. Socioscientific articles do not need to go through the same process. They may be written by scientists, but more often than not are written by journalists, non-government organisations or people with an interest in the topic. The information presented may be inaccurate (i.e. it contains errors or incorrect data analysis), or it may be biased (where only one view is expressed) or written by someone with a vested interest (e.g. they own a business that could benefit from people reading the article). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: NUTRITION IN MAMMALS Teeth and Ingestion There are three main diets in the mammalian world. Mammals whose diets are similar belong to a trophic group (“trophic” is derived from the Greek “trophikos”, meaning ‘nourishment’). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: NUTRITION IN MAMMALS Digestive Processes - Digestion (The Stomach) The oesophagus leads to the stomach. The stomach is a large, elastic sac that can expand to hold many litres of food (typically 2 - 4 litres in humans). This means a meal can be ingested quickly and digested over a longer period of time. Carbohydrates arriving at the stomach have already begun to be turned into simple sugars by the enzyme amylase. Other nutrients remain undigested. The interior of the stomach is lined with holes, called gastric pits. Cells within the gastric pits secrete three types of fluid, collectively called gastric fluid: • Hydrochloric acid (HCl). The corrosive nature of this strong acid (pH 1-2) is able to dissolve many types of food. The acid causes proteins to denature, unravelling them and exposing the bonds holding the molecule together. This exposure allows digestive enzymes to break the long chains of amino acids into individual molecules. The acidic nature of HCl also kills many pathogens (disease causing micro-organisms) that enter the body with food. • Pepsin. The enzyme pepsin catalyses the breakdown of proteins into amino acids. • Mucus. Secreted to form a protective layer that prevents the acid and enzymes digesting the stomach itself. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: GAS EXCHANGE Gas Exchange in Fish Animals that live under water are disadvantaged because water has a much lower percentage of oxygen when compared to the same volume of air. This disadvantage is counteracted by two key adaptations found in most fish. Adaptation 1 - Ventilation of the Gills By working together the pharynx and the operculum supply an almost continuous, unidirectional supply of water. They also ensure there is no ‘dead-space’ as there is in lungs. Inspiration Expiration Mouth Oral valve Operculum (gills underneath) Pharynx (buccal chamber) Gill arches Operculum valve The mouth opens and water is drawn into it as the floor of the pharynx is lowered, increasing the volume of the buccal chamber. At the same time the gill covers (operculum) open, sucking water over the gills. The mouth then closes, the floor of the pharynx is raised, the operculum closes resulting in water being pushed over the gills. Adaptation 2 - Countercurrent Exchange Blood flows in the opposite direction to the water. This means blood is always flowing next to water that has given up less of its oxygen and it is able to absorb more and more oxygen as it moves along the capillary. Even as blood reaches the end of the lamella it is flowing past water which is at the beginning of the lamella and therefore high in dissolved oxygen. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: GAS EXCHANGE Gas Exchange in Mammals Because oxygen is relatively abundant in air (when compared to water), the major issue faced by terrestrial air breathers is the gas exchange surface drying out. The lungs of mammals are adapted to overcome this problem. Lungs are sac-like organs. The mammalian torso contains two lungs. Air passes between the lungs and the outside of the body through the windpipe (called the trachea). The trachea divides into two bronchi, with one bronchus for each lung. Mucus produced by cells in the bronchi help maintain a moist environment. Each bronchus divides further in the lungs into smaller tubes called bronchioles. At the end of each bronchiole, there is a group of tiny air sacs called alveoli. These alveoli provide a large surface area through which gases can diffuse. The distance between the alveolus and the blood supply (capillaries) is short because the lining of the lung and the capillary are both only one cell thick. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: GENETIC CHANGE Mechanisms for Evolution - Migration (Gene Flow) Migration occurs when individuals move into (immigration) or out of (emigration) a population. When the migrating individuals interbreed with the new population, they contribute their alleles to the gene pool of the local population, distribute favourable mutations and reduce genetic variation between the populations. A high rate of migration can have a significant effect on allele frequencies of both the population they leave, and the population they enter. In small populations migration can have a major effect on allele frequencies. In general terms, migration tends to increase variation within populations and decrease variation between populations. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: INVESTIGATE AN ECOLOGICAL COMMUNITY Interactions Between Species within a Community Most resources (food, space, mates, shelter, etc.) are in limited supply in a community, so individuals must compete for them. Whenever resources are in short supply, they become a limiting factor and only those individuals that are able to out-compete others will survive. Interspecific competition describes competition between individuals of different species. This form of competition can be so strong that it causes the exclusion of one species by the other. Intraspecific competition describes the competition between members of the same species. Predation describes the consumption of other species for food. The predator species benefits while the prey species is harmed. Some predators kill their prey before eating them while other predators are described as parasites that feed on prey while it is still alive. Herbivory is a form of predation whereby an animal feeds on plants. Mutualism is a symbiotic interaction between species in which both benefit. Commensalism is a type of relationship among organisms in which one organism benefits while the other organism neither benefits nor is harmed. Parasitism results in one species benefitting, while the other species is harmed. 1. Give four examples of resources the following groups would compete for. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: BIOLOGICAL MATERIAL AT THE MICROSCOPIC LEVEL Drawing Cells Scientists need to use microscopes to observe cells. They often make drawings of what they have seen to show other scientists and communicate their findings. Your ability to make a biological drawing will be assessed in this achievement standard. Rules for making a biological drawing • Draw what you see, not what you expect to see. • Use a sharp HB pencil and a clean eraser. • Make the drawing as large as possible. • Draw the main features. Cells are relatively complicated and there is no need to draw every detail. • Use clear bold lines. Sketches and lines that cross over each other are unacceptable. • Don’t use shading or cross hatching. Generally stippling (using dots) is not allowed but permitted by some schools - check with your teacher. • Plant cells generally don’t exist in insolation so you shouldn’t have gaps between plant cells • Add an appropriate title that identifies the biological material used, shows the magnification used (e.g. x 400) and any stain used. • Label organelles AND features of the cells (e.g. large number of chloroplasts in palisade layer of leaf). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: NON-LINEAR MATHEMATICAL RELATIONSHIP Significant Figures The use of the correct number of significant figures in final answers is crucial. Too many significant figures in your answers demonstrates a lack of understanding about the degree of accuracy that can be obtained from an experiment. Some simple rules need to be followed to ensure answers are rounded to the correct number of significant figures: • All non-zero digits are significant. • 12.34 has four significant figures. Zeros appearing anywhere between two non-zero digits are significant. 1001 has four significant figures. • Leading zeros are not significant. • 0.001234 has four significant figures. Trailing zeros in a number with a decimal point are significant. 0.1000 has four significant figures. • Trailing zeros are not significant unless indicated. 1000 (2 sig. figs.) has two significant figures as stated. Significant figures become important when doing calculations. The accuracy of the final answer is limited by the lowest number of significant figures, for example: QUESTION ONE Calculate the time taken for light to travel to Earth from the Sun. Distance to Earth is 149 600 000 000 m (4 sig. figs.) Speed of light is 299 792 458 m s-1 (9 sig. figs.) uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: NON-LINEAR MATHEMATICAL RELATIONSHIP Experimental Variables Experiments are used to investigate the relationship between two quantities. Quantities that are measured or recorded in experiments are called variables. During an experiment one variable is changed, and a second variable is measured to record the effect of the change. Only one variable can be changed during an experiment to ensure the relationship between variables is definitely linked. If more than one variable was changed, the change in the second variable could be linked to either change and the relationship to each variable would be uncertain. Variables are named depending on the role they play in the experiment: Independent variable: The variable that is changed by the person conducting the experiment. There can be only one independent variable per experiment. Dependent variable: The variable that is measured by the person conducting the experiment. There is only one dependent variable per experiment. Control variables: These are any variables, other than the dependent and independent variables, that could affect the results of the experiment. There can be an unlimited number of control variables for any experiment. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: NON-LINEAR MATHEMATICAL RELATIONSHIP Finding a Range And Collecting Data Most experiments will have a limited range over which data should be gathered. The range may be limited due to physical constraints (e.g. a maximum weight that a spring can support), or theoretical constraints (e.g. no noticeable difference in wave speed once water gets above a certain depth, even though the formula predicts there is). Most restrictions on the range of school laboratory experiments will be due to physical constraints. Before the experimental design is finalised, it is important to do trial runs to establish the range from which data can be collected. Once an upper and lower limit has been established, at least three other (intermediate) data points should be specified. Ideally these are evenly spaced across the entire range that is available. If data is not collected over the entire range an inaccurate relationship may result. Below are some illustrations of what might happen if the range is too small. Data collected only in the shaded area would give a steeper gradient than data over the entire range. Data collected only in the shaded area would appear linear, but the true shape is parabolic. Time must be spent planning data collection methods that minimise the effect of errors on the results. The methods used to minimise these errors are called accuracy improving techniques. Techniques used may minimise errors but may not completely eliminate them. It is important to note that when accuracy improving techniques are explained, the explanation indicates that you understand what the type of error is, and how it applies to your experiment. General statements such as "it removes random error" do not indicate that you understand the type of error or how it applies to your particular experiment. To avoid confusion, explain in plain terms what could happen and how you tried to prevent it happening. 1 - Consistent Start/Stop Positions A number of experiments have specific start or stop positions that must be used consistently throughout the experiment to ensure measurements are accurate. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: TRANSPORT IN ANGIOSPERMS Transpiration Transpiration is the process whereby water moves up the plant against gravity, without the expenditure of energy. Most of the water in a leaf evaporates before it can be used in photosynthesis. If you imagine the xylem cells as one long continuous drinking straw, removing water at the top of the straw will result in water been drawn into it at the bottom. Xylem tissue acts just like a straw. The effect of evaporation at the top of the plant literally pulls a column of water up the plant. The ability of these thin columns of water to be pulled in this way – without breaking – is caused by the characteristics of cohesion and adhesion in water. Cohesion is the ability of water molecules to stick to one another. Adhesion is the ability of water molecules to stick to other substances (such as the wall of the xylem tube). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: GAS EXCHANGE Gas Exchange in Terrestrial Insects The circulatory system of insects is not used for gas exchange so gases need to be transported directly to the respiring tissues via a tracheal system. Tracheal System Spiracle The spiracles are openings of small tubes running into the insect’s body. There may be up to 20 spiracles on an insect. Some insects may also have air sacs present that increase the efficiency of the tracheal system during periods of vigorous movement. Spiracle opening controlled by valves that can be opened and closed to reduce water loss. Detail of Tracheole End Exoskeleton helps minimise water loss. Trachea are covered in chitin to prevent them closing. Insects ventilate the trachea by making rhythmic body movements. Tracheole fluid Tracheoles lack chitin and reach to individual cells. Dissolved oxygen in tracheole fluid moves into the surrounding muscle tissue when the muscle contracts. When the muscle relaxes the fluid flows back into the tracheole. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Early Atomic Models The first model of the atom is credited to the Greek philosopher Democritus (460 – 370 BC). Democritus proposed that matter could not be divided into smaller parts forever. Eventually the matter would reach its smallest possible state and could not be divided further. This smallest particle was called ‘atomos’ which means uncuttable or indivisible. Democritus believed that the atomos were very small hard particles of varying shapes and sizes that could join together. Another Greek philosopher, Aristotle (384 – 322 BC), disagreed with the idea of atomos. He believed matter could be divided infinitely as there was no single particle that made up matter. Aristotle believed matter was made from the four ‘elements’- fire, earth, water and air. A fifth element called aether was a divine element that made up the sky and planets. Aristotle’s theory became the accepted model and stood for about 2 000 years. John Dalton’s ‘Billiard Ball’ Model John Dalton (1766 - 1844) was an English chemist who, in the 1800s, was performing a number of experiments with gases. Through these experiments Dalton re-introduced Democritus’ idea that matter is made up of smaller fundamental particles called atoms. Dalton made the following five statements about matter and its composition: • All matter is made up of atoms. • Atoms cannot be created or destroyed. •

uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Rutherford’s Model of the Atom Rutherford’s model of the atom introduced the concept of a nucleus - a very small positively charged region of the atom that contains most of the atomic mass. The negatively charged electrons orbit the nucleus like planets around the Sun. Rutherford also proposed that the atom is nearly all empty space. The Rutherford model is sometimes called the planetary model because the electrons are described as orbiting the nucleus just like planets orbiting a star. Electrons surround the nucleus at a distance very much greater than the nuclear diameter. The nucleus is very small, lies at the centre of the atom, contains almost all of the mass (Thomson had shown that electrons were about 1 / 2 000 the mass of a proton) and contains all of the positive charge. Most of the space occupied by an atom contains nothing. It is a vacuum bounded by the orbiting electrons. It is important to note that Rutherford’s model does not place the electrons in orbits with set energy levels, nor does it include neutrons in the positively charged nucleus. These ideas came later. Flaws with Rutherford’s model of the atom include: • It cannot explain why the orbiting electrons do not spiral into the nucleus. • The photo-electric effect could not be explained. Apart from atoms of hydrogen, that contain only a single proton and one electron, all atoms contain these three types of particle. Electrons are much smaller than neutrons and protons (~1 / 2000 the size) and occupy space (shells) around the nucleus. ‘Room’ in the shells is limited, and only a fixed number of electrons ‘fit’ in each shell. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Getting To Know The Periodic Table If you look at the NCEA Periodic Table, you will notice that each element has two numbers associated with it. The smaller number is called the atomic number (Z) and represents the number of protons found in the nucleus of a single atom of that element. Since the number of protons is equal to the number of electrons, the atomic number also tells you how many electrons there are in the energy levels around the nucleus. The larger number you will find on the NCEA Periodic Table is called the mass number. This tells you the total number of particles, protons plus neutrons, found in the nucleus of an atom. So, if you know the mass number and the atomic number of an element, it is possible to work out the number of neutrons in the nucleus. By subtracting the number of protons from the mass number, you can calculate the total number of neutrons. Worked Example 1. A lithium atom has a mass number of 7. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons found in this atom. 3 Li Lithium 7 1. 54 Number of protons or electrons = The atomic number. Therefore, the lithium atom has 3 protons and 3 electrons. Number of neutrons = Mass number - Atomic number. Therefore, the lithium atom has 7 - 3 = 4 neutrons. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS The Results of Rutherford’s Experiment The Expected Results Rutherford’s experiment was performed to support Thomson’s Plum Pudding model of the atom. He expected the alpha particles to pass through the gold foil, with perhaps a few of the particles deviating a small amount. The ‘Plum Pudding’ model describes a positively charged mass with electrons embedded throughout. This would mean that the atom’s positive charge was spread throughout the atom. There would be no region of high charge density to interact with the positively charged alpha particles so only a small amount of deviation was expected. 1. Outline why Rutherford did not expect the alpha particles to be deflected by the gold atoms.  The plum pudding model was still believed to be accurate, meaning  the positive charge of the atom was evenly distributed throughout. As a  consequence the positively charged alpha particles would not experience  strong electrostatic forces and would not be deviated a great distance/  angle. The Actual Results As expected, most of the alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, while a small number experienced a small amount of deviation. However, about 1 in 8 000 alpha particles were deflected through large angles. Some even bounced backwards. The large deflections and rebounding were unexpected and indicated a flaw with Thomson’s Plum Pudding model

uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Radiation Different forms of radiation may be emitted from the nucleus of radioactive atoms. There are three types of radiation that you need to be familiar with: Alpha Particles (α) Alpha particles are the largest and slowest moving of the three types of radiation. An alpha particle 4 has the same structure as a helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons). It is given the symbol 2 α. The speed of an alpha particle is approximately 15 000 000 m s-1 (5% of the speed of light). Beta Particles (β) Beta particles are formed when a neutron breaks down into a proton, giving off a negatively charged beta particle. This negatively charged particle can be described as a high speed electron that has been emitted from the nucleus. Beta particles have the symbol -10 β, which shows the beta particle has a charge of negative 1, and essentially no mass. Beta particles travel near the speed of light, although the exact speed (and energy) can vary. 90% of the speed of light (270 000 000 m s-1) is a typical value for the speed of a beta particle. Gamma Rays (γ) Gamma rays are an electromagnetic wave and therefore travel at the speed of light. Nuclei that have too much energy, often due to a previous nuclear reaction, are unstable and release the excess in the form of gamma rays. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Isotopes Atoms of an element can exist in different forms. Different forms of the same element are called isotopes. Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but a different mass number. This means they have the same number of protons (and electrons), but different numbers of neutrons. Isotopes with more neutrons than usual may cause the nucleus to become unstable. These isotopes may be radioactive, even if the majority of the element’s other atoms are stable. The word isotope comes from Greek and means “the same place”. It is used because isotopes of an atom are located at the same place on the Periodic Table. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Ionising the contents of cells can cause cancer (among other things). Ionisation Ionisation is the process whereby radiation changes atoms into ions. During ionisation, radiation causes atoms to lose electrons and become positively charged. Ionisation by radiation is classified into two types: Direct Ionisation Both alpha and beta radiation are charged particles. When these charged particles move near electrons there is an electrostatic force between the particle and the electron. If the force is large the electron may be pushed far enough that it leaves its orbit around the atom and becomes free. The size of the electrostatic force between the electron and the radiation depends on: • The distance between the electron and the radiation (closer means greater force). • The size of the charge on the radiation (greater charge means greater force). Indirect Ionisation Gamma rays do not have a charge so they cannot exert electrostatic force on electrons they interact with. However, gamma rays are highly energised and some of this energy can be passed on to electrons. Energising the electrons allows them to move further away from the nucleus. If sufficient energy is provided to the electron, it may leave the atom altogether. Indirect ionisation has a lesser effect on matter than direct ionisation. Ionising Ability Weak Gamma rays 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Radiation in Medicine Radiation has various uses in medicine including diagnosis and treatment of diseases, and sterilisation of medical equipment. These uses involve high energy or ionising radiation that has the ability to damage healthy cells, as well as unhealthy ones. The use of radiation must be carefully monitored, and radioactive sources with short half-lives used in order to keep patients safe. Diagnosis One form of diagnosis uses radioactive tracers. This involves a small amount of radioactive material being injected into the bloodstream. When the tracer reaches a cancerous tumour (tumours usually have increased blood supply) the radioactivity becomes concentrated. Sensors are then used to detect the radiation emitted and locate the cancer. Treatment When a cancerous tumour has been identified the patient may undergo radiation treatment. Treatments involving radiation can either be done by placing a radioactive source (temporarily) inside the patient, allowing the radiation emitted to destroy the unhealthy cells, or by using an external source to direct radiation at the tumour. During Cobalt-60 therapy gamma rays are emitted from a radioactive source and directed towards the cancer. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: TRANSPORT IN ANGIOSPERMS Transpiration Transpiration is the process whereby water moves up the plant against gravity, without the expenditure of energy. Most of the water in a leaf evaporates before it can be used in photosynthesis. If you imagine the xylem cells as one long continuous drinking straw, removing water at the top of the straw will result in water been drawn into it at the bottom. Xylem tissue acts just like a straw. The effect of evaporation at the top of the plant literally pulls a column of water up the plant. The ability of these thin columns of water to be pulled in this way – without breaking – is caused by the characteristics of cohesion and adhesion in water. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: NON-LINEAR MATHEMATICAL RELATIONSHIP Experimental Variables Experiments are used to investigate the relationship between two quantities. Quantities that are measured or recorded in experiments are called variables. During an experiment one variable is changed, and a second variable is measured to record the effect of the change. Only one variable can be changed during an experiment to ensure the relationship between variables is definitely linked. If more than one variable was changed, the change in the second variable could be linked to either change and the relationship to each variable would be uncertain. Variables are named depending on the role they play in the experiment: Independent variable: The variable that is changed by the person conducting the experiment. There can be only one independent variable per experiment. Dependent variable: The variable that is measured by the person conducting the experiment. There is only one dependent variable per experiment. Control variables: These are any variables, other than the dependent and independent variables, that could affect the results of the experiment. There can be an unlimited number of control variables for any experiment. One type of smoke detector uses a radiation source (normally americium-241 - an alpha emitter) to ionise the air between two charged plates. The ionised air is attracted to the charged plates, and is detected as a flowing current. If smoke particles move between the charged plates, they interact with the ionised particles and disrupt the pathway between the two plates. This reduces the current flowing between the two plates and an alarm is set off. Alpha emission ionises air molecules that are then attracted to the charged plates of the detector. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: NON-LINEAR MATHEMATICAL RELATIONSHIP Finding a Range And Collecting Data Most experiments will have a limited range over which data should be gathered. The range may be limited due to physical constraints (e.g. a maximum weight that a spring can support), or theoretical constraints (e.g. no noticeable difference in wave speed once water gets above a certain depth, even though the formula predicts there is). Most restrictions on the range of school laboratory experiments will be due to physical constraints. Before the experimental design is finalised, it is important to do trial runs to establish the range from which data can be collected. Once an upper and lower limit has been established, at least three other (intermediate) data points should be specified. Ideally these are evenly spaced across the entire range that is available. If data is not collected over the entire range an inaccurate relationship may result. Below are some illustrations of what might happen if the range is too small. Data collected only in the shaded area would give a steeper gradient than data over the entire range. Data collected only in the shaded area would appear linear, but the true shape is parabolic. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: NON-LINEAR MATHEMATICAL RELATIONSHIP Accuracy Improving Techniques Recording data accurately, and explaining how you ensured accuracy in your data collection, is crucial to obtaining higher grades. Time must be spent planning data collection methods that minimise the effect of errors on the results. The methods used to minimise these errors are called accuracy improving techniques. Techniques used may minimise errors but may not completely eliminate them. It is important to note that when accuracy improving techniques are explained, the explanation indicates that you understand what the type of error is, and how it applies to your experiment. General statements such as "it removes random error" do not indicate that you understand the type of error or how it applies to your particular experiment. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Early Atomic Models The first model of the atom is credited to the Greek philosopher Democritus (460 – 370 BC). Democritus proposed that matter could not be divided into smaller parts forever. Eventually the matter would reach its smallest possible state and could not be divided further. This smallest particle was called ‘atomos’ which means uncuttable or indivisible. Democritus believed that the atomos were very small hard particles of varying shapes and sizes that could join together. Another Greek philosopher, Aristotle (384 – 322 BC), disagreed with the idea of atomos. He believed matter could be divided infinitely as there was no single particle that made up matter. Aristotle believed matter was made from the four ‘elements’- fire, earth, water and air. A fifth element called aether was a divine element that made up the sky and planets. Aristotle’s theory became the accepted model and stood for about 2 000 years. John Dalton’s ‘Billiard Ball’ Model John Dalton (1766 - 1844) was an English chemist who, in the 1800s, was performing a number of experiments with gases. Through these experiments Dalton re-introduced Democritus’ idea that matter is made up of smaller fundamental particles called atoms. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Rutherford’s Model of the Atom Rutherford’s model of the atom introduced the concept of a nucleus - a very small positively charged region of the atom that contains most of the atomic mass. The negatively charged electrons orbit the nucleus like planets around the Sun. Rutherford also proposed that the atom is nearly all empty space. The Rutherford model is sometimes called the planetary model because the electrons are described as orbiting the nucleus just like planets orbiting a star. Most of the space occupied by an atom contains nothing. It is a vacuum bounded by the orbiting electrons. Electrons surround the nucleus at a distance very much greater than the nuclear diameter. The nucleus is very small, lies at the centre of the atom, contains almost all of the mass (Thomson had shown that electrons were about 1 / 2 000 the mass of a proton) and contains all of the positive charge. It is important to note that Rutherford’s model does not place the electrons in orbits with set energy levels, nor does it include neutrons in the positively charged nucleus. These ideas came later. Flaws with Rutherford’s model of the atom include: • It cannot explain why the orbiting electrons do not spiral into the nucleus. • The photo-electric effect could not be explained. The ‘Plum Pudding’ model describes a positively charged mass with electrons embedded throughout. This would mean that the atom’s positive charge was spread throughout the atom. There would be no region of high charge density to interact with the positively charged alpha particles so only a small amount of deviation was expected. 1. The large deflections and rebounding were unexpected and indicated a flaw with Thomson’s Plum Pudding model. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Getting To Know The Periodic Table If you look at the NCEA Periodic Table, you will notice that each element has two numbers associated with it. The smaller number is called the atomic number (Z) and represents the number of protons found in the nucleus of a single atom of that element. Since the number of protons is equal to the number of electrons, the atomic number also tells you how many electrons there are in the energy levels around the nucleus. The larger number you will find on the NCEA Periodic Table is called the mass number. This tells you the total number of particles, protons plus neutrons, found in the nucleus of an atom. So, if you know the mass number and the atomic number of an element, it is possible to work out the number of neutrons in the nucleus. Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but a different mass number. This means they have the same number of protons (and electrons), but different numbers of neutrons. Isotopes with more neutrons than usual may cause the nucleus to become unstable. These isotopes may be radioactive, even if the majority of the element’s other atoms are stable. The word isotope comes from Greek and means “the same place”. It is used because isotopes of an atom are located at the same place on the Periodic Table. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Radiation Different forms of radiation may be emitted from the nucleus of radioactive atoms. There are three types of radiation that you need to be familiar with: Alpha Particles (α) Alpha particles are the largest and slowest moving of the three types of radiation. An alpha particle 4 has the same structure as a helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons). It is given the symbol 2 α. The speed of an alpha particle is approximately 15 000 000 m s-1 (5% of the speed of light). Beta Particles (β) Beta particles are formed when a neutron breaks down into a proton, giving off a negatively charged beta particle. This negatively charged particle can be described as a high speed electron that has been emitted from the nucleus. Beta particles have the symbol -10 β, which shows the beta particle has a charge of negative 1, and essentially no mass. Beta particles travel near the speed of light, although the exact speed (and energy) can vary. 90% of the speed of light (270 000 000 m s-1) is a typical value for the speed of a beta particle. Gamma Rays (γ) Gamma rays are an electromagnetic wave and therefore travel at the speed of light. Nuclei that have too much energy, often due to a previous nuclear reaction, are unstable and release the excess in the form of gamma rays. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Ionising the contents of cells can cause cancer (among other things). Ionisation Ionisation is the process whereby radiation changes atoms into ions. During ionisation, radiation causes atoms to lose electrons and become positively charged. Ionisation by radiation is classified into two types: Direct Ionisation Both alpha and beta radiation are charged particles. When these charged particles move near electrons there is an electrostatic force between the particle and the electron. If the force is large the electron may be pushed far enough that it leaves its orbit around the atom and becomes free. The size of the electrostatic force between the electron and the radiation depends on: • The distance between the electron and the radiation (closer means greater force). • The size of the charge on the radiation (greater charge means greater force). Indirect Ionisation Gamma rays do not have a charge so they cannot exert electrostatic force on electrons they interact with. However, gamma rays are highly energised and some of this energy can be passed on to electrons. Energising the electrons allows them to move further away from the nucleus. If sufficient energy is provided to the electron, it may leave the atom altogether. Indirect ionisation has a lesser effect on matter than direct ionisation. Ionising Ability Weak Gamma rays 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Radiation in Medicine Radiation has various uses in medicine including diagnosis and treatment of diseases, and sterilisation of medical equipment. These uses involve high energy or ionising radiation that has the ability to damage healthy cells, as well as unhealthy ones. The use of radiation must be carefully monitored, and radioactive sources with short half-lives used in order to keep patients safe. Diagnosis One form of diagnosis uses radioactive tracers. This involves a small amount of radioactive material being injected into the bloodstream. When the tracer reaches a cancerous tumour (tumours usually have increased blood supply) the radioactivity becomes concentrated. Sensors are then used to detect the radiation emitted and locate the cancer. Treatment When a cancerous tumour has been identified the patient may undergo radiation treatment. Treatments involving radiation can either be done by placing a radioactive source (temporarily) inside the patient, allowing the radiation emitted to destroy the unhealthy cells, or by using an external source to direct radiation at the tumour. During Cobalt-60 therapy gamma rays are emitted from a radioactive source and directed towards the cancer. It is exceptionally difficult and therefore is mostly seen in high-energy environments such as stars. One type of smoke detector uses a radiation source (normally americium-241 - an alpha emitter) to ionise the air between two charged plates. The ionised air is attracted to the charged plates, and is detected as a flowing current. If smoke particles move between the charged plates, they interact with the ionised particles and disrupt the pathway between the two plates. This reduces the current flowing between the two plates and an alarm is set off. Alpha emission ionises air molecules that are then attracted to the charged plates of the detector. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Introduction to Responses The primary interest of ecologists is how organisms interact with, and respond to, their environment. Non-living objects do not “interact” with their environment - they are simply acted upon by forces in the environment. In order to survive, living organisms need to respond and adapt to changes. The various ways in which an animal responds to its environment is called the organism’s ‘behaviour’. Any behaviour that enables an organism to adjust to a particular situation or environmental factor is called an adaptive behaviour. Adaptive behaviours may contribute directly or indirectly to an individual’s survival or reproductive success and is thus subject to the forces of natural selection. Why Organisms Need to Respond to their Environment 1 To find a more favourable environment, where they can obtain resources (food, water, nutrients, oxygen, etc.), or alternatively, to be able to move away from unfavourable favourable environments. 2 To reduce competition between members of the same species (intraspecific competition) or competition between members of different species (interspecific competition). 3 To avoid being eaten. This is called predation if it relates to an animal, or herbivory if it relates to a plant. 4 To find another member of the same species, but opposite sex, for reproduction. 1. Just because a certain behaviour is innate does not necessarily mean it is simple. Innate behaviours can be sophisticated. For example, the ‘waggle-dance’ of the honey bee. Innate behaviours are: • Heritable - encoded in DNA and passed from one generation to the next. • Intrinsic - present in animals raised in isolation from others. • Stereotypic - performed in the same way each time by each individual. • Inflexible - not modified by development or experience. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Nuclear Fission Fission reactions occur when nuclides split into smaller, lighter nuclei. In large unstable elements fission reactions can occur without any external input. This is called spontaneous fission. For more stable elements the fission reaction is caused by making the nucleus unstable. This can be done by colliding a neutron with the nucleus, and is called a stimulated or induced fission reaction. Fission product A chain reaction may occur Nucleus begins to transform Neutron Energy released Fissionable nucleus Fission product The neutrons emitted may collide with other fissionable nuclei that are present. This may result in further fission reactions, leading to the emission of even more neutrons that may also cause even more fission reactions. When this process continues to grow, it is known as a chain reaction. Chain reactions can be very dangerous. If they become uncontrollable they can emit very large amounts of energy. When nuclear fission reactions are created for power generation, the conditions must be carefully managed to minimise the chance of a dangerous chain reaction occurring. 1. Common Methods of Navigation As the Sun moves across the sky from east to west, animals are able to use its position to navigate. However, over long journeys animals must compensate for the movement of the Sun by using some form of biological clock or other navigation mechanism. Animals travelling at night may orientate to a particular constellation or to a celestial pole (the point at which all stars appear to rotate around). Constellations move across the sky with time so animals require an internal clock for compensation. Celestial poles do not move so no clock is required. The angle of the Earth’s magnetic field varies with latitude so many animals use this for navigation. The strength of the field and local anomalies (iron rich rocks, etc.) may also help animals build up a mental map of their territory. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Orthokinesis and klinokinesis may occur in the same animal at the same time. Kineses Kinesis (plural kineses) is another innate behavioural response of an organism to an external nondirectional stimulus such as humidity or the temperature. The response of the organism can be seen by the speed of movement or frequency of turning, which are further classified as orthokinesis or klinokinesis: • Orthokinesis occurs when the rate of locomotion (speed) is proportional to the tolerance levels of an organism. In the optimum range, movement would be slow. Outside this range, the organism is in a zone of physiological stress and would move more rapidly to seek refuge from the stimulus. • Klinokinesis is specific to the rate of turning of an organism proportional to the external stimulus. The more physiological stress an organism is under, the more it will twist and turn in search of a more tolerable environment. When describing an organism’s kinesis, the appropriate prefix is placed in front of the suffix kinesis (similar to taxes). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Migration Migration is the regular, mass movement of organisms of the same species, usually on a seasonal basis and typically to a predetermined location. Migration may be a cyclical event (the migrants eventually return to their origin), or it may be one-way (the migrants die at the end of the migration). The reasons animals migrate varies between species. However, migrating animals will usually be doing so for one of the following reasons: • Food: To find food or essential nutrients. • Shelter: To find shelter, avoid harsh climate or to moult in a safe place. • Reproduction: To search for a mate, to give birth, lay eggs or raise young in favourable environmental conditions. Migration typically involves travel over very long distances and, therefore, migratory animals need to navigate using a combination of techniques. 1. Outline how migration is different from homing.   Migration typically involves a  mass seasonal movement of organisms, often between a feeding location and  a breeding location. Homing is focussed on individuals returning specifically  to that animal’s home base.     Migration is a large investment in energy. There has to be a survival advantage, otherwise it would be pointless for the organism to do it. 2. 22 3. State three reasons why animals may migrate. (a) To locate a mate, breed and raise young. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Knowing When To Migrate The most important consequence of migration is keeping individuals in favourable environments. Rather than adapting to life in a single location, migrants have evolved the means to move repeatedly between habitats in order to complete their life cycles. This migratory behaviour is innate and genetically controlled, but in most species it is initiated by the environment. External Migration Cues Internal Migration Cues Photoperiod Longer days in the summer or shorter days in the winter cue some animals to migrate. Less sunlight results in lower rates of photosynthesis and, therefore, less food. It also means lower temperatures. Circadian Rhythms The ‘internal calendar’ in an animal’s nervous system can help an animal know when to migrate. Experimental evidence suggests that some species have an innate sense of when to migrate even without exposure to external stimuli. Shifting Seasons In many areas the temperature and levels of precipitation change, resulting in distinct wet and dry seasons. Fat Reserves Low fat reserves may cue some species to move in search of food. In other species, migration only occurs after fat reserves have been built up. Food and/or Water Availability Lack of food and/or water, as a result of extremes in temperature, lack of precipitation, or because of population pressure in an area reaching its carrying capacity.
