uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Homing Homing refers to the ability of an animal to return to its home location after travelling away from it. Animals will travel away from a home location in order to find food or other resources, to meet and mate at a breeding site and/or to return to a well resourced location. It is thought that returning to breed at the same location provides an adaptive advantage as eggs and hatchlings will be well adapted to the specific conditions of the habitat where they are laid as their ancestors survived the selective pressures at that same location. In order to navigate animals will use topographical memory (i.e. visual clues such as landmarks, seas, rivers, mountains, etc.) or magnetic navigation (i.e. use the Earth’s magnetic field), celestial (star) navigation or navigation by smell. Generally, the time away from home is short. Due to the short distances, many animals rely on visual cues to return to their home site. However, the seasonal return from migration to a familiar site is also considered to be a type of homing. Navigation techniques other than visual cues may be used in these instances. For example, albatrosses (toroa) exhibit homing behaviours. Once the chicks have fledged, they leave the nest site and fly across vast areas of the southern ocean before returning to their breeding grounds in New Zealand. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: INVESTIGATE AN ECOLOGICAL COMMUNITY Ecological Succession The composition and type of species within a community can change over time. Some species may become more abundant, less abundant, new species may be introduced, or species may disappear from the community altogether. Changes in species’ composition over time is called ‘ecological succession’. Ecological succession is most easily observed when the environment suddenly and drastically changes (fire, human activity, landslides, etc.) or new land is formed (uplift, volcanism, etc.). Succession that occurs on bare land that had not previously supported life is called ‘primary succession’. ‘Secondary succession’ occurs on bare land that previously supported life. The environment suddenly and drastically changes. No, or very few, organisms remain. 1. The bare land is colonised by mosses, lichens and grasses. These plants stabilise the land and provide organic matter from which a soil develops. Small shrubs and trees are now able to grow in the ever thickening soil layer. These plants provide shelter and food for other organisms that may bring the seeds of new species to the area. The thick soil layer is able to support large trees. Some species may not be able to compete and may disappear from the community. A dynamically stable climax community is formed. Distinguish between ‘primary succession’ and ‘secondary succession’.

However, the productivity in the sea around Tonga is also low due to a lack of nutrients in the water. Therefore, during winter Southern Ocean months, adults do not eat (or eat very little), but will live off their layer of blubber (fat reserves). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Introduction to Circadian Rhythms Daily rhythms are found in most organisms. These rhythms are cyclic, repeating activity patterns that are often seen in biochemical, physiological and behavioural processes. If these rhythms continue under constant environmental conditions, then we know that the organisms are not simply responding to sunrise and sunset. Such rhythms are defined as circadian. Circadian rhythms have a free-running period of approximately 24 hours and are endogenous (built-in). They are adjusted (entrained) to the local environment by external cues called zeitgebers (from German, ‘time giver’), which include light and temperature. Circadian rhythms can be further divided into three groups based on when the organism is most active: diurnal (active during hours of daylight), nocturnal (active during hours of darkness), crepuscular (active at dawn and dusk). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Circatidal Rhythms Circatidal rhythms are cycles synchronised by the tides and commonly seen in organisms living in the littoral (intertidal) zone. As tides are linked to the phases of the Moon (with unusually high tides being seen at the full and new moons, and unusually low tides being seen in the first and third quarters of the Moon), circatidal cycles could be seen as being partly circalunal cycles. Many marine organisms inhabiting the tidal zones around New Zealand exhibit clear endogenous circatidal rhythmicity. Shell gaping (opening)and siphon extension (for feeding) in bivalve molluscs occur at the times of expected high tides. This may help to avoid dessication at low tide and increase the feeding time. Studies have shown that circatidal rhythms do not seem to be affected by inundation (wetting) and it has been proposed that mechanical agitation from the waves, water pressure, changes in temperature or water turbidity may act as zeitgebers. Marine animals may also travel vertically (either up or down) through the water column during periods of high tide. This behaviour may act to reduce predation by surface-feeding animals, reduce the risk of being stranded at low tide or assist with horizontal dispersal of juveniles. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Circannual Rhythms Seasonal migration is a common example of a circannual rhythm. In extreme climate zones where migration is not possible (i.e. the animals cannot travel out of that zone), the animals will often hibernate. Hibernation is when an animal spends many weeks in a dormant state in a protected area. Hibernating animals are able to lower their body temperature and slow their breathing and heart rate as they sleep. As a result, they use very little energy and do not need to eat to obtain more energy. If it has eaten enough food during the year and stored energy in the form of body fat, the animal may sleep until climatic conditions improve (generally in spring) without eating anything. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Biology -.searchText: INVESTIGATE AN ECOLOGICAL COMMUNITY Ecological Succession The composition and type of species within a community can change over time. Some species may become more abundant, less abundant, new species may be introduced, or species may disappear from the community altogether. Changes in species’ composition over time is called ‘ecological succession’. Ecological succession is most easily observed when the environment suddenly and drastically changes (fire, human activity, landslides, etc.) or new land is formed (uplift, volcanism, etc.). Succession that occurs on bare land that had not previously supported life is called ‘primary succession’. ‘Secondary succession’ occurs on bare land that previously supported life. The environment suddenly and drastically changes. No, or very few, organisms remain. The bare land is colonised by mosses, lichens and grasses. These plants stabilise the land and provide organic matter from which a soil develops. Small shrubs and trees are now able to grow in the ever thickening soil layer. These plants provide shelter and food for other organisms that may bring the seeds of new species to the area. The thick soil layer is able to support large trees. Some species may not be able to compete and may disappear from the community. A dynamically stable climax community is formed. 1. Distinguish between ‘primary succession’ and ‘secondary succession’.

uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Introduction to Plant Responses As autotrophs (organisms that manufacture their own food, usually by photosynthesis) plants need to absorb carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O) as well as trace minerals. Because they need to absorb water and minerals from the soil, terrestrial plants are anchored to their substrate by their roots. Therefore, plants have limited mobility and few ways in which they can respond to environmental stimuli. Secondly, with no bones for support, plant cells are surrounded by rigid cell walls made predominantly of cellulose. These cell walls prevent plants from undertaking the type of rapid movements seen in animals. However, the lack of a central nervous system and the general lack of receptor or effector cells seen in animals is no barrier to plants being able to respond to stimuli. There are two primary ways in which plants can respond to stimuli: • Growth movements (called ‘tropisms’) are the long-term, slow growth of the plant toward or away from a stimulus. They result in permanent changes in the size of some cells. • Turgor movements (called ‘nastic responses’) occur more rapidly than tropisms and are reversible. They rely on changes in turgor pressure (exerted by water on cell walls) within certain plant cells. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Effects of Temperature on Aspects of Growth The changing of seasons brings about variation in day length, temperature and rainfall levels. In order to exploit favourable conditions (such as those found in spring) and protect themselves from unfavourable conditions (such as those found in winter) plants need to time their activities. Dormancy Almost all plants experience a period of suspended growth (dormancy) when climatic conditions become unfavourable in winter; seeds and buds lie dormant over winter or during periods when rainfall is low. Dormant periods mean that energy requirements are lowered to a minimum and scare resources can be conserved. When favourable conditions return, various positive environmental cues trigger renewed activity. Vernalisation Many plants grown in temperate climates must experience a period of low winter temperature to initiate or accelerate bud burst and the flowering process - called vernalisation (from Latin ‘vernus’, meaning “of the spring”). Vernalisation ensures that reproductive development and seed production occurs in spring and summer, rather than in autumn. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Phytohormones Plant hormones (phytohormones) are used to control most aspects of a plant’s life cycle, from germination to the formation of flowers, stems, leaves, the shedding of leaves, to the development and ripening of fruit. Hormones are ‘signalling molecules’ that are produced in very small amounts in one part of the plant and transported to other parts, where they bind to a specific receptor and trigger responses in the target cells/tissues. Abscisic Acid (ABA) ABA promotes seed dormancy. ABA accumulates within seeds during fruit maturation, thus preventing seed germination within the fruit. ABA also inhibits germination during periods of unfavourably low temperatures (i.e. winter). Without ABA, buds and seeds would start to grow during warm periods in winter, only to be killed when temperatures fell again. It was thought that ABA played a role in abscission (leaf fall seen in deciduous plants). However, recent evidence suggests auxins and ethylene are responsible. Gibberellin (GA) GAs break dormancy and initiate germination. Absorption of water by the seed causes production of GA. The presence of GA initiates the breakdown of energy-rich reserves of starch within the seed, providing the embryo with the energy required for germination. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 2 Physics I.searchText: ATOMIC AND NUCLEAR PHYSICS Nuclear Fission Fission reactions occur when nuclides split into smaller, lighter nuclei. In large unstable elements fission reactions can occur without any external input. This is called spontaneous fission. For more stable elements the fission reaction is caused by making the nucleus unstable. This can be done by colliding a neutron with the nucleus, and is called a stimulated or induced fission reaction. Fission product A chain reaction may occur Nucleus begins to transform Neutron Energy released Fissionable nucleus Fission product The neutrons emitted may collide with other fissionable nuclei that are present. This may result in further fission reactions, leading to the emission of even more neutrons that may also cause even more fission reactions. When this process continues to grow, it is known as a chain reaction. Chain reactions can be very dangerous. If they become uncontrollable they can emit very large amounts of energy. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: Biological clocks allow organisms to anticipate environmental changes, before the change happens. For example, a nocturnal animal can return to its burrow before sunrise occurs. ANIMAL RESPONSES Biological Clocks Organisms have adapted to take advantage of the daily cycle of light and dark via internal endogenous (originating within an organism) biological clocks. Biological clocks are innate and genetically determined. However, an organism’s biological clock can be altered or entrained using various environmental cues called zeitgebers (from German, meaning ‘time keeper’). The alternation of the light/dark cycle of a 24-hour day is an important natural zeitgeber. In natural conditions the internal clock must be continually ‘re-set’ or entrained by the environment. Otherwise the biological rhythm and external rhythm would become unsynchronised as day length changes with the seasons. For most humans the biological clock runs at about 25.5 hours. To keep it synchronised with the 24-hour period of day length, it needs to be entrained using outside stimuli. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Photoperiodism The amount and intensity of sunlight, temperature, levels of precipitation and availability of pollinators vary markedly between the seasons. Staying synchronised with these seasonal rhythms is critical in life cycles of most plants. Although temperature seems like an obvious cue to use, it is not a reliable indicator of a change of season, as warm periods can occur in winter and cold periods can occur in summer. Plants use the relative lengths of night and day - called the photoperiod - as the environmental stimulus to detect time of year (i.e. the seasons). Any physiological responses to changes in photoperiod (e.g. flowering) is called photoperiodism. American scientists Allard and Garner developed the concept of critical day length for two groups of plants - short-day plants (SDP) and long-day plants (LDP). The terms SDP and LDP are not referring to the actual day length, but whether the plant will begin to flower when the days are longer or shorter than the plant’s individual critical day length. PLANT RESPONSES Auxin and Phototropism Auxin is a hormone that controls a number of plant functions, especially phototropisms. Phototropism combines the Greek words ‘photo’ meaning ‘light’ and ‘tropos’ meaning ‘to turn’. Therefore, a phototropism is a growth response in which the direction of the growth is determined by the direction of the source of light source. A positive phototropism occurs when a plant grows towards the light. Auxin is produced in cells of the apical meristem (the tips of shoots and roots) and transported to regions of growth. Auxin normally migrates evenly down both sides of a growing stem. However, when light from a certain direction reaches the apical meristem, most of the auxin produced migrates down the unlit side of the stem. Auxin causes cells to elongate by increasing the elasticity of the cell and by promoting the intake of water. Therefore, although all cells will elongate to a certain extent, the higher concentration of auxin on the shaded side of the plant causes greater elongation. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Auxin and Gravitropism Because plants photosynthesise, it is not surprising that mechanisms for growing towards light have evolved. However, when a seed is planted underground and there is no light to detect, the plumule (shoot) always grows upwards and the radicle (root) grows downwards. This is because the plant can detect gravity. Roots exhibit a positive gravitropism and shoots exhibit a negative gravitropism. Several hypotheses about how plants perceive gravity have been advanced, and although none of them are entirely satisfactory, the statolith hypothesis is generally accepted to explain the positive gravitropic response of primary roots. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Interspecific Symbiotic Relationships Symbiosis is a close (usually involving direct contact) relationship between two different species in which at least one species benefits (shown with a ‘+’ sign). For the other species, the relationship may be positive (+), negative (-), or neutral (0). There are three basic types of symbiosis: parasitism, mutualism and commensalism. Parasitism is a symbiotic relationship in which one species (the parasite) benefits (+), while the other species (the host) is harmed (-). Parasitism can also be described as an example of exploitation. Mutualism is a symbiotic relationship between two individuals of different species in which both species benefit (both +). Commensalism is a symbiotic relationship between two species in which one species benefits (+) while the other species is not affected (0). Commensalism usually occurs when one species uses the other for a purpose other than food (e.g. shelter or protection). In return, the clownfish defends the anemone from its predators and parasites. The anemone gains nutrients from the fish’s excrement and functions as a safe nest site. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Mutualism in Plants Living organisms need nitrogen to make the proteins needed for growth and repair of tissue. Lack of nitrogen is often the limiting factor in plant nutrition and growth. Nitrogen gas (N2) is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere (78%). However, N2 cannot be used by plants and animals. Plants need nitrogen in soluble form, usually ammonium (NH4+) and nitrate (NO3-) ions. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen containing compounds such as nitrates. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria are found in the soil. However, a group of plants called legumes (peas, beans, clover, etc.) have adapted to form a symbiotic relationship with nitrogen fixing bacteria. Legumes have root nodules (small swellings) that contain nitrogen fixing bacteria. The bacteria fix nitrogen by converting it to ammonia and nitrates which the plant can absorb. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Plant Defence Mechanisms In order to grow stems, leaves, roots and reproductive tissues plants must invest energy and nutrients. Herbivory reduces the plant’s ability to convert nutrients and energy into offspring as these tissues are lost. Therefore, natural selection favours plant traits that limit the negative impact of herbivores. Plant defence mechanisms can be broadly categorised into two groups: • Chemical defences: Plants may produce organic compounds with chemical properties that directly deter herbivores from feeding on them. Chemical deterrents can take the form of noxious odours, bitter oils, or cause excessive stimulation (e.g. caffeine) or lethargy (e.g. cannabis). Some compounds become toxic after ingestion. For example, foxgloves produce chemicals that can cause nausea, vomiting, hallucinations, convulsions and death. • Structural defences: Once herbivores find a plant, structural defences may discourage consumption. These structures include thorns (modified branches), spines (modified leaves) and hairs that discourage animals by causing physical damage or by inducing rashes and allergic reactions. Plants may also produce thick, waxy leaves that make browsing and digestion difficult. 1. Gorse is a major invasive plant species in New Zealand. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: Predators and their prey evolve together. INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Exploitation - Predation Predation is a relationship in which one species acts as a predator that captures and feeds on another species that serves as the prey. The predator is advantaged (+) and the prey is disadvantaged (-). Therefore, predation is an example of exploitation. Predator/prey relationships not only influence population numbers in the short term, but in the long term predation influences the genetic fitness and, therefore, evolution of both predators and prey. In order to survive until maturity and breed, predators must exhibit traits that allow them to successfully capture prey and feed. Similarly, prey species must be able to avoid being eaten to survive and reproduce. Traits associated with improved predation for predators and escaping predation for prey tend to be positively selected by natural selection. Common Adaptations of Large Predators Camouflage Camouflage consists of not only colour but also shape and pattern. Camouflage can help a predator blend into its background, hiding its location from prey species. Eye Position Forward-facing eyes allow for accurate detection of prey animals from locations and distances where they themselves are still undetected. Defences evolve through natural selection because they increase the fitness of the prey. The increase of fitness leads to a better reproductive success of the individual possessing the favourable trait, and thus results in the persistence of the trait in the population over time. Predator avoidance strategies can be divided into two major categories: morphological and behavioural defences. 1. Morphological Defences Behavioural Defences Structural adaptations such as horns, spikes, stingers, claws, fangs and toxins, etc. Some may relate to the prey’s appearance to avoid detection (e.g. camouflage and mimicry). Behavioural defences involve acts performed by the prey to avoid or reduce predation. These include actions such as pursuit deterrent signals, nocturnality and group living. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Mimicry Mimicry is a form of defence against predators. It occurs when a species evolves to appear similar to another, where either one or both are protected when a third organism cannot tell them apart. Mimicry happens in both animal and plant species. The term mimic applies to the species which looks like the model, in order to confuse another (the dupe), usually a predator. Batesian Mimicry Batesian mimicry is a specific type of mimicry where the model is dangerous (usually unpalatable) and the mimic has evolved similar features, but is harmless (palatable) - such as the hoverfly shown on the right. This type of mimicry is thought to have evolved because once a predator has learned from harsh experience not to eat the model organism, it will be likely to avoid anything that looks similar in the future (i.e. the mimic). Mullerian Mimicry Mullerian mimicry occurs when two or more poisonous species (that may or may not be closely related) share one or more common predators and have come to mimic each other’s warning signals. A predator that has learnt to avoid one species will avoid all other similar-looking species. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Gause’s Principle The term ‘fundamental niche’ describes the total tolerance range of a species. It is the total possible niche a species could occupy based on its range of tolerances for the various abiotic factors present. However, when the fundamental niche overlaps with another species’ fundamental niche, competition for resources leads to a narrower realised niche. This competitive exclusion is known as Gause’s principle. Gause’s principle states that two species, competing for the same resources, cannot coexist if their ecological niches are the same. When one species has even the slightest advantage over another, then the one with the advantage will outcompete, and potentially eliminate, the other species from the habitat. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Competition and Ecological Patterns of Distribution In order to reduce interspecific competition, species have evolved various adaptations to live in certain conditions and within their niche. This allows different species to coexist and results in patterns of distribution including stratification, zonation and succession. Stratification Stratification is a word used to describe the formation of layers. For example, within a mature forest community the plants occupy various horizontal layers based on their adaptations to the varying abiotic factors. In stratified forest in New Zealand there are usually four distinct layers. Canopy Layer (Kauri, rimu, totara, beech, kahikatea) Sub-Canopy Layer (Lancewood, ponga, nikau, kowhai, manuka) Shrub Layer (Kawakawa, rangiora, putaputaweta and Coprosma sp.) Ground Layer (Ground ferns, mosses, various grasses and seedlings) The main environmental factors causing the stratification of plant species is light intensity and relative humidity. Plants that require more light are found in the canopy layer, and plants that can survive with lower light intensities and higher humidities are found in the lower layers. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Intraspecific Relationships Intraspecific relationships are interactions among organisms of the same species. Competition between members of the same species occurs because they have the same niche and so compete for exactly the same resources. Therefore, intraspecific competition tends to be more intense than interspecific competition. Population increases Less intraspecific competition More intraspecific competition Population decreases Population Numbers Intraspecific competition tends to have a stabilising influence on population size. If the population gets too big, intraspecific competition increases, so the population falls. If the population gets too small, intraspecific competition decreases, so the population increases. Intraspecific competition is therefore classified as being ‘density-dependent’. Time Competition has an overall negative effect on populations as it leads to increased aggression between members of that population and physiological stress in individuals. Aggressive behaviour can lead to injury and possibly death, while increased stress can lead to poorer health, increased mortality, increased risk of disease and reduced natality (births). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Living in Cooperative Groups Many animals of the same species live together in cooperative groups. In some species, membership to the group is open, whereas in others membership is closed or closely guarded. In closed groups, a hierarchy of dominance is likely to form to minimise aggression within the group. Group members may display altruistic behaviour where they may endanger themselves for the benefit of unrelated individuals (e.g. defending the offspring of another group member against a predatory attack). Group members may also show altruism towards relatives - called kin selection (e.g. raising and defending the offspring of relatives). This form of behaviour promotes the survival of genes which the relatives may have in common, ensuring they have a greater chance of being passed on to the next generation. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Dominance Hierarchies A dominance hierarchy is the organisation of individuals in a group according to their status (or rank) within that group. Hierarchies arise when members of a social group repeatedly interact (often aggressively) which leads to the creation of a social order. The order is maintained by ritualised activities such as grooming, threats, displays and vocalisations. The order is subject to change if a dominant animal is successfully challenged by a subordinate one. Such challenges are often very aggressive as both individuals fight to either maintain their position or improve it. A B C D E F G Alpha Individual Omega Individual Dominance hierarchies are often linear (or near linear) where each individual dominates the individuals below them, but is subordinate to (dominated by) those above. The most dominant individual is often referred to as the alpha individual, followed by a beta individual and so on. The lowest is referred to as the omega individual. The position of an individual in a hierarchy is often determined by the sex of the individual, their age, size, familial relations (relationship to more dominant individuals), presence of special features (tusks, horns, combs, etc), and their health. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS The Costs and Benefits of Dominance Benefits High-ranking individuals have first access to prey that has been caught by the group, and they feed for longer without being interrupted. Therefore, dominant individuals spend less time foraging/ hunting, which reduces their risk of predation. This means they have an increased chance of survival because of increased nutrition and decreased predation. Higher-ranking males have higher reproductive success due to increased female acquisition and higher mating frequency. Dominant females benefit from increased rank because they produce more surviving offspring, reproduce at shorter intervals, produce offspring that grow faster and are weaned at earlier ages compared to lower-ranking females. The offspring of high-ranking individuals have better fitness and thus an increased rate of survival. This is most likely a function of high rank correlating with higher fitness and fighting ability, meaning these traits will be passed on to their offspring. Higher-ranking parents are also likely to provide better protection to their offspring and thus ensure higher survival rates. Costs High-ranking individuals generally have higher metabolic rates and higher levels of stress hormones. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Complex Hierarchies - Olive Baboons When in the trees, a baboon troop shows no particular organisation. However, when the troop moves out onto open ground, a clear order of progression appears. Boldest troop members lead the troop. Following them are pregnant and oestrus adult females and juveniles. The rear of the troop is a ‘mirror image’ of its front. Baboon hierarchy is a complex social organisation and non-linear, as there are subordinate groups and affiliations within the overall group, such as mating pairs and families. Associations are constantly changing, however, there is an alpha male in charge overall. Dominance relationships are most obvious among males, who aggressively compete over the highest positions in the hierarchy, engaging in frequent aggressive competition over females. They use vocalisations to signal competitive ability. Females also maintain dominance relationships within linear, stable dominance hierarchies. Female dominance is hereditary, with each female generally ranking just below her mother and below her older sisters. Complex hierarchies exist within troops, with both sexes maintaining separate dominance hierarchies. Females socially dominate males in all circumstances, including feeding priority. Dominance is enforced by lunging, chasing, grabbing and biting. Male involvement in infant rearing is limited, although the entire troop, regardless of age or sex, can be seen caring for the young. Home range and territory size varies depending on resource availability, season and population density. It is the dominant female’s responsibility to defend the troop’s territory. Agonistic encounters include staring, lunging approaches and occasional physical aggression, and conclude with troop members retreating toward the centre of the home range. Within the home range there may be a core area that contains a food supply, nesting site, water source or other valuable resources. This area will be actively and aggressively defended and is known as the animal’s territory. The boundary of the territory is usually defined with scent markings, displays, calls, or physical marks (rubbings and scratches, etc.). Where home ranges overlap, the animals will try to avoid each other, rather than seeking to expel each other. The size of the territory can change with the seasons (e.g. during mating), and can be density-dependent. A high population density correlates to smaller territories. Reproduction requires a large investment of energy. However, after the physical process of mating has occurred, the number of offspring produced and the amount of energy devoted to the care of each fertilised egg differs between species. Two main strategies exist: K-selection (also referred to as K-strategists or K-selected) and r-selection. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Mating Systems There are four basic types of mating systems, each differentiated by the sexual behaviour between mates. The Four Basic Mating Systems Monogamy Monogamy (monos - “single”, and gamos “marriage”) is a mating system in which an individual has only one partner during his or her lifetime or at any one time. The benefits of monogamy become apparent in habitats where resources and mates are scarce, or offspring require a high level of parental care. For example, in birds, each pair will have a greater number of offspring if they share in raising a brood as it takes a long time to raise flight-capable offspring. Sometimes males feed females on the nest, or share in incubation and feeding of the chick. Polygyny Polygyny (poly- “many”, and gyne - woman”) is a mating system in which a male mates with multiple females, but each female only mates with a single male. Generally in polygynous systems, females will provide the majority of parental care, leaving the male free to seek further mates. For males, the greatest advantage is increased reproductive success because he will father a large number of offspring. However, this may be detrimental as this may lead to reduced genetic diversity and increases the chance of inbreeding and the passing on of genetic disorders. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Territorial and Breeding Behaviour in Gannets Australasian gannets (Morus serrator) breed in dense colonies on coastal islands and on cliffs and beaches of some headlands of the New Zealand mainland, They feed mainly on small fish and are often seen dive-bombing into schools of these fish. Gannets usually breed with the same partner over consecutive seasons. However, members of a pair might not see each other for months at a time. After wintering out at sea, they return to their nesting colony in spring. Male birds are the first to arrive and quickly re-occupy or establish and defend a nest site. They prefer flat ground for nesting, rather than cliff ledges. Breeding colonies are situated at sites that are completely or largely surrounded by the sea, i.e. on islands or headlands such as those found at Cape Kidnappers, Muriwai and Farewell Spit. When the females arrive they are greeted with a series of synchronised performances, such as preening, pointing, calling, mutual bill fencing and bowing. After copulation, a single egg is laid which is incubated between the webbing on the gannet’s feet. Both sexes share the incubation duty. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Courtship Behaviour Courtship can be described as mate-selection rituals. Animal courtship may involve complicated dances or touching, vocalisations, visual displays of beauty or fighting prowess, or via chemical production (pheromones, etc.). Courtship rituals are species specific. Even closely related species have different courtship behaviours. This ensures that energy is not wasted on interspecific mating. Generally, the male of the species initiates the courtship and the female selects (or rejects) the male based on his ‘performance’. Performing a display allows the male to present his traits or abilities to a female, allowing her to select the best mate in terms of strength, size, plumage, etc. This method of sexual selection ensures that the best genes are passed on the next generation and can lead to sexual dimorphism. If the female is selecting for size or colour as an indication of male fitness, these genes will also be selected for. This explains why male and female birds of the same species often show dramatic differences in colouration. Such bright colouration may make the male more conspicuous to predators. However, if he is also able to avoid predation it may give the female another clue as to his fitness. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Parental Care Parental care can be defined as any investment of time and energy in the raising of offspring, often to the detriment of the parent as the investment of time and energy means the parent has a decreased ability to invest in their own fitness. The ultimate aim of all organisms is to pass on their genes to reproductively successful offspring. An organism can increase their chances of achieving this by either producing a large number of offspring, and/or protecting and nurturing their offspring, thereby increasing their chances of survival. Reproductive effort is a measure of the total amount of energy an organism spends on reproduction. This includes the effort required to produce gametes, court and mate, and care for their offspring. r-selected organisms place most of their reproductive effort into producing large numbers of offspring and very little into parental care. K-selected organisms generally produce few offspring but place a large amount of reproductive effort into caring for their offspring. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Biological Rhythms Our environment undergoes predictable, cyclical fluctuations as a result of changes in seasons, tides, and the time of day. When events and conditions repeat in a rhythmic pattern, the ability to predict, anticipate and prepare for them is a highly beneficial trait. After millions of years of evolution it is not surprising that most organisms on Earth show rhythmic changes in activity linked to these cyclical changes in their environment. For example, kiwi begin to stir in the late afternoon and evening, awaiting the emergence of invertebrates at dusk, and migrating birds lay down fat reserves in late summer in preparation for their annual migration. The timing of a cycle’s events can operate at many different time scales. Some cycles are linked to obvious external patterns, including: • Sun The day-night cycle caused by the Earth rotating on its axis. Daily rhythms are classified as ‘circadian’ (from the Latin circa, meaning “about” and diem meaning “day”). • Moon The orbit of the Moon around the Earth and its gravitational pull on the oceans causes the tidal rhythms with a period of 12.4 hours. The illumination of the moon by the Sun causes the ‘phases of the moon’. • Earth The tilt of Earth’s axis and its orbit around the Sun cause changes in temperature, precipitation, and photoperiod corresponding to the Earth’s seasons. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: MECHANISMS OF EVOLUTION Sexual Selection The appearance of males and females of many animal species are very similar. However, there are species where the sexes display dimorphism (a physical difference). In particular, the males of many bird and mammal species are larger, more brightly coloured, and/or adorned with conspicuous ornaments such as antlers and horns, etc. These traits appear disadvantageous, as they make the animals more visible to predators, hinder movement and are energetically expensive to grow and maintain. You would expect that natural selection would act against them. However, it is worth remembering that natural selection is not simply a battle to survive, but a battle to pass on genes (reproduce). If these exaggerated traits are advantageous in terms of increasing an individual’s ability to reproduce, then they would be selected for. This type of selection is called sexual selection. Sexual selection can be very strong because, in terms of fitness, failing to mate is equivalent to dying young. Hybrid inviability: The hybrid embryos are often not viable because the genes of the two species are incompatible and the hybrid dies before birth. If the hybrid survives, it may die before reaching reproductive age. Hybrid sterility: Hybrid offspring that do survive birth and reach sexual maturity are sterile so they cannot produce viable gametes. Hybrid breakdown: Hybrids may be viable, fertile and capable of producing offspring. However, these and any subsequent generations harbour detrimental genetic abnormalities, ultimately resulting in reduced fitness and fertility. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: THE ORIGIN OF SPECIES Polyploid Advantage In contrast with the relatively slow process of allopatric speciation, polyploidy can result in the rapid development of new species. Studies have shown that polyploidy events have played a significant role in the evolution of plants, especially ferns and angiosperms. Therefore, in some cases, polyploidy must provide an adaptive advantage. The presence of more chromosomes means larger nuclei, which results in larger cells in general. The large cell size can result in larger leaves, stems and wider branch angles. These traits may allow the plants to grow in a wider range of habitats and be more resistant to pests and disease. Flowers and fruit are also larger. However, if the polyploid plant contains an uneven number of chromosomes they will be sterile, so any resulting fruit will be seedless. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: pre = before, post = after, zygote = fertilized egg THE ORIGIN OF SPECIES Modes of Reproductive Isolation The biological definition of the term ‘species’ relies primarily on reproductive isolation rather than trait differences. A species must be able to produce fertile offspring with members of the same species but not with other species. Reproductive isolation, through mechanical, behavioural and physiological barriers, is an important component of speciation. Reproductive isolating mechanisms (RIMs) are barriers that prevent members of one species mating with different species - they prevent gene flow. RIMs can be prezygotic (barriers that prevent reproduction from taking place), or they can be postzygotic (barriers that occurs after zygote formation). Ecological Isolation Species occupy or exploit different habitats within an area. Behavioural Isolation Different courtship rituals, sounds, calls or colouration. Temporal Isolation Activity, mating or flowering occurs at different times of the day, month or year. Mechanical Isolation Reproductive structures are incompatible and prevent the delivery or acceptance of gametes. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: THE ORIGIN OF SPECIES poly = many ploidy = number of chromosomes Instant Speciation - Polyploidy Polyploidy is caused by errors during cell division that result in cells with more than two copies of each chromosomes (>2n). The resulting organism is genetically, and therefore reproductively, unique. However, this is not necessarily a problem in plant species that carry both male and female sex organs, and can therefore reproduce via self-fertilisation. Autopolyploidy Autopolyploidy involves the multiplication of the genome of a single species. It occurs when homologous chromosomes do not separate (non-disjunction) during meiosis. This results in non-reduced, diploid gametes (with two sets of chromosomes) instead of haploid gametes (with one set of chromosomes). If these diploid (2n) gametes fuse with a normal haploid (1n) gamete during fertilisation, the result will be a triploid (3n) organism with three sets of chromosomes. If the diploid gamete fuses with another diploid gamete (potentially via self-fertilisation) the resulting zygote will be tetraploid (4n). Some lineages are surprisingly complete, linking ancient long-extinct species with their modern descendants. This is particularly evident with marine organisms who, upon death, are more likely to be buried in sediments. Over thousands of years the sediment becomes compacted into sedimentary rocks. As further sediments are deposited, layers of sedimentary rocks (called ‘strata’) form. Because the layers at the bottom of a column of strata are the oldest, fossils within the strata can be dated, relative to those in other layers. Reproductive isolation isolates gene pools Biologists generally classify a species as “a group of organisms that interbreed under natural conditions and are reproductively isolated from other species”. In other words, one species cannot mate with other species and produce fertile offspring - if they could, it would suggest they are genetically similar and, therefore, are probably the same species. When populations become geographically isolated from each other, gene flow between them stops. In the absence of gene flow, the accumulation of favourable mutations and changes in allele frequencies will differ between the two populations. This means the populations will start to genetically diverge. Divergence will continue and the populations will gradually become more and more genetically different. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PATTERNS OF EVOLUTION Evidence for Evolution - Molecular Biology The chemistry, structures and processes of all cells are remarkably similar. For example, all animal cells contain mitochondria (for cellular respiration) and the cells of all three domains of life (Eukarya, Bacteria, Archaea) contain ribosomes which help to assemble proteins in a process that is basically the same across all living things. Secondly, the codons on DNA specify the same amino acids in all organisms, from bacteria to plants and animals. The conservation of structures and processes across all organisms provides evidence for a shared ancestry. The tools of modern molecular biology allow biologists to determine the nucleotide sequence of particular genes. If the nucleotide sequences of two species are analysed and if it is found that they contain a large number of genetic differences (due to mutation), it is unlikely that they shared a relatively recent common ancestor. Since mutations take time to accumulate, the number of differences can be considered a measure of the passage of time. So, if two species are found to contain genes with very similar nucleotide sequences, it can be concluded that they must have inherited the genes from a recent common ancestor. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PATTERNS OF EVOLUTION Evidence from mtDNA and Y Chromosome Analysis Great Grandparents Inheritance of Y chromosome Father Mother Y chromosome The Y chromosome is one of two sexdetermining chromosomes found in the nucleus of males. Due to its small size (compared to the X chromosome it is paired with) during meiosis it can only exchange alleles from its very tips (known as ‘pseudoautosomal regions’). This means over 95% of the Y chromosome is conserved and is passed on from father to son largely unchanged. Any changes that occur are the result of mutation. Mutations in modern populations can be traced back to their origin. Son 1. 2. Daughter Inheritance of mtDNA Grandparents Mitochondrial DNA Mitochondria contain their own DNA (mtDNA). Since mitochondria are outside the nucleus, mtDNA is not subject to meiosis. Therefore, the only way for genetic variation in mtDNA to occur is via mutation. When two groups diverge, each accumulates different mutations at a fairly consistent rate. Therefore, the number of mutations present in their mtDNA is proportional to the time since divergence. Secondly, at conception, sperm do not pass on any mtDNA, it comes only from the ovum. Therefore, both males and females get mtDNA from their mother. It is thought that the two main groups of moa (Dinornithidae and Emeidae) diverged as recently as 5.3 mya, around the time that rapid tectonic uplift was happening in the South Island. Evidence from fossils indicates that moa established in the North Island less than 2 mya (prior to this they only existed on the South Island). This correlates to glaciation events that resulted in lower sea levels, creating relatively short-lived land bridges linking the main land masses that allowed movement between the two islands. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PATTERNS OF EVOLUTION Darwin’s Orchids Using insects and birds for pollination is energetically expensive for plants. If the pollinator visits flowers of numerous species, the chances that any one plant will be successfully pollinated is lower than if the pollinator was a specialist, encouraged to only visit one particular plant species. One way of restricting access to nectar is to elongate the part of the flower that holds this sugary liquid, ensuring that only the longest-tongued of insects can reach it. In 1862, Darwin received an orchid from Madagascar, Angraecum sesquipedale. It had an exceptionally long nectary (up to 30 cm). In a letter he wrote to a friend at Kew Gardens he remarked “I have just received such a box full from Mr Bateman with the astounding Angraecum with a nectary a foot long. Good heavens what insect can suck it”, and in a second letter just a few days later suggested “in Madagascar there must be moths with a proboscis capable of extension to a length of between ten and eleven inches”. Later, in a book on orchid pollination, Darwin suggested that this extreme feature may have evolved alongside a moth with an exceptionally long tongue to pollinate it. At the time no such moth had been discovered. In 1907, more than 20 years after Darwin’s death, a moth from Madagascar with a suitable proboscis was identified. 1. Humans have lost the grasping ability in our feet because our feet serve as a platform for walking. • Sensitive fingers and toes with dermal ridges (fingerprints) that enhance the sense of touch. Primates rely heavily on their sense of touch to explore and investigate their environments. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Ecological Succession The composition and type of species within a community can change over time. Some species may become more abundant, less abundant, new species may be introduced, or species may disappear from the community altogether. Changes in community composition over time is called ‘ecological succession’. Ecological succession is most easily observed when the environment suddenly and drastically changes (fire, human activity, landslides, etc.) or new land is formed by uplift, volcanism, etc. Succession that occurs on bare land that had not previously supported life is called ‘primary succession’. ‘Secondary succession’ occurs on bare land that previously supported life. The environment suddenly and drastically changes. No, or very few, organisms remain. 1. The bare land is colonised by mosses, lichens and grasses. They stabilise the land and provide organic matter from which a soil develops. Small shrubs and trees are now able to grow in the ever-thickening soil layer. These plants provide shelter and food for other organisms that may bring the seeds of new species to the area. The thick soil layer is able to support large trees. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: MECHANISMS OF EVOLUTION This was extensively covered in the Level 2 Biology sciPAD Genetic Drift Genetic drift describes how the frequency of alleles can change over time due to chance events rather than selection pressure. Small populations are more susceptible to the forces of genetic drift. The random mating or the death of one or two individuals in a small population can have a dramatic effect on the allele frequency of the entire population. Large populations with more individuals are buffered against chance events. Genetic drift tends to decrease the variation within a population. However, it tends to increase variation between populations - potentially leading to speciation (the formation of new species). Genetic drift is more likely to occur after a ‘founder effect’ event (a population descending from a few founders), or a ‘bottleneck effect’ event (a sharp decline in population size). The Founder Effect The founder effect occurs when a small number of individuals emigrate from a population, or become geographically isolated from their original population. Geographical isolating mechanisms such as the formation of a mountain range, or land masses moving apart due to tectonic activity, are thought to have played a major role in the evolution of New Zealand’s native species. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: MECHANISMS OF EVOLUTION It is a misconception to assume that organisms evolve, natural selection acts on individuals, but only populations evolve. Natural Selection Biologists use the word ‘fitness’ to describe how good a particular genotype is at surviving to reproductive age, finding a mate and producing offspring. Fitness involves an individual’s ability to survive ‘selection pressures’ (environmental factors which may reduce reproductive success, e.g. predators, disease, ability to obtain food, resistance to drought, etc.). Natural selection occurs when populations of organisms are subjected to selection pressures. The fittest creatures are more likely to survive and pass their genes on to their offspring, producing a population that is better adapted to the selection pressures of that particular environment. The genes of less-fit individuals are unlikely to be passed on to the next generation. Variation Individuals within the population vary in many heritable traits. 1. Overproduction Populations produce more offspring than can survive until maturity. This leads to competition. Selection Selection pressures acting on variation results in some individuals surviving better than others. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: HUMANS AS BIPEDAL PRIMATES The Problems With Being Bipedal Humans are remarkably well adapted for bipedalism - we have an ‘S’ shaped spine, arched feet, agile hands and large brains. As remarkable as our adaptations for bipedalism are, they are, like all evolutionary transformations, a compromise with our history. We are by no means perfectly adapted for bipedal locomotion. Our spines are derived from our distant ancestors who walked on all four limbs. In these ancestors, like modern quadrupeds, the spine functioned more like a flexible suspension bridge, supporting the body’s organs. The human spine has been transformed into a vertical, weight-bearing column, putting it under unprecedented stresses. This means that humans are highly likely to suffer from back injuries and pain. Forces travelling down the spine transfer to the knees, ankles and feet, also resulting in increased susceptibility to injury. The most significant trade-offs in human evolution are evidenced at the time of birth. The evolutionary development of the human pelvis, towards bipedal locomotion, required a narrow pelvis and a decrease in the size of the bony birth-canal. The trend toward increased intelligence required a larger cranium, which would need a wider pelvic area and birth canal. It is a common misconception to think that a large brain equates to intelligence. There are animals with larger brains than humans. Scientists believe that intelligence may be better measured by relative brain size to body mass ratio and by looking at the structure and organisation of the various parts of the brain. When compared to chimpanzees, we have a larger brain size to body mass ratio and our brains are structurally more complex. Human brains have a high surface area because they are much more wrinkled and folded than chimpanzee brains, with greater numbers of connections between many of its parts. Humans also have a relatively larger frontal lobe, which gives us the ability to have abstract and logical thought, imagination, complex language and artistic ability. The cerebellum is associated with balancing and coordination. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: HUMANS AS BIPEDAL PRIMATES Modes of Primate Locomotion Most primates are adapted to an arboreal (tree-living) niche. All primates (except humans) move on all four limbs (quadrupedal) when on the ground. Our closest extant (living) relatives, the gorillas and chimpanzees, are knuckle-walkers. Knuckle-walking is a form of quadrupedal walking in which the forelimbs hold the fingers in a partially flexed posture that allows body weight to press down on the ground through the knuckles. Gorillas and humans are the only primates that do not sleep in the canopy. When chimpanzees are in the trees, they move by swinging through the branches (brachiation). Other more distant extant relatives such as orangutans and monkeys move primarily by brachiation. Very distant extant relatives (e.g. the prosimians) move via brachiation or by climbing vertical surfaces and leaping. Humans are the only bipedal (using only their legs for walking) members of the primate family. Almost all primates habitually engage in upright sitting so that they can manipulate objects with their hands, and thus all are capable of supporting their weight vertically through the spine. Brachiators generally have a short lumbar spine, long curved fingers, reduced thumbs, long forelimbs, flexible shoulder joints and freely rotating wrists. Many hypotheses regarding bipedalism have arisen and been debated. One of the reasons it remains unsolved is that these ideas are hard to test, and the selection pressures that led to bipedalism do not show up in the fossil record. It is generally accepted that our early ancestors took their first bipedal steps in order to free their arms and hands to carry valuable resources (food, offspring, tools, weapons etc.). Most of the more accepted hypotheses attempt to reconstruct paleoenvironmental changes (‘paleo’ means ancient, especially relating to the geological past) in which these early bipeds lived, in order to understand and explain how bipedalism emerged as a need of daily activity. Bipedalism and the Hand The degree of curvature of the fingers of primates is directly related to the frequency of arboreal behaviour. Arboreal primate species that spend most of their time grasping or suspended from branches have highly curved fingers and toes. The curvature provides them with a more powerful grip but reduces the capacity for more precise grips, such as those required for manipulating tools. Humans have almost no curvature of the fingers. This reflects a reduction in arboreal activity and the shift to bipedal locomotion. The freeing of the hands due to bipedalism facilitated the evolution of precise hand movements necessary for making and using tools, throwing and thrusting weapons enabling the hunting of large game, and carrying large items over long distances. Fingers Long, curved fingers assist with brachiating but inhibit the ability to form precision and some power grips. Humans have shorter, straighter fingers as they are no longer required for brachiation. The proportional lengths of the thumb and other fingers give us an opposable thumb with precise, firm contact between its tip and the ends of each of the other fingers. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Hominins The terms ‘hominid’ and ‘hominin’ are both used to describe members of the primate family. • Hominids are the group consisting of all extant and extinct great apes - modern humans, chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans and their immediate ancestors. • Hominins are a sub-group of the hominids consisting of modern humans, extinct human species and all immediate ancestors including so called ‘dead-ends’ - ancestral lines that became extinct after diverging from the direct line between humans and even earlier lines. The hominin line begins where the line that leads to modern humans diverged from the chimpanzees, around 7 million years ago. Palaeoanthropologists (scientists who study ancient humans) have identified over 20 species of extinct hominins in the fossil record. While the relationships to each other remains unresolved, features of the fossils allow them to be grouped into genera including Homo - the genus of modern humans. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Australopithecus afarensis Australopithecus afarensis is perhaps the most well-known member of the australopithecines. This is largely due to the very famous and relatively complete female specimen nicknamed ‘Lucy’ (3.2 mya) as well as numerous other fossil examples. More is known about its anatomy and behaviour than any other earlier hominin. A. afarensis is thought to be closely related to the genus Homo, whether as a direct ancestor or a close relative of an unknown ancestor. Radiometric dating indicates that they lived 3.7 - 2.9 mya. A. afarensis was slenderly built (females 30 kg and 1.05 m and males 55 kg and 1.51 m). Analysis of sediment, pollen and fossilised plant material suggests they lived in a wooded-savannah type habitat. A. afarensis had a chimpanzee-like face that projects forward below the nose, with a low forehead, a bony ridge over the eyes, a flat nose and no chin. They had protruding jaws with large back teeth. Cranial capacity varied from about 350 to 600 cm3 (the cranial capacity varies widely in this species due to a high degree of sexual dimorphism). Based on the wear patterns observed on the teeth of several A. afarensis specimens, it is thought that their diet was largely plant based (similar to modern gorillas). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS mya = million years ago Ardipithecus ramidus Fossil evidence shows that A. ramidus lived about 4.4 mya during the early Pliocene. The last common ancestor shared by humans and chimpanzees is thought to have lived six or more million years ago. Although Ardipithecus is not itself this last common ancestor, it likely shared many of this ancestor’s characteristics. Analysis of plant and animal fossils in the region where A. ramidus was found indicates that they lived in a lush, humid woodland, similar to the habitat of modern chimpanzees. They were short, standing only 1.20 m tall. Like most hominids, but unlike all previously recognised hominins, A. ramidus had a grasping big toe (hallux) adapted for gripping branches, suggesting some sort of arboreal lifestyle. However, other aspects of its skeleton show that A. ramidus was capable of bipedal locomotion when moving on the ground. The pelvis, for example, shows features only found in bipedal hominins and although their hands could easily grasp branches, they lacked the powerful upper torso needed for brachiation. Ardipithecus ramidus had a small brain, measuring between 300 and 350 cm3. This is slightly smaller than a modern female chimpanzee brain, but much smaller than the brain of australopithecines (~400 to 625 cm3) and roughly 20% the size of the modern Homo sapien brain. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Australopithecus africanus Australopithecus africanus was described in the 1920s and was the first specimen found that proved that human evolution started in Africa (at the time it was thought modern humans came out of Europe/Asia). It also showed that, despite having a small brain, these early hominins could walk upright. A. africanus fossils have been dated to the end of the Early Pliocene, between 3.3 – 2.1 mya. The cranial capacity of A. africanus (420 - 625 cm3) is slightly larger than that of A. afarensis and the overall morphology of the face is quite different. A. africanus had a less prognathic face with a smaller brow ridge and a slightly arched (rather than flat) forehead area, resulting in a flatter face than observed in A. afarensis. The attachment points for the neck muscles are low on the back of the skull, which sits on a vertical spine. A sagittal crest is absent and the zygomatic arches are smaller than previous species, traits that are shared with early members of the Homo lineage. However, it still retains some ape-like features, particularly a cone-shaped ribcage and relatively long arms. A. africanus (like A. afarensis) is small-bodied (males 1.35 m, females 1.10 m) when compared to later hominins. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Paranthropus boisei Paranthropus boisei lived in eastern Africa during the Pleistocene epoch, from about 2.3 until about 1.2 mya. They are often described as ‘robust’ australopithecines, hence they are sometimes referred to as Australopithecus boisei. As is the case with virtually all australopithecine species, there is a high degree of sexual dimorphism. Males weighed about 49 kg and stood about 1.37 m tall, while females weighed about 34 kg and were 1.24 m tall. The cranial capacity (475 to 550 cm³) is within a similar range to that of A. afarensis, A. africanus and modern-day chimpanzees. The skull is highly specialized for heavy chewing and shares several traits seen in modern-day gorillas. The premolar and molar teeth were very large (up to four times the size of modern human molars) and they had the thickest tooth enamel of any known hominin. The large muscles needed for chewing were attached to a pronounced sagittal crest. To accommodate their enormous teeth and the muscles associated with chewing, P. boisei had pronounced and flared zygomatic arches resulting in a very wide, dish-shaped face. Large teeth and strong jaw muscles suggest that P. boisei consumed large quantities of plant matter, including nuts, seeds and fruit. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS H. ergaster is sometimes categorized as a subspecies of Homo erectus. Homo ergaster Homo ergaster lived in eastern and southern Africa between 1.9 million and 1.5 mya. It was the first hominin with a human-like body shape, stature and limb proportions. Their gait and running stride would have been very similar to modern humans and well-adapted for long-distance travel. About 1.8 mya, the climate over most of Africa became drier and more seasonal with extensive savannahs. Shortly after H. ergaster appeared, members of the Homo genus began to leave Africa for the first time and migrate to other continents. Their faces project forwards but to a smaller degree than in earlier hominins. The lower jaw slopes backward and does not form a pointed chin like that of modern humans. The arrangement of the teeth within the jaws was intermediate between that of apes and modern humans. When compared to the australopithecines the incisors are more vertical and the post-canine teeth are much smaller, and more human-like. This implies that they ate foods that required less chewing. The overall shape of the skull had developed a more human-like shape including a higher, more domed cranium. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Homo erectus Homo erectus (meaning “upright man”) lived throughout most of the Pleistocene epoch. The earliest fossil specimens date from 1.9 mya to potentially as recent as 30 000 years ago. It is generally thought that H. erectus originated in Africa and spread from there, migrating throughout Eurasia, India, Sri Lanka, China and Indonesia. However, controversy surrounds this species and how it relates to H. ergaster and H. heidelbergensis. An increasing number of anthropologists have redefined the species so that it now contains only east Asian fossils. The older African fossils are classified as Homo ergaster. Homo erectus is now generally believed to be a side branch on our family tree whereas Homo ergaster is now viewed as one of H. sapiens’ direct ancestors. However, the evolution of H. erectus represents a major adaptive shift in human evolution in terms of brain size, body size and behaviour. Fossil evidence suggests that they had human-like limb proportions and body mass (1.6 m - 1.8 m and 40 - 68 kg). They were fully bipedal and possessed a relative large brain (750 - 1 300 cm3) that shared a similar structure to modern humans. Their skull is characterized by a long, low cranial vault and a distinct sagittal keel running down the mid-line. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS H.habilis’ rather primitive attributes have led some experts to propose reclassifying them as australopithecines (Australopithecus habilis). Homo habilis Homo habilis, the “handy man”, was so called because of evidence of tool use found with some remains. H. habilis, the first member of the genus Homo to appear in the fossil record, lived between 2.4 and 1.6 mya. They were similar in size to the australopithecines (males 1.35 m and females 1.10 m) but had a much larger brain capacity of 600 - 700 cm³. This is on average 50% larger than australopithecines, but considerably smaller than modern humans (~1 350 cm³). A few specimens show an endocranial bulge in the Broca’s area (essential for speech). This suggests H. habilis was capable of rudimentary speech, although a developed language is unlikely. Their short stature and disproportionately long arms are similar to those of the australopithecines from which they are thought to have descended. The finger bones are slightly curved and intermediate in shape between the curved finger bones of quadrupedal apes and the straight finger bones of modern humans. The proportions of the finger bones suggest the human-like ability to form a precision grip. Compared to the australopithecines, H. habilis had a more vertical forehead and a weaker brow ridge. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Homo heidelbergensis Homo heidelbergensis lived between 600 000 and 200 000 years ago and evidence suggests they lived over a wide area from southern Africa to Northern Europe. They were tall (1.45 -1.85 m) with strongly built bodies (50 - 68 kg). The skull accommodated a large brain (1 280 cm3), well within the range of modern humans. Their faces were relatively flat and still lacked the pointed chins typical of modern humans. Substantial brow ridges are evident in front of a low, sloping forehead. The jawbone is strongly built for the attachment of powerful chewing muscles. Their teeth were smaller than those of earlier species, but were still slightly larger than those of modern humans. The teeth were arranged so that they formed a parabolic dental arcade. The pelvis is adapted for efficient bipedal walking, although it is wider and more robust than that of modern humans. Wide knees and strong muscle attachment points suggest there was considerable loading on the legs. Stone tools associated with H. heidelbergensis fossils were more complex than those made by H. ergaster and include a variety of tools such as stone hand axes and wooden spears set with stone spearheads. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Homo neanderthalensis Homo neanderthalensis lived 350 000 to 28 000 years ago. They occupied a range of environments across Europe and the Middle East and lived through a period of changing climatic conditions. Ice ages in Europe were interspersed with warmer periods but by 110 000 years ago average temperatures were on the decline and full glacial conditions had appeared by 40 000 years ago. A vast fossil record consisting of over 270 individuals from foetuses to adults provides extensive information about this species. Current thinking is that populations of H. heidelbergensis in Africa evolved into H. sapiens while those in Europe and Asia evolved into the H. neanderthalensis. Neanderthals are recognisably human but were generally shorter (males 1.68 m, females 1.56 m) and had more robust skeletons and muscular bodies than modern humans. These features are considered to be an adaptation to cold, dry environments. They had a distinctive skull shape that was long and low, with a rounded brain case that housed a relatively large brain (1 200 - 1 750 cm3) which is slightly larger than modern humans. The face is not as vertical as modern humans. Two separate arched brow ridges are seen over large, rounded eye sockets. The nasal cavity is large and a wide, fleshy nose was probably prominent. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Trends in Cranial Capacity Over the past 4 million years of hominin evolution average brain size has more than tripled, increasing from approximately 400 cm3 in the early australopithecines to approximately 1 350 cm3 in modern humans. During this time, the rate of change has been variable, with periods of gradual increase punctuated by periods of dramatic change. Intelligence is not just a function of cranial capacity; there are animals with larger brains than ours. Scientists think that relative brain size (cranial capacity as a percentage of total body mass) is a more important indicator. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Homo sapiens After more than 7 million years of hominin evolution, Homo sapiens is the only surviving member of the hominin family. Although we appeared relatively recently (200 000 years ago) our complex culture and technology has enabled us to spread throughout the world and occupy a range of different niches. This resulted in a species that is highly variable in physical appearance, despite the fact that we are almost genetically identical to each other. Fossils of early H. sapiens (referred to as ‘archaic Homo sapiens’), have all been found in Africa and these fossils provide the best evidence for the evolutionary transition from H. heidelbergensis. Archaic H. sapiens had bodies with short, slender trunks and long limbs, possibly an adaptation for cooling the body in tropical regions. As populations spread to cooler regions stocky builds gradually evolved as an adaptation that helped the body retain heat. Modern humans now have an average height of approximately 1.60 m in females and 1.75 m in males. Archaic H. sapiens also had a slightly larger brain size (1 500 cm3) whereas modern H. sapiens have an average brain size of about 1 350 cm3 (2.2% of our body weight). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Cultural Evolution Biological evolution (sometimes called ‘genetic evolution’) occurs through genetic variation, reproduction and natural selection. Transmission of traits can only occur from one generation to the next via directly related individuals (i.e. from parents to offspring). Biological evolution is only one aspect of evolution. Cultural evolution is the change in culture that occurs due to the transmission of learned behaviour, ideas and knowledge. Cultural evolution occurs through the development of language and customs. Unlike biological evolution, transmission of cultural evolution can occur between unrelated individuals within a generation, or across many generations. Data transmitted by behaviour, written or spoken language. • • Transmission only occurs from one generation to the next. Traits can be transmitted between both related and unrelated individuals. • Transmission can occur within and/or between generations. • Occurs slowly. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Reduced genetic variability in non-African populations is a result of the ‘Founder Effect’. Genetic Diversity and Dispersal Models Most genetic evidence supports the Out of Africa hypothesis, or a close variant of it. Humans as a species have very little genetic diversity when compared to other mammalian species. For example, there is much more genetic diversity between two randomly selected, unrelated chimpanzees than there is between two randomly selected, unrelated humans. Within the human population, nearly all genetic studies indicate greater diversity within African populations. This is consistent with an African origin of modern humans since diversity is a function of both time (we’ve been present in Africa longer than anywhere else) and population size. Non-African populations also tend to be more similar to one another than they are to African populations, suggesting that a subset of the African population left the continent and colonised the rest of the world. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Scientists can also use the Y-chromosome (inherited from father to son) to trace all modern males back to a man (called “Y-chromosomal Adam”) who lived 120 000 to 200 000 ya Mitochondrial DNA Mitochondria have their own DNA called mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). mtDNA is totally separate from nuclear DNA in chromosomes. Mitochondria are found in eggs and not in the head of a sperm cell, so mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from our mothers. mtDNA does not recombine during meiosis. The process of recombination in nuclear DNA mixes sections of DNA from the mother and the father, creating a garbled genetic history. This means that the variation in mtDNA between individuals can only be caused by mutation. The rate at which these mutations occur is fairly consistent and so acts as a ‘biological clock’ as they can be traced back in time. In the late 1980s New Zealand geneticist Allan Wilson tested the mtDNA of 137 people from different parts of the world. He found that the mtDNA of these people could all be traced back to one common mitochondrial sequence that existed between 100 000 and 200 000 years ago nicknamed “Mitochondrial Eve” (note that this name has nothing to do with biblical Eve). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Not Quite so Human Recent scientific advances in DNA techniques have enabled scientists to sequence entire genomes of some fossil hominins. Notably, they have been able to sequence the entire genome of a few Neanderthals. Analysis of this genome shocked the scientific community. The results showed that between 1% and 4% of the modern Eurasian human genome is derived from Neanderthal DNA. Since the genome of modern Africans shows no sign of Neanderthal DNA, these results suggest that a small population of H. sapiens outside of Africa, encountered and interbred with a population of Neanderthals. Furthermore, in 2010, scientists announced the discovery of a finger bone from a hominin who lived about 41 000 years ago. The fossils was found in the remote Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of Siberia, a cave which is known to have been inhabited by both H. neanderthalensis and H. sapiens. Analysis of the mtDNA of the finger bone showed it was genetically distinct from both the Neanderthals and modern humans - it was a different species, scientists called “the Denisovans”. In 2015, a number of Denisovan teeth were found. Genetic analysis showed that Denisovans shared a common ancestor with Neanderthals.
