uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Using Fire Controlling fire is generally considered to be one of humankinds’ greatest achievements. Wherever humans have gone, they have taken fire, or the memory of how to make it, with them. It is easy to imagine a primitive human society without the ability to make fire, existing purely on raw food. However, no such society has ever known to have existed. Due to their chemical complexity, raw starch and proteins take a long time to be digested and require a lot of chewing. As a result, only a small percentage of the calories found in raw starch and protein are absorbed by the small intestine. Cooking causes a number of chemical changes that make starches and protein easier to digest. For example, for the same amount of calories ingested, the body gets roughly 30% more energy from a cooked potato when compared to a raw one, and as much as 80% more energy from the protein in a cooked egg. Secondly, cooking kills most pathogens, parasites and detoxifies some plant poisons making food safer to eat. Hominins using fire were able to exploit a larger range of food sources and reduce disease transmission. Thirdly, by making food more digestible, the need for large digestive tracts is reduced, as is the need for large jaws and teeth along with the muscles associated with them. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Leaving Africa Homo sapiens were not the first species to emerge from Africa. According to current evidence, the first dispersal out of Africa happened around 1.8 mya. It is widely accepted that Homo ergaster left Africa and spread across Asia. After hominins dispersed from Africa towards the north, they interacted with, and learnt to exploit, different types of habitats and fauna. These populations became geographically and reproductively isolated, ultimately evolving into variants (e.g. H. erectus and H. neanderthalensis). Approximately 100 000 years ago there was a second emigration out of Africa - Homo sapiens. This new species of hominin gradually replaced the other Homo populations that occupied Asia and Europe. This dispersal of hominins from Africa to Eurasia occurred at approximately the same time as climatic changes linked to glacial/interglacial cycles. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Shelter Shelters provide protection from adverse climatic conditions and predation from wild animals. They also provide a place to store tools and food. Shelters also promote social interactions as individuals gather into groups. The ability to obtain or construct shelter would have provided a clear selection advantage. Early hominins would have used the natural environment for various forms of shelter. From simply climbing trees to avoid predators, to using natural rock formations and caves. The first evidence of sites that were used repeatedly have been found in association with fossils of Homo habilis. Individuals may have returned to a particular area due to its resources, but there is little or no evidence that they settled in any one particular area. This is likely because of their constant need to forage for food. Homo heidelbergensis were also mobile foragers. As well as using caves and rock formations for shelter, there is some evidence to show that they were possibly one of the first species to construct simple freestanding shelters. Homo neanderthalensis are associated with cave dwelling as many of their fossils have been found in caves - hence the ‘cave man’ title associated with Neanderthals. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Clothing The development of clothing was most probably driven primarily by the need to gain increased insulation due to loss of body fur and for protection from direct sunlight on the skin. Additionally, studies of modern hunter gatherer tribes also suggest that clothing was used to communicate social identity, status and tribal affiliation. The earliest forms of clothing were undoubtedly animal furs and skins worn over the body. Unfortunately, furs and skins do not fossilise, so palaeoanthropologists largely rely on indirect methods to date the origin of the evolution of clothing use. A 2011 study on human lice suggested that 170 000 years ago head lice and the species of lice that live in our clothes diverged from a common ancestor. It is hypothesised that once hominins started to wear clothing, lice speciation occurred. Their research suggests that the invention of clothing may have coincided with the northward migration of modern Homo sapiens away from the warm climate of Africa. Homo neanderthalensis lived in cold climates outside of Africa and clothing would have been vital for survival. Their clothing was likely to have been based upon animal furs and skins. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Humans are apex predators despite our lack of claws, razor-sharp teeth, or the other adaptations found in carnivores because from the very inception of the genus Homo we have used technology. Hunting Early hominins were not at the top of the food chain. Early stone tools (Oldowan) enabled us to scavenge from the leftovers of apex predators. However, the rate of our cultural evolution quickly outpaced the biological evolution of these predators. The arrival of Homo sapiens in Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas was soon followed by the extinction of many megafaunal (large animal) species. Although climate change may have contributed in part to reducing the population size of some species, the correlation between the arrival of humans and the rapid extinction of most megafaunal species suggests Homo sapiens were most likely the direct cause of their extinction. Human desire for animal protein as the mainstay of their diet, sophisticated hunting techniques, combined with the inexperience of native animals, quickly led to the extermination of almost all megafaunal species. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS From Hunters to Farmers When the ice sheets retreated after the last glacial maximum (~20 kya) the world underwent many changes. It became warmer, the sea level rose, rainfall increased, and forested and grassland areas spread. During this period the first evidence of agriculture appears. In a favourable region, with food resources that were available year-round, previously nomadic hunter-gatherer populations could remain in one location. This simple form of settlement, where less time was required to ensure adequate food supplies, gave them time to observe and experiment with plants and animals. Humans learnt how to control the environment (clearing fertile land, etc.) and how to control the growth and breeding of selected plants and animals - ultimately leading to domestication. By ensuring they had a regular supply of high quality food these settlements could support a larger population. Secondly, as not everyone was needed to ensure an adequate food supply, they could develop skills in other areas such as carpentry, medicine, music, art, etc. and thereby, accelerate the rate of cultural evolution. Ants, bees, cicadas, cows and dogs all communicate with each other. All of the primates have been shown to have language - gestures or sounds that mean specific things. When researchers played a recorded ‘leopard’ alarm call, the monkeys would scamper up the nearest tree. An ‘eagle’ call caused the monkeys to look up at the sky and head for thick, low-lying bushes. The evolution and origin of speech (i.e. the ability to connect a limited number of sounds to produce an infinite number of sentences) is a widely debated and controversial topic. However, once it appeared, it is relatively easy to see how it advanced. Feeding them with excess crops would have turned the animal into an energy (food) reserve. However, eating an animal ends its usefulness. Animals would have become far more valuable if they could be exploited without having to be killed (e.g. for wool, eggs, pulling ploughs or transport). Whether by accident or on purpose, breeding animals for these traits genetically modified them, ultimately resulting in today’s domesticated breeds. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Introduction to Responses The primary interest of ecologists is how organisms interact with, and respond to, their environment. Non-living objects do not “interact” with their environment - they are simply acted upon by forces in the environment. In order to survive, living organisms need to respond and adapt to changes. The various ways in which an animal responds to its environment is called the organism’s ‘behaviour’. Any behaviour that enables an organism to adjust to a particular situation or environmental factor is called an adaptive behaviour. Adaptive behaviours may contribute directly or indirectly to an individual’s survival or reproductive success and is thus subject to the forces of natural selection. Why Organisms Need to Respond to their Environment 1 To find a more favourable environment, where they can obtain resources (food, water, nutrients, oxygen, etc.), or alternatively, to be able to move away from unfavourable favourable environments. 2 To reduce competition between members of the same species (intraspecific competition) or competition between members of different species (interspecific competition). 3 To avoid being eaten. This is called predation if it relates to an animal, or herbivory if it relates to a plant. 4 To find another member of the same species, but opposite sex, for reproduction. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Innate and Learned Behaviours Innate Behaviour Learned Behaviour Innate behaviour is genetically programmed. Individuals not only inherit a range of physical traits (such as body size, hair colour, eye colour, etc.) but also a suite of behaviours. Just because a certain behaviour is innate does not necessarily mean it is simple. Innate behaviours can be sophisticated. For example, the ‘waggle-dance’ of the honey bee. Innate behaviours are: • Heritable - encoded in DNA and passed from one generation to the next. • Intrinsic - present in animals raised in isolation from others. • Stereotypic - performed in the same way each time by each individual. • Inflexible - not modified by development or experience. Learned behaviour occurs as a result of experience. Newborn individuals have no prior experience so their first behaviours will be entirely innate. New skills are acquired through trial and error, observation of other individuals, or memory of past events. 1. Learned behaviours are: • Non-inheritable - acquired only through observation or experience. • Extrinsic - absent in animals raised in isolation from others. • Adaptable - capable of modification to suit changing conditions. • Progressive - subject to improvement or refinement through practice. This innate behaviour (although it can be refined by experience and learning) makes use of a range of sensory receptors, allowing animals to respond to environmental stimuli and navigate across unfamiliar territories. Common Methods of Navigation As the Sun moves across the sky from east to west, animals are able to use its position to navigate. However, over long journeys animals must compensate for the movement of the Sun by using some form of biological clock or other navigation mechanism. Animals travelling at night may orientate to a particular constellation or to a celestial pole (the point at which all stars appear to rotate around). Constellations move across the sky with time so animals require an internal clock for compensation. Celestial poles do not move so no clock is required. The angle of the Earth’s magnetic field varies with latitude so many animals use this for navigation. The strength of the field and local anomalies (iron rich rocks, etc.) may also help animals build up a mental map of their territory. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Orthokinesis and klinokinesis may occur in the same animal at the same time. Kineses Kinesis (plural kineses) is another innate behavioural response of an organism to an external nondirectional stimulus such as humidity or the temperature. The response of the organism can be seen by the speed of movement or frequency of turning, which are further classified as orthokinesis or klinokinesis: • Orthokinesis occurs when the rate of locomotion (speed) is proportional to the tolerance levels of an organism. In the optimum range, movement would be slow. Outside this range, the organism is in a zone of physiological stress and would move more rapidly to seek refuge from the stimulus. • Klinokinesis is specific to the rate of turning of an organism proportional to the external stimulus. The more physiological stress an organism is under, the more it will twist and turn in search of a more tolerable environment. When describing an organism’s kinesis, the appropriate prefix is placed in front of the suffix kinesis (similar to taxes). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Migration Migration is the regular, mass movement of organisms of the same species, usually on a seasonal basis and typically to a predetermined location. Migration may be a cyclical event (the migrants eventually return to their origin), or it may be one-way (the migrants die at the end of the migration). The reasons animals migrate varies between species. However, migrating animals will usually be doing so for one of the following reasons: • Food: To find food or essential nutrients. • Shelter: To find shelter, avoid harsh climate or to moult in a safe place. • Reproduction: To search for a mate, to give birth, lay eggs or raise young in favourable environmental conditions. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Knowing When To Migrate The most important consequence of migration is keeping individuals in favourable environments. Rather than adapting to life in a single location, migrants have evolved the means to move repeatedly between habitats in order to complete their life cycles. This migratory behaviour is innate and genetically controlled, but in most species it is initiated by the environment. External Migration Cues Internal Migration Cues Photoperiod Longer days in the summer or shorter days in the winter cue some animals to migrate. Less sunlight results in lower rates of photosynthesis and, therefore, less food. It also means lower temperatures. Circadian Rhythms The ‘internal calendar’ in an animal’s nervous system can help an animal know when to migrate. Experimental evidence suggests that some species have an innate sense of when to migrate even without exposure to external stimuli. Shifting Seasons In many areas the temperature and levels of precipitation change, resulting in distinct wet and dry seasons. Fat Reserves Low fat reserves may cue some species to move in search of food. In other species, migration only occurs after fat reserves have been built up. Food and/or Water Availability Lack of food and/or water, as a result of extremes in temperature, lack of precipitation, or because of population pressure in an area reaching its carrying capacity.

uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Homing Homing refers to the ability of an animal to return to its home location after travelling away from it. Animals will travel away from a home location in order to find food or other resources, to meet and mate at a breeding site and/or to return to a well resourced location. It is thought that returning to breed at the same location provides an adaptive advantage as eggs and hatchlings will be well adapted to the specific conditions of the habitat where they are laid as their ancestors survived the selective pressures at that same location. In order to navigate animals will use topographical memory (i.e. visual clues such as landmarks, seas, rivers, mountains, etc.) or magnetic navigation (i.e. use the Earth’s magnetic field), celestial (star) navigation or navigation by smell. Generally, the time away from home is short. Due to the short distances, many animals rely on visual cues to return to their home site. However, the seasonal return from migration to a familiar site is also considered to be a type of homing. Navigation techniques other than visual cues may be used in these instances. For example, albatrosses (toroa) exhibit homing behaviours. Once the chicks have fledged, they leave the nest site and fly across vast areas of the southern ocean before returning to their breeding grounds in New Zealand. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Introduction to Circadian Rhythms Daily rhythms are found in most organisms. These rhythms are cyclic, repeating activity patterns that are often seen in biochemical, physiological and behavioural processes. If these rhythms continue under constant environmental conditions, then we know that the organisms are not simply responding to sunrise and sunset. Such rhythms are defined as circadian. Circadian rhythms have a free-running period of approximately 24 hours and are endogenous (built-in). They are adjusted (entrained) to the local environment by external cues called zeitgebers (from German, ‘time giver’), which include light and temperature. Circadian rhythms can be further divided into three groups based on when the organism is most active: diurnal (active during hours of daylight), nocturnal (active during hours of darkness), crepuscular (active at dawn and dusk). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Circatidal Rhythms Circatidal rhythms are cycles synchronised by the tides and commonly seen in organisms living in the littoral (intertidal) zone. As tides are linked to the phases of the Moon (with unusually high tides being seen at the full and new moons, and unusually low tides being seen in the first and third quarters of the Moon), circatidal cycles could be seen as being partly circalunal cycles. Many marine organisms inhabiting the tidal zones around New Zealand exhibit clear endogenous circatidal rhythmicity. Shell gaping (opening)and siphon extension (for feeding) in bivalve molluscs occur at the times of expected high tides. This may help to avoid dessication at low tide and increase the feeding time. Studies have shown that circatidal rhythms do not seem to be affected by inundation (wetting) and it has been proposed that mechanical agitation from the waves, water pressure, changes in temperature or water turbidity may act as zeitgebers. Marine animals may also travel vertically (either up or down) through the water column during periods of high tide. This behaviour may act to reduce predation by surface-feeding animals, reduce the risk of being stranded at low tide or assist with horizontal dispersal of juveniles. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Circannual Rhythms Seasonal migration is a common example of a circannual rhythm. In extreme climate zones where migration is not possible (i.e. the animals cannot travel out of that zone), the animals will often hibernate. Hibernation is when an animal spends many weeks in a dormant state in a protected area. Hibernating animals are able to lower their body temperature and slow their breathing and heart rate as they sleep. As a result, they use very little energy and do not need to eat to obtain more energy. If it has eaten enough food during the year and stored energy in the form of body fat, the animal may sleep until climatic conditions improve (generally in spring) without eating anything. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Actograms When organisms that exhibit biorhythms are kept in constant conditions (e.g. darkness), the period (the length of the activity cycle) of their rhythm will continue. The period of the rhythm in constant conditions is called the free-running period. Initially, the start of activity during the free-running period will correspond with the start of activity under normal conditions. Gradually, however, the rhythm will drift out of synchrony with the rhythm of the environment. By measuring when activity started and stopped in relation to time and environmental cues, scientists can produce graphs of activity patterns called actograms. Actograms are read from top to bottom. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: HUMANS AS BIPEDAL PRIMATES Selecting for Bipedalism Thermoregulation Bipeds are subject to less solar radiation whilst standing upright, absorbing up to 60% less heat, meaning they could have ranged further without having to increase water intake. Secondly, the upper bodies of bipeds, being placed higher from the ground, would be subject to stronger air currents, helping them to keep cool. However, early hominins lived in at least partially wooded habitats, meaning shade was never too far away. Solar radiation Energy Efficiency Bipedal locomotion is no faster than quadrupedal locomotion. However, recent studies have shown that walking on two legs may have evolved because it uses less energy than knuckle-walking. Humans walking on two legs only used one-quarter of the energy that chimpanzees who knuckle-walked on four legs do. This means less energy would be expended during foraging and allowed for longer and more rewarding foraging journeys. Solar radiation Wind speed decreases closer to the ground Predator Avoidance Bipedalism may have allowed some of our early ancestors to stand up to look over tall grass on the savannah of Africa and thereby identify and avoid predators. The problem with this hypothesis is that standing upright might have actually made it easier for predators to spot these hominins! 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Mechanisms of Plant Growth Primary growth refers to the elongation of the plant. Primary growth occurs in cells found in the tips of roots and shoots. These cells are called apical meristematic cells. Meristematic cells are undifferentiated (i.e. they have not yet acquired any specific structure or function) but are capable of dividing rapidly. Growth at the meristem occurs in three stages: 1 Zone of cell division - cells multiply by the process of mitosis. 2 Zone of cell elongation - cells grow in both length and width as water fills the vacuole and the elastic cell stretches. 3 Zone of differentiation - elongated cells become specialised. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Introduction to Plant Responses As autotrophs (organisms that manufacture their own food, usually by photosynthesis) plants need to absorb carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O) as well as trace minerals. Because they need to absorb water and minerals from the soil, terrestrial plants are anchored to their substrate by their roots. Therefore, plants have limited mobility and few ways in which they can respond to environmental stimuli. Secondly, with no bones for support, plant cells are surrounded by rigid cell walls made predominantly of cellulose. These cell walls prevent plants from undertaking the type of rapid movements seen in animals. However, the lack of a central nervous system and the general lack of receptor or effector cells seen in animals is no barrier to plants being able to respond to stimuli. There are two primary ways in which plants can respond to stimuli: • Growth movements (called ‘tropisms’) are the long-term, slow growth of the plant toward or away from a stimulus. They result in permanent changes in the size of some cells. • Turgor movements (called ‘nastic responses’) occur more rapidly than tropisms and are reversible. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Effects of Temperature on Aspects of Growth The changing of seasons brings about variation in day length, temperature and rainfall levels. In order to exploit favourable conditions (such as those found in spring) and protect themselves from unfavourable conditions (such as those found in winter) plants need to time their activities. Dormancy Almost all plants experience a period of suspended growth (dormancy) when climatic conditions become unfavourable in winter; seeds and buds lie dormant over winter or during periods when rainfall is low. Dormant periods mean that energy requirements are lowered to a minimum and scare resources can be conserved. When favourable conditions return, various positive environmental cues trigger renewed activity. Vernalisation Many plants grown in temperate climates must experience a period of low winter temperature to initiate or accelerate bud burst and the flowering process - called vernalisation (from Latin ‘vernus’, meaning “of the spring”). Vernalisation ensures that reproductive development and seed production occurs in spring and summer, rather than in autumn. Abscission Abscission is defined as the natural detachment of parts of a plant, typically leaves and ripe fruit. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Phytohormones Plant hormones (phytohormones) are used to control most aspects of a plant’s life cycle, from germination to the formation of flowers, stems, leaves, the shedding of leaves, to the development and ripening of fruit. Hormones are ‘signalling molecules’ that are produced in very small amounts in one part of the plant and transported to other parts, where they bind to a specific receptor and trigger responses in the target cells/tissues. Abscisic Acid (ABA) ABA promotes seed dormancy. ABA accumulates within seeds during fruit maturation, thus preventing seed germination within the fruit. ABA also inhibits germination during periods of unfavourably low temperatures (i.e. winter). Without ABA, buds and seeds would start to grow during warm periods in winter, only to be killed when temperatures fell again. It was thought that ABA played a role in abscission (leaf fall seen in deciduous plants). However, recent evidence suggests auxins and ethylene are responsible. Gibberellin (GA) GAs break dormancy and initiate germination. Absorption of water by the seed causes production of GA. The presence of GA initiates the breakdown of energy-rich reserves of starch within the seed, providing the embryo with the energy required for germination. It describes the processes by which a large number of new species evolve over a relatively short period of time from a common ancestor. It often occurs following major tectonic processes, natural disasters, extinction events or during colonisation of an unexploited habitat. As new, unoccupied niches become available, populations adapt to fill the new habitats and potentially form new species. PLANT RESPONSES Auxin and Phototropism Auxin is a hormone that controls a number of plant functions, especially phototropisms. Phototropism combines the Greek words ‘photo’ meaning ‘light’ and ‘tropos’ meaning ‘to turn’. Therefore, a phototropism is a growth response in which the direction of the growth is determined by the direction of the source of light source. A positive phototropism occurs when a plant grows towards the light. Auxin is produced in cells of the apical meristem (the tips of shoots and roots) and transported to regions of growth. Auxin normally migrates evenly down both sides of a growing stem. However, when light from a certain direction reaches the apical meristem, most of the auxin produced migrates down the unlit side of the stem. Auxin causes cells to elongate by increasing the elasticity of the cell and by promoting the intake of water. Therefore, although all cells will elongate to a certain extent, the higher concentration of auxin on the shaded side of the plant causes greater elongation. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Thigmotropism Thigmotropism is a movement in which a plant moves or grows in response to touch or contact stimuli. The prefix thigmo- comes from the Greek for ‘touch’. It is a directional response commonly seen in climbing plants with coil-like structures called tendrils. Tendrils coil around solid objects supporting the plant while it is growing toward sunlight. Thigmotropic responses can be relatively rapid (complete rotation in less than an hour in some species). The mechanism that gives rise to thigmotropism is not well understood but it is thought that auxin plays a role in this response. Cells on the side of the plant touching the object produce auxin and transport it to cells on the opposite side of the tendril. High concentrations of auxin in these ‘untouched’ cells stimulates elongation and faster growth rates, resulting in the tendril bending around the object. 1. Describe thigmotropism. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: Biological clocks allow organisms to anticipate environmental changes, before the change happens. For example, a nocturnal animal can return to its burrow before sunrise occurs. ANIMAL RESPONSES Biological Clocks Organisms have adapted to take advantage of the daily cycle of light and dark via internal endogenous (originating within an organism) biological clocks. Biological clocks are innate and genetically determined. However, an organism’s biological clock can be altered or entrained using various environmental cues called zeitgebers (from German, meaning ‘time keeper’). The alternation of the light/dark cycle of a 24-hour day is an important natural zeitgeber. In natural conditions the internal clock must be continually ‘re-set’ or entrained by the environment. Otherwise the biological rhythm and external rhythm would become unsynchronised as day length changes with the seasons. For most humans the biological clock runs at about 25.5 hours. To keep it synchronised with the 24-hour period of day length, it needs to be entrained using outside stimuli. Allopatric speciation is the  formation of a new species as a result of physical separation (geographical Sympatric = same place Sympatric speciation is the formation of a new species without geographical isolation. The new species becomes reproductively isolated even though they are surrounded by their parent population. It is rare in animal species, although biologists have observed cases in which a subpopulation may be in the process of sympatric speciation via niche specialisation. For example, in order to reduce intraspecific competition, members of a bird population may begin to forage for insects higher in the canopy than other members of their species who spend more time on the ground and, as such, different adaptations for exploiting these different food resources are selected for, which may ultimately lead to reproductive isolation. Sympatric speciation is more common in plants and usually occurs by polyploidy. Polyploidy is caused by errors during cell division that result in the cell having more than two copies of each chromosome (>2n). The resulting organism is genetically unique. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Thigmonastic Responses osmotic loss of water rapid loss of turgor in pulvini = flaccid cells Mimosa pudica (also called the “touch-me-not”) is a small herb with compound leaves that fold inward and droop when touched or shaken. The intensity of the response depends on the magnitude of the stimulus. Hitting the leaf hard will cause the leaf to close rapidly whereas a gentle touch at the tip of a leaf will result in a slower response and the propagation of the stimulus along the leaf can be observed. This response is easily reversed so that the plant can resume photosynthesising. Closing of the leaves may lead to lowered carbohydrate production in the short term. Pulvini Compound leaf of Mimosa pudica composed of many smaller leaflets in an open and undisturbed position. Upon stimulation (touching the leaf), the leaflets fold upwards. The movement of the leaflets results from changes in osmotic potential in specialised ‘motor cells’ called pulvini (sing. pulvinus). The pulvini are specialised regions containing large, water-filled cells. Water in these cells creates turgor pressure. This pressure pushes on both the cell membrane and cell wall, resulting in a firm and rigid cell (turgid). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Auxin and Gravitropism Because plants photosynthesise, it is not surprising that mechanisms for growing towards light have evolved. However, when a seed is planted underground and there is no light to detect, the plumule (shoot) always grows upwards and the radicle (root) grows downwards. This is because the plant can detect gravity. Roots exhibit a positive gravitropism and shoots exhibit a negative gravitropism. Several hypotheses about how plants perceive gravity have been advanced, and although none of them are entirely satisfactory, the statolith hypothesis is generally accepted to explain the positive gravitropic response of primary roots. The Statolith Hypothesis Statoliths Specialised organelles containing dense starch grains called statoliths are found in certain cells in the root cap. Statoliths within a horizontally orientated root will quickly settle on the lower sides of the root cap cells. Over the course of a few hours, the root gravitropically orientates downwards. 1. 2. It is thought that the settling of statoliths causes auxin to accumulate along the underside of the root. A high concentration of auxin in the roots inhibits the elongation of cells and slows their growth. Cells on the opposite side (the top) still receive auxin, but at a lower concentration. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Measuring Photoperiod Experimental evidence has shown that when different wavelengths of light are used to interrupt the period of darkness, flowering in both short-day plants and long-day plants can be affected. When red light is used, flowering can be inhibited in short-day plants, and induced in long-day plants. However, if red light is immediately followed by a brief flash of far-red light, the effect of the red light is cancelled out. SDP LDP Far Red Red light Red light Light Regime This suggests that the mechanism by which plants measure photoperiod involves the light-sensitive protein phytochrome. Phytochrome exists in two forms - phytochrome red (Pr) and phytochrome far-red (Pfr). During a 24-hour period, there is a shift in ratio of these two pigments. When Pr absorbs light, it is converted to Pfr. Sunlight contains more red light than far-red light, so Pfr predominates during the day. Absorbs red light. Inactive form. When Pfr absorbs far-red light it is rapidly converted back into Pr. During darkness, there is a slow conversion of Pfr back to Pr. Absorbs far-red light. Active form. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PLANT RESPONSES Photoperiodism The amount and intensity of sunlight, temperature, levels of precipitation and availability of pollinators vary markedly between the seasons. Staying synchronised with these seasonal rhythms is critical in life cycles of most plants. Although temperature seems like an obvious cue to use, it is not a reliable indicator of a change of season, as warm periods can occur in winter and cold periods can occur in summer. Plants use the relative lengths of night and day - called the photoperiod - as the environmental stimulus to detect time of year (i.e. the seasons). Any physiological responses to changes in photoperiod (e.g. flowering) is called photoperiodism. American scientists Allard and Garner developed the concept of critical day length for two groups of plants - short-day plants (SDP) and long-day plants (LDP). The terms SDP and LDP are not referring to the actual day length, but whether the plant will begin to flower when the days are longer or shorter than the plant’s individual critical day length. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Interspecific Symbiotic Relationships Symbiosis is a close (usually involving direct contact) relationship between two different species in which at least one species benefits (shown with a ‘+’ sign). For the other species, the relationship may be positive (+), negative (-), or neutral (0). There are three basic types of symbiosis: parasitism, mutualism and commensalism. Parasitism is a symbiotic relationship in which one species (the parasite) benefits (+), while the other species (the host) is harmed (-). Parasitism can also be described as an example of exploitation. Mutualism is a symbiotic relationship between two individuals of different species in which both species benefit (both +). Commensalism is a symbiotic relationship between two species in which one species benefits (+) while the other species is not affected (0). Commensalism usually occurs when one species uses the other for a purpose other than food (e.g. shelter or protection). In return, the clownfish defends the anemone from its predators and parasites. The anemone gains nutrients from the fish’s excrement and functions as a safe nest site. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Mutualism in Plants Living organisms need nitrogen to make the proteins needed for growth and repair of tissue. Lack of nitrogen is often the limiting factor in plant nutrition and growth. Nitrogen gas (N2) is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere (78%). However, N2 cannot be used by plants and animals. Plants need nitrogen in soluble form, usually ammonium (NH4+) and nitrate (NO3-) ions. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen containing compounds such as nitrates. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria are found in the soil. However, a group of plants called legumes (peas, beans, clover, etc.) have adapted to form a symbiotic relationship with nitrogen fixing bacteria. Legumes have root nodules (small swellings) that contain nitrogen fixing bacteria. The bacteria fix nitrogen by converting it to ammonia and nitrates which the plant can absorb. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: Predators and their prey evolve together. INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Exploitation - Predation Predation is a relationship in which one species acts as a predator that captures and feeds on another species that serves as the prey. The predator is advantaged (+) and the prey is disadvantaged (-). Therefore, predation is an example of exploitation. Predator/prey relationships not only influence population numbers in the short term, but in the long term predation influences the genetic fitness and, therefore, evolution of both predators and prey. In order to survive until maturity and breed, predators must exhibit traits that allow them to successfully capture prey and feed. Similarly, prey species must be able to avoid being eaten to survive and reproduce. Traits associated with improved predation for predators and escaping predation for prey tend to be positively selected by natural selection. Common Adaptations of Large Predators Camouflage Camouflage consists of not only colour but also shape and pattern. Camouflage can help a predator blend into its background, hiding its location from prey species. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Plant Defence Mechanisms In order to grow stems, leaves, roots and reproductive tissues plants must invest energy and nutrients. Herbivory reduces the plant’s ability to convert nutrients and energy into offspring as these tissues are lost. Therefore, natural selection favours plant traits that limit the negative impact of herbivores. Plant defence mechanisms can be broadly categorised into two groups: • Chemical defences: Plants may produce organic compounds with chemical properties that directly deter herbivores from feeding on them. Chemical deterrents can take the form of noxious odours, bitter oils, or cause excessive stimulation (e.g. caffeine) or lethargy (e.g. cannabis). Some compounds become toxic after ingestion. For example, foxgloves produce chemicals that can cause nausea, vomiting, hallucinations, convulsions and death. • Structural defences: Once herbivores find a plant, structural defences may discourage consumption. These structures include thorns (modified branches), spines (modified leaves) and hairs that discourage animals by causing physical damage or by inducing rashes and allergic reactions. Plants may also produce thick, waxy leaves that make browsing and digestion difficult. 1. Gorse is a major invasive plant species in New Zealand. Defences evolve through natural selection because they increase the fitness of the prey. The increase of fitness leads to a better reproductive success of the individual possessing the favourable trait, and thus results in the persistence of the trait in the population over time. Predator avoidance strategies can be divided into two major categories: morphological and behavioural defences. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Mimicry Mimicry is a form of defence against predators. It occurs when a species evolves to appear similar to another, where either one or both are protected when a third organism cannot tell them apart. Mimicry happens in both animal and plant species. The term mimic applies to the species which looks like the model, in order to confuse another (the dupe), usually a predator. Batesian Mimicry Batesian mimicry is a specific type of mimicry where the model is dangerous (usually unpalatable) and the mimic has evolved similar features, but is harmless (palatable) - such as the hoverfly shown on the right. This type of mimicry is thought to have evolved because once a predator has learned from harsh experience not to eat the model organism, it will be likely to avoid anything that looks similar in the future (i.e. the mimic). Mullerian Mimicry Mullerian mimicry occurs when two or more poisonous species (that may or may not be closely related) share one or more common predators and have come to mimic each other’s warning signals. A predator that has learnt to avoid one species will avoid all other similar-looking species. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Gause’s Principle The term ‘fundamental niche’ describes the total tolerance range of a species. It is the total possible niche a species could occupy based on its range of tolerances for the various abiotic factors present. However, when the fundamental niche overlaps with another species’ fundamental niche, competition for resources leads to a narrower realised niche. This competitive exclusion is known as Gause’s principle. Gause’s principle states that two species, competing for the same resources, cannot coexist if their ecological niches are the same. When one species has even the slightest advantage over another, then the one with the advantage will outcompete, and potentially eliminate, the other species from the habitat. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Living in Cooperative Groups Many animals of the same species live together in cooperative groups. In some species, membership to the group is open, whereas in others membership is closed or closely guarded. In closed groups, a hierarchy of dominance is likely to form to minimise aggression within the group. Group members may display altruistic behaviour where they may endanger themselves for the benefit of unrelated individuals (e.g. defending the offspring of another group member against a predatory attack). Group members may also show altruism towards relatives - called kin selection (e.g. raising and defending the offspring of relatives). This form of behaviour promotes the survival of genes which the relatives may have in common, ensuring they have a greater chance of being passed on to the next generation. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Intraspecific Relationships Intraspecific relationships are interactions among organisms of the same species. Competition between members of the same species occurs because they have the same niche and so compete for exactly the same resources. Therefore, intraspecific competition tends to be more intense than interspecific competition. Population increases Less intraspecific competition More intraspecific competition Population decreases Population Numbers Intraspecific competition tends to have a stabilising influence on population size. If the population gets too big, intraspecific competition increases, so the population falls. If the population gets too small, intraspecific competition decreases, so the population increases. Intraspecific competition is therefore classified as being ‘density-dependent’. Time Competition has an overall negative effect on populations as it leads to increased aggression between members of that population and physiological stress in individuals. Aggressive behaviour can lead to injury and possibly death, while increased stress can lead to poorer health, increased mortality, increased risk of disease and reduced natality (births). Stratification Stratification is a word used to describe the formation of layers. For example, within a mature forest community the plants occupy various horizontal layers based on their adaptations to the varying abiotic factors. In stratified forest in New Zealand there are usually four distinct layers. Canopy Layer (Kauri, rimu, totara, beech, kahikatea) Sub-Canopy Layer (Lancewood, ponga, nikau, kowhai, manuka) Shrub Layer (Kawakawa, rangiora, putaputaweta and Coprosma sp.) Ground Layer (Ground ferns, mosses, various grasses and seedlings) The main environmental factors causing the stratification of plant species is light intensity and relative humidity. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: ANIMAL RESPONSES Biological Rhythms Our environment undergoes predictable, cyclical fluctuations as a result of changes in seasons, tides, and the time of day. When events and conditions repeat in a rhythmic pattern, the ability to predict, anticipate and prepare for them is a highly beneficial trait. After millions of years of evolution it is not surprising that most organisms on Earth show rhythmic changes in activity linked to these cyclical changes in their environment. For example, kiwi begin to stir in the late afternoon and evening, awaiting the emergence of invertebrates at dusk, and migrating birds lay down fat reserves in late summer in preparation for their annual migration. The timing of a cycle’s events can operate at many different time scales. Some cycles are linked to obvious external patterns, including: • Sun The day-night cycle caused by the Earth rotating on its axis. Daily rhythms are classified as ‘circadian’ (from the Latin circa, meaning “about” and diem meaning “day”). • Moon The orbit of the Moon around the Earth and its gravitational pull on the oceans causes the tidal rhythms with a period of 12.4 hours. The illumination of the moon by the Sun causes the ‘phases of the moon’. • Earth The tilt of Earth’s axis and its orbit around the Sun cause changes in temperature, precipitation, and photoperiod corresponding to the Earth’s seasons. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Dominance Hierarchies A dominance hierarchy is the organisation of individuals in a group according to their status (or rank) within that group. Hierarchies arise when members of a social group repeatedly interact (often aggressively) which leads to the creation of a social order. The order is maintained by ritualised activities such as grooming, threats, displays and vocalisations. The order is subject to change if a dominant animal is successfully challenged by a subordinate one. Such challenges are often very aggressive as both individuals fight to either maintain their position or improve it. A B C D E F G Alpha Individual Omega Individual Dominance hierarchies are often linear (or near linear) where each individual dominates the individuals below them, but is subordinate to (dominated by) those above. The most dominant individual is often referred to as the alpha individual, followed by a beta individual and so on. The lowest is referred to as the omega individual. The position of an individual in a hierarchy is often determined by the sex of the individual, their age, size, familial relations (relationship to more dominant individuals), presence of special features (tusks, horns, combs, etc), and their health. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS The Costs and Benefits of Dominance Benefits High-ranking individuals have first access to prey that has been caught by the group, and they feed for longer without being interrupted. Therefore, dominant individuals spend less time foraging/ hunting, which reduces their risk of predation. This means they have an increased chance of survival because of increased nutrition and decreased predation. Higher-ranking males have higher reproductive success due to increased female acquisition and higher mating frequency. Dominant females benefit from increased rank because they produce more surviving offspring, reproduce at shorter intervals, produce offspring that grow faster and are weaned at earlier ages compared to lower-ranking females. The offspring of high-ranking individuals have better fitness and thus an increased rate of survival. This is most likely a function of high rank correlating with higher fitness and fighting ability, meaning these traits will be passed on to their offspring. Higher-ranking parents are also likely to provide better protection to their offspring and thus ensure higher survival rates. Costs High-ranking individuals generally have higher metabolic rates and higher levels of stress hormones. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Maintaining Hierarchies Maintaining a hierarchy has adaptive advantages for the entire group. Less time and energy spent fighting means more time and energy can be used foraging/hunting, breeding, raising young and defending territories. Various agonistic displays are used to assert dominance. For example, dominant animals will often make themselves appear bigger by raising hackles/fur, spreading wings, standing upright or assuming an aggressive stance. They may open their mouth and show their teeth, or use various vocalisations (threats, calls, etc.). Submissive animals will often make themselves smaller by bowing, crouching, lying down and may roll on their backs to expose vulnerable areas. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.originalPath: uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology External/Worksheets/122 - Complex Hierarchies - Olive Baboons - Worksheet.pdf
uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Complex Hierarchies - Olive Baboons When in the trees, a baboon troop shows no particular organisation. However, when the troop moves out onto open ground, a clear order of progression appears. Boldest troop members lead the troop. Following them are pregnant and oestrus adult females and juveniles. The rear of the troop is a ‘mirror image’ of its front. Baboon hierarchy is a complex social organisation and non-linear, as there are subordinate groups and affiliations within the overall group, such as mating pairs and families. Associations are constantly changing, however, there is an alpha male in charge overall. Dominance relationships are most obvious among males, who aggressively compete over the highest positions in the hierarchy, engaging in frequent aggressive competition over females. They use vocalisations to signal competitive ability. Females also maintain dominance relationships within linear, stable dominance hierarchies. Female dominance is hereditary, with each female generally ranking just below her mother and below her older sisters. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Home Ranges and Territories An animal’s home range is the area in which it lives and travels. Within the home range there may be a core area that contains a food supply, nesting site, water source or other valuable resources. This area will be actively and aggressively defended and is known as the animal’s territory. The boundary of the territory is usually defined with scent markings, displays, calls, or physical marks (rubbings and scratches, etc.). Where home ranges overlap, the animals will try to avoid each other, rather than seeking to expel each other. The size of the territory can change with the seasons (e.g. during mating), and can be density-dependent. A high population density correlates to smaller territories. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Territorial Behaviour Ring-tailed lemurs (Lemur catta) are social primates endemic to the island of Madagascar who live in cooperative groups (troops) usually containing 13 to 15 individuals. Complex hierarchies exist within troops, with both sexes maintaining separate dominance hierarchies. Females socially dominate males in all circumstances, including feeding priority. Dominance is enforced by lunging, chasing, grabbing and biting. Male involvement in infant rearing is limited, although the entire troop, regardless of age or sex, can be seen caring for the young. Home range and territory size varies depending on resource availability, season and population density. It is the dominant female’s responsibility to defend the troop’s territory. Agonistic encounters include staring, lunging approaches and occasional physical aggression, and conclude with troop members retreating toward the centre of the home range. Marking Territorial Boundaries Males and females scent mark both vertical and horizontal surfaces at the boundary of their home ranges using their anogenital scent glands. They perform a handstand to mark vertical surfaces, grasping the highest point with their feet while applying scent. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Mating Systems There are four basic types of mating systems, each differentiated by the sexual behaviour between mates. The Four Basic Mating Systems Monogamy Monogamy (monos - “single”, and gamos “marriage”) is a mating system in which an individual has only one partner during his or her lifetime or at any one time. The benefits of monogamy become apparent in habitats where resources and mates are scarce, or offspring require a high level of parental care. For example, in birds, each pair will have a greater number of offspring if they share in raising a brood as it takes a long time to raise flight-capable offspring. Sometimes males feed females on the nest, or share in incubation and feeding of the chick. Polygyny Polygyny (poly- “many”, and gyne - woman”) is a mating system in which a male mates with multiple females, but each female only mates with a single male. Generally in polygynous systems, females will provide the majority of parental care, leaving the male free to seek further mates. For males, the greatest advantage is increased reproductive success because he will father a large number of offspring. However, this may be detrimental as this may lead to reduced genetic diversity and increases the chance of inbreeding and the passing on of genetic disorders. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Courtship Behaviour Courtship can be described as mate-selection rituals. Animal courtship may involve complicated dances or touching, vocalisations, visual displays of beauty or fighting prowess, or via chemical production (pheromones, etc.). Courtship rituals are species specific. Even closely related species have different courtship behaviours. This ensures that energy is not wasted on interspecific mating. Generally, the male of the species initiates the courtship and the female selects (or rejects) the male based on his ‘performance’. Performing a display allows the male to present his traits or abilities to a female, allowing her to select the best mate in terms of strength, size, plumage, etc. This method of sexual selection ensures that the best genes are passed on the next generation and can lead to sexual dimorphism. If the female is selecting for size or colour as an indication of male fitness, these genes will also be selected for. This explains why male and female birds of the same species often show dramatic differences in colouration. Such bright colouration may make the male more conspicuous to predators. However, if he is also able to avoid predation it may give the female another clue as to his fitness. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Reproductive Strategies Obviously, successful reproduction is essential to the survival of any species. Reproduction requires a large investment of energy. However, after the physical process of mating has occurred, the number of offspring produced and the amount of energy devoted to the care of each fertilised egg differs between species. Two main strategies exist: K-selection (also referred to as K-strategists or K-selected) and r-selection. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Parental Care Parental care can be defined as any investment of time and energy in the raising of offspring, often to the detriment of the parent as the investment of time and energy means the parent has a decreased ability to invest in their own fitness. The ultimate aim of all organisms is to pass on their genes to reproductively successful offspring. An organism can increase their chances of achieving this by either producing a large number of offspring, and/or protecting and nurturing their offspring, thereby increasing their chances of survival. Reproductive effort is a measure of the total amount of energy an organism spends on reproduction. This includes the effort required to produce gametes, court and mate, and care for their offspring. r-selected organisms place most of their reproductive effort into producing large numbers of offspring and very little into parental care. K-selected organisms generally produce few offspring but place a large amount of reproductive effort into caring for their offspring. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTRASPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Territorial and Breeding Behaviour in Gannets Australasian gannets (Morus serrator) breed in dense colonies on coastal islands and on cliffs and beaches of some headlands of the New Zealand mainland, They feed mainly on small fish and are often seen dive-bombing into schools of these fish. Gannets usually breed with the same partner over consecutive seasons. However, members of a pair might not see each other for months at a time. After wintering out at sea, they return to their nesting colony in spring. Male birds are the first to arrive and quickly re-occupy or establish and defend a nest site. They prefer flat ground for nesting, rather than cliff ledges. Breeding colonies are situated at sites that are completely or largely surrounded by the sea, i.e. on islands or headlands such as those found at Cape Kidnappers, Muriwai and Farewell Spit. When the females arrive they are greeted with a series of synchronised performances, such as preening, pointing, calling, mutual bill fencing and bowing. After copulation, a single egg is laid which is incubated between the webbing on the gannet’s feet. Both sexes share the incubation duty. Nesting gannets are strongly territorial and will aggressively defend their nesting site. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: MECHANISMS OF EVOLUTION Sexual Selection The appearance of males and females of many animal species are very similar. However, there are species where the sexes display dimorphism (a physical difference). In particular, the males of many bird and mammal species are larger, more brightly coloured, and/or adorned with conspicuous ornaments such as antlers and horns, etc. These traits appear disadvantageous, as they make the animals more visible to predators, hinder movement and are energetically expensive to grow and maintain. You would expect that natural selection would act against them. However, it is worth remembering that natural selection is not simply a battle to survive, but a battle to pass on genes (reproduce). If these exaggerated traits are advantageous in terms of increasing an individual’s ability to reproduce, then they would be selected for. This type of selection is called sexual selection. Sexual selection can be very strong because, in terms of fitness, failing to mate is equivalent to dying young. The Peacock’s Tail 8 7 6 Number of mates Egg production is more costly than producing sperm and, in general, females engage more in parenting after reproduction than males. Hybrid inviability: The hybrid embryos are often not viable because the genes of the two species are incompatible and the hybrid dies before birth. If the hybrid survives, it may die before reaching reproductive age. Hybrid sterility: Hybrid offspring that do survive birth and reach sexual maturity are sterile so they cannot produce viable gametes. Hybrid breakdown: Hybrids may be viable, fertile and capable of producing offspring. However, these and any subsequent generations harbour detrimental genetic abnormalities, ultimately resulting in reduced fitness and fertility. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: MECHANISMS OF EVOLUTION The Importance of Genetic Variation Genetic variation is advantageous to a population because it enables some individuals to exploit a changing environment, thereby ensuring the survival of the population. Without genetic variation the basic mechanisms of evolutionary change cannot operate. There are two primary sources of genetic variation - sexual reproduction and mutation. Sexual Reproduction Sexual reproduction requires the production of gametes through the process of meiosis. Meiosis produces new combinations of alleles, and so genetic variation arises from this unique combination of alleles that each individual inherits from their parents. New combinations of alleles occur every generation from the random processes of independent assortment, crossing over and segregation. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: THE ORIGIN OF SPECIES Polyploid Advantage In contrast with the relatively slow process of allopatric speciation, polyploidy can result in the rapid development of new species. Studies have shown that polyploidy events have played a significant role in the evolution of plants, especially ferns and angiosperms. Therefore, in some cases, polyploidy must provide an adaptive advantage. The presence of more chromosomes means larger nuclei, which results in larger cells in general. The large cell size can result in larger leaves, stems and wider branch angles. These traits may allow the plants to grow in a wider range of habitats and be more resistant to pests and disease. Flowers and fruit are also larger. However, if the polyploid plant contains an uneven number of chromosomes they will be sterile, so any resulting fruit will be seedless. Reproductive isolation isolates gene pools Biologists generally classify a species as “a group of organisms that interbreed under natural conditions and are reproductively isolated from other species”. In other words, one species cannot mate with other species and produce fertile offspring - if they could, it would suggest they are genetically similar and, therefore, are probably the same species. When populations become geographically isolated from each other, gene flow between them stops. In the absence of gene flow, the accumulation of favourable mutations and changes in allele frequencies will differ between the two populations. This means the populations will start to genetically diverge. Divergence will continue and the populations will gradually become more and more genetically different. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: THE ORIGIN OF SPECIES poly = many ploidy = number of chromosomes Instant Speciation - Polyploidy Polyploidy is caused by errors during cell division that result in cells with more than two copies of each chromosomes (>2n). The resulting organism is genetically, and therefore reproductively, unique. However, this is not necessarily a problem in plant species that carry both male and female sex organs, and can therefore reproduce via self-fertilisation. Autopolyploidy Autopolyploidy involves the multiplication of the genome of a single species. It occurs when homologous chromosomes do not separate (non-disjunction) during meiosis. This results in non-reduced, diploid gametes (with two sets of chromosomes) instead of haploid gametes (with one set of chromosomes). If these diploid (2n) gametes fuse with a normal haploid (1n) gamete during fertilisation, the result will be a triploid (3n) organism with three sets of chromosomes. If the diploid gamete fuses with another diploid gamete (potentially via self-fertilisation) the resulting zygote will be tetraploid (4n). Fossils are the preserved remains of organisms and include impressions, casts, moulds of their shape or marks left behind in sediment by their activities. The fossil record provides irrefutable evidence for evolution as it shows: • Very early life was simple. The very earliest fossils are of bacteria and algae. • Organisms change over time. Some lineages are surprisingly complete, linking ancient long-extinct species with their modern descendants. This is particularly evident with marine organisms who, upon death, are more likely to be buried in sediments. Over thousands of years the sediment becomes compacted into sedimentary rocks. As further sediments are deposited, layers of sedimentary rocks (called ‘strata’) form. Because the layers at the bottom of a column of strata are the oldest, fossils within the strata can be dated, relative to those in other layers. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PATTERNS OF EVOLUTION Evidence for Evolution - Molecular Biology The chemistry, structures and processes of all cells are remarkably similar. For example, all animal cells contain mitochondria (for cellular respiration) and the cells of all three domains of life (Eukarya, Bacteria, Archaea) contain ribosomes which help to assemble proteins in a process that is basically the same across all living things. Secondly, the codons on DNA specify the same amino acids in all organisms, from bacteria to plants and animals. The conservation of structures and processes across all organisms provides evidence for a shared ancestry. The tools of modern molecular biology allow biologists to determine the nucleotide sequence of particular genes. If the nucleotide sequences of two species are analysed and if it is found that they contain a large number of genetic differences (due to mutation), it is unlikely that they shared a relatively recent common ancestor. Since mutations take time to accumulate, the number of differences can be considered a measure of the passage of time. So, if two species are found to contain genes with very similar nucleotide sequences, it can be concluded that they must have inherited the genes from a recent common ancestor. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PATTERNS OF EVOLUTION Evidence from mtDNA and Y Chromosome Analysis Great Grandparents Inheritance of Y chromosome Father Mother Y chromosome The Y chromosome is one of two sexdetermining chromosomes found in the nucleus of males. Due to its small size (compared to the X chromosome it is paired with) during meiosis it can only exchange alleles from its very tips (known as ‘pseudoautosomal regions’). This means over 95% of the Y chromosome is conserved and is passed on from father to son largely unchanged. Any changes that occur are the result of mutation. Mutations in modern populations can be traced back to their origin. Son 1. 2. Daughter Inheritance of mtDNA Grandparents Mitochondrial DNA Mitochondria contain their own DNA (mtDNA). Since mitochondria are outside the nucleus, mtDNA is not subject to meiosis. Therefore, the only way for genetic variation in mtDNA to occur is via mutation. When two groups diverge, each accumulates different mutations at a fairly consistent rate. Therefore, the number of mutations present in their mtDNA is proportional to the time since divergence. Secondly, at conception, sperm do not pass on any mtDNA, it comes only from the ovum. Therefore, both males and females get mtDNA from their mother. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PATTERNS OF EVOLUTION Adaptive Radiation - The Moa New Zealand’s moa show significant adaptive radiation. It is thought that the two main groups of moa (Dinornithidae and Emeidae) diverged as recently as 5.3 mya, around the time that rapid tectonic uplift was happening in the South Island. Evidence from fossils indicates that moa established in the North Island less than 2 mya (prior to this they only existed on the South Island). This correlates to glaciation events that resulted in lower sea levels, creating relatively short-lived land bridges linking the main land masses that allowed movement between the two islands. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: PATTERNS OF EVOLUTION Darwin’s Orchids Using insects and birds for pollination is energetically expensive for plants. If the pollinator visits flowers of numerous species, the chances that any one plant will be successfully pollinated is lower than if the pollinator was a specialist, encouraged to only visit one particular plant species. One way of restricting access to nectar is to elongate the part of the flower that holds this sugary liquid, ensuring that only the longest-tongued of insects can reach it. In 1862, Darwin received an orchid from Madagascar, Angraecum sesquipedale. It had an exceptionally long nectary (up to 30 cm). In a letter he wrote to a friend at Kew Gardens he remarked “I have just received such a box full from Mr Bateman with the astounding Angraecum with a nectary a foot long. Good heavens what insect can suck it”, and in a second letter just a few days later suggested “in Madagascar there must be moths with a proboscis capable of extension to a length of between ten and eleven inches”. Later, in a book on orchid pollination, Darwin suggested that this extreme feature may have evolved alongside a moth with an exceptionally long tongue to pollinate it. At the time no such moth had been discovered. In 1907, more than 20 years after Darwin’s death, a moth from Madagascar with a suitable proboscis was identified. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: pre = before, post = after, zygote = fertilized egg THE ORIGIN OF SPECIES Modes of Reproductive Isolation The biological definition of the term ‘species’ relies primarily on reproductive isolation rather than trait differences. A species must be able to produce fertile offspring with members of the same species but not with other species. Reproductive isolation, through mechanical, behavioural and physiological barriers, is an important component of speciation. Reproductive isolating mechanisms (RIMs) are barriers that prevent members of one species mating with different species - they prevent gene flow. RIMs can be prezygotic (barriers that prevent reproduction from taking place), or they can be postzygotic (barriers that occurs after zygote formation). Prezygotic Reproductive Isolating Mechanisms Geographic Isolation Species occur in different areas with no geographical overlap. Ecological Isolation Species occupy or exploit different habitats within an area. Behavioural Isolation Different courtship rituals, sounds, calls or colouration. Temporal Isolation Activity, mating or flowering occurs at different times of the day, month or year. Mechanical Isolation Reproductive structures are incompatible and prevent the delivery or acceptance of gametes. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: HUMANS AS BIPEDAL PRIMATES Typical Feature of Primates • Monkeys, apes and humans have much larger brains for their body size than nearly all other mammals. Humans are the most extreme of all animals in this feature. • Primates have eyes that are forward-facing, which in turn leads to greater overlap in the visual fields of the eyes. This overlap creates a stereoscopic view that enhances depth perception, allowing primates to perceive the world three-dimensionally. The ability to see the world in 3D with good depth perception is a significant asset for life in an arboreal (tree-living) environment. • A reduced snout as they rely less on their sense of smell and more on vision. • A reduced number of teeth compared to other mammals allows them to eat and process a variety of foods efficiently. • Digits are prehensile (capable of grasping) with opposable thumbs and big toes for manipulating objects, climbing and gripping branches. Humans have lost the grasping ability in our feet because our feet serve as a platform for walking. • Sensitive fingers and toes with dermal ridges (fingerprints) that enhance the sense of touch. Primates rely heavily on their sense of touch to explore and investigate their environments. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: HUMANS AS BIPEDAL PRIMATES Modes of Primate Locomotion Most primates are adapted to an arboreal (tree-living) niche. All primates (except humans) move on all four limbs (quadrupedal) when on the ground. Our closest extant (living) relatives, the gorillas and chimpanzees, are knuckle-walkers. Knuckle-walking is a form of quadrupedal walking in which the forelimbs hold the fingers in a partially flexed posture that allows body weight to press down on the ground through the knuckles. Gorillas and humans are the only primates that do not sleep in the canopy. When chimpanzees are in the trees, they move by swinging through the branches (brachiation). Other more distant extant relatives such as orangutans and monkeys move primarily by brachiation. Very distant extant relatives (e.g. the prosimians) move via brachiation or by climbing vertical surfaces and leaping. Humans are the only bipedal (using only their legs for walking) members of the primate family. Almost all primates habitually engage in upright sitting so that they can manipulate objects with their hands, and thus all are capable of supporting their weight vertically through the spine. Brachiators generally have a short lumbar spine, long curved fingers, reduced thumbs, long forelimbs, flexible shoulder joints and freely rotating wrists. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: MECHANISMS OF EVOLUTION This was extensively covered in the Level 2 Biology sciPAD Genetic Drift Genetic drift describes how the frequency of alleles can change over time due to chance events rather than selection pressure. Small populations are more susceptible to the forces of genetic drift. The random mating or the death of one or two individuals in a small population can have a dramatic effect on the allele frequency of the entire population. Large populations with more individuals are buffered against chance events. Genetic drift tends to decrease the variation within a population. However, it tends to increase variation between populations - potentially leading to speciation (the formation of new species). Genetic drift is more likely to occur after a ‘founder effect’ event (a population descending from a few founders), or a ‘bottleneck effect’ event (a sharp decline in population size). The Founder Effect The founder effect occurs when a small number of individuals emigrate from a population, or become geographically isolated from their original population. Geographical isolating mechanisms such as the formation of a mountain range, or land masses moving apart due to tectonic activity, are thought to have played a major role in the evolution of New Zealand’s native species. Endocranial Features The brain size of humans (approximately 1 350 cm3) is much larger than the brains of chimpanzees (approximately 400 cm3). It is a common misconception to think that a large brain equates to intelligence. There are animals with larger brains than humans. Scientists believe that intelligence may be better measured by relative brain size to body mass ratio and by looking at the structure and organisation of the various parts of the brain. When compared to chimpanzees, we have a larger brain size to body mass ratio and our brains are structurally more complex. Human brains have a high surface area because they are much more wrinkled and folded than chimpanzee brains, with greater numbers of connections between many of its parts. Humans also have a relatively larger frontal lobe, which gives us the ability to have abstract and logical thought, imagination, complex language and artistic ability. The cerebellum is associated with balancing and coordination. The large cerebellum in humans allows us to have refined fine motor skills, particularly those associated with finely coordinated finger movements. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: HUMANS AS BIPEDAL PRIMATES Evolution of Bipedalism One of the biggest questions in human evolution is why hominins evolved into upright, obligate bipeds. Many hypotheses regarding bipedalism have arisen and been debated. One of the reasons it remains unsolved is that these ideas are hard to test, and the selection pressures that led to bipedalism do not show up in the fossil record. It is generally accepted that our early ancestors took their first bipedal steps in order to free their arms and hands to carry valuable resources (food, offspring, tools, weapons etc.). Most of the more accepted hypotheses attempt to reconstruct paleoenvironmental changes (‘paleo’ means ancient, especially relating to the geological past) in which these early bipeds lived, in order to understand and explain how bipedalism emerged as a need of daily activity.
