uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: HUMANS AS BIPEDAL PRIMATES The Problems With Being Bipedal Humans are remarkably well adapted for bipedalism - we have an ‘S’ shaped spine, arched feet, agile hands and large brains. As remarkable as our adaptations for bipedalism are, they are, like all evolutionary transformations, a compromise with our history. We are by no means perfectly adapted for bipedal locomotion. Our spines are derived from our distant ancestors who walked on all four limbs. In these ancestors, like modern quadrupeds, the spine functioned more like a flexible suspension bridge, supporting the body’s organs. The human spine has been transformed into a vertical, weight-bearing column, putting it under unprecedented stresses. This means that humans are highly likely to suffer from back injuries and pain. Forces travelling down the spine transfer to the knees, ankles and feet, also resulting in increased susceptibility to injury. The most significant trade-offs in human evolution are evidenced at the time of birth. The evolutionary development of the human pelvis, towards bipedal locomotion, required a narrow pelvis and a decrease in the size of the bony birth-canal. The trend toward increased intelligence required a larger cranium, which would need a wider pelvic area and birth canal. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: INTERSPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS Ecological Succession The composition and type of species within a community can change over time. Some species may become more abundant, less abundant, new species may be introduced, or species may disappear from the community altogether. Changes in community composition over time is called ‘ecological succession’. Ecological succession is most easily observed when the environment suddenly and drastically changes (fire, human activity, landslides, etc.) or new land is formed by uplift, volcanism, etc. Succession that occurs on bare land that had not previously supported life is called ‘primary succession’. ‘Secondary succession’ occurs on bare land that previously supported life. The environment suddenly and drastically changes. No, or very few, organisms remain. 1. The bare land is colonised by mosses, lichens and grasses. They stabilise the land and provide organic matter from which a soil develops. Small shrubs and trees are now able to grow in the ever-thickening soil layer. These plants provide shelter and food for other organisms that may bring the seeds of new species to the area. The thick soil layer is able to support large trees. Some species may not be able to compete and may disappear from the community. A dynamically stable climax community is formed. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: HUMANS AS BIPEDAL PRIMATES All primates have opposable thumbs - only humans have FULLY opposable thumbs. Bipedalism and the Hand The degree of curvature of the fingers of primates is directly related to the frequency of arboreal behaviour. Arboreal primate species that spend most of their time grasping or suspended from branches have highly curved fingers and toes. The curvature provides them with a more powerful grip but reduces the capacity for more precise grips, such as those required for manipulating tools. Humans have almost no curvature of the fingers. This reflects a reduction in arboreal activity and the shift to bipedal locomotion. The freeing of the hands due to bipedalism facilitated the evolution of precise hand movements necessary for making and using tools, throwing and thrusting weapons enabling the hunting of large game, and carrying large items over long distances. Fingers Long, curved fingers assist with brachiating but inhibit the ability to form precision and some power grips. Humans have shorter, straighter fingers as they are no longer required for brachiation. The proportional lengths of the thumb and other fingers give us an opposable thumb with precise, firm contact between its tip and the ends of each of the other fingers. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: MECHANISMS OF EVOLUTION It is a misconception to assume that organisms evolve, natural selection acts on individuals, but only populations evolve. Natural Selection Biologists use the word ‘fitness’ to describe how good a particular genotype is at surviving to reproductive age, finding a mate and producing offspring. Fitness involves an individual’s ability to survive ‘selection pressures’ (environmental factors which may reduce reproductive success, e.g. predators, disease, ability to obtain food, resistance to drought, etc.). Natural selection occurs when populations of organisms are subjected to selection pressures. The fittest creatures are more likely to survive and pass their genes on to their offspring, producing a population that is better adapted to the selection pressures of that particular environment. The genes of less-fit individuals are unlikely to be passed on to the next generation. Variation Individuals within the population vary in many heritable traits. 1. Overproduction Populations produce more offspring than can survive until maturity. This leads to competition. Selection Selection pressures acting on variation results in some individuals surviving better than others. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Hominins The terms ‘hominid’ and ‘hominin’ are both used to describe members of the primate family. • Hominids are the group consisting of all extant and extinct great apes - modern humans, chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans and their immediate ancestors. • Hominins are a sub-group of the hominids consisting of modern humans, extinct human species and all immediate ancestors including so called ‘dead-ends’ - ancestral lines that became extinct after diverging from the direct line between humans and even earlier lines. The hominin line begins where the line that leads to modern humans diverged from the chimpanzees, around 7 million years ago. Palaeoanthropologists (scientists who study ancient humans) have identified over 20 species of extinct hominins in the fossil record. While the relationships to each other remains unresolved, features of the fossils allow them to be grouped into genera including Homo - the genus of modern humans. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Australopithecus africanus Australopithecus africanus was described in the 1920s and was the first specimen found that proved that human evolution started in Africa (at the time it was thought modern humans came out of Europe/Asia). It also showed that, despite having a small brain, these early hominins could walk upright. A. africanus fossils have been dated to the end of the Early Pliocene, between 3.3 – 2.1 mya. The cranial capacity of A. africanus (420 - 625 cm3) is slightly larger than that of A. afarensis and the overall morphology of the face is quite different. A. africanus had a less prognathic face with a smaller brow ridge and a slightly arched (rather than flat) forehead area, resulting in a flatter face than observed in A. afarensis. The attachment points for the neck muscles are low on the back of the skull, which sits on a vertical spine. A sagittal crest is absent and the zygomatic arches are smaller than previous species, traits that are shared with early members of the Homo lineage. However, it still retains some ape-like features, particularly a cone-shaped ribcage and relatively long arms. A. africanus (like A. afarensis) is small-bodied (males 1.35 m, females 1.10 m) when compared to later hominins. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Australopithecus afarensis Australopithecus afarensis is perhaps the most well-known member of the australopithecines. This is largely due to the very famous and relatively complete female specimen nicknamed ‘Lucy’ (3.2 mya) as well as numerous other fossil examples. More is known about its anatomy and behaviour than any other earlier hominin. A. afarensis is thought to be closely related to the genus Homo, whether as a direct ancestor or a close relative of an unknown ancestor. Radiometric dating indicates that they lived 3.7 - 2.9 mya. A. afarensis was slenderly built (females 30 kg and 1.05 m and males 55 kg and 1.51 m). Analysis of sediment, pollen and fossilised plant material suggests they lived in a wooded-savannah type habitat. A. afarensis had a chimpanzee-like face that projects forward below the nose, with a low forehead, a bony ridge over the eyes, a flat nose and no chin. They had protruding jaws with large back teeth. Cranial capacity varied from about 350 to 600 cm3 (the cranial capacity varies widely in this species due to a high degree of sexual dimorphism). Based on the wear patterns observed on the teeth of several A. afarensis specimens, it is thought that their diet was largely plant based (similar to modern gorillas). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS mya = million years ago Ardipithecus ramidus Fossil evidence shows that A. ramidus lived about 4.4 mya during the early Pliocene. The last common ancestor shared by humans and chimpanzees is thought to have lived six or more million years ago. Although Ardipithecus is not itself this last common ancestor, it likely shared many of this ancestor’s characteristics. Analysis of plant and animal fossils in the region where A. ramidus was found indicates that they lived in a lush, humid woodland, similar to the habitat of modern chimpanzees. They were short, standing only 1.20 m tall. Like most hominids, but unlike all previously recognised hominins, A. ramidus had a grasping big toe (hallux) adapted for gripping branches, suggesting some sort of arboreal lifestyle. However, other aspects of its skeleton show that A. ramidus was capable of bipedal locomotion when moving on the ground. The pelvis, for example, shows features only found in bipedal hominins and although their hands could easily grasp branches, they lacked the powerful upper torso needed for brachiation. Ardipithecus ramidus had a small brain, measuring between 300 and 350 cm3. This is slightly smaller than a modern female chimpanzee brain, but much smaller than the brain of australopithecines (~400 to 625 cm3) and roughly 20% the size of the modern Homo sapien brain. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS H. ergaster is sometimes categorized as a subspecies of Homo erectus. Homo ergaster Homo ergaster lived in eastern and southern Africa between 1.9 million and 1.5 mya. It was the first hominin with a human-like body shape, stature and limb proportions. Their gait and running stride would have been very similar to modern humans and well-adapted for long-distance travel. About 1.8 mya, the climate over most of Africa became drier and more seasonal with extensive savannahs. Shortly after H. ergaster appeared, members of the Homo genus began to leave Africa for the first time and migrate to other continents. Their faces project forwards but to a smaller degree than in earlier hominins. The lower jaw slopes backward and does not form a pointed chin like that of modern humans. The arrangement of the teeth within the jaws was intermediate between that of apes and modern humans. When compared to the australopithecines the incisors are more vertical and the post-canine teeth are much smaller, and more human-like. This implies that they ate foods that required less chewing. The overall shape of the skull had developed a more human-like shape including a higher, more domed cranium. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Paranthropus boisei Paranthropus boisei lived in eastern Africa during the Pleistocene epoch, from about 2.3 until about 1.2 mya. They are often described as ‘robust’ australopithecines, hence they are sometimes referred to as Australopithecus boisei. As is the case with virtually all australopithecine species, there is a high degree of sexual dimorphism. Males weighed about 49 kg and stood about 1.37 m tall, while females weighed about 34 kg and were 1.24 m tall. The cranial capacity (475 to 550 cm³) is within a similar range to that of A. afarensis, A. africanus and modern-day chimpanzees. The skull is highly specialized for heavy chewing and shares several traits seen in modern-day gorillas. The premolar and molar teeth were very large (up to four times the size of modern human molars) and they had the thickest tooth enamel of any known hominin. The large muscles needed for chewing were attached to a pronounced sagittal crest. To accommodate their enormous teeth and the muscles associated with chewing, P. boisei had pronounced and flared zygomatic arches resulting in a very wide, dish-shaped face. Large teeth and strong jaw muscles suggest that P. boisei consumed large quantities of plant matter, including nuts, seeds and fruit. H. habilis, the first member of the genus Homo to appear in the fossil record, lived between 2.4 and 1.6 mya. They were similar in size to the australopithecines (males 1.35 m and females 1.10 m) but had a much larger brain capacity of 600 - 700 cm³. This is on average 50% larger than australopithecines, but considerably smaller than modern humans (~1 350 cm³). A few specimens show an endocranial bulge in the Broca’s area (essential for speech). This suggests H. habilis was capable of rudimentary speech, although a developed language is unlikely. Their short stature and disproportionately long arms are similar to those of the australopithecines from which they are thought to have descended. The finger bones are slightly curved and intermediate in shape between the curved finger bones of quadrupedal apes and the straight finger bones of modern humans. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Homo erectus Homo erectus (meaning “upright man”) lived throughout most of the Pleistocene epoch. The earliest fossil specimens date from 1.9 mya to potentially as recent as 30 000 years ago. It is generally thought that H. erectus originated in Africa and spread from there, migrating throughout Eurasia, India, Sri Lanka, China and Indonesia. However, controversy surrounds this species and how it relates to H. ergaster and H. heidelbergensis. An increasing number of anthropologists have redefined the species so that it now contains only east Asian fossils. The older African fossils are classified as Homo ergaster. Homo erectus is now generally believed to be a side branch on our family tree whereas Homo ergaster is now viewed as one of H. sapiens’ direct ancestors. However, the evolution of H. erectus represents a major adaptive shift in human evolution in terms of brain size, body size and behaviour. Fossil evidence suggests that they had human-like limb proportions and body mass (1.6 m - 1.8 m and 40 - 68 kg). They were fully bipedal and possessed a relative large brain (750 - 1 300 cm3) that shared a similar structure to modern humans. Their skull is characterized by a long, low cranial vault and a distinct sagittal keel running down the mid-line. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Homo heidelbergensis Homo heidelbergensis lived between 600 000 and 200 000 years ago and evidence suggests they lived over a wide area from southern Africa to Northern Europe. They were tall (1.45 -1.85 m) with strongly built bodies (50 - 68 kg). The skull accommodated a large brain (1 280 cm3), well within the range of modern humans. Their faces were relatively flat and still lacked the pointed chins typical of modern humans. Substantial brow ridges are evident in front of a low, sloping forehead. The jawbone is strongly built for the attachment of powerful chewing muscles. Their teeth were smaller than those of earlier species, but were still slightly larger than those of modern humans. The teeth were arranged so that they formed a parabolic dental arcade. The pelvis is adapted for efficient bipedal walking, although it is wider and more robust than that of modern humans. Wide knees and strong muscle attachment points suggest there was considerable loading on the legs. Stone tools associated with H. heidelbergensis fossils were more complex than those made by H. ergaster and include a variety of tools such as stone hand axes and wooden spears set with stone spearheads. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Homo sapiens After more than 7 million years of hominin evolution, Homo sapiens is the only surviving member of the hominin family. Although we appeared relatively recently (200 000 years ago) our complex culture and technology has enabled us to spread throughout the world and occupy a range of different niches. This resulted in a species that is highly variable in physical appearance, despite the fact that we are almost genetically identical to each other. Fossils of early H. sapiens (referred to as ‘archaic Homo sapiens’), have all been found in Africa and these fossils provide the best evidence for the evolutionary transition from H. heidelbergensis. Archaic H. sapiens had bodies with short, slender trunks and long limbs, possibly an adaptation for cooling the body in tropical regions. As populations spread to cooler regions stocky builds gradually evolved as an adaptation that helped the body retain heat. Modern humans now have an average height of approximately 1.60 m in females and 1.75 m in males. Archaic H. sapiens also had a slightly larger brain size (1 500 cm3) whereas modern H. sapiens have an average brain size of about 1 350 cm3 (2.2% of our body weight). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Homo neanderthalensis Homo neanderthalensis lived 350 000 to 28 000 years ago. They occupied a range of environments across Europe and the Middle East and lived through a period of changing climatic conditions. Ice ages in Europe were interspersed with warmer periods but by 110 000 years ago average temperatures were on the decline and full glacial conditions had appeared by 40 000 years ago. A vast fossil record consisting of over 270 individuals from foetuses to adults provides extensive information about this species. Current thinking is that populations of H. heidelbergensis in Africa evolved into H. sapiens while those in Europe and Asia evolved into the H. neanderthalensis. Neanderthals are recognisably human but were generally shorter (males 1.68 m, females 1.56 m) and had more robust skeletons and muscular bodies than modern humans. These features are considered to be an adaptation to cold, dry environments. They had a distinctive skull shape that was long and low, with a rounded brain case that housed a relatively large brain (1 200 - 1 750 cm3) which is slightly larger than modern humans. The face is not as vertical as modern humans. Two separate arched brow ridges are seen over large, rounded eye sockets. The nasal cavity is large and a wide, fleshy nose was probably prominent. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Scientists can also use the Y-chromosome (inherited from father to son) to trace all modern males back to a man (called “Y-chromosomal Adam”) who lived 120 000 to 200 000 ya Mitochondrial DNA Mitochondria have their own DNA called mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). mtDNA is totally separate from nuclear DNA in chromosomes. Mitochondria are found in eggs and not in the head of a sperm cell, so mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from our mothers. mtDNA does not recombine during meiosis. The process of recombination in nuclear DNA mixes sections of DNA from the mother and the father, creating a garbled genetic history. This means that the variation in mtDNA between individuals can only be caused by mutation. The rate at which these mutations occur is fairly consistent and so acts as a ‘biological clock’ as they can be traced back in time. In the late 1980s New Zealand geneticist Allan Wilson tested the mtDNA of 137 people from different parts of the world. He found that the mtDNA of these people could all be traced back to one common mitochondrial sequence that existed between 100 000 and 200 000 years ago nicknamed “Mitochondrial Eve” (note that this name has nothing to do with biblical Eve). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Cultural Evolution Biological evolution (sometimes called ‘genetic evolution’) occurs through genetic variation, reproduction and natural selection. Transmission of traits can only occur from one generation to the next via directly related individuals (i.e. from parents to offspring). Biological evolution is only one aspect of evolution. Cultural evolution is the change in culture that occurs due to the transmission of learned behaviour, ideas and knowledge. Cultural evolution occurs through the development of language and customs. Unlike biological evolution, transmission of cultural evolution can occur between unrelated individuals within a generation, or across many generations. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Not Quite so Human Recent scientific advances in DNA techniques have enabled scientists to sequence entire genomes of some fossil hominins. Notably, they have been able to sequence the entire genome of a few Neanderthals. Analysis of this genome shocked the scientific community. The results showed that between 1% and 4% of the modern Eurasian human genome is derived from Neanderthal DNA. Since the genome of modern Africans shows no sign of Neanderthal DNA, these results suggest that a small population of H. sapiens outside of Africa, encountered and interbred with a population of Neanderthals. Furthermore, in 2010, scientists announced the discovery of a finger bone from a hominin who lived about 41 000 years ago. The fossils was found in the remote Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of Siberia, a cave which is known to have been inhabited by both H. neanderthalensis and H. sapiens. Analysis of the mtDNA of the finger bone showed it was genetically distinct from both the Neanderthals and modern humans - it was a different species, scientists called “the Denisovans”. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Reduced genetic variability in non-African populations is a result of the ‘Founder Effect’. Genetic Diversity and Dispersal Models Most genetic evidence supports the Out of Africa hypothesis, or a close variant of it. Humans as a species have very little genetic diversity when compared to other mammalian species. For example, there is much more genetic diversity between two randomly selected, unrelated chimpanzees than there is between two randomly selected, unrelated humans. Within the human population, nearly all genetic studies indicate greater diversity within African populations. This is consistent with an African origin of modern humans since diversity is a function of both time (we’ve been present in Africa longer than anywhere else) and population size. Non-African populations also tend to be more similar to one another than they are to African populations, suggesting that a subset of the African population left the continent and colonised the rest of the world. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Using Fire Controlling fire is generally considered to be one of humankinds’ greatest achievements. Wherever humans have gone, they have taken fire, or the memory of how to make it, with them. It is easy to imagine a primitive human society without the ability to make fire, existing purely on raw food. However, no such society has ever known to have existed. Due to their chemical complexity, raw starch and proteins take a long time to be digested and require a lot of chewing. As a result, only a small percentage of the calories found in raw starch and protein are absorbed by the small intestine. Cooking causes a number of chemical changes that make starches and protein easier to digest. For example, for the same amount of calories ingested, the body gets roughly 30% more energy from a cooked potato when compared to a raw one, and as much as 80% more energy from the protein in a cooked egg. Secondly, cooking kills most pathogens, parasites and detoxifies some plant poisons making food safer to eat. Hominins using fire were able to exploit a larger range of food sources and reduce disease transmission. Thirdly, by making food more digestible, the need for large digestive tracts is reduced, as is the need for large jaws and teeth along with the muscles associated with them. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Humans are apex predators despite our lack of claws, razor-sharp teeth, or the other adaptations found in carnivores because from the very inception of the genus Homo we have used technology. Hunting Early hominins were not at the top of the food chain. Early stone tools (Oldowan) enabled us to scavenge from the leftovers of apex predators. However, the rate of our cultural evolution quickly outpaced the biological evolution of these predators. The arrival of Homo sapiens in Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas was soon followed by the extinction of many megafaunal (large animal) species. Although climate change may have contributed in part to reducing the population size of some species, the correlation between the arrival of humans and the rapid extinction of most megafaunal species suggests Homo sapiens were most likely the direct cause of their extinction. Human desire for animal protein as the mainstay of their diet, sophisticated hunting techniques, combined with the inexperience of native animals, quickly led to the extermination of almost all megafaunal species. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Leaving Africa Homo sapiens were not the first species to emerge from Africa. According to current evidence, the first dispersal out of Africa happened around 1.8 mya. It is widely accepted that Homo ergaster left Africa and spread across Asia. After hominins dispersed from Africa towards the north, they interacted with, and learnt to exploit, different types of habitats and fauna. These populations became geographically and reproductively isolated, ultimately evolving into variants (e.g. H. erectus and H. neanderthalensis). Approximately 100 000 years ago there was a second emigration out of Africa - Homo sapiens. This new species of hominin gradually replaced the other Homo populations that occupied Asia and Europe. This dispersal of hominins from Africa to Eurasia occurred at approximately the same time as climatic changes linked to glacial/interglacial cycles. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Shelter Shelters provide protection from adverse climatic conditions and predation from wild animals. They also provide a place to store tools and food. Shelters also promote social interactions as individuals gather into groups. The ability to obtain or construct shelter would have provided a clear selection advantage. Early hominins would have used the natural environment for various forms of shelter. From simply climbing trees to avoid predators, to using natural rock formations and caves. The first evidence of sites that were used repeatedly have been found in association with fossils of Homo habilis. Individuals may have returned to a particular area due to its resources, but there is little or no evidence that they settled in any one particular area. This is likely because of their constant need to forage for food. Homo heidelbergensis were also mobile foragers. As well as using caves and rock formations for shelter, there is some evidence to show that they were possibly one of the first species to construct simple freestanding shelters. Homo neanderthalensis are associated with cave dwelling as many of their fossils have been found in caves - hence the ‘cave man’ title associated with Neanderthals. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS Clothing The development of clothing was most probably driven primarily by the need to gain increased insulation due to loss of body fur and for protection from direct sunlight on the skin. Additionally, studies of modern hunter gatherer tribes also suggest that clothing was used to communicate social identity, status and tribal affiliation. The earliest forms of clothing were undoubtedly animal furs and skins worn over the body. Unfortunately, furs and skins do not fossilise, so palaeoanthropologists largely rely on indirect methods to date the origin of the evolution of clothing use. A 2011 study on human lice suggested that 170 000 years ago head lice and the species of lice that live in our clothes diverged from a common ancestor. It is hypothesised that once hominins started to wear clothing, lice speciation occurred. Their research suggests that the invention of clothing may have coincided with the northward migration of modern Homo sapiens away from the warm climate of Africa. Homo neanderthalensis lived in cold climates outside of Africa and clothing would have been vital for survival. Their clothing was likely to have been based upon animal furs and skins. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: DISPERSAL AND CULTURAL EVOLUTION OF HOMININS From Hunters to Farmers When the ice sheets retreated after the last glacial maximum (~20 kya) the world underwent many changes. It became warmer, the sea level rose, rainfall increased, and forested and grassland areas spread. During this period the first evidence of agriculture appears. In a favourable region, with food resources that were available year-round, previously nomadic hunter-gatherer populations could remain in one location. This simple form of settlement, where less time was required to ensure adequate food supplies, gave them time to observe and experiment with plants and animals. Humans learnt how to control the environment (clearing fertile land, etc.) and how to control the growth and breeding of selected plants and animals - ultimately leading to domestication. By ensuring they had a regular supply of high quality food these settlements could support a larger population. Secondly, as not everyone was needed to ensure an adequate food supply, they could develop skills in other areas such as carpentry, medicine, music, art, etc. and thereby, accelerate the rate of cultural evolution. 1. Ants, bees, cicadas, cows and dogs all communicate with each other. All of the primates have been shown to have language - gestures or sounds that mean specific things. When researchers played a recorded ‘leopard’ alarm call, the monkeys would scamper up the nearest tree. An ‘eagle’ call caused the monkeys to look up at the sky and head for thick, low-lying bushes. The evolution and origin of speech (i.e. the ability to connect a limited number of sounds to produce an infinite number of sentences) is a widely debated and controversial topic. However, once it appeared, it is relatively easy to see how it advanced. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: CARRY OUT A PRACTICAL INVESTIGATION Finding a Range And Collecting Data Most biological investigations will have a limited range over which data should be gathered. Sometimes there will be an upper limit beyond which there will be no change in the independent variable. Before the experimental design is finalised, it is important to establish the range from which data should be collected. Research into the biological concept or idea will help to establish a valid range. Remember that it is necessary to establish a clear trend or relationship between the dependent and independent variables. Once an upper and lower limit has been determined, at least three other (intermediate) data points should be specified. Ideally these data points are evenly spread across the range that is available. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: CARRY OUT A PRACTICAL INVESTIGATION Writing a Conclusion, Discussion and Evaluation The purpose of a conclusion is to summarize the findings presented in the results section. It is a written description of the processed data and should refer to the purpose (aim and hypothesis) of the investigation. The discussion section is where you interpret your results using relevant biological concepts and knowledge. You should analyse and describe the trends, patterns and results, and compare them to your hypothesis and the findings of others. During an evaluation you should analyse the accuracy of the investigation and describe how you ensured the validity and reliability of your results. Explain what went well and what didn’t. Outline any changes you would make for future investigations by describing any anomalies or outliers. Explain what caused them and how they could be eliminated. You should also comment on the validity of your data (i.e. was it consistent within your trials?). 1. Distinguish between a conclusion and a discussion. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: RESPONSE TO A SOCIO-SCIENTIFIC ISSUE Analysing Socio-scientific Information Socio-scientific issues are controversial social issues that relate to science in New Zealand and/or the Pacific region. Examples of socio-scientific issues include issues such as genetic engineering, climate change, animal testing for medical purposes, oil drilling in national parks, “fat taxes” on “unhealthy” foods, and oil extraction by fracking, etc. Research that is published in scientific journals (for example ‘Nature’, and ‘The Lancet’) must go through a rigorous peer review process. Peer review means that the research is evaluated by one or more people of similar competence to the producers of the work. Socio-scientific articles published in newspapers and magazines do not need to go through the same process. They may be written by scientists, but more often they are written by journalists, non-government organisations or are interviews of people with an interest in the topic. The information presented may be inaccurate (i.e. it contains errors or incorrect data analysis), or it may be biased (where only one view is expressed) or written by someone with a vested interest (e.g. they own a business that could benefit from people being influenced by the article). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Homeostasis The human body is comprised of trillions of cells that work together for the maintenance and survival of the entire organism. Metabolic reactions that take place in these cells can only do so efficiently within a narrow range of conditions (e.g. within a certain pH or temperature). Maintaining a constant internal environment despite fluctuations in the external environment is known as homeostasis - literally ‘same’ (homeo-) ‘state’ (-stasis). The body acts to restore an equilibrium to a predetermined ‘set point’. Homeostatic feedback mechanisms sense a change in the internal environment (e.g. temperature, CO2 concentration, etc.) and turn on, or off, various internal systems in order to return the body back to the set point. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Introduction to Feedback Control The purpose of homeostasis is to maintain a state of dynamic equilibrium within the body. It is an interplay between external factors that can change the internal environment, and internal control mechanisms that oppose these changes. Negative feedback is a type of control in which the regulated conditions are brought back to equilibrium once it starts to deviate. It is called ‘negative feedback’ as the body will maintain a stable environment by opposing the change that deviates from the normal. A negative feedback system requires a receptor to measure a variable and transmit this information to a controller. The controller compares the input from the receptor to a pre-set value (called the set point). If the value from the receptor is outside the optimum range for metabolic processes, the controller activates an effector. Once the influence of the effector has brought the variable back to the optimum range, the control unit switches off the effector. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Thermoregulation Endothermic animals are warmed primarily by the heat generated by their metabolism. Humans and other mammals are endothermic. Many reptiles, fish, amphibians and most invertebrates are ectothermic, meaning they gain most of their heat from external sources. Thermoregulation in organisms runs along a spectrum from endothermy to ectothermy and the two processes are not mutually exclusive (e.g. an endothermic animal can still warm itself in the sun on cold days). Heat Exchange Between an Organism and its Environment Radiation is the emission of electromagnetic waves produced by warm objects, including an animal’s body and the sun. Radiation can transfer heat between objects that are not in direct contact with each other. Convection is the transfer of heat by movement of air or liquid past a body surface. On a cool day, warm bodies lose heat by convection because skin temperature is higher than the surrounding air temperature. Evaporation is the loss of heat from a surface as water molecules escape in the form of a gas. Liquid from moist surfaces in the body or on the skin absorb latent heat energy and depart from the surface in the form of gas, carrying heat with them. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Hypothermia Definition Hypothermia is a dangerous drop in body temperature, usually caused by prolonged exposure to cold environmental temperatures resulting in the body dissipating more heat than it can absorb or produce. However, it can also be caused by substances that decrease heat production, increase heat loss or impair thermoregulation (e.g. certain medical conditions, some medications, severe trauma, alcohol and some illegal drugs). Risk factors Exposure to cold conditions, medical conditions, some medications, alcohol and some drugs. Age - older people cannot regulate their core temperature as well. Thermoregulatory response In the early stages; shivering, high blood pressure, fast heart rate, fast respiratory rate, and vasoconstriction of blood vessels. These are all physiological responses to preserve heat within the core. Progressive symptoms As the temperature decreases; further physiological systems falter and heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure all decrease. Soon the person has difficulty speaking, has ‘sluggish’ thinking and amnesia start to appear. Often inability to use hands and stumbling are also usually present. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Hyperthermia Definition Hyperthermia is elevated body temperature due to failed thermoregulation. It occurs when the body produces or absorbs more heat than it dissipates. Extreme temperature elevation then becomes a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment to prevent disability or death. Risk factors Significant physical exertion in hot conditions. Some drugs cause excessive internal heat production. Heat waves are often followed by a rise in the death rate. Thermoregulatory response The increase in body temperature that results from a breakdown in thermoregulation affects the body biochemically. Enzymes involved in metabolic pathways within the body, such as cellular respiration, fail to work effectively at higher temperatures. Further increases can lead them to denature, reducing their ability to catalyse essential chemical reactions. This loss of enzymatic control affects the functioning of major organs with high energy demands such as the heart and brain. Progressive symptoms Accompanying dehydration can produce nausea, vomiting, headaches and low blood pressure. The latter can lead to fainting or dizziness. In severe heat stroke, there may be confusion and disorientation. Heart rate and respiration rate will increase. In advanced cases; organ failure, unconsciousness and death will result. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Fever Fever describes an elevated body temperature substantially higher than the normal range. Fever is not by itself an illness, but it is usually a symptom of an underlying condition, most often an infection. Fever can be caused by a number of factors, including pathogens, trauma and certain drugs and chemicals, all of which incite the release of substances collectively called ‘pyrogens’ (from the Greek ‘pyro-’ meaning “fire” and ‘-gen’ meaning “produced by”). Pyrogens act on the hypothalamus to increase its thermoregulatory set point. When the set point is raised, the body is perceived to be cold. The hypothalamus initiates heat conserving behaviours such as vasoconstriction, shivering, and inhibiting sweat production, etc. White blood cells (WBCs) can produce pyrogens in the presence of pathogens. For example, the pyrogen interleukin-1 (IL-1) is produced by macrophages (a type of WBC) when they detect pathogens. IL-1 enters the bloodstream and (a) causes the hypothalamic thermostat to increase, (b) signals other macrophages to increase their motility and activity, and (c) signals to T-cells (another type of WBC) to attack and destroy the pathogens. Homeotherms maintain a constant body temperature, usually above that of their environment, by metabolic activity. To experience the cooling effects of sweating, dab some methanol or ethanol on the back of your hand. Homeotherms have a number of structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations that enable them to exploit a number of different external environments. All this while keeping their body temperature within the narrow range required for metabolic reactions to occur. Components of the Human Thermoregulatory System In humans, core body temperature is controlled by the thermoregulatory centre in the hypothalamus. It maintains the set point for body temperature. The hypothalamus receives input from two sets of thermoreceptors. Receptors in the hypothalamus itself Thalamus monitor the temperature of the blood as it passes Hypothalamus through the brain (core temperature) and receptors in the skin monitor the external temperature. Important biological solutes include ions such as Na+ and K+ and organic molecules such as glucose and urea. Osmoregulation is a homeostatic mechanism which maintains the level of water (and therefore, the concentration of solutes) within three major fluids: blood plasma, extracellular fluid (in the spaces between cells), and intracellular fluid (within cells). Osmoregulation is maintained despite the influence of external factors such as environmental temperature and humidity, diet and metabolic rate. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Hypernatremia Definition Hypernatremia results when there is a net water loss or a sodium gain, and it reflects too little water in relation to total body sodium and potassium. Risk factors Hypernatremia can occur from sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, diuretic medication, or kidney disease and in severe cases hyperaldosteronism. Osmoregulatory response An increased osmolality draws water from cells into the blood, thus dehydrating specific neurons in the brain that serve as osmoreceptors or “tonicity receptors”, leading to a breakdown in the regulation of the person. Progressive symptoms Early symptoms may include a strong feeling of thirst, weakness, nausea and loss of appetite. Severe symptoms include confusion, muscle twitching and bleeding in or around the brain. Treatment Administration of water to correct the relative water deficit. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Hyponatremia Definition Hyponatremia is a condition that occurs when the level of sodium in your blood is abnormally low. It is generally defined as a sodium concentration of less than 135 mmol/L (135 mEq/L), with severe hyponatremia being below 120 mEql/L. Risk factors Low sodium can be caused by: Diarrhea, diuretic medicines (water pills), which increase urine output. Heart failure, kidney diseases, liver cirrhosis, sweating, vomiting. Osmoregulatory response When the amount of sodium in fluids outside cells drops below normal, water moves into the cells via osmosis to balance the levels. This causes the cells to swell with too much water. Brain cells are especially sensitive to swelling, and this causes a breakdown in regulation within the body. Progressive symptoms Symptoms can be absent, mild or severe. Mild symptoms include a decreased ability to think, headaches, nausea and poor balance. Severe symptoms include confusion, seizures, and coma. Treatment The intravenous administration of fluids and electrolytes. 44 NCEA BIOLOGY 3.4 SCIPAD PHOTOCOPYING PROHIBITED © Silverback Academic Media

uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Introduction to Selective Breeding Selective breeding (sometimes called ‘artificial selection’) involves choosing individuals with desirable characteristics to breed in order to produce offspring with the same desirable characteristics. Humans have selectively bred plants and animals for thousands of years in order to produce crop plants with better yields, ornamental plants with particular flower shapes and colours, animals that produce better quality meat or wool and working animals with particular physiques and temperaments, suited to do jobs like herd sheep or to move heavy equipment. Selective breeding aims to change an organism’s characteristics, over successive generations, in a way that is desirable to the humans that breed them. This is based on the assumption that an organism’s characteristics are primarily determined by the combination of genes that are passed on from one generation to the next (i.e. the offspring of tall parents will also grow tall because they inherit the genes for ‘tallness’). Wild Ancestral Avocado Modern Avocado Archeologists in Mexico have found evidence that humans were consuming avocado almost 10 000 years ago. They were likely to simply be gathering and eating wild avocados. Evidence of avocado cultivation dates back to about 5 000 years ago. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Methods of Selective Breeding In order to establish a population of organisms with predictable, uniform characteristics the individuals must be genetically similar. Remember that an individual has two copies of any given gene, one derived from each parent. If the parents are closely related, there is a high probability that the genes passed on to the offspring will also be similar. This is why most forms of selective breeding involve some form of inbreeding. Continued inbreeding results in genetically similar individuals with uniform traits. Mating two individuals that are unrelated (for at least 6 generations) is called an out-cross. Out-crossing increases genetic diversity and reduces the probability of offspring inheriting recessive genetic disorders. G1 G2 Mating two animals that are closely related is called inbreeding. Since all breeds trace back to small number of ancestors, all purebred organisms have arisen due to inbreeding. Inbreeding reduces the pool of available genes. G3 Linebreeding is a type of inbreeding between distantly related individuals in order to capitalise on the particular genes of a recent common ancestor. Compared to inbreeding, linebreeding can reduce the possibility of genetic defects occurring. However, selective breeding also has a number of disadvantages. 1. Discuss the disadvantages of selective breeding in terms of: Inbreeding depression This is the result of successively inbreeding related individuals. It describes the abnormally high expression of recessive allele mutations that are harmful to the organism. Recessive alleles are alleles that are only expressed in the phenotype if two copies are present in the genotype. Inbreeding tends to concentrate these alleles in the gene pool of a population. Loss of genetic diversity within a population If wild types are displaced by a domesticated type then genetic diversity will decrease. The domesticated type has been bred for conformity to a type, often with removal or minimisation of undesirable traits, as well as amplification of desirable ones. This may have flow on effects in food chains and webs, unsettling the natural ecological balance. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Search for “Featherless broilers on British TV” on YouTube The Naked Chicken Broiler chickens have been bred to gain weight rapidly. In doing so they generate a lot of heat. The optimum temperature for weight gain has been found to be 20°C. In warm countries this temperature can only be obtained with expensive air conditioning. In the 1950s, scientists identified a recessive mutation, called ‘scaleless’, in a breed of chickens called ‘New Hampshire’. In homozygous recessive individuals, the mutation blocked feather formation. Unfortunately, the mutation also caused a substantial reduction in growth rate. In an effort to eliminate the gene’s impact on growth rate, the mutant chickens were crossed with commercial broilers. The growth rates of the resultant offspring only showed a marginal improvement and, as such, they were of no commercial value. In 2014, Israeli scientists crossed chickens from the original New Hampshire breed with females from modern, high growth rate broilers. The resulting offspring were repeatedly backcrossed with the female broilers. After just one cycle of backcross, the featherless birds showed superior growth rates under hot conditions and reached slaughter weight quicker than standard broilers under the same conditions. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Controlling Breeding - Artificial Insemination Artificial insemination (AI) is the process of collecting sperm cells from a male animal and manually depositing them in the reproductive tract of a female. Collected semen is diluted to increase the number of doses and put into a small plastic tube (referred to as a ‘straw’). Although the straw can be used immediately, most straws are cryopreserved (frozen). Cryogenic preservation makes the semen easier to transport to other populations separated by distance or time. Advantages Disadvantages Increased efficiency: During natural breeding, more semen is deposited than is required for conception and the physical act of mating is energetically expensive. These factors limit the number of mating efforts a male can make. Decreased conception rate: When compared to natural breeding, the percentage of successful births in artificially inseminated animals is almost always lower. Using lowquality semen, incorrect handling or poor placement of semen may be factors. It is also thought that the physical act of intercourse may induce biochemical reactions in the female reproductive tract that assist in conception. Rapid genetic improvement: Superior genes can be quickly disseminated to a large number of individuals. Increased health: No risk of large, aggressive males injuring females during mating. This means less energy would be expended during foraging and allowed for longer and more rewarding foraging journeys. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Transgenesis Transgenesis is a biotechnological process whereby a gene from one species (the ‘transgene’), is inserted into the genome of another species. The recipient (the 'transgenic organism’) will express the foreign gene and also pass it on to its offspring. For example, the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), contains a gene (the ‘Bt-gene’) that produces a protein toxic to insect larvae. After its discovery, this ‘Bt-protein’ became a common ingredient in pesticide sprays. Sprays, although generally effective, have limitations. They are easily washed off the plant by rain, and Bt-protein is degraded by sunlight. These limit its long term effectiveness. Sprays are unable to reach pest insects living underground or in parts of the plant the spray can’t reach. Although some insects aren’t affected by the Bt-protein, it was found to be highly effective against almost all moth larvae, and in particular the Corn Borer moth (Ostrinia nubilalis). This particular moth was nicknamed the “billion dollar bug” because it was the major pest associated with corn plantations. In the 1990s, scientists utilised advances in genetic engineering to insert the Bt-gene into the genome of corn plants. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Introduction to Genetic Engineering Genetic engineering (GE) (also called ‘genetic modification’) is the manipulation of an organism’s genes using biotechnology. Unlike traditional selective breeding, genetic engineering involves the direct transfer of genes from one organism to another. Compared to traditional selective breeding techniques, genetic engineering is faster, can produce more accurate results and it reduces the possibility of undesirable traits emerging. It can be used to transfer desirable genes from one species to a completely unrelated species (transgenesis). As well as inserting new genes, genetic engineering can also be used to remove harmful genes or disrupt their expression. This means genetic engineering could be used to eliminate inherited genetic disorders. Existing genes can be modified to fix defects or amplify effects. Foreign genes from other species can be added (transgenesis). 1. Existing genes can be deleted or deactivated (turned off). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Controlling Breeding - IVF, Embryo Selection and Transfer The resulting embryos then undergo ‘embryo screening’ and ‘embryo selection’ to ensure that the most viable and healthy ones are used for implantation. During embryo screening a single cell is removed from the developing embryo and subjected to pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) which can include karyotyping, DNA fingerprinting and testing for specific sequences or genetic markers associated with genetic defects or inherited diseases. In vitro is Latin for ‘within glass’ In vitro fertilisation (IVF) is a technique used to create embryos outside the body of the animal. Oocytes (unfertilised egg cells) are first collected from the ovaries of a donor. The oocytes are matured in a Petri dish and fertilised 20-24 hours later. They are then left to develop in an incubator for up to seven days. Since most female animals only release a small number of eggs every cycle, drugs are often used to stimulate the release of a large number of eggs (super ovulation). Once checked, the embryo will either be implanted into the uterus of the original donor, or transferred to a genetically unrelated surrogate (called ‘embryo transfer’). They found that the enzymes were chopping up the viral DNA and ‘restricting’ the viruses’ activity. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: CARRY OUT A PRACTICAL INVESTIGATION Finding a Range And Collecting Data Most biological investigations will have a limited range over which data should be gathered. Sometimes there will be an upper limit beyond which there will be no change in the independent variable. Before the experimental design is finalised, it is important to establish the range from which data should be collected. Research into the biological concept or idea will help to establish a valid range. Remember that it is necessary to establish a clear trend or relationship between the dependent and independent variables. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Cloning Whole Organisms Reproductive cloning is the creation of an individual with identical DNA to that of an existing individual. Cloning provides certainty that existing favourable genes will be replicated in offspring as those genes are not combined with any other. Nor are they subjected to the ‘genetic lottery’ that occurs during meiosis and sexual reproduction. Plants are much easier to clone than animals. Most plants cells are totipotent, meaning that under certain conditions plant cells are able to change into other types of cells. Many gardeners clone plants simply by taking ‘cuttings’ from an existing plant and inserting the cutting into a suitable substrate. The cells within the stem section of the cutting that are subsequently covered by substrate will change into root cells and the cutting will grow into a genetic copy of the original plant from which the cutting was taken. Cloning Plants - Micropropagation Tissue samples are cleaned and sterilised to ensure they are free of microbes and viruses. They are grown on a substrate containing nutrients and hormones to promote growth and root development. The resulting plants are clones of the parent and each other. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: RESPONSE TO A SOCIO-SCIENTIFIC ISSUE Analysing Socio-scientific Information Socio-scientific issues are controversial social issues that relate to science in New Zealand and/or the Pacific region. Examples of socio-scientific issues include issues such as genetic engineering, climate change, animal testing for medical purposes, oil drilling in national parks, “fat taxes” on “unhealthy” foods, and oil extraction by fracking, etc. Research that is published in scientific journals (for example ‘Nature’, and ‘The Lancet’) must go through a rigorous peer review process. Peer review means that the research is evaluated by one or more people of similar competence to the producers of the work. Socio-scientific articles published in newspapers and magazines do not need to go through the same process. They may be written by scientists, but more often they are written by journalists, non-government organisations or are interviews of people with an interest in the topic. The information presented may be inaccurate (i.e. it contains errors or incorrect data analysis), or it may be biased (where only one view is expressed) or written by someone with a vested interest (e.g. they own a business that could benefit from people being influenced by the article). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Introduction to Feedback Control The purpose of homeostasis is to maintain a state of dynamic equilibrium within the body. It is an interplay between external factors that can change the internal environment, and internal control mechanisms that oppose these changes. Negative feedback is a type of control in which the regulated conditions are brought back to equilibrium once it starts to deviate. It is called ‘negative feedback’ as the body will maintain a stable environment by opposing the change that deviates from the normal. A negative feedback system requires a receptor to measure a variable and transmit this information to a controller. The controller compares the input from the receptor to a pre-set value (called the set point). If the value from the receptor is outside the optimum range for metabolic processes, the controller activates an effector. Once the influence of the effector has brought the variable back to the optimum range, the control unit switches off the effector. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Fever Fever describes an elevated body temperature substantially higher than the normal range. Fever is not by itself an illness, but it is usually a symptom of an underlying condition, most often an infection. Fever can be caused by a number of factors, including pathogens, trauma and certain drugs and chemicals, all of which incite the release of substances collectively called ‘pyrogens’ (from the Greek ‘pyro-’ meaning “fire” and ‘-gen’ meaning “produced by”). Pyrogens act on the hypothalamus to increase its thermoregulatory set point. When the set point is raised, the body is perceived to be cold. The hypothalamus initiates heat conserving behaviours such as vasoconstriction, shivering, and inhibiting sweat production, etc. White blood cells (WBCs) can produce pyrogens in the presence of pathogens. For example, the pyrogen interleukin-1 (IL-1) is produced by macrophages (a type of WBC) when they detect pathogens. IL-1 enters the bloodstream and (a) causes the hypothalamic thermostat to increase, (b) signals other macrophages to increase their motility and activity, and (c) signals to T-cells (another type of WBC) to attack and destroy the pathogens. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Methods of Selective Breeding In order to establish a population of organisms with predictable, uniform characteristics the individuals must be genetically similar. Remember that an individual has two copies of any given gene, one derived from each parent. If the parents are closely related, there is a high probability that the genes passed on to the offspring will also be similar. This is why most forms of selective breeding involve some form of inbreeding. Continued inbreeding results in genetically similar individuals with uniform traits. Mating two individuals that are unrelated (for at least 6 generations) is called an out-cross. Out-crossing increases genetic diversity and reduces the probability of offspring inheriting recessive genetic disorders. G1 G2 Mating two animals that are closely related is called inbreeding. Since all breeds trace back to small number of ancestors, all purebred organisms have arisen due to inbreeding. Inbreeding reduces the pool of available genes. G3 Linebreeding is a type of inbreeding between distantly related individuals in order to capitalise on the particular genes of a recent common ancestor. Compared to inbreeding, linebreeding can reduce the possibility of genetic defects occurring. Humans have selectively bred plants and animals for thousands of years in order to produce crop plants with better yields, ornamental plants with particular flower shapes and colours, animals that produce better quality meat or wool and working animals with particular physiques and temperaments, suited to do jobs like herd sheep or to move heavy equipment. Selective breeding aims to change an organism’s characteristics, over successive generations, in a way that is desirable to the humans that breed them. This is based on the assumption that an organism’s characteristics are primarily determined by the combination of genes that are passed on from one generation to the next (i.e. the offspring of tall parents will also grow tall because they inherit the genes for ‘tallness’). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Search for “Featherless broilers on British TV” on YouTube The Naked Chicken Broiler chickens have been bred to gain weight rapidly. In doing so they generate a lot of heat. The optimum temperature for weight gain has been found to be 20°C. In warm countries this temperature can only be obtained with expensive air conditioning. In the 1950s, scientists identified a recessive mutation, called ‘scaleless’, in a breed of chickens called ‘New Hampshire’. In homozygous recessive individuals, the mutation blocked feather formation. Unfortunately, the mutation also caused a substantial reduction in growth rate. In an effort to eliminate the gene’s impact on growth rate, the mutant chickens were crossed with commercial broilers. The growth rates of the resultant offspring only showed a marginal improvement and, as such, they were of no commercial value. In 2014, Israeli scientists crossed chickens from the original New Hampshire breed with females from modern, high growth rate broilers. The resulting offspring were repeatedly backcrossed with the female broilers. After just one cycle of backcross, the featherless birds showed superior growth rates under hot conditions and reached slaughter weight quicker than standard broilers under the same conditions. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Glucoregulation Glucose is the primary source of usable energy for the body. It is predominantly received through the consumption of food. Because glucose is used for cellular respiration, the concentration of glucose in the blood affects every cell within the body. Therefore, an efficient homeostatic control mechanism is needed in order to survive. Control of blood glucose concentration is called glucoregulation. Glucose concentration is controlled by the pancreas. It contains receptor cells which not only monitor the concentration of glucose in the blood, but it also contains endocrine cells (called the ‘Islets of Langerhans’), which secrete hormones. Alpha (α)-cells secrete the hormone glucagon, while beta (β)-cells secrete the hormone insulin. These two hormones are antagonistic - they have an opposite effect on blood glucose. Body cells take in glucose for respiration. INSULIN INSULIN Beta (β) cells of the pancreas release insulin into the blood. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Controlling Breeding - Artificial Insemination Artificial insemination (AI) is the process of collecting sperm cells from a male animal and manually depositing them in the reproductive tract of a female. Collected semen is diluted to increase the number of doses and put into a small plastic tube (referred to as a ‘straw’). Although the straw can be used immediately, most straws are cryopreserved (frozen). Cryogenic preservation makes the semen easier to transport to other populations separated by distance or time. Advantages Disadvantages Increased efficiency: During natural breeding, more semen is deposited than is required for conception and the physical act of mating is energetically expensive. These factors limit the number of mating efforts a male can make. Decreased conception rate: When compared to natural breeding, the percentage of successful births in artificially inseminated animals is almost always lower. Using lowquality semen, incorrect handling or poor placement of semen may be factors. It is also thought that the physical act of intercourse may induce biochemical reactions in the female reproductive tract that assist in conception. Rapid genetic improvement: Superior genes can be quickly disseminated to a large number of individuals. Increased health: No risk of large, aggressive males injuring females during mating. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Transgenesis Transgenesis is a biotechnological process whereby a gene from one species (the ‘transgene’), is inserted into the genome of another species. The recipient (the 'transgenic organism’) will express the foreign gene and also pass it on to its offspring. For example, the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), contains a gene (the ‘Bt-gene’) that produces a protein toxic to insect larvae. After its discovery, this ‘Bt-protein’ became a common ingredient in pesticide sprays. Sprays, although generally effective, have limitations. They are easily washed off the plant by rain, and Bt-protein is degraded by sunlight. These limit its long term effectiveness. Sprays are unable to reach pest insects living underground or in parts of the plant the spray can’t reach. Although some insects aren’t affected by the Bt-protein, it was found to be highly effective against almost all moth larvae, and in particular the Corn Borer moth (Ostrinia nubilalis). This particular moth was nicknamed the “billion dollar bug” because it was the major pest associated with corn plantations. In the 1990s, scientists utilised advances in genetic engineering to insert the Bt-gene into the genome of corn plants. During embryo screening a single cell is removed from the developing embryo and subjected to pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) which can include karyotyping, DNA fingerprinting and testing for specific sequences or genetic markers associated with genetic defects or inherited diseases. In vitro is Latin for ‘within glass’ In vitro fertilisation (IVF) is a technique used to create embryos outside the body of the animal. Oocytes (unfertilised egg cells) are first collected from the ovaries of a donor. The oocytes are matured in a Petri dish and fertilised 20-24 hours later. They are then left to develop in an incubator for up to seven days. Since most female animals only release a small number of eggs every cycle, drugs are often used to stimulate the release of a large number of eggs (super ovulation). Once checked, the embryo will either be implanted into the uterus of the original donor, or transferred to a genetically unrelated surrogate (called ‘embryo transfer’). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: PROPERTIES OF PARTICLES AND SUBSTANCES Electron Configurations and Sub-shells Electrons in atoms and ions occupy shells, with each shell having a limited number of ‘spaces’ available. Once an inner shell is full further electrons will need to occupy a shell further away from the nucleus. Each shell may also be described as a principal energy level as electrons within that shell have similar energy. The further an electron is away from the nucleus the higher its energy level. Studies of the light emitted when excited electrons drop from higher energy levels to lower energy levels showed that shells were further divided into sub-shells (or sub-levels). Each sub-shell represents a slightly different energy level within a shell. Electrons in the same sub-shell have the same energy. Sub-shells contain atomic orbitals that hold two electrons each. Orbitals are given the notation s, p, d and f (respectively: sharp, principal, diffuse and faint - based upon the spectral lines (light) produced when electrons drop from higher energy levels). An s sub-shell has one orbital, p has three orbitals, d has five orbitals and f has seven. The f orbitals are not studied at Level 3. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: PROPERTIES OF PARTICLES AND SUBSTANCES Periodic Trends - Electronegativity Electronegativity is a relative measure of how strongly an atom attracts a bonding pair of electrons. A ‘bonding pair’ is the pair of shared electrons in a covalent bond. The attraction that a bonding pair of electrons feels for a nucleus depends upon: • The number of protons in the nucleus. • The distance from the nucleus. • The amount of screening by inner shells of electrons. The most commonly used scale is one derived by Linus Pauling in 1932. He assigned a value of 4.0 to the most electronegative element (fluorine). The other elements are assigned values relative to fluorine. The lowest value is given to francium (0.7) - the element at the bottom of group 1. As fluorine is the most electronegative element, the periodic trends are: • Electronegativity increases moving up a group. The noble gases (He - Kr) are not usu ally assigned electronegativity • Electronegativity increases moving across a period. values. 1. Heating the DNA fragment breaks the hydrogen bonding between the complementary bases and the DNA denatures (separates) into two single strands. Primers are short, artificial DNA strands engineered to flank the region of interest on the DNA fragment. When the temperature is lowered to 50°C, the primers anneal (bind) to complementary sequences on each DNA strand. 4 Exponential Amplification Two new DNA double stranded DNA molecules are produced. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: GENETIC TRANSFER Cloning Whole Organisms Reproductive cloning is the creation of an individual with identical DNA to that of an existing individual. Cloning provides certainty that existing favourable genes will be replicated in offspring as those genes are not combined with any other. Nor are they subjected to the ‘genetic lottery’ that occurs during meiosis and sexual reproduction. Plants are much easier to clone than animals. Most plants cells are totipotent, meaning that under certain conditions plant cells are able to change into other types of cells. Many gardeners clone plants simply by taking ‘cuttings’ from an existing plant and inserting the cutting into a suitable substrate. The cells within the stem section of the cutting that are subsequently covered by substrate will change into root cells and the cutting will grow into a genetic copy of the original plant from which the cutting was taken. Cloning Plants - Micropropagation Tissue samples are cleaned and sterilised to ensure they are free of microbes and viruses. They are grown on a substrate containing nutrients and hormones to promote growth and root development. The resulting plants are clones of the parent and each other. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: PROPERTIES OF PARTICLES AND SUBSTANCES Covalent Bonds Covalent bonds are formed when a pair of electrons are shared between two atoms. They form from the overlap of singly occupied electron orbitals. If the electronegativity of the atoms are different then the pair of electrons will not be shared equally between the atoms. The electrons will spend more time closer to the most electronegative atom giving that atom a slight negative charge - called a negative dipole (∂-). The less electronegative atom will carry a positive dipole (∂+). These types of bonds are called ‘polar covalent bonds’. Atoms with the same electronegativity will share the bonding electrons equally, no dipoles will occur on the atoms and the bond will be classified as a ‘non-polar covalent bond’. 1. 2. 3. Outline the difference between a polar covalent bond and a non-polar covalent bond. In non-polar covalent bonds the pair of electrons are shared equally   between to the atoms. In a polar covalent bond the pair of electrons are   shared unequally. The more electronegative atom will have a slight negative   charge, and the less electronegative atom, a slight positive charge. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: PROPERTIES OF PARTICLES AND SUBSTANCES Solubility A molecular substance will dissolve in a solvent if the attractive forces between the molecules and solvent are stronger than the attractive forces between molecules and stronger than the attractive forces between solvent molecules. The rule “like dissolves like” is often used to explain the observation that polar molecules are soluble in polar solvents, and non-polar molecules are soluble in non-polar solvents. It does not explain the observation that many polar molecules are insoluble (or only sparingly so) in water. This can be explained by the strong hydrogen bonding in water. Water molecules are strongly attracted to other water molecules, and less so to some polar molecules. Chloromethane (CH3Cl) has a solubility in water of only 5.3 g L-1 while methanol CH3OH is soluble in water in all proportions (infinite solubility). The electrons are mobile and can change position within the cloud. At any particular time the electron cloud may be more dense on one side of the molecule compared to the other side. ∂- This uneven distribution of charge creates a temporary dipole on the molecule. These types of dipole are weak (only a small amount of charge separation occurs) and they disappear very quickly. It is important to remember that the molecule remains electronically neutral. For non-polar molecules to be able to form liquids and solids there must be some form of attraction between molecules. We know that the attractive forces must be very weak because non-polar molecular substances have very low melting and boiling points. The attractive forces occur because of the temporary dipoles that arise on these type of molecules, and the temporary dipoles they induce in neighbouring molecules. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology E.searchText: THE ORIGIN OF SPECIES Sympatric Speciation 1. Distinguish between allopatric and sympatric speciation.   Sympatric = same place Sympatric speciation is the formation of a new species without geographical isolation. The new species becomes reproductively isolated even though they are surrounded by their parent population. It is rare in animal species, although biologists have observed cases in which a subpopulation may be in the process of sympatric speciation via niche specialisation. For example, in order to reduce intraspecific competition, members of a bird population may begin to forage for insects higher in the canopy than other members of their species who spend more time on the ground and, as such, different adaptations for exploiting these different food resources are selected for, which may ultimately lead to reproductive isolation. Sympatric speciation is more common in plants and usually occurs by polyploidy. Polyploidy is caused by errors during cell division that result in the cell having more than two copies of each chromosome (>2n). The resulting organism is genetically unique. This is why polyploidy is often called ‘instant speciation’.         2. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: THERMOCHEMICAL PRINCIPLES Spontaneity of Reactions - Gibbs Free Energy A reaction is said to be spontaneous if it occurs without outside intervention. They may occur rapidly (e.g. the reaction of magnesium with oxygen), or slowly (e.g. the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen gas). There are two factors that drive chemical reactions: enthalpy AND entropy. Chemical reactions tend to be spontaneous when the products have less enthalpy than the reactants. High energy states are considered to be less stable than low energy states. Reactions are also ‘driven’ forward by increases in entropy. The spontaneity of chemical reactions can be determined mathematically: ∆G = ∆H - T∆S G = Gibbs free energy ∆H = Change in enthalpy T = Temperature in K ΔS = Change in entropy The sign of ∆G for a reaction must be negative if the reaction is to be spontaneous. From the equation we can see that even if ∆H is positive, if ∆S is sufficiently large AND positive the value of ∆G may be negative. 1. Not spontaneous (b) Positive ∆H and negative ∆S.   Not enough information (c) Positive ∆S.   Not enough information (d) Negative ∆H and negative ∆S.   Not Spontaneous (e) Positive value for ∆G.
