uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: THERMOCHEMICAL PRINCIPLES Accuracy of Calorimetry Several factors can affect the accuracy of calorimetry experiments. Most important is the ability of the calorimeter to retain all of the enthalpy change within the water. It is difficult to prevent some heat being either lost to the surroundings or gained from them. Typically, the values of ∆rH for exothermic reactions calculated from laboratory experimental data are lower than the ‘true’ figure. This is because not all the heat released in the reaction is gained by the water in the calorimeter. School laboratory experiments using polystyrene cups, or other types of improvised equipment, as insulating vessels will lose a significant amount of heat and give a calculated figure of ∆rH that is lower than the true figure. Heat is also absorbed by the thermometer (both the glass and the liquid in it) in order for it to show the temperature change. When the enthalpy of the reaction is small, these loses can severely affect the calculated result. It is also difficult to control experiments to standard conditions (1 atmosphere of pressure and a starting temperature of 25°C). Problems may also arise with the quality of the equipment used to weigh both the water and the reactant(s). Small amounts of reactants are difficult to weigh accurately. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: HYDROCARBONS Geometric (cis-trans) Isomers The single C-C bond found in alkanes allows for rotation of the groups of atoms attached to carbon atoms. The double C=C bond in alkenes prevents rotation. Any atoms or groups of atoms attached either side of a double bond are fixed in space and always have the same orientation to each other. It is therefore possible for alkenes with the same molecular formula, and the same name, to have geometric isomers, (where two different groups/atoms bonded to each C atom of the double bond), occupy different positions in space. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Biology I.searchText: MAINTAINING A STABLE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Glucoregulation Glucose is the primary source of usable energy for the body. It is predominantly received through the consumption of food. Because glucose is used for cellular respiration, the concentration of glucose in the blood affects every cell within the body. Therefore, an efficient homeostatic control mechanism is needed in order to survive. Control of blood glucose concentration is called glucoregulation. Glucose concentration is controlled by the pancreas. It contains receptor cells which not only monitor the concentration of glucose in the blood, but it also contains endocrine cells (called the ‘Islets of Langerhans’), which secrete hormones. Alpha (α)-cells secrete the hormone glucagon, while beta (β)-cells secrete the hormone insulin. These two hormones are antagonistic - they have an opposite effect on blood glucose. Body cells take in glucose for respiration. INSULIN INSULIN Beta (β) cells of the pancreas release insulin into the blood. Liver takes in glucose, converts it to glycogen (glycogenesis) and stores it. Blood glucose levels decline to the set point. Insulin production is inhibited. Elevated levels of glucose in the blood are detected by receptors in the pancreas. Increase due to excessive consumption, particularly foods high in sugar/carbohydrate. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: HYDROCARBONS Introduction to Optical Isomers Optical isomers (a type of stereoisomer) are molecules with the same formula but with a different 3-D arrangement of the atoms in the molecule. The molecules are mirror images of each and are therefore non-superimposable. Optical isomers are called enantiomers. Enantiomers may be identified by locating a chiral carbon - a carbon atom with four different groups attached to it. 1 The numbers 1-4 represent 4 different atoms or groups of atoms attached to the chiral carbon atom. 1 C 2 4 C 2 3 The molecules are mirror images of each other. Each molecule has a different arrangement of atoms or groups in space. 4 3 Enantiomers have identical molecular weights, and are chemically nearly identical apart from how they rotate plane-polarised light. Each enantiomer will rotate the plane-polarised light equal amounts but in opposite directions, classifying them as ‘optically active’. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: HYDROCARBONS Addition Reactions - Hydrohalogenation Hydrogen halides include the molecules HF, HCl, HBr and HI. They are relatively reactive species and will react with alkenes without the need for a catalyst. The reaction takes a similar form to that of reactions with the halogens (Cl2, Br2 etc.), but with the halogen atom AND a hydrogen atom being added to the alkene to form a haloalkane. Alkene + Hydrogen halide For example: C2H4 + HCl C2H5Cl Haloalkane CH3CHCH2 + HBr CH3CHBrCH3 For symmetrical alkenes (carbon atoms either side of the double bond have the same number of hydrogen atoms bonded) only one type of product is possible. Asymmetric alkenes will produce two possible products. The more common product is called the major product and the least common product is called the minor product. Markovnikov’s Rule Sometimes known as ‘the rich get richer’ rule, Markovnikov’s rule infers that “the carbon atom in the double bond with the most hydrogen atoms already bonded will get another hydrogen atom and the carbon atom with the least hydrogen atoms will get the halogen atom bonded to it”. For example, the removal of a halogen atom and a hydrogen atom from a haloalkane using potassium hydroxide in alcohol (KOH(alc)). Alcohol is used as the solvent as the presence of water would ‘push’ the equilibrium to the left: Haloalkane + KOH(alc) Alkene + H2O + KX With some haloalkanes, only one type of organic product is possible. Consider the elimination of HF from 2-fluoropropane: HF could be formed from the hydrogen to the ‘left’... H When the haloalkane is asymmetric (the carbon atoms either side of the halogen-carbon bond have different numbers of hydrogen atoms attached), Saytzeff’s rule must be used to identify major and minor products. Saytzeff’s rule states: “an elimination will occur such that a hydrogen atom is removed from an adjacent carbon with the fewest hydrogens attached to it”. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: THERMOCHEMICAL PRINCIPLES Entropy The term ‘entropy’ (symbol: S) describes the amount of order (or disorder) within a substance or chemical system. An increase in entropy occurs when the degree of disorder increases. For example, particles in a solid are considered to have low entropy - they are held in a structure with a high level of order. When a solid melts, its particles gain entropy as they begin to move more freely and have a less ordered structure. The total entropy of a substance or system is difficult to measure, so chemists are usually only concerned with changes in entropy (∆S). There is a statistical basis to entropy. A chemical system will tend to increase its entropy, and therefore disorder, to the maximum possible. This is because there are more possible arrangements of disordered states than ordered states. Consider what happens when a partition is removed from between two different but miscible liquids: 1 There is order and therefore low entropy in the system when the two liquids are separated. This is not the lowest entropy possible. Lower entropy would occur if the samples were solids. 1. 2 When the partition is removed random movement of the particles will begin to mix the liquids into higher and higher states of disorder. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ALCOHOLS, ALDEHYDES AND KETONES Lucas’ Reagent In 1930, American chemist Howard J. Lucas, devised a chemical test to differentiate between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols of low molecular weight. Using a saturated solution of anhydrous zinc chloride and concentrated hydrochloric acid a substitution reaction occurs. The hydroxyl group is substituted with a chlorine atom, resulting in two layers forming. A cloudy non-polar layer is the newly formed haloalkane, and a polar layer of aqueous HCl and ZnCl2. Alcohol + ZnCl2 HCl Haloalkane + H2O For example: H H OH H H C C C C H H H C H H H + HCl ZnCl2 H H Cl H H C C C C H H H C H H H + H2O H H The classification of alcohols is revealed by the length of time it takes for the reaction to occur at room temperature. Tertiary alcohols react readily and therefore a positive test is observed in seconds. Secondary alcohols take more time to show a positive test, generally around 3-5 minutes. Primary alcohols will eventually react with Lucas’ reagent but it is incredibly slow. For the purposes of identification in the laboratory, it is implied that a primary alcohol will not react with the Lucas’ reagent at room temperature. It is this lack of reaction that positively identifies a primary alcohol by a process of elimination. Anhydrous 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ALCOHOLS, ALDEHYDES AND KETONES Solubility of Alcohols The trend in solubility for primary alcohols is opposite to that of their melting and boiling points. As the molecules get larger their solubility decreases. Think of alcohol molecules as having a hydrophilic (water liking) end and a hydrophobic (water hating) end. The hydroxyl (-OH) group links strongly to surrounding water molecules, while the ‘chain’ of carbon and hydrogen atoms does not. Short chain alcohols will dissolve in all proportions with water. From butan-1-ol onwards, the alcohols show rapidly decreasing solubility. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ALCOHOLS, ALDEHYDES AND KETONES Elimination Reactions - Alcohol to Alkene Concentrated sulfuric acid is such a strong dehydrating agent that it will remove a hydrogen atom and the hydroxyl group from an alcohol and combine them to form a water molecule. The hydrogen atom and hydroxyl group are taken from adjacent carbon atoms, and those carbon atoms are then joined with a double bond, creating an alkene. Production of alkenes from alcohols using concentrated sulfuric acid is rarely done in the school laboratory. The reaction requires the sulfuric acid catalyst to be heated to around 170°C and ‘side’ reactions produce carbon, carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide. The two gases need to be removed by passing them through sodium hydroxide solution. The use of hot sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide make the process extremely dangerous. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ALCOHOLS, ALDEHYDES AND KETONES Aldehyde or Ketone? Three commonly used laboratory reagents are able to distinguish between aldehydes and ketones. All use the fact that aldehydes are readily oxidised, even by weak oxidants, while ketones are not. For this reason, acidified dichromate solution may also be used to distinguish between aldehydes and ketones, while the stronger oxidant, acidified permanganate solution cannot. Remember: Aldehydes are readily oxidised. Ketones are not. Tollens’ Reagent Tollens’ reagent contains the diammine silver complex ion, [Ag(NH3)2]+. Aldehydes are able to reduce the silver ions (Ag+) to metallic silver, while ketones cannot. The silver atoms precipitate out of solution and will cover glass surfaces with a silver coating if the glass is clean. If the silver atoms do not form a coating on the glass they are observed as a black/dark grey precipitate. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ALCOHOLS, ALDEHYDES AND KETONES Solubility (in Water) The solubility of molecular compounds in water, a polar solvent, is related to the strength of the intermolecular attractions between the solute molecules and the solvent molecules. Essentially, the energy needed to separate the solvent molecules must be ‘recovered’ by the bonds formed between the solute and solvent. Aldehydes and ketones both contain the strongly polarised carbonyl group (C=O), and so the negative dipole on the oxygen atom will be attracted to the positive dipole of the hydrogen in water molecules. Note that while aldehydes and ketones cannot hydrogen bond with themselves, they do form hydrogen bonds with water molecules. Smaller aldehydes and ketones are infinitely soluble in water. As carbon chain length increases, the non-polar hydrocarbon ‘tail’ makes the larger molecules increasingly insoluble. Unless very small amounts are added to water (the solvent), they will form a layer above the water due to their immiscibility and lower density. Aldehydes and ketones with carbon chains longer than 7 atoms are insoluble in water. Table of Solubilities - Selected Aldehydes and Ketones 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: AMINES AND CARBOXYLIC ACID DERIVATIVES Reactions of Acid Chlorides Acid chlorides are highly reactive. The high electronegativity of the oxygen and chlorine atoms attached to the same carbon atom draws electrons away from the carbon atom, giving it a strong positive dipole. Reactants with negative dipoles or lone-pair electrons (called ‘nucleophiles’) are attracted to the positive dipole and may form covalent bonds with the carbon atom. Acid chlorides have a carbon atom that strongly attracts nucleophiles. Reactions of acid chlorides and nucleophilic species are often vigorous and highly exothermic, and may be used as distinguishing tests. (‘R’ represents any organic group) Carbon-2 in the above diagram is known as the α-carbon as it is the first carbon atom bonded to the carbonyl carbon atom. Although the amine group can be attached to any carbon atom in the molecule, all naturally occurring amino acids are α-amino acids. Amino acids may be named using IUPAC conventions, however their common name is almost always used. For example: Alanine H H O H C H3C OH C NH2 SH H H2C C O C Cysteine C OH O H 2N Glycine C NH2 OH Note that in all α-amino acids except glycine the α-carbon atom is chiral. The acidic hydrogen dissociates and bonds to the amine group, giving the ion both negatively and positively charged regions. This makes amino acids highly soluble in water. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECIES IN SOLUTION Ka and Conjugate Base Strength Strong acids have weak conjugate bases. In a solution of hydrochloric acid, for example, the conjugate base (Cl-) has a very weak affinity for protons. The amount of HCl in the solution will be so small as to be negligible for the purposes of calculation. Conversely, the conjugate bases of weak acids will have higher affinity for protons, so significant amounts of the acid will occur in equilibrium with their ions. ACID STRENGTH Ka is the strength of dissociation specifically for a weak acid. Like Ks (covered in the previous chapter), the larger a Ka value - the more it has dissociated. Weak bases are similar in that they have a Kb value; a base dissociation constant. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECIES IN SOLUTION Acids and Bases The chemists Brønsted and Lowry independently proposed the theory (the Brønsted-Lowry theory) that when an acid and a base react with each other, the acid will form its conjugate base and the base will form its conjugate acid by exchanging a proton. By this definition, a Brønsted-Lowry acid is a species that ‘donates’ a proton (H+) to a water molecule when in aqueous solution, forming a hydronium ion (H3O+). A Brønsted-Lowry base is a species that ‘accepts’ a proton to become a conjugate acid. Weak acids and bases will react to form solutions in equilibrium: Acid + Base Conjugate Base + Conjugate Acid Acids have a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom. The strong polarisation of the bond allows the proton to ‘leave’ the acid. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECIES IN SOLUTION Acidic Metal Cations Many metal cations form acidic solutions, particularly those that carry 3+ charges. Aqueous solutions of metal cations form complex ions with water molecules as ligands. Electrons on the oxygen atom are drawn towards the positively charged metal cation. This draws the electrons in the O-H bond in the water molecule towards the oxygen atom, and further polarises the bond. Hydrogen ions (H+) are more likely to leave the water molecule. The higher the positive charge on the metal cation, the stronger the effect on polarisation of the O-H bond. H 2O Each of six water molecules is bonded to the metal ion by one of the lone pairs on an oxygen atom. Withdrawal of electrons in the O-H bonds towards the oxygen further polarises each of the bonds. H 2O H 2O H 2O One (or possibly more) protons may leave the complex and form a hydronium ion with a water molecule. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: BUFFER SOLUTIONS & TITRATION CURVES Buffer Solutions A buffer is a solution that undergoes a minimal change of pH when small amounts of base or acid are added. Essentially, when small amounts of hydronium or hydroxide ions are added, they react with species in the buffer solution and do not contribute to a large change in pH, as would be expected if they were added to pure water. An acidic buffer solution may be prepared by mixing a weak acid with its conjugate base. For example, a mixture of solutions of ethanoic acid and ethanoate ions (typically as sodium ethanoate). The weak acid will react with small amounts of base added to form water and ethanoate ions. The ethanoate ions will react with small amounts of hydronium ions added to form water and the weak acid. How A Buffer Solution Works Below is an example on how an ethanoic/sodium ethanoate buffer solution works in resisting a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. Small amount of base added CH3COOH(aq) + OH-(aq) CH3COO-(aq) + H2O(l) Small amount of acid added CH3COO-(aq) + H3O+(aq) CH3COOH(aq) + H2O(l) If the acid and the conjugate base are at the same concentration (equimolar) then pH = pKa of the acid. In the case of a CH3COOH/CH3COO- buffer the pH would be 4.76, the pKa of ethanoic acid. By varying the ratio of acid to conjugate base the pH of the buffer solution can be varied within a narrow range

uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: BUFFER SOLUTIONS & TITRATION CURVES Effectiveness of Buffer Solutions If the weak acid and its conjugate base are in equal concentrations, then the buffer solution will be just as effective at resisting a change in pH with excess acid or base being added. This will also mean that the pH of the solution is equal to the pKa value. 1. Calculate the pH of a buffer made of ammonia and ammonium chloride, both with a concentration of 0.150 mol L-1. pKa(NH4+) = 9.24.  pH = pKa + log([NH3]/[NH4+]   = 9.24 + log (0.150/0.150) = 9.24 However, if the pH is not equal to the pKa, then a buffer solution will be more effective at resisting a change in pH with either an acid or a base. If pH is less than pKa then there is more weak acid present than its conjugate base. With more weak acid present the buffer solution is better able to resist changes in pH to having base added. pH < pKa pH > pKa pH = pKa [Acid]>[Base] More effective at overcoming addition of excess base. Weak acid and conjugate base are in equal concentrations. The buffer is equally effective. [Acid]<[Base] More effective at overcoming addition of excess acid. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: BUFFER SOLUTIONS & TITRATION CURVES Selecting Indicators for Titrations Indicators are used in titrations to show when the equivalence point has been reached. They are weak acids that change colour when they are converted to their conjugate base as the pH of their environment changes. Le Châtelier’s principle can be used to explain how an indicator will work based on the effect of relative concentration changes of hydronium ions on the position of equilibrium. Consider the use of litmus to indicate the equivalence point of a strong acid/strong base titration: HLit(aq) + H2O(l) Lit-(aq) Red Species + H3O+ (aq) Blue Species With an excess of hydronium ions, H3O+, the position of equilibrium shifts to the left and the redcoloured, protonated form of litmus (HLit) will be at a higher concentration than its conjugate base (Lit-). If hydroxide ions, OH-, are added to the solution hydronium ions will be removed and equilibrium position will shift to the right, converting the red HLit to the blue Lit-. At equivalence, there will be equal amounts of red HLit and blue Lit-, and the solution will be purple. The endpoint of a titration occurs when the indicator changes colour, indicating that the equivalence point has been reached. Ideally this happens on the steepest part of the titration curve. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: PROPERTIES OF PARTICLES AND SUBSTANCES Periodic Trends - Electronegativity Electronegativity is a relative measure of how strongly an atom attracts a bonding pair of electrons. A ‘bonding pair’ is the pair of shared electrons in a covalent bond. The attraction that a bonding pair of electrons feels for a nucleus depends upon: • The number of protons in the nucleus. • The distance from the nucleus. • The amount of screening by inner shells of electrons. The most commonly used scale is one derived by Linus Pauling in 1932. He assigned a value of 4.0 to the most electronegative element (fluorine). The other elements are assigned values relative to fluorine. The lowest value is given to francium (0.7) - the element at the bottom of group 1. As fluorine is the most electronegative element, the periodic trends are: • Electronegativity increases moving up a group. The noble gases (He - Kr) are not usu ally assigned electronegativity • Electronegativity increases moving across a period. values. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: PROPERTIES OF PARTICLES AND SUBSTANCES Electron Configurations and Sub-shells Electrons in atoms and ions occupy shells, with each shell having a limited number of ‘spaces’ available. Once an inner shell is full further electrons will need to occupy a shell further away from the nucleus. Each shell may also be described as a principal energy level as electrons within that shell have similar energy. The further an electron is away from the nucleus the higher its energy level. Studies of the light emitted when excited electrons drop from higher energy levels to lower energy levels showed that shells were further divided into sub-shells (or sub-levels). Each sub-shell represents a slightly different energy level within a shell. Electrons in the same sub-shell have the same energy. Sub-shells contain atomic orbitals that hold two electrons each. Orbitals are given the notation s, p, d and f (respectively: sharp, principal, diffuse and faint - based upon the spectral lines (light) produced when electrons drop from higher energy levels). An s sub-shell has one orbital, p has three orbitals, d has five orbitals and f has seven. The f orbitals are not studied at Level 3. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: PROPERTIES OF PARTICLES AND SUBSTANCES Covalent Bonds Covalent bonds are formed when a pair of electrons are shared between two atoms. They form from the overlap of singly occupied electron orbitals. If the electronegativity of the atoms are different then the pair of electrons will not be shared equally between the atoms. The electrons will spend more time closer to the most electronegative atom giving that atom a slight negative charge - called a negative dipole (∂-). The less electronegative atom will carry a positive dipole (∂+). These types of bonds are called ‘polar covalent bonds’. Atoms with the same electronegativity will share the bonding electrons equally, no dipoles will occur on the atoms and the bond will be classified as a ‘non-polar covalent bond’. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: PROPERTIES OF PARTICLES AND SUBSTANCES Solubility A molecular substance will dissolve in a solvent if the attractive forces between the molecules and solvent are stronger than the attractive forces between molecules and stronger than the attractive forces between solvent molecules. The rule “like dissolves like” is often used to explain the observation that polar molecules are soluble in polar solvents, and non-polar molecules are soluble in non-polar solvents. It does not explain the observation that many polar molecules are insoluble (or only sparingly so) in water. This can be explained by the strong hydrogen bonding in water. Water molecules are strongly attracted to other water molecules, and less so to some polar molecules. Chloromethane (CH3Cl) has a solubility in water of only 5.3 g L-1 while methanol CH3OH is soluble in water in all proportions (infinite solubility). They may occur rapidly (e.g. the reaction of magnesium with oxygen), or slowly (e.g. the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen gas). There are two factors that drive chemical reactions: enthalpy AND entropy. Chemical reactions tend to be spontaneous when the products have less enthalpy than the reactants. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: THERMOCHEMICAL PRINCIPLES Accuracy of Calorimetry Several factors can affect the accuracy of calorimetry experiments. Most important is the ability of the calorimeter to retain all of the enthalpy change within the water. It is difficult to prevent some heat being either lost to the surroundings or gained from them. Typically, the values of ∆rH for exothermic reactions calculated from laboratory experimental data are lower than the ‘true’ figure. This is because not all the heat released in the reaction is gained by the water in the calorimeter. School laboratory experiments using polystyrene cups, or other types of improvised equipment, as insulating vessels will lose a significant amount of heat and give a calculated figure of ∆rH that is lower than the true figure. Heat is also absorbed by the thermometer (both the glass and the liquid in it) in order for it to show the temperature change. When the enthalpy of the reaction is small, these loses can severely affect the calculated result. It is also difficult to control experiments to standard conditions (1 atmosphere of pressure and a starting temperature of 25°C). Problems may also arise with the quality of the equipment used to weigh both the water and the reactant(s). Small amounts of reactants are difficult to weigh accurately. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: PROPERTIES OF PARTICLES AND SUBSTANCES Temporary Dipole-Dipole Attractions ∂+ Br Br The electrons in a bromine molecule (Br2) form an ovalshaped cloud. The electrons are mobile and can change position within the cloud. At any particular time the electron cloud may be more dense on one side of the molecule compared to the other side. ∂- This uneven distribution of charge creates a temporary dipole on the molecule. These types of dipole are weak (only a small amount of charge separation occurs) and they disappear very quickly. It is important to remember that the molecule remains electronically neutral. For non-polar molecules to be able to form liquids and solids there must be some form of attraction between molecules. We know that the attractive forces must be very weak because non-polar molecular substances have very low melting and boiling points. The attractive forces occur because of the temporary dipoles that arise on these type of molecules, and the temporary dipoles they induce in neighbouring molecules. Weak Attractive Force Induced dipoles may also be referred to as ‘dispersion forces’, ‘Van der Waals forces’ or ‘Instantaneous dipoles’. ∂+ Br Br ∂- Assume a temporary dipole has arisen on the molecule above. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: HYDROCARBONS Geometric (cis-trans) Isomers The single C-C bond found in alkanes allows for rotation of the groups of atoms attached to carbon atoms. The double C=C bond in alkenes prevents rotation. Any atoms or groups of atoms attached either side of a double bond are fixed in space and always have the same orientation to each other. It is therefore possible for alkenes with the same molecular formula, and the same name, to have geometric isomers, (where two different groups/atoms bonded to each C atom of the double bond), occupy different positions in space. For example, the removal of a halogen atom and a hydrogen atom from a haloalkane using potassium hydroxide in alcohol (KOH(alc)). Alcohol is used as the solvent as the presence of water would ‘push’ the equilibrium to the left: Haloalkane + KOH(alc) Alkene + H2O + KX With some haloalkanes, only one type of organic product is possible. Consider the elimination of HF from 2-fluoropropane: HF could be formed from the hydrogen to the ‘left’... H When the haloalkane is asymmetric (the carbon atoms either side of the halogen-carbon bond have different numbers of hydrogen atoms attached), Saytzeff’s rule must be used to identify major and minor products. Saytzeff’s rule states: “an elimination will occur such that a hydrogen atom is removed from an adjacent carbon with the fewest hydrogens attached to it”. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: HYDROCARBONS Addition Reactions - Hydrohalogenation Hydrogen halides include the molecules HF, HCl, HBr and HI. They are relatively reactive species and will react with alkenes without the need for a catalyst. The reaction takes a similar form to that of reactions with the halogens (Cl2, Br2 etc.), but with the halogen atom AND a hydrogen atom being added to the alkene to form a haloalkane. Alkene + Hydrogen halide For example: C2H4 + HCl C2H5Cl Haloalkane CH3CHCH2 + HBr CH3CHBrCH3 For symmetrical alkenes (carbon atoms either side of the double bond have the same number of hydrogen atoms bonded) only one type of product is possible. Asymmetric alkenes will produce two possible products. The more common product is called the major product and the least common product is called the minor product. Markovnikov’s Rule Sometimes known as ‘the rich get richer’ rule, Markovnikov’s rule infers that “the carbon atom in the double bond with the most hydrogen atoms already bonded will get another hydrogen atom and the carbon atom with the least hydrogen atoms will get the halogen atom bonded to it”. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: HYDROCARBONS Introduction to Optical Isomers Optical isomers (a type of stereoisomer) are molecules with the same formula but with a different 3-D arrangement of the atoms in the molecule. The molecules are mirror images of each and are therefore non-superimposable. Optical isomers are called enantiomers. Enantiomers may be identified by locating a chiral carbon - a carbon atom with four different groups attached to it. 1 The numbers 1-4 represent 4 different atoms or groups of atoms attached to the chiral carbon atom. 1 C 2 4 C 2 3 The molecules are mirror images of each other. Each molecule has a different arrangement of atoms or groups in space. 4 3 Enantiomers have identical molecular weights, and are chemically nearly identical apart from how they rotate plane-polarised light. Each enantiomer will rotate the plane-polarised light equal amounts but in opposite directions, classifying them as ‘optically active’. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ALCOHOLS, ALDEHYDES AND KETONES Lucas’ Reagent In 1930, American chemist Howard J. Lucas, devised a chemical test to differentiate between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols of low molecular weight. Using a saturated solution of anhydrous zinc chloride and concentrated hydrochloric acid a substitution reaction occurs. The hydroxyl group is substituted with a chlorine atom, resulting in two layers forming. A cloudy non-polar layer is the newly formed haloalkane, and a polar layer of aqueous HCl and ZnCl2. Alcohol + ZnCl2 HCl Haloalkane + H2O For example: H H OH H H C C C C H H H C H H H + HCl ZnCl2 H H Cl H H C C C C H H H C H H H + H2O H H The classification of alcohols is revealed by the length of time it takes for the reaction to occur at room temperature. Tertiary alcohols react readily and therefore a positive test is observed in seconds. Secondary alcohols take more time to show a positive test, generally around 3-5 minutes. Primary alcohols will eventually react with Lucas’ reagent but it is incredibly slow. For the purposes of identification in the laboratory, it is implied that a primary alcohol will not react with the Lucas’ reagent at room temperature. It is this lack of reaction that positively identifies a primary alcohol by a process of elimination. 1. State the chemicals used in Lucas’ reagent.     2. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ALCOHOLS, ALDEHYDES AND KETONES Solubility of Alcohols The trend in solubility for primary alcohols is opposite to that of their melting and boiling points. As the molecules get larger their solubility decreases. Think of alcohol molecules as having a hydrophilic (water liking) end and a hydrophobic (water hating) end. The hydroxyl (-OH) group links strongly to surrounding water molecules, while the ‘chain’ of carbon and hydrogen atoms does not. Short chain alcohols will dissolve in all proportions with water. From butan-1-ol onwards, the alcohols show rapidly decreasing solubility. The reaction requires the sulfuric acid catalyst to be heated to around 170°C and ‘side’ reactions produce carbon, carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ALCOHOLS, ALDEHYDES AND KETONES Aldehyde or Ketone? Three commonly used laboratory reagents are able to distinguish between aldehydes and ketones. All use the fact that aldehydes are readily oxidised, even by weak oxidants, while ketones are not. For this reason, acidified dichromate solution may also be used to distinguish between aldehydes and ketones, while the stronger oxidant, acidified permanganate solution cannot. Aldehydes are able to reduce the silver ions (Ag+) to metallic silver, while ketones cannot. The silver atoms precipitate out of solution and will cover glass surfaces with a silver coating if the glass is clean. If the silver atoms do not form a coating on the glass they are observed as a black/dark grey precipitate. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: THERMOCHEMICAL PRINCIPLES Entropy The term ‘entropy’ (symbol: S) describes the amount of order (or disorder) within a substance or chemical system. An increase in entropy occurs when the degree of disorder increases. For example, particles in a solid are considered to have low entropy - they are held in a structure with a high level of order. When a solid melts, its particles gain entropy as they begin to move more freely and have a less ordered structure. The total entropy of a substance or system is difficult to measure, so chemists are usually only concerned with changes in entropy (∆S). There is a statistical basis to entropy. A chemical system will tend to increase its entropy, and therefore disorder, to the maximum possible. This is because there are more possible arrangements of disordered states than ordered states. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ALCOHOLS, ALDEHYDES AND KETONES Solubility (in Water) The solubility of molecular compounds in water, a polar solvent, is related to the strength of the intermolecular attractions between the solute molecules and the solvent molecules. Essentially, the energy needed to separate the solvent molecules must be ‘recovered’ by the bonds formed between the solute and solvent. Aldehydes and ketones both contain the strongly polarised carbonyl group (C=O), and so the negative dipole on the oxygen atom will be attracted to the positive dipole of the hydrogen in water molecules. Note that while aldehydes and ketones cannot hydrogen bond with themselves, they do form hydrogen bonds with water molecules. Smaller aldehydes and ketones are infinitely soluble in water. As carbon chain length increases, the non-polar hydrocarbon ‘tail’ makes the larger molecules increasingly insoluble. Unless very small amounts are added to water (the solvent), they will form a layer above the water due to their immiscibility and lower density. Aldehydes and ketones with carbon chains longer than 7 atoms are insoluble in water. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: AMINES AND CARBOXYLIC ACID DERIVATIVES Reactions of Acid Chlorides Acid chlorides are highly reactive. The high electronegativity of the oxygen and chlorine atoms attached to the same carbon atom draws electrons away from the carbon atom, giving it a strong positive dipole. Reactants with negative dipoles or lone-pair electrons (called ‘nucleophiles’) are attracted to the positive dipole and may form covalent bonds with the carbon atom. Acid chlorides have a carbon atom that strongly attracts nucleophiles. Reactions of acid chlorides and nucleophilic species are often vigorous and highly exothermic, and may be used as distinguishing tests. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM Calculating Ks Using Solubility (AB type) Ionic solids that were described in Level 2 Chemistry as insoluble are better described as sparingly soluble. Because Ks is derived from an expression including reactants at very low concentrations, sparingly soluble ionic compounds will have very small values of Ks. For example, aluminium hydroxide: Ks(Al(OH)3) = 3.00 × 10-34. Conversely, a large value for Ks indicates a high solubility. The solubility of ionic solids is usually given as a number of moles per litre of water (mol L-1). Solubility is calculated experimentally, and may then be used to calculate Ks of the compound. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: EQUILIBRIUM The Common Ion Effect The solubility of an ionic compound is reduced if it is added to a solution already containing one of its ions (a common ion). Because Ks is a constant, the increase in concentration of one ion means that the concentration of the other must fall to maintain the same value of Ks. It is also useful to consider Le Châtelier’s principle when solving problems concerning the common ion effect. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECIES IN SOLUTION Ka and Conjugate Base Strength Strong acids have weak conjugate bases. In a solution of hydrochloric acid, for example, the conjugate base (Cl-) has a very weak affinity for protons. The amount of HCl in the solution will be so small as to be negligible for the purposes of calculation. Conversely, the conjugate bases of weak acids will have higher affinity for protons, so significant amounts of the acid will occur in equilibrium with their ions. ACID STRENGTH Ka is the strength of dissociation specifically for a weak acid. Like Ks (covered in the previous chapter), the larger a Ka value - the more it has dissociated. Weak bases are similar in that they have a Kb value; a base dissociation constant. The higher the value of Kb the more it will dissociate. 1. • Strong acids have high values for Ka and therefore low values of pKa. • Strong acids have weak conjugate bases. • As acid strength decreases so does Ka, therefore pKa value increases. • The weaker of two acids will have a lower Ka and therefore a higher pKa. • The conjugate base of weak acids accepts protons to form the acid in equilibrium with its ions. • The weaker of two acids will have the stronger conjugate base - i.e. it will accept protons more readily so there will be a higher concentration of the acid in equilibrium. • Very weak acids have strong conjugate bases. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECIES IN SOLUTION Acids and Bases The chemists Brønsted and Lowry independently proposed the theory (the Brønsted-Lowry theory) that when an acid and a base react with each other, the acid will form its conjugate base and the base will form its conjugate acid by exchanging a proton. By this definition, a Brønsted-Lowry acid is a species that ‘donates’ a proton (H+) to a water molecule when in aqueous solution, forming a hydronium ion (H3O+). A Brønsted-Lowry base is a species that ‘accepts’ a proton to become a conjugate acid. Weak acids and bases will react to form solutions in equilibrium: Acid + Base Conjugate Base + Conjugate Acid Acids have a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom. The strong polarisation of the bond allows the proton to ‘leave’ the acid. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: BUFFER SOLUTIONS & TITRATION CURVES Buffer Solutions A buffer is a solution that undergoes a minimal change of pH when small amounts of base or acid are added. Essentially, when small amounts of hydronium or hydroxide ions are added, they react with species in the buffer solution and do not contribute to a large change in pH, as would be expected if they were added to pure water. An acidic buffer solution may be prepared by mixing a weak acid with its conjugate base. For example, a mixture of solutions of ethanoic acid and ethanoate ions (typically as sodium ethanoate). The weak acid will react with small amounts of base added to form water and ethanoate ions. The ethanoate ions will react with small amounts of hydronium ions added to form water and the weak acid. How A Buffer Solution Works Below is an example on how an ethanoic/sodium ethanoate buffer solution works in resisting a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. Small amount of base added CH3COOH(aq) + OH-(aq) CH3COO-(aq) + H2O(l) Small amount of acid added CH3COO-(aq) + H3O+(aq) CH3COOH(aq) + H2O(l) If the acid and the conjugate base are at the same concentration (equimolar) then pH = pKa of the acid. In the case of a CH3COOH/CH3COO- buffer the pH would be 4.76, the pKa of ethanoic acid. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECIES IN SOLUTION Acidic Metal Cations Many metal cations form acidic solutions, particularly those that carry 3+ charges. Aqueous solutions of metal cations form complex ions with water molecules as ligands. Electrons on the oxygen atom are drawn towards the positively charged metal cation. This draws the electrons in the O-H bond in the water molecule towards the oxygen atom, and further polarises the bond. Hydrogen ions (H+) are more likely to leave the water molecule. The higher the positive charge on the metal cation, the stronger the effect on polarisation of the O-H bond. The Hexaaquairon(III) Complex Ion H 2O The pH of solutions containing hexaaqua ions varies for different metals of equal concentration. However, the reason for their acidity is the same. H 2O Each of six water molecules is bonded to the metal ion by one of the lone pairs on an oxygen atom. Withdrawal of electrons in the O-H bonds towards the oxygen further polarises each of the bonds. H 2O H 2O H 2O One (or possibly more) protons may leave the complex and form a hydronium ion with a water molecule. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: BUFFER SOLUTIONS & TITRATION CURVES Selecting Indicators for Titrations Indicators are used in titrations to show when the equivalence point has been reached. They are weak acids that change colour when they are converted to their conjugate base as the pH of their environment changes. Le Châtelier’s principle can be used to explain how an indicator will work based on the effect of relative concentration changes of hydronium ions on the position of equilibrium. Consider the use of litmus to indicate the equivalence point of a strong acid/strong base titration: HLit(aq) + H2O(l) Lit-(aq) Red Species + H3O+ (aq) Blue Species With an excess of hydronium ions, H3O+, the position of equilibrium shifts to the left and the redcoloured, protonated form of litmus (HLit) will be at a higher concentration than its conjugate base (Lit-). If hydroxide ions, OH-, are added to the solution hydronium ions will be removed and equilibrium position will shift to the right, converting the red HLit to the blue Lit-. At equivalence, there will be equal amounts of red HLit and blue Lit-, and the solution will be purple. The endpoint of a titration occurs when the indicator changes colour, indicating that the equivalence point has been reached. Ideally this happens on the steepest part of the titration curve. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ANALYTICAL TECHNIQUES Colorimetric Analysis Colorimetry relies upon the property of some substances to absorb certain wavelengths of visible light and to transmit others. The strength of colour of a sample can be compared to a standard curve - a curve which shows the strength of colour recorded from prepared (known) samples. Colorimetry is limited to analysis of coloured compounds such as Fe3+ and Cu2+ ions, etc, although it is possible to undertake chemical reactions that create coloured substances from uncoloured ones. To be accurate, special equipment is needed to measure the strength of the colour. Without colorimeters, the test is limited to subjective analysis such as no colour, weak colour, strong colour etc, which is not suitably accurate for the purposes of this standard. Creating a Standard Curve Research into the expected results is necessary. This is so an appropriate range for the standard curve can be chosen. For example, if the sample to be tested is expected to be between 2 g L-1 and 5 g L-1, then reference samples of 0, 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, and 6.0 g L-1 should be prepared and their absorbance measured. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ANALYTICAL TECHNIQUES Gravimetric Analysis Gravimetry involves calculating the concentration or amount of a substance in a sample by measuring mass. A simple example would be the determination of total solids in a sample of river water by evaporating off the water (and other volatiles) and weighing the residue. The mass of the residue divided by the mass of the water sample (×100) would give a percentage of dissolved solids. More complicated analyses may involve the precipitation of ions in solution, filtration, dessication and weighing. Once again, the mass or volume of the aqueous sample can be used to calculate the concentration of the ions in solution. Gravimetric analysis allows for very precise analysis if methods are simple and followed correctly. It does not require preparation of a series of standards and does not require expensive equipment. However, if there are several steps necessary to prepare the precipitate, errors may accumulate. The effect of each step must be considered when deciding whether the analysis will be accurate. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECTROSCOPY Infrared Spectra IR spectra are produced by placing a sample of the compound to be investigated in a machine called an IR spectrometer (or IR photospectrometer). IR light is shone through the sample, and the amount of each frequency that is transmitted through the sample is measured. Frequencies that pass through the sample are recorded as having a high percentage transmission. Frequencies that are absorbed by interaction with covalent bonds show up as troughs on the spectrum because a lesser amount of that frequency is transmitted through the sample. Note that it is conventional to call troughs on spectra “peaks”. An example of an IR spectrum is shown below: Infrared Absorption Spectrum - Methanol % Transmittance 100 50 C-H OH C-O 0 4000 3000 2000 1500 1000 500 Wavenumber (cm-1­) The left-hand side of spectra (above 1 500 cm-1) is called the diagnostic side. Strong (deep) peaks on this side are diagnostic of particular types of bonds. Both the depth, width and position (wavenumber) must be considered. For example a strong peak around 1 700 cm-1 indicates the presence of a C=O (carbonyl) group. Some diagnostic peaks are found below 1 500 cm-1. For example, a strong peak at 1 050 - 1 300 cm-1 indicates C-O stretch. The right-hand side of a spectrum is called the fingerprint side. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECTROSCOPY Infrared Spectroscopy Spectroscopy is the study of the interaction between matter and radiated energy. Infrared (IR) spectroscopy exploits the interaction between light in the infrared part of the spectrum and the bonds between atoms in molecules. IR spectroscopy is of particular use in identifying types of bonds, and therefore functional groups, present in organic molecules. Covalent bonds behave like springs. They are not rigid connections; bonds are able to bend and stretch, and like springs they are able to absorb energy. Bonds Bending Bonds Stretching There are other ways that bonds may bend and stretch. These examples are indicative only. IR light with a frequency close to the vibrational frequency of a particular bond will be ‘absorbed’ by the bond as the bond begins to bend and/or stretch. Because molecules can bend, stretch and vibrate, the same bond can give more than one ‘signal’ on infrared spectra. Because stretching usually gives a sharper and stronger ‘peak’, and at higher frequencies, it is these that are mostly used for identifying the type of bonds present. It is important to note that IR spectroscopy uses wavenumber (v (cm-1)) rather than using frequency (f (Hz or s-1)) or wavelength (λ (m)). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECTROSCOPY Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy Any nucleus with an odd mass number or atomic number has a property called nuclear spin. These nuclei behave like tiny magnets, and in most situations they will have a random alignment of their magnetic fields. When an external magnetic field is applied to the atoms, the nuclei’s magnetic field will align with the external field. Most will align their magnetic field with the external field, but a small percentage will (mis)align their field in the opposite direction. No Magnetic Field External Magnetic Field Applied Key Direction of magnetic field Spinning nucleus The aligned state is the lower energy state. The higher energy, misaligned nuclei may be ‘flipped’ into the lower energy state by absorbing electromagnetic radiation. The frequency required to ‘flip’ the nuclei is called the resonance frequency (hence the term NMR), and varies according to the type of atom and the type of atom(s) that they are bonded to. NMR is especially useful in analysing organic compounds because of the presence of 1H and 13C in organic molecules. 13C NMR is able to measure the number of chemical environments that 13C atoms have in a compound. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECTROSCOPY Mass Spectroscopy Mass spectrometry is a technique used to help determine the composition of unknown compounds. The compound is placed in the mass spectrometer, vaporised and bombarded with high energy electrons. These electrons ‘knock’ electrons off of molecules of the compound, forming positive ions called carbocations. The high energy electrons may also fragment the molecule, with the fragments also having electrons removed forming positive ions. The positive ions are accelerated towards a magnetic field which deflects the ‘beam’ of particles into a detector. The amount of deflection depends upon the mass of the particle (heavy particles deflect less than lighter particles), and the charge on the particle (higher positive charge causes higher deflection). Note that charges higher than +1 are rare and usually ignored by the detector. A mass spectrum is a graph of relative abundance vs. the ratio of mass to charge (m/z). Mass spectra can be used to determine the ratio of isotopes of an element. For example, there are three naturally occurring isotopes of carbon, 12C, 13C and 14C. Their proportions in a pure sample of carbon are approximately 99%, 1% and trace respectively. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECTROSCOPY Mass Spectra of Organic Molecules Mass spectra of organic molecules generally show a number of peaks. The peak with the highest m/z ratio will be that caused by the molecular ion (M+). The presence of isotopes such as 35Cl/37Cl and 79Br/81Br, where the abundance of both isotopes is high, may show as two peaks at the upper end of the m/z ratios. Molecular ions are unstable and it is common to see spectra showing taller peaks for the fragments they separate into than the peak caused by the molecular ion itself. Fragments of the molecule may show up as a number of closely grouped peaks separated in their m/z ratio because of the presence of isotopes, or the removal of a hydrogen atom from the fragment (lower m/z than expected). To determine the structure of the fragment, generally only the highest peak in the cluster is considered. The easiest way to determine what fragment has created the peak, ‘separate’ the molecule into two fragments at a C-C bond and calculate the mass of the various fragment. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: OXIDATION-REDUCTION PROCESSES The Standard Hydrogen Electrode The voltage produced by a galvanic cell depends upon the combination of reductants and oxidants (among other things, including their concentration and temperature). Higher voltages will be produced if the reductant is very willing to release electrons and the oxidant is very willing to accept them. Chemists agreed that in order to measure the potential of any particular redox couple, it needed to be measured against a standard electrode. The standard chosen was the ‘standard hydrogen electrode - SHE’: Platinum wire Hydrogen gas (101 kPa - 298 K) Well-constructed standard hydrogen electrodes provide very accurate readings and, most importantly, reproducibility. Platinum is used as the electrode because it is inert, does not corrode and catalyses the reaction. The electrode potential (E°) of the SHE is arbitrarily taken as 0.0 V. When combined with other redox couples (under standard conditions), the voltage produced is taken as the standard electrode potential of that couple. Some easily remembered rules help identify the anode and cathode in electrochemical cells: Vowels go together (A & O) Consonants go together (C & R). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ANALYTICAL TECHNIQUES Preparation of Standard Solutions A standard solution is a solution in which the concentration of a reagent is known to a high degree of accuracy. They may be used in titrations, gravimetric and colorimetric analyses. A primary standard is prepared by adding a weighed amount of a reactant that is stable - for example, it does not oxidise in air and does not decompose in sunlight, can be obtained as a pure substance, does not absorb water (not hygroscopic) or carbon dioxide from the air, and ideally has a high molecular weight. The amount added and the volume can be used to calculate the concentration of the reagent accurately. A secondary standard can be prepared in a similar manner, but from a reagent that lacks the desirable qualities of a primary standard. A primary standard can then be used in a titration with the secondary standard to determine its concentration. Preparation of at least one standard solution is required to pass this AS. Preparing a Primary Standard 1 Do a calculation to find an exact mass that would give the desired concentration. It is almost impossible to weigh out this mass exactly - a mass close to the exact mass is weighed, and a calculation done to find out the actual concentration. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: 0XIDATION-REDUCTION PROCESSES Electrolysis - Aqueous Solutions Electrolysis is the use of electrical current to drive a non-spontaneous electrochemical reaction. A power supply provides a voltage that pulls electrons from species that would not otherwise give them up, and force them onto species that would not accept them otherwise. Electrolysis is important in the commercial production of many metals that occur as ions in their ores, and in oxidising halogen ions to form elemental chlorine, bromine and iodine. As with galvanic cells, the anode is the site of oxidation - anions lose electrons with a subsequent increase in oxidation number. The anode is therefore the positive electrode - it attracts anions and removes electrons from them. The electrodes are inert materials - usually carbon (graphite) or platinum. e- The cathode is the site of reduction - it is the negative electrode and it provides electrons to cations that are attracted to it. By accepting electrons the cations are reduced with a subsequent reduction in oxidation number. X+ Y- APPROXIMATE VOLUMES e- SILVERBACK SCIENTIFIC INSTRUMENTS 1. Colorimetry is limited to analysis of coloured compounds such as Fe3+ and Cu2+ ions, etc, although it is possible to undertake chemical reactions that create coloured substances from uncoloured ones. To be accurate, special equipment is needed to measure the strength of the colour. Without colorimeters, the test is limited to subjective analysis such as no colour, weak colour, strong colour etc, which is not suitably accurate for the purposes of this standard. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ANALYTICAL TECHNIQUES Gravimetric Analysis Gravimetry involves calculating the concentration or amount of a substance in a sample by measuring mass. A simple example would be the determination of total solids in a sample of river water by evaporating off the water (and other volatiles) and weighing the residue. The mass of the residue divided by the mass of the water sample (×100) would give a percentage of dissolved solids. More complicated analyses may involve the precipitation of ions in solution, filtration, dessication and weighing. Once again, the mass or volume of the aqueous sample can be used to calculate the concentration of the ions in solution. Gravimetric analysis allows for very precise analysis if methods are simple and followed correctly. It does not require preparation of a series of standards and does not require expensive equipment. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECTROSCOPY Infrared Spectra IR spectra are produced by placing a sample of the compound to be investigated in a machine called an IR spectrometer (or IR photospectrometer). IR light is shone through the sample, and the amount of each frequency that is transmitted through the sample is measured. Frequencies that pass through the sample are recorded as having a high percentage transmission. Frequencies that are absorbed by interaction with covalent bonds show up as troughs on the spectrum because a lesser amount of that frequency is transmitted through the sample. Note that it is conventional to call troughs on spectra “peaks”. An example of an IR spectrum is shown below: Infrared Absorption Spectrum - Methanol % Transmittance 100 50 OH 0 4000 3000 2000 1500 1000 500 Wavenumber (cm-1­) The left-hand side of spectra (above 1 500 cm-1) is called the diagnostic side. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECTROSCOPY Infrared Spectroscopy Spectroscopy is the study of the interaction between matter and radiated energy. Infrared (IR) spectroscopy exploits the interaction between light in the infrared part of the spectrum and the bonds between atoms in molecules. IR spectroscopy is of particular use in identifying types of bonds, and therefore functional groups, present in organic molecules. Covalent bonds behave like springs. They are not rigid connections; bonds are able to bend and stretch, and like springs they are able to absorb energy. Bonds Bending Bonds Stretching There are other ways that bonds may bend and stretch. These examples are indicative only. IR light with a frequency close to the vibrational frequency of a particular bond will be ‘absorbed’ by the bond as the bond begins to bend and/or stretch. Because molecules can bend, stretch and vibrate, the same bond can give more than one ‘signal’ on infrared spectra. Because stretching usually gives a sharper and stronger ‘peak’, and at higher frequencies, it is these that are mostly used for identifying the type of bonds present. It is important to note that IR spectroscopy uses wavenumber (v (cm-1)) rather than using frequency (f (Hz or s-1)) or wavelength (λ (m)). uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: ANALYTICAL TECHNIQUES Preparation of Standard Solutions A standard solution is a solution in which the concentration of a reagent is known to a high degree of accuracy. They may be used in titrations, gravimetric and colorimetric analyses. A primary standard is prepared by adding a weighed amount of a reactant that is stable - for example, it does not oxidise in air and does not decompose in sunlight, can be obtained as a pure substance, does not absorb water (not hygroscopic) or carbon dioxide from the air, and ideally has a high molecular weight. The amount added and the volume can be used to calculate the concentration of the reagent accurately. A secondary standard can be prepared in a similar manner, but from a reagent that lacks the desirable qualities of a primary standard. A primary standard can then be used in a titration with the secondary standard to determine its concentration. Preparation of at least one standard solution is required to pass this AS. Preparing a Primary Standard 1 Do a calculation to find an exact mass that would give the desired concentration. It is almost impossible to weigh out this mass exactly - a mass close to the exact mass is weighed, and a calculation done to find out the actual concentration. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECTROSCOPY Mass Spectra of Organic Molecules Mass spectra of organic molecules generally show a number of peaks. The peak with the highest m/z ratio will be that caused by the molecular ion (M+). The presence of isotopes such as 35Cl/37Cl and 79Br/81Br, where the abundance of both isotopes is high, may show as two peaks at the upper end of the m/z ratios. Molecular ions are unstable and it is common to see spectra showing taller peaks for the fragments they separate into than the peak caused by the molecular ion itself. Fragments of the molecule may show up as a number of closely grouped peaks separated in their m/z ratio because of the presence of isotopes, or the removal of a hydrogen atom from the fragment (lower m/z than expected). To determine the structure of the fragment, generally only the highest peak in the cluster is considered. The easiest way to determine what fragment has created the peak, ‘separate’ the molecule into two fragments at a C-C bond and calculate the mass of the various fragment. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECTROSCOPY Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy Any nucleus with an odd mass number or atomic number has a property called nuclear spin. These nuclei behave like tiny magnets, and in most situations they will have a random alignment of their magnetic fields. When an external magnetic field is applied to the atoms, the nuclei’s magnetic field will align with the external field. Most will align their magnetic field with the external field, but a small percentage will (mis)align their field in the opposite direction. No Magnetic Field External Magnetic Field Applied Key Direction of magnetic field Spinning nucleus The aligned state is the lower energy state. The higher energy, misaligned nuclei may be ‘flipped’ into the lower energy state by absorbing electromagnetic radiation. The frequency required to ‘flip’ the nuclei is called the resonance frequency (hence the term NMR), and varies according to the type of atom and the type of atom(s) that they are bonded to. NMR is especially useful in analysing organic compounds because of the presence of 1H and 13C in organic molecules. 13C NMR is able to measure the number of chemical environments that 13C atoms have in a compound. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: SPECTROSCOPY Mass Spectroscopy Mass spectrometry is a technique used to help determine the composition of unknown compounds. The compound is placed in the mass spectrometer, vaporised and bombarded with high energy electrons. These electrons ‘knock’ electrons off of molecules of the compound, forming positive ions called carbocations. The high energy electrons may also fragment the molecule, with the fragments also having electrons removed forming positive ions. The positive ions are accelerated towards a magnetic field which deflects the ‘beam’ of particles into a detector. The amount of deflection depends upon the mass of the particle (heavy particles deflect less than lighter particles), and the charge on the particle (higher positive charge causes higher deflection). Note that charges higher than +1 are rare and usually ignored by the detector. A mass spectrum is a graph of relative abundance vs. the ratio of mass to charge (m/z). Mass spectra can be used to determine the ratio of isotopes of an element. For example, there are three naturally occurring isotopes of carbon, 12C, 13C and 14C. Their proportions in a pure sample of carbon are approximately 99%, 1% and trace respectively. Consider the following galvanic cell: External circuit KNO3(aq) Zn2+ + 2e- Cu2+ + 2e- Solution of Zn2+ ions APPROXIMATE VOLUMES Cu metal APPROXIMATE VOLUMES Zn Zn metal Zn2+/Zn and Cu2+/Cu are called redox couples. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: OXIDATION-REDUCTION PROCESSES Electrolysis - Molten Ionic Compounds Electrolysis requires ions to be free to move to the electrodes so that electron transfer may occur. Heating ionic substances until they become liquids frees the ions, and has important applications in industry. The Reduction of Aluminium from Molten Bauxite Carbon electrodes Power Supply 3-5 V Hundreds of thousands of amps are consumed. Carbon dioxide gas Molten aluminium oxide/cryolite Carbon lining Molten aluminium The Hall-Héroult Electrochemical Cell Unprocessed aluminium ore (bauxite) is washed with hot sodium hydroxide solution, NaOH(aq), under pressure. uploads/science/Scipad/Level 3 Chemistry.searchText: 0XIDATION-REDUCTION PROCESSES Electrolysis - Aqueous Solutions Electrolysis is the use of electrical current to drive a non-spontaneous electrochemical reaction. A power supply provides a voltage that pulls electrons from species that would not otherwise give them up, and force them onto species that would not accept them otherwise. Electrolysis is important in the commercial production of many metals that occur as ions in their ores, and in oxidising halogen ions to form elemental chlorine, bromine and iodine. As with galvanic cells, the anode is the site of oxidation - anions lose electrons with a subsequent increase in oxidation number. The anode is therefore the positive electrode - it attracts anions and removes electrons from them. The electrodes are inert materials - usually carbon (graphite) or platinum. e- The cathode is the site of reduction - it is the negative electrode and it provides electrons to cations that are attracted to it. By accepting electrons the cations are reduced with a subsequent reduction in oxidation number. X+ Y- APPROXIMATE VOLUMES e- SILVERBACK SCIENTIFIC INSTRUMENTS 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Mechanics/13 - Po.searchText: POWER, WORK AND ENERGY Calculating Gravitational Potential Energy When an object is lifted up against the force of gravity it gains gravitational potential energy. For example, if you place a cup on a shelf you have to do work against the force of gravity. The cup has gained gravitational potential energy. The amount of gravitational potential energy depends on its height above Earth and its mass. The cup and glasses on the two shelves have gravitational potential energy. The cup and glass on the top shelf have more gravitational potential energy than the glasses on the bottom because they are higher. The cup on the top shelf has more gravitational potential energy than the glass on the same shelf because it has more mass. The glasses on the bottom shelf have the same amount of gravitational potential energy because they have the same mass and are the same height above the Earth. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS What is Electricity? There are two types of electricity. When electrical charge gathers in one place it is known as static electricity (the word static means something that does not move). Charge that moves from one place to another is called current electricity (or usually just electricity). Electricity is caused by electrons, the particles that surround the nucleus of atoms. Each electron has a negative charge. An atom has an equal number of electrons and protons (positively charged particles in its nucleus), so atoms have no overall electrical charge. You can observe the effects of static electricity right now by rubbing a plastic pen in your hair. After a few seconds you can use the pen to pick up small pieces of torn paper. Static electricity is created when certain materials rub against each other and some of the electrons are transferred from one material to the other. If a material gains electrons it will have a negative charge. If a material loses electrons it will have a positive charge. Lightning is created when electrons move within a cloud. You may also have experienced static electricity after jumping on a trampoline or wearing a polar fleece garment that has just come out of the dryer. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Atomic Review Everything is made from atoms, including you. Atoms are tiny particles that are far too small to see, even with a microscope. If people were the same size as atoms, the entire population of the world could stand on the point of a pin! Atoms are made up of 3 main types of particles: electrons, protons and neutrons. These particles have different properties. Electrons are tiny particles that have a negative electrical charge (-). They surround around the centre of the atom. Protons are much larger and heavier than electrons and have the opposite charge. Protons have a positive charge (+). Neutrons are large and have a similar mass to protons. However, neutrons have no electrical charge (0). The nucleus is at the centre of the atom and contains the protons and neutrons. Virtually all the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus, because electrons have very little mass. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Electrons - A Review All atoms are neutral, as they have the same number of electrons and protons. Therefore, the positive and negative charges are balanced and cancel each other out, giving an overall charge of 0. An object becomes positively charged if it has more protons than electrons and negatively charged if it has more electrons than protons. But what’s moving to produce the charge imbalance? The protons are locked in the nucleus and are not easily released from the atom. However, electrons exist in shells relatively far from the nucleus and can be moved from atom to atom. Therefore, electrons are the particle which moves to charge an object. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Mechanics/08 - Fo.searchText: FORCES Force, Mass and Acceleration The amount of force acting on an object can be calculated using its mass and its acceleration. In simple terms, if a car and a bus were accelerating at the same rate, the bus would have a greater force acting on it (think about it hitting the wall) than the car, because the bus has a greater mass. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Electrostatic Painting Electrostatic painting is a method that is widely used to coat metal objects. It is used to paint cars, metal fences, gates, office furniture and many other metal objects. Electrostatic painting uses a special spray gun. The spray gun nozzle gives the paint droplets a negative charge. The object being painted is given a positive charge. The opposite charges of the paint droplets and the metal create an attractive force. This means the paint is drawn towards the metal object, rather than being blown around the surrounding area. The advantages of this technique over traditional painting methods include less wastage, a more even coverage of paint and no paint drips on the painted object. The attractive force means that the paint droplets are pulled into all the gaps and hard-to-reach regions of the object, minimising time consuming work and ensuring that the finished product has a smooth, even coverage. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Charging with Friction The most common way in which electrically neutral objects become charged is by friction. Charging by friction involves two objects rubbing against each other. Electrons are scraped off one of the objects and transferred to the other object. The object that gains electrons becomes negatively charged and the object that loses electrons gains an equally positive charge. These charges are called static charge. The example below involves rubbing a glass rod with a silk cloth. During rubbing Electrons from the glass rod are removed and deposited on the silk cloth. This means that both the rod and the cloth have an imbalance of charge. After rubbing The cloth has more electrons than protons and ends up negatively charged. The rod has more protons than electrons and ends up positively charged. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Electrical Discharge - Earthing (Grounding) A build-up of electrical charge is dangerous as it can lead to electrical shocks, sparks and fires. A common method of stopping the build-up of charge is to ‘earth’ the object. Earthing is the process whereby a pathway is provided so that excess electrons can flow to the ground or, conversely, electrons from the ground can flow to the object to cancel out any excess of positive charge. Since the Earth has such a massive number of charges, these excess charges do not make a noticeable difference to the Earth’s overall charge. A useful analogy is to imagine the effect of earthing like pouring a cup of water into the ocean. Earthing is also used as a safety mechanism for current electricity. Houses are earthed by metal rods pushed into the ground. If there is a fault with an electrical appliance the excess electricity flows down this rod and safely into the ground. A New Zealand power plug has three pins, although some appliances only use the top two. The bottom/third pin is for safety and is connected to the Earth. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: CURRENT ELECTRICITY Understanding Current When lamps are placed in closed circuits they will glow, but in open circuits they won’t. The reason for this is that the charges require a closed loop so that they can flow from one terminal of the power source to the other. In the electrostatics unit you learnt that the charges that are able to move are electrons. Each electron that flows around the circuit has a very small amount of charge. The amount of charge that passes a certain point per second is defined as current. Scientists express the relationship between charge and current with the following formula. I=Q/t I = Q = t = current (Amperes, A) charge (Coulomb, C) time (seconds, s) 1 C = 6.24 x 18 10 electr ons From the formula, we can see that 1 Ampere is 1 Coulomb flowing through a circuit in 1 second. Early investigators into electrical current decided that because one terminal of a power supply seemed to have an excess of charge, it should be labelled “+ve”. They did not know that the charge-carrying particle was the negatively charged electron. Only later was it discovered that electrons were flowing from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. Today, we still use the ‘old’ idea that current is travelling from positive to negative, and call this “conventional current”. 1. Define the term ‘electrical current’.   The amount of charge flowing past a point  per second.

uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: CURRENT ELECTRICITY Understanding Voltage Voltage (or potential difference) is a measure of the amount of electrical energy changed (∆E) to other forms of energy by one unit of charge (coulomb) as it moves between two positions. 10 V 10 V The voltage source (battery/power-pack) raises the electrical potential energy of the electrons (that are distributed evenly and everywhere within the circuit). However, no work can be done to the electrons (i.e. they can't be moved) unless there is a difference in electrical potential energy. 10 V 5V Kinetic energy + Heat There is now a difference in voltage in the wire. Because of this, all the electrons move at the same time from an area of high electrical potential energy to an area of lower electrical potential energy. This potential difference can be measured (in volts (V)) using a voltmeter. The voltmeter measures the electric potential energy of electrons before and after a component. For example, in a light bulb, voltmeters measure the electrical energy (per coulomb) changed to heat and light. Therefore, voltmeters must be connected in parallel to the component to be able to record the difference. Scientists express this relationship with the following formula: V = ∆E / q V = Voltage (volts , V) ∆E = Change in Potential Energy (joules , J) q = Charge (coulombs, C) 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: CURRENT ELECTRICITY Properties of Lamps Lamps are a very commonly assessed electrical component in NCEA exams. Shorting lamps, brightness, and blowing bulbs are all important contexts. Shorting Lamps: Placing a wire in parallel with a lamp shorts it (creates a short circuit). This means that all the current flows along the wire and bypasses the lamp. Since no current flows through the lamp, it uses no voltage and does not glow. Brightness: Lamps convert electrical energy to light energy. A bright lamp will convert more energy than a dim lamp. The rate which a component transforms energy is called power. Therefore, to determine if one lamp is brighter than another, you must figure out which lamp has the greatest power. Blowing Bulbs: Lamps are designed to operate at a certain voltage. They can handle a small percentage higher voltage (20% more will generally work), but once that margin is exceeded the bulb will burn out. With most bulbs this means the filament has melted. 1. When current flows through the coils a magnetic field is set up, such that the  right hand side becomes a north pole and the left hand side is a south pole.  Due to the north pole that is created at the right end, the reed attached to  the right also becomes magnetised, with a north at its right end and a south at  its left end. The south pole at the left end caused the reed attached to the  left end to also become magnetised (north at its right end and a south at its  left end). However, the two reeds overlap such that the north pole of the left  reed is directly opposite the south pole of the right reed. This means they are  attracted to each other and the switch closes.       Electronic Door Locks A lot of modern security systems use electronic door locks.
