uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS What is Electricity? There are two types of electricity. When electrical charge gathers in one place it is known as static electricity (the word static means something that does not move). Charge that moves from one place to another is called current electricity (or usually just electricity). Electricity is caused by electrons, the particles that surround the nucleus of atoms. Each electron has a negative charge. An atom has an equal number of electrons and protons (positively charged particles in its nucleus), so atoms have no overall electrical charge. You can observe the effects of static electricity right now by rubbing a plastic pen in your hair. After a few seconds you can use the pen to pick up small pieces of torn paper. Static electricity is created when certain materials rub against each other and some of the electrons are transferred from one material to the other. If a material gains electrons it will have a negative charge. If a material loses electrons it will have a positive charge. Lightning is created when electrons move within a cloud. You may also have experienced static electricity after jumping on a trampoline or wearing a polar fleece garment that has just come out of the dryer. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Electrostatic Painting Electrostatic painting is a method that is widely used to coat metal objects. It is used to paint cars, metal fences, gates, office furniture and many other metal objects. Electrostatic painting uses a special spray gun. The spray gun nozzle gives the paint droplets a negative charge. The object being painted is given a positive charge. The opposite charges of the paint droplets and the metal create an attractive force. This means the paint is drawn towards the metal object, rather than being blown around the surrounding area. The advantages of this technique over traditional painting methods include less wastage, a more even coverage of paint and no paint drips on the painted object. The attractive force means that the paint droplets are pulled into all the gaps and hard-to-reach regions of the object, minimising time consuming work and ensuring that the finished product has a smooth, even coverage. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS The Gold-Leaf Electroscope In 1787 physicist Abraham Bennet developed an instrument to measure the presence and strength of charge. This instrument is called the ‘Gold-Leaf Electroscope’ and is still used today. When the cap is touched with a charged object, the charge flows down the metal stem and the gold leaf. Since both conductors will have an excess of the same type of charge, the repulsion between like charges causes the gold leaf to be deflected from the end of the rod. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Electrical Discharge - Earthing (Grounding) A build-up of electrical charge is dangerous as it can lead to electrical shocks, sparks and fires. A common method of stopping the build-up of charge is to ‘earth’ the object. Earthing is the process whereby a pathway is provided so that excess electrons can flow to the ground or, conversely, electrons from the ground can flow to the object to cancel out any excess of positive charge. Since the Earth has such a massive number of charges, these excess charges do not make a noticeable difference to the Earth’s overall charge. A useful analogy is to imagine the effect of earthing like pouring a cup of water into the ocean. Earthing is also used as a safety mechanism for current electricity. Houses are earthed by metal rods pushed into the ground. If there is a fault with an electrical appliance the excess electricity flows down this rod and safely into the ground. A New Zealand power plug has three pins, although some appliances only use the top two. The bottom/third pin is for safety and is connected to the Earth. The reason for this is that the charges require a closed loop so that they can flow from one terminal of the power source to the other. In the electrostatics unit you learnt that the charges that are able to move are electrons. Each electron that flows around the circuit has a very small amount of charge. The amount of charge that passes a certain point per second is defined as current. Scientists express the relationship between charge and current with the following formula. Early investigators into electrical current decided that because one terminal of a power supply seemed to have an excess of charge, it should be labelled “+ve”. They did not know that the charge-carrying particle was the negatively charged electron. Only later was it discovered that electrons were flowing from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: CURRENT ELECTRICITY Understanding Voltage Voltage (or potential difference) is a measure of the amount of electrical energy changed (∆E) to other forms of energy by one unit of charge (coulomb) as it moves between two positions. 10 V 10 V The voltage source (battery/power-pack) raises the electrical potential energy of the electrons (that are distributed evenly and everywhere within the circuit). However, no work can be done to the electrons (i.e. they can't be moved) unless there is a difference in electrical potential energy. 10 V 5V Kinetic energy + Heat There is now a difference in voltage in the wire. Because of this, all the electrons move at the same time from an area of high electrical potential energy to an area of lower electrical potential energy. This potential difference can be measured (in volts (V)) using a voltmeter. The voltmeter measures the electric potential energy of electrons before and after a component. For example, in a light bulb, voltmeters measure the electrical energy (per coulomb) changed to heat and light. Therefore, voltmeters must be connected in parallel to the component to be able to record the difference. Scientists express this relationship with the following formula: V = ∆E / q V = Voltage (volts , V) ∆E = Change in Potential Energy (joules , J) q = Charge (coulombs, C) 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: CURRENT ELECTRICITY Properties of Lamps Lamps are a very commonly assessed electrical component in NCEA exams. Shorting lamps, brightness, and blowing bulbs are all important contexts. Shorting Lamps: Placing a wire in parallel with a lamp shorts it (creates a short circuit). This means that all the current flows along the wire and bypasses the lamp. Since no current flows through the lamp, it uses no voltage and does not glow. Brightness: Lamps convert electrical energy to light energy. A bright lamp will convert more energy than a dim lamp. The rate which a component transforms energy is called power. Therefore, to determine if one lamp is brighter than another, you must figure out which lamp has the greatest power. Blowing Bulbs: Lamps are designed to operate at a certain voltage. They can handle a small percentage higher voltage (20% more will generally work), but once that margin is exceeded the bulb will burn out. With most bulbs this means the filament has melted. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Mechanics/09 - Fr.searchText: FORCES Friction Friction is a force that occurs when an object moves, or tries to move, against another object or fluid. Friction often acts to oppose (prevent or stop) the movement of an object. Friction can generate heat, causes wear and tear, and slow moving objects down. The effects of friction can be reduced if the surfaces of the two materials are lubricated (with water or oil, etc). Friction can be increased by making one or more of the surfaces rougher or by pressing them together more strongly. 1. 2. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.3 Elect.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Bar Magnets Magnets are made from magnetic materials. These are metals that can be magnetised or will be attracted to a magnet. Most metals are not magnetic, but iron, cobalt and nickel are. Steel is mostly iron, so steel is magnetic too. Bar magnets are permanent magnets. This means that their magnetism is there all the time and cannot be turned on or off. They have two poles; north pole (or north-seeking pole, usually shown with an ‘N’) and a south pole (or south-seeking pole, usually shown with an ‘S’). All bar magnets have similar properties: • North poles are attracted to south poles. • North poles will repel north poles. • South poles will repel south poles. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Refraction Ever noticed how a drinking straw appears to bend in two when it's viewed in a glass filled with water? This is due to refraction. Refraction occurs because light changes speed when it moves from one medium into another. Medium is the word used by scientists to describe any region that allows waves to travel through it. Air, water and glass are all different mediums. Each allows waves to travel through them, but with varying amounts of ease. How easily light can travel through a medium depends on its optical density. If the medium is more optically dense the light travels slower, and vice versa. The straw appears bent because the light travels faster through air than through water. Because it slows down as it enters the liquid, the light bends towards the normal. Investigating Refraction – Bending Light Aim: To investigate how light is affected by changing the substance it is travelling through. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Lateral Inversion In the previous experiment it was shown that when you wave your right hand at a mirror, the image waves back with its left hand. This is known as lateral inversion (‘lateral’ comes from the Latin word for ‘side’ and ‘invert’ comes from the word for ‘reverse’). When you wave the hand that is on the right side of the mirror, the image also waves back with its hand that is on the mirror’s right side. This can be explained by using the ‘apparent depth backtracking method’ from both ends of the submerged object. If the observer is looking at the object from an angle, the rays from the front and the back of submerged object must travel at different angles to reach the observer's eye. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: LIGHT What is Light? Light is a form of energy called electromagnetic radiation. Electromagnetic radiation occurs as waves and includes visible light, invisible light (such as infrared and ultraviolet), x-rays, microwaves and radio waves. The components of visible light can be memorised by using the mnemonic ROYGBIV: an abbreviation of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. ROYGBIV also helps you to remember the wavelength of the different colours. Red has the longest wavelength and these decrease in order through to violet which has the smallest wavelength. Light has properties that are responsible for the phenomena that will be studied in this course. These properties are: • Light travels in straight lines. • Light travels at 300 000 000 m s-1 (3 x 108 m s-1) in a vacuum. • Light can travel through a vacuum (empty space). The difference between waves and other forms of energy transfer is that the energy moves from one place to another without any transfer of matter. An example of this is a singer at a concert. The singer’s voice creates sound waves that the concert-goers hear. However, when hearing the music, they do not receive the original particles that were in contact with the singer’s voice box. The sound energy has been transferred without the particles travelling to the listener’s ears. 1. Mechanical waves require a medium to travel through such as water, air, glass or earth. Therefore, transverse waves oscillate particles 90° to the direction the waves are travelling. An easy way to visualise a transverse wave is to think of it as a piece of string. Without a wave travelling along it, the string lies in a straight line. This is called the equilibrium position. When a wave travels along the string it oscillates (moves back and forth at a regular speed). The highest point of the wave is called the crest or peak. The lowest point of the wave is called the trough. The wavelength (symbol = l) of the wave is the distance it takes for the wave to repeat itself. This can be found by either measuring the distance between successive peaks or the distance between successive troughs. Wavelength is measured in metres (m). The amplitude (symbol = A) is the maximum distance moved from the equilibrium position. It can be measured above (crest) or below (trough) the equilibrium position. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: WAVES Longitudinal Waves The particles in longitudinal waves vibrate/oscillate parallel to the direction the wave is moving. As the oscillations are parallel to the wave direction, the particles can be moving in the same direction as the wave, as well as in the opposite direction. Since longitudinal waves have particles that oscillate backwards and forwards, the wave has regions where the particles are squashed up and other regions where the particles are spread out. The squashed-up regions are called compressions and the spread regions are called rarefactions. The distance between successive compressions or successive rarefactions is the wavelength (symbol = l) of a longitudinal wave. Sound waves and the primary waves created by earthquakes (seismic waves) are longitudinal. 1. Label the diagram below using the following words. Some words may be used more than once. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: WAVES Musical Instruments Musical instruments are designed to create sound waves at varying frequencies/pitches. The interaction between the instrument and the surrounding air particles is important. It is this that allows the sound to travel from the instrument to the listener at the desired frequency. Sound waves are longitudinal. Air particles need to squash up (compressions) at certain times and spread out (rarefactions) at other times. To do that the air particles are oscillated parallel to the direction that they travel. The oscillation of air particles is driven by the musical instrument. When the instrument’s vibration moves in the same direction as the wave is travelling, the air particles are pushed together, forming compressions. When the instrument’s vibration moves in the opposite direction to the wave’s travel, the air particles become spread out, and rarefactions are formed. Since the direction of the instrument’s vibration/oscillation creates the compressions and rarefactions in the air, the frequency of the sound waves is identical to the frequency of the musical instrument. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: LIGHT What is Light? Light is a form of energy called electromagnetic radiation. Electromagnetic radiation occurs as waves and includes visible light, invisible light (such as infrared and ultraviolet), x-rays, microwaves and radio waves. The components of visible light can be memorised by using the mnemonic ROYGBIV: an abbreviation of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. ROYGBIV also helps you to remember the wavelength of the different colours. Red has the longest wavelength and these decrease in order through to violet which has the smallest wavelength. Light has properties that are responsible for the phenomena that will be studied in this course. These properties are: • Light travels in straight lines. • Light travels at 300 000 000 m s-1 (3 x 108 m s-1) in a vacuum. • Light can travel through a vacuum (empty space). Reflection is easily seen in mirrors because they have smooth, shiny surfaces. When a light ray hits a smooth surface it bounces off in a predictable direction. To measure the angle of incidence (the angle that light is hitting a mirror) a line is drawn 90° to the surface of the mirror. This line is called the normal line. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Refraction Ever noticed how a drinking straw appears to bend in two when it's viewed in a glass filled with water? This is due to refraction. Refraction occurs because light changes speed when it moves from one medium into another. Medium is the word used by scientists to describe any region that allows waves to travel through it. Air, water and glass are all different mediums. Each allows waves to travel through them, but with varying amounts of ease. How easily light can travel through a medium depends on its optical density. If the medium is more optically dense the light travels slower, and vice versa. The straw appears bent because the light travels faster through air than through water. Because it slows down as it enters the liquid, the light bends towards the normal. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Magnification With Refraction As well as appearing shallower than they really are, images of submerged objects often appear larger. This can be explained by using the ‘apparent depth backtracking method’ from both ends of the submerged object. If the observer is looking at the object from an angle, the rays from the front and the back of submerged object must travel at different angles to reach the observer's eye. Rays from the back of the object travel a 'flatter' path than those from the front. When the brain 'backtracks' these rays, the back rays must travel a further horizontal distance. This increased distance results in the image appearing larger, as well as shallower, than the actual object. 1. Sarah is fishing with her friends when she hooks a snapper. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Using Total Internal Reflection - Fibre Optics An optic fibre is a thin fibre of glass or plastic that carries light from one end to the other. The study of optical fibres is called fibre optics. Optical fibres enable the transmission of large amounts of information over greater distances at quicker speeds than traditional copper wires. An optical fibre is a long, flexible, transparent cable of a very small diameter. When light is shone in one end it is totally internally reflected (no light escapes or bounces backwards) along its entire length, until it emerges at the end. Light ray exits optic fibre Light is totally internally reflected along optic fibre Light ray enters optic fibre Fibre-optic cable contains the optical fibre in the centre. This optical fibre is usually made of glass or plastic with a low optical density. Around the core is a layer called the cladding. If the cladding of the fibre is scratched, the fibre may break. A plastic coating called the buffer covers the cladding to protect it. Often, the buffered fibre is put inside an even tougher layer, called the jacket. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: WAVES What is a Wave? Waves are a regular pattern of disturbance. They transfer energy from one position to another. The difference between waves and other forms of energy transfer is that the energy moves from one place to another without any transfer of matter. An example of this is a singer at a concert. The singer’s voice creates sound waves that the concert-goers hear. However, when hearing the music, they do not receive the original particles that were in contact with the singer’s voice box. The sound energy has been transferred without the particles travelling to the listener’s ears. 1. 2. Light Waves Mechanical Waves Light waves belong to a special type of wave called electromagnetic radiation. These are special because they are able to travel through a vacuum. Not all light waves can be seen and include things like infrared and x-rays. Mechanical waves include sound, water and seismic waves, and are the waves that people are the most familiar with. Mechanical waves require a medium to travel through such as water, air, glass or earth. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: WAVES Transverse Waves The word ‘trans’ means across. Therefore, transverse waves oscillate particles 90° to the direction the waves are travelling. An easy way to visualise a transverse wave is to think of it as a piece of string. Without a wave travelling along it, the string lies in a straight line. This is called the equilibrium position. When a wave travels along the string it oscillates (moves back and forth at a regular speed). The highest point of the wave is called the crest or peak. The lowest point of the wave is called the trough. The wavelength (symbol = l) of the wave is the distance it takes for the wave to repeat itself. This can be found by either measuring the distance between successive peaks or the distance between successive troughs. Wavelength is measured in metres (m). The amplitude (symbol = A) is the maximum distance moved from the equilibrium position. It can be measured above (crest) or below (trough) the equilibrium position. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: WAVES Longitudinal Waves The particles in longitudinal waves vibrate/oscillate parallel to the direction the wave is moving. As the oscillations are parallel to the wave direction, the particles can be moving in the same direction as the wave, as well as in the opposite direction. Since longitudinal waves have particles that oscillate backwards and forwards, the wave has regions where the particles are squashed up and other regions where the particles are spread out. The squashed-up regions are called compressions and the spread regions are called rarefactions. The distance between successive compressions or successive rarefactions is the wavelength (symbol = l) of a longitudinal wave. Sound waves and the primary waves created by earthquakes (seismic waves) are longitudinal. 1. Label the diagram below using the following words. Some words may be used more than once. Amplitude 2. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.4 Waves.searchText: WAVES Musical Instruments Musical instruments are designed to create sound waves at varying frequencies/pitches. The interaction between the instrument and the surrounding air particles is important. It is this that allows the sound to travel from the instrument to the listener at the desired frequency. Sound waves are longitudinal. Air particles need to squash up (compressions) at certain times and spread out (rarefactions) at other times. To do that the air particles are oscillated parallel to the direction that they travel. The oscillation of air particles is driven by the musical instrument. When the instrument’s vibration moves in the same direction as the wave is travelling, the air particles are pushed together, forming compressions. When the instrument’s vibration moves in the opposite direction to the wave’s travel, the air particles become spread out, and rarefactions are formed. Since the direction of the instrument’s vibration/oscillation creates the compressions and rarefactions in the air, the frequency of the sound waves is identical to the frequency of the musical instrument. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Heat Transfer Heating an object describes the process by which thermal (thermal means ‘heat’) energy is transferred to that object. It is important to remember that heat can only move from a hot object to a cold object, not the other way around. If the heating is positive, then the heat energy is being added to the object and it will become hotter, and may change state. The hot gas from the Bunsen burner is transferring heat to the test tube, which in turn is transferring heat to the liquid through the glass. If the heating is negative, then the heat energy is being removed from the object and it cools down (becomes colder). It may also change to a lower energy state. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Conduction Questions 1. Jimmy walks around his house barefoot first thing in the morning. When he walks on the carpet the floor feels warmer than when he walks on the tiles, despite the temperature of the two surfaces being the same. Explain why this happens. The tiles are a thermal conductor. Heat flows from Jimmy’s feet into the tiles and makes Jimmy’s feet feel cold. However, the carpet is a thermal insulator which means that heat is not drawn away from Jimmy’s feet and the carpet feels warmer. 2. Performance sports shirts are designed to draw sweat away from the body. Use the appropriate physics theory to explain why this is an advantage when running. Sweat cannot evaporate when it is against the body and covered with a shirt that prevents air-flow. Some types of sports shirts draw sweat from the body and distribute it evenly on the surface of the shirt where air-flow can evaporate it and cool down the person doing exercise. 3. Robert wants to remove a hot tray from the oven. Would he be better to use the wet dishcloth or an identical dry dish-cloth? Explain your answer. The dry cloth is full of air holes, and air is a thermal insulator, which will protect Robert’s hands when he lifts the hot tray. In a wet cloth the air holes are replaced with water which is a better thermal conductor. This means that Robert will burn his hands when he picks up the hot tray.

uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Radiation Radiation is able to transfer heat energy without involving particles of matter. The most obvious example of heat transfer via radiation is the Sun. Nuclear reactions within the Sun give off large amounts of energy that travels through space (a vacuum) as radiation. When this radiation strikes an object, energy is either absorbed, partially absorbed, reflected or partially reflected. Absorption of the radiation increases the thermal energy of the object and causes its temperature to increase. Whether a surface will absorb or reflect radiation is due to the type of radiation, and the colour and shininess of the surface. Dull, dark objects are very good at absorbing radiation, which is the reason why solar panels and portable camping showers are black. Shiny, bright surfaces reflect radiation, which is the reason why it is better to wear light-coloured shirts in the summer. Reflective, shiny surfaces are useful when trying to minimise the heat absorbed from radiation. Note: It is important to realise that radiation does not just occur in the Sun. All objects radiate energy. Black surfaces are not only the best absorbers of radiation, they are also the best emitters of radiation (white shiny objects are poor emitters of radiation). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Convection Unlike conduction, where the atoms and particles remain stationary, convection occurs when the particles are free to move (i.e. they are fluid). This means that the object must either be a liquid or a gas. When a fluid’s particles are heated, they gain kinetic energy. This causes them to move faster and further apart. If some regions of a fluid become less dense then those particles rise upwards. The region will become more dense and move downwards as it cools down. This difference in density is the main reason why thermal energy is able to be transferred from one area to another in liquids and gases. Convection currents are the most common example of convection that people are familiar with. They are responsible for a wide range of phenomena, from an oil heater warming a room to the tectonic plates moving, and the occurrence of sea breezes. It was originally devised by Sir James Dewar for storing liquefied gases at a very low temperature. The nature of heat transfer means that the substance contained in a vacuum flask remains at its temperature for much longer than if it were in an ordinary vessel. It does this by reducing heat transfer via all three heat transfer methods. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Types of Heat Transfer There are three methods by which heat energy can be transferred from one region to another. These are: conduction, convection and radiation. Conduction Conduction is a term used to describe the flow of heat through an object. As heat energy flows the particles themselves do not change position. This is most easily explained by considering a solid metal rod. 1 Particles inside a solid object vibrate in a fixed position. When the heating process begins, the particles closest to the heat source gain kinetic energy and vibrate more vigorously. These more energetic particles collide with unheated particles, passing some of their kinetic energy on and causing those particles to also start vibrating more vigorously. HEAT 2 The process of particles colliding continues along the metal rod. In this way the heat energy is transferred from the hot end of the rod to the cold end, until the entire rod is hot. An object’s ability to transfer heat energy via conduction depends of the properties of the object. Metals allow conduction to occur easily and are called thermal conductors. This is the reason why most cooking utensils are made of metal. Objects that resist conduction are called thermal insulators. Some examples of these are plastic, wood and air. These are the materials that are used to make handles on frying pans, soldering irons, etc. Conduction

uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: EFFECTS OF HEATING Sublimation Some substances change directly from a solid state to a gaseous state without changing to a liquid. This process is called sublimation. The opposite process, where a gas changes directly to a solid, is deposition. Common examples of substances which undergo sublimation and deposition are carbon dioxide (dry ice), iodine and naphthalene. Naphthalene is an active ingredient in mothballs, and the change of state from solid to gas is useful for the fumigation of moths that attack clothing. Subliming means that the moths are eradicated without making clothes damp or marking them. Sublimation is also the reason why iodine can be used to lift fingerprints off paper. If the change of state of iodine included a liquid transition, the paper would become wet and the fingerprints would be damaged. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Heat Transfer Heating an object describes the process by which thermal (thermal means ‘heat’) energy is transferred to that object. It is important to remember that heat can only move from a hot object to a cold object, not the other way around. If the heating is positive, then the heat energy is being added to the object and it will become hotter, and may change state. The hot gas from the Bunsen burner is transferring heat to the test tube, which in turn is transferring heat to the liquid through the glass. If the heating is negative, then the heat energy is being removed from the object and it cools down (becomes colder). It may also change to a lower energy state. Thermal Energy Transfer when Evaporating Methylated Spirits Method: Add a few drops of methylated spirits to the underside of your wrist and observe what happens. Methylated spirits Put a few drops of methylated spirits on the underside of your wrist. Conclusion: Outline • What you observed. • The direction the heat has moved. • How your senses provide evidence for the direction. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Radiation Radiation is able to transfer heat energy without involving particles of matter. The most obvious example of heat transfer via radiation is the Sun. Nuclear reactions within the Sun give off large amounts of energy that travels through space (a vacuum) as radiation. When this radiation strikes an object, energy is either absorbed, partially absorbed, reflected or partially reflected. Absorption of the radiation increases the thermal energy of the object and causes its temperature to increase. Whether a surface will absorb or reflect radiation is due to the type of radiation, and the colour and shininess of the surface. Dull, dark objects are very good at absorbing radiation, which is the reason why solar panels and portable camping showers are black. Shiny, bright surfaces reflect radiation, which is the reason why it is better to wear light-coloured shirts in the summer. Reflective, shiny surfaces are useful when trying to minimise the heat absorbed from radiation. Note: It is important to realise that radiation does not just occur in the Sun. All objects radiate energy. Black surfaces are not only the best absorbers of radiation, they are also the best emitters of radiation (white shiny objects are poor emitters of radiation). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Convection Unlike conduction, where the atoms and particles remain stationary, convection occurs when the particles are free to move (i.e. they are fluid). This means that the object must either be a liquid or a gas. When a fluid’s particles are heated, they gain kinetic energy. This causes them to move faster and further apart. If some regions of a fluid become less dense then those particles rise upwards. The region will become more dense and move downwards as it cools down. This difference in density is the main reason why thermal energy is able to be transferred from one area to another in liquids and gases. Convection currents are the most common example of convection that people are familiar with. They are responsible for a wide range of phenomena, from an oil heater warming a room to the tectonic plates moving, and the occurrence of sea breezes. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Types of Heat Transfer There are three methods by which heat energy can be transferred from one region to another. These are: conduction, convection and radiation. Conduction Conduction is a term used to describe the flow of heat through an object. As heat energy flows the particles themselves do not change position. This is most easily explained by considering a solid metal rod. 1 Particles inside a solid object vibrate in a fixed position. When the heating process begins, the particles closest to the heat source gain kinetic energy and vibrate more vigorously. These more energetic particles collide with unheated particles, passing some of their kinetic energy on and causing those particles to also start vibrating more vigorously. HEAT 2 The process of particles colliding continues along the metal rod. In this way the heat energy is transferred from the hot end of the rod to the cold end, until the entire rod is hot. An object’s ability to transfer heat energy via conduction depends of the properties of the object. Metals allow conduction to occur easily and are called thermal conductors. This is the reason why most cooking utensils are made of metal. Objects that resist conduction are called thermal insulators. Some examples of these are plastic, wood and air. This process is called sublimation. The opposite process, where a gas changes directly to a solid, is deposition. Common examples of substances which undergo sublimation and deposition are carbon dioxide (dry ice), iodine and naphthalene. Naphthalene is an active ingredient in mothballs, and the change of state from solid to gas is useful for the fumigation of moths that attack clothing. Subliming means that the moths are eradicated without making clothes damp or marking them. Sublimation is also the reason why iodine can be used to lift fingerprints off paper. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: EFFECTS OF HEATING Investigating Cooling Cooling curves are the opposite of heating curves. They have the same melting and boiling points as the heating curve for the same substance. Assuming the rate of cooling is the same as the rate of heating, the steepness of the gradients and length of flat regions of cooling curves are identical to that of the heating curve. Aim: To investigate how removing heat energy affects a substance. Equipment: 1 x 250 mL beaker 1 boiling tube 1 thermometer (0-100°C type) 1 stopwatch 1 hotplate 1 test tube rack Method: Risk of burning 15 g stearic acid 1. Fill a 250 mL beaker with 150 mL of water and place it on the hotplate. 2. Heat the water until it reaches 80°C, then adjust the hotplate so the water maintains that temperature. 3. Place the stearic acid in a boiling tube. Then put the boiling tube inside the heated 250 mL beaker. Leave it there until all of the stearic acid has melted. 4. Transfer the boiling tube of stearic acid from the beaker to a test tube rack. 5. Measure the temperature of the stearic acid every 30 seconds for 15 minutes. Do not stop recording the temperature if your stearic acid solidifies. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Components of Curved Mirror Reflection Concave Mirrors r Radius of curvature Focal point Pole P C F Principal axis Centre of curvature Focal length f When rays of light parallel to the principal axis hit a concave mirror, all rays of light are reflected into a single spot called the focal point (F). The focal point lies on the primary axis - an imaginary line that passes through the centre of the mirror. The position of the mirror that the principal axis passes through is called the pole (P). At the pole, the mirror can be thought of as a plane/flat mirror. The distance between the pole and focal point is called the focal length (f). If the curved mirror was extended it would eventually form a circle. At the centre of this circle is the centre of curvature (C). The radius of curvature (r) is measured from the centre of curvature to the pole. Halfway between the centre of curvature (C) and the mirror is the focal point, therefore C = 2f or alternatively r = 2f. A concave mirror has a real focal point (i.e. the rays of light actually pass through it). Convex Mirrors In order to determine the focal point and length, centre and radius of curvature, dotted lines (without arrows) are drawn inside the mirror to show the path of light. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Refraction Ever noticed how a drinking straw appears to bend in two when it's viewed in a glass filled with water? This is because of refraction. Refraction occurs because light changes speed when it moves from one medium into another. Medium is the word used by scientists to describe any region that allows waves to travel through it. Air, water and glass are all different mediums. Each allows waves to travel through them, but with varying amounts of ease. How easily light can travel through a medium depends on its optical density. If the medium is more optically dense the light travels slower, and vice versa. The straw appears bent because the light travels faster through air than through water. Because it slows down as it enters the liquid, the light bends towards the normal. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Magnification With Refraction As well as appearing shallower than they really are, images of submerged objects often appear larger. This can be explained by using the ‘apparent depth backtracking method’ from both ends of the submerged object. If the observer is looking at the object from an angle, the rays from the front and the back of the submerged object must travel at different angles to reach the observer's eye. Rays from the back of the object travel a 'flatter' path than those from the front. When the brain 'backtracks' these rays, the back rays must travel a further horizontal distance. This increased distance results in the image appearing larger, as well as shallower, than the actual object. 1. Sarah is fishing with her friends when she hooks a snapper. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: LIGHT What is Light? Light is a form of energy called electromagnetic radiation. Electromagnetic radiation occurs as waves and includes visible light, invisible light (such as infrared and ultraviolet), x-rays, microwaves and radio waves. The components of visible light can be memorised by using the mnemonic ROYGBIV: an abbreviation of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. ROYGBIV also helps you to remember the wavelength of the different colours. Red has the longest wavelength and these decrease in order through to violet which has the smallest wavelength. Light has properties that are responsible for the phenomena that will be studied in this course. These properties are: • Light travels in straight lines. • Light travels at 300 000 000 m s-1 (c = 3 x 108 m s-1) in a vacuum. • Light can travel through a vacuum (empty space). Speed of Light Light travels at approximately 300 000 000 m s-1 (metres per second) or 300 000 km s-1 (kilometres per second). This speed is almost unimaginable to us. If you were travelling by road at the speed of light it would take 0.0067 seconds to get from Cape Reinga (the top of the North Island) to Bluff (the bottom of the South Island). White light is made up of a whole range (or spectrum) of colours mixed together. We can see this spectrum if we pass white light through a glass prism (a triangular glass block). This rainbow of colours is called the ‘visible spectrum’. The visible spectrum contains the colours red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. The colours of the light spectrum are easy to remember if you recall ‘ROYGBIV’. The reason white light splits into the colours of the spectrum is because each colour is refracted (or bent) at slightly different amounts as it changes mediums. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES What is a Wave? Waves are a regular pattern of disturbance. They transfer energy from one position to another. The difference between waves and other forms of energy transfer is that the energy moves from one place to another without any transfer of matter. An example of this is a singer at a concert. The singer’s voice creates sound waves that the concert-goers hear. However, when hearing the music, they do not receive the original particles that were in contact with the singer’s voice box. The sound energy has been transferred without the particles travelling to the listeners’ ears. 1. Light Waves Mechanical Waves Light waves are a special type of wave called electromagnetic radiation. They are special because they are able to travel through a vacuum. Not all light waves are visible and include things such as infrared light and x-rays. Mechanical waves include sound, water and seismic waves, and are the waves that people are most familiar with. Mechanical waves require a medium to travel through such as water, air, glass or the earth. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Longitudinal Waves The particles in longitudinal waves vibrate/oscillate parallel to the direction the wave is moving. As the oscillations are parallel to the wave direction, the particles can be moving in the same direction as the wave, as well as in the opposite direction. Since longitudinal waves have particles that oscillate backwards and forwards, the wave has regions where the particles are squashed up and other regions where the particles are spread out. The squashed-up regions are called compressions and the spread regions are called rarefactions. The distance between successive compressions or successive rarefactions is the wavelength (symbol = l) of a longitudinal wave. Sound waves and the primary waves created by earthquakes (seismic waves) are longitudinal. 1. Label the diagram below using the following words. Some words may be used more than once. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.originalPath: uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves/Answers/069 - Transverse Waves - Answers.pdf
uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Transverse Waves The word ‘trans’ means across. Transverse waves oscillate particles at 90° to the direction the waves are travelling. An easy way to visualise a transverse wave is to think of it as a piece of string. Without a wave travelling along it, the string lies in a straight line. This is called the equilibrium position. When a wave travels along the string it oscillates (moves back and forth at a regular speed). The highest point of the wave is called the crest or peak. The lowest point of the wave is called the trough. When interference happens, positions where the wave is at the equilibrium position are called nodes, while troughs and peaks are known as antinodes. The wavelength (symbol = l) of the wave is the distance it takes for the wave to repeat itself. This can be found either by measuring the distance between successive peaks or the distance between successive troughs. Wavelength is measured in metres (m). The amplitude (symbol = A) is the maximum distance moved from the equilibrium position. It can be measured above (crest) or below (trough) the equilibrium position. Amplitude is measured in metres (m). 1. Label the diagram below using the following words. Some words may be used more than once. Transmission can also be thought of as refraction since the transmitted wave experiences a change in speed. Moving from a Less Dense to a More Dense Medium When the pulse moves from a less dense to a more dense medium, the boundary will act in a similar manner to a fixed boundary - the reflected pulse will experience a phase change. The amplitude of the reflected portion is less than the amplitude of the incident wave as some of the energy from the pulse has been taken by the transmitted/refracted pulse. Less Dense Medium More Dense Medium BEFORE Boundary AFTER The pulse will move slower in the more dense medium. Therefore, the refracted pulse will not have travelled as far from the boundary, and will have a smaller wavelength than the reflected pulse. Moving from a More Dense to a Less Dense Medium The boundary between the two mediums acts as a free end, meaning that the reflected pulse will be in phase with the incident pulse. Note the longer wave in the thin rope compared to the thick rope. The waves are moving, but some places have a very large amplitude oscillation (called antinodes) while others have zero amplitude and completely destructive interference (called nodes). The resultant wave does not appear to be travelling forward, hence the terms ‘standing wave’ or ‘stationary wave’. Most stringed instruments are designed to produce a standing wave pattern. 1 2 Antinodes Nodes A wave approaches a fixed, reflective end. The wave is reflected and inverted. The two waves interfere with each other to produce a new wave form. There is no displacement at the nodes. The antinodes move up and down but in opposite directions to each other. However, only the change of speed is refraction. The change in direction is an observable effect due to the light changing direction. Consider a lawnmower that is moving from a concrete surface (fast medium - equivalent to small index of refraction) to a grassy surface (slow medium - equivalent to a large index of refraction). uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Components of Curved Mirror Reflection Concave Mirrors r Radius of curvature Focal point Pole P C F Principal axis Centre of curvature Focal length f When rays of light parallel to the principal axis hit a concave mirror, all rays of light are reflected into a single spot called the focal point (F). The focal point lies on the primary axis - an imaginary line that passes through the centre of the mirror. The position of the mirror that the principal axis passes through is called the pole (P). At the pole, the mirror can be thought of as a plane/flat mirror. The distance between the pole and focal point is called the focal length (f). If the curved mirror was extended it would eventually form a circle. At the centre of this circle is the centre of curvature (C). The radius of curvature (r) is measured from the centre of curvature to the pole. Halfway between the centre of curvature (C) and the mirror is the focal point, therefore C = 2f or alternatively r = 2f. A concave mirror has a real focal point (i.e. the rays of light actually pass through it). Convex Mirrors In order to determine the focal point and length, centre and radius of curvature, dotted lines (without arrows) are drawn inside the mirror to show the path of light. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Refraction Ever noticed how a drinking straw appears to bend in two when it's viewed in a glass filled with water? This is because of refraction. Refraction occurs because light changes speed when it moves from one medium into another. Medium is the word used by scientists to describe any region that allows waves to travel through it. Air, water and glass are all different mediums. Each allows waves to travel through them, but with varying amounts of ease. How easily light can travel through a medium depends on its optical density. If the medium is more optically dense the light travels slower, and vice versa. The straw appears bent because the light travels faster through air than through water. Because it slows down as it enters the liquid, the light bends towards the normal. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: LIGHT What is Light? Light is a form of energy called electromagnetic radiation. Electromagnetic radiation occurs as waves and includes visible light, invisible light (such as infrared and ultraviolet), x-rays, microwaves and radio waves. The components of visible light can be memorised by using the mnemonic ROYGBIV: an abbreviation of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. ROYGBIV also helps you to remember the wavelength of the different colours. Red has the longest wavelength and these decrease in order through to violet which has the smallest wavelength. Light has properties that are responsible for the phenomena that will be studied in this course. These properties are: • Light travels in straight lines. • Light travels at 300 000 000 m s-1 (c = 3 x 108 m s-1) in a vacuum. • Light can travel through a vacuum (empty space). Speed of Light Light travels at approximately 300 000 000 m s-1 (metres per second) or 300 000 km s-1 (kilometres per second). This speed is almost unimaginable to us. If you were travelling by road at the speed of light it would take 0.0067 seconds to get from Cape Reinga (the top of the North Island) to Bluff (the bottom of the South Island). uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: LIGHT Magnification With Refraction As well as appearing shallower than they really are, images of submerged objects often appear larger. This can be explained by using the ‘apparent depth backtracking method’ from both ends of the submerged object. If the observer is looking at the object from an angle, the rays from the front and the back of the submerged object must travel at different angles to reach the observer's eye. Rays from the back of the object travel a 'flatter' path than those from the front. When the brain 'backtracks' these rays, the back rays must travel a further horizontal distance. This increased distance results in the image appearing larger, as well as shallower, than the actual object. 1. Sarah is fishing with her friends when she hooks a snapper. Looking over the side of the boat, Sarah sees her fish and starts boasting that it is the catch of the day. However, upon landing the fish she discovers that it does not even reach the legal length. MP 80:4 G3 3G DAPICS 4:08 PM SCIPAD © © kcolnu ot edils slide to unlock HO (Height of Object) People see objects because light travels from the object into the person’s eye. Since light is given off in all directions, and the pupil is not an infinitely small dot, more than one ray from any point of the object can enter the person’s eye. These rays are diverging (spreading out) and by tracing the rays back to where they come from, the person can locate the position of the object. di (Image distance) When the rays of light have reflected off a mirror before entering the eye, they have changed direction. However, the person’s brain is unaware of this change of direction and the person traces the rays back as if they have always been travelling in that direction. As a consequence the image appears behind the mirror. Rays behind the mirror are dotted, as they do not actually exist. These are called ‘virtual rays’, and the image is a ‘virtual image’. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES What is a Wave? Waves are a regular pattern of disturbance. They transfer energy from one position to another. The difference between waves and other forms of energy transfer is that the energy moves from one place to another without any transfer of matter. An example of this is a singer at a concert. The singer’s voice creates sound waves that the concert-goers hear. However, when hearing the music, they do not receive the original particles that were in contact with the singer’s voice box. The sound energy has been transferred without the particles travelling to the listeners’ ears. 1. 2. Light Waves Mechanical Waves Light waves are a special type of wave called electromagnetic radiation. They are special because they are able to travel through a vacuum. Not all light waves are visible and include things such as infrared light and x-rays. Mechanical waves include sound, water and seismic waves, and are the waves that people are most familiar with. Mechanical waves require a medium to travel through such as water, air, glass or the earth. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Longitudinal Waves The particles in longitudinal waves vibrate/oscillate parallel to the direction the wave is moving. As the oscillations are parallel to the wave direction, the particles can be moving in the same direction as the wave, as well as in the opposite direction. Since longitudinal waves have particles that oscillate backwards and forwards, the wave has regions where the particles are squashed up and other regions where the particles are spread out. The squashed-up regions are called compressions and the spread regions are called rarefactions. The distance between successive compressions or successive rarefactions is the wavelength (symbol = l) of a longitudinal wave. Sound waves and the primary waves created by earthquakes (seismic waves) are longitudinal. 1. Label the diagram below using the following words. Some words may be used more than once. Amplitude 2. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Transverse Waves The word ‘trans’ means across. Transverse waves oscillate particles at 90° to the direction the waves are travelling. An easy way to visualise a transverse wave is to think of it as a piece of string. Without a wave travelling along it, the string lies in a straight line. This is called the equilibrium position. When a wave travels along the string it oscillates (moves back and forth at a regular speed). The highest point of the wave is called the crest or peak. The lowest point of the wave is called the trough. When interference happens, positions where the wave is at the equilibrium position are called nodes, while troughs and peaks are known as antinodes. The wavelength (symbol = l) of the wave is the distance it takes for the wave to repeat itself. This can be found either by measuring the distance between successive peaks or the distance between successive troughs. Wavelength is measured in metres (m). The amplitude (symbol = A) is the maximum distance moved from the equilibrium position. It can be measured above (crest) or below (trough) the equilibrium position. A wavefront represents the peaks of the waves as they appear from a ‘bird’s-eye view’. Wavefronts combine ray diagrams with a method for illustrating wavelength. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Standing Waves Standing waves (also known as ‘stationary waves’) are produced when two waves with the same amplitude and frequency are travelling in opposite directions. The waves are moving, but some places have a very large amplitude oscillation (called antinodes) while others have zero amplitude and completely destructive interference (called nodes). The resultant wave does not appear to be travelling forward, hence the terms ‘standing wave’ or ‘stationary wave’. Most stringed instruments are designed to produce a standing wave pattern. 1 2 Antinodes Nodes A wave approaches a fixed, reflective end. The wave is reflected and inverted. The two waves interfere with each other to produce a new wave form. There is no displacement at the nodes. The antinodes move up and down but in opposite directions to each other. The result is a standing wave. 1. Distinguish between a ‘node’ and an ‘antinode’.             2. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Two Point Source Interference Point sources produce curved wavefronts. When two point sources create waves near to each other the following situation can arise: • Constructive interference occurs where troughs meet troughs and crests meet crests. • Destructive interference occurs where troughs meet crests. In this region no displacement will occur. This can also occur in sound waves (compressions/rarefactions instead of peak/trough). Two point sources can be created in different ways: • Two gaps in a barrier causing diffracted wavefronts. • Two sound sources emitting circular wavefronts. • Two point sources in water (refer to the image above). All of these contexts rely on the wavefronts having the same wavelengths and being in phase with each other. They can be represented by the following type of diagram: A C D E B Point Source (S1) Point Source (S2) The lines are wavefronts. They illustrate the crests or ‘peaks’ of the waves. In the middle, between successive crests, are the troughs. Where two lines (crests) intersect there will be constructive interference. Two troughs meeting will also create constructive interference. Where a line (crest) is mid-way between lines from the other source (a trough) destructive interference will occur. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.4 Mecha.searchText: MOTION If a change in distance or displacement, and the amount of time required to cover that distance, is known then the following equation can used to used to calculate the average speed or velocity. vav = ∆d/∆t vav = average speed/velocity (m s-1) ∆d = change in distance/displacement (m) ∆t = change in time (s) This equation is useful if the object is travelling at a constant speed or velocity, or if an average value is sufficient. However, instantaneous speeds or velocities cannot be calculated from this equation. For example, if a sprinter runs 100 m in 10 s, his average speed is 10 m s-1. However, the sprinter starts from rest and accelerates to his maximum speed and may even begin to slow down over the last section of the race. The sprinter will reach speeds in excess of 10 m s-1. The average speed/velocity equation cannot be used to calculate any of these instantaneous speeds. If scalar quantities are used in this equation, the answer will be a scalar, and vector quantities will give a vector answer. If the medium (and its properties) is changed, the speed of the waves also changes. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.4 Mecha.searchText: MOTION Horizontal Projectile Motion Horizontal projectile motion is a form of motion in which an object is projected at an angle to the Earth’s surface. The object will move along a curved path due to the force of gravity alone. The path followed by the projectile is called its trajectory. If we ignore the air friction or drag, we can assume that the curved trajectory is caused by the object moving at a constant horizontal velocity, while accelerating downwards due to gravity. The object’s vertical velocity decreases as it moves upwards, and increases as it moves downwards. At the top of the path, the vertical instantaneous velocity is zero, but the ball still has its constant horizontal velocity. The horizontal velocity of a projectile does not change with time. The vertical component decreases in magnitude as the ball rises, then increases as it falls. To solve projectile motion problems it is necessary to separate the initial motion into horizontal and vertical components. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.3 Waves.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Refraction of Wavefronts The speed of a wave is dependent upon the properties of the medium through which the waves travel. If the medium (and its properties) is changed, the speed of the waves also changes. The most significant property of water that affects the speed of waves travelling on its surface is the depth of the water. Water waves travel fastest when the medium is the deepest. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.4 Mecha.searchText: ENERGY AND MOMENTUM Conservation of Momentum The principle of conservation of momentum states that "the total momentum before a collision (or explosion) is equal to the total momentum after the collision, unless acted upon by an external net force". It is important to remember that momentum is a vector. When finding the total momentum the direction of the vector components must be taken into account. An external net force is a force from something that is not initially considered to be part of the system. If two trolleys collide they should rebound away so that the sum of their initial momentums is equal to the sum of their final momentums. It is important to realise that this does not mean that the principle of the conservation of momentum has been broken. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.4 Mecha.searchText: MOTION If a change in distance or displacement, and the amount of time required to cover that distance, is known then the following equation can used to used to calculate the average speed or velocity. vav = ∆d/∆t vav = average speed/velocity (m s-1) ∆d = change in distance/displacement (m) ∆t = change in time (s) This equation is useful if the object is travelling at a constant speed or velocity, or if an average value is sufficient. However, instantaneous speeds or velocities cannot be calculated from this equation. For example, if a sprinter runs 100 m in 10 s, his average speed is 10 m s-1. However, the sprinter starts from rest and accelerates to his maximum speed and may even begin to slow down over the last section of the race. The sprinter will reach speeds in excess of 10 m s-1. The average speed/velocity equation cannot be used to calculate any of these instantaneous speeds. If scalar quantities are used in this equation, the answer will be a scalar, and vector quantities will give a vector answer. For example, using displacement and time will give a velocity (a vector quantity), as displacement is also a vector quantity. 1. Use the average speed/velocity equation to find the unknown variables. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.4 Mecha.searchText: MOTION Vectors and Scalars Physical quantities can be separated into two categories: vectors, that show a size and a direction, and scalars that only show a size. The difference between vectors and scalars can be demonstrated by considering the quantities speed and velocity. Speed is a scalar; it indicates how fast an object is travelling. Velocity is a vector; it indicates how quickly an object is moving and the direction that the object is moving. Think about a car travelling north at 28 m s-1. It has a speed of 28 m s-1, and a velocity of 28 m s-1 north. There are vector and scalar quantities that represent similar concepts, such as speed and velocity. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.4 Mecha.searchText: MOTION Horizontal Projectile Motion Horizontal projectile motion is a form of motion in which an object is projected at an angle to the Earth’s surface. The object will move along a curved path due to the force of gravity alone. The path followed by the projectile is called its trajectory. If we ignore the air friction or drag, we can assume that the curved trajectory is caused by the object moving at a constant horizontal velocity, while accelerating downwards due to gravity. The object’s vertical velocity decreases as it moves upwards, and increases as it moves downwards. At the top of the path, the vertical instantaneous velocity is zero, but the ball still has its constant horizontal velocity. The horizontal velocity of a projectile does not change with time. The vertical component decreases in magnitude as the ball rises, then increases as it falls. To solve projectile motion problems it is necessary to separate the initial motion into horizontal and vertical components. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.4 Mecha.searchText: ENERGY AND MOMENTUM Conservation of Momentum The principle of conservation of momentum states that "the total momentum before a collision (or explosion) is equal to the total momentum after the collision, unless acted upon by an external net force". It is important to remember that momentum is a vector. When finding the total momentum the direction of the vector components must be taken into account. An external net force is a force from something that is not initially considered to be part of the system. If two trolleys collide they should rebound away so that the sum of their initial momentums is equal to the sum of their final momentums. INITIAL FINAL pTOTAL = 0.5 kg m s left -1 pLEFT = 2 kg m s-1 pRIGHT = 2.5 kg m s-1 pTOTAL = 0.5 kg m s-1 left pLEFT = 2 kg m s-1 pRIGHT = 1.5 kg m s-1 However, if the two trolleys collide and frictional forces are large the total momentum will not be conserved. It is important to realise that this does not mean that the principle of the conservation of momentum has been broken. Friction is an external net force, so it accounts for the change in total momentum. 1. Dave is driving a bumper boat (m = 250 kg) and collides with another boat driven by Angela (m = 220 kg). uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Calculating Total Charge Objects become charged because they have gained or lost electrons. Gaining or losing electrons creates an imbalance of charge and results in the object gaining an overall charge. If electrons are gained, the object will become negatively charged and positively charged if electrons are lost. The size of an object’s overall charge depends on the number of electrons that have been gained or lost. An object that has gained 4 x 106 electrons will be twice as negatively charged as an object that has gained only 2 x 106 electrons. The following equation can be used to calculate the total charge on an object: Q = nq Q = total charge n = number of charged particles q = charge on the particle 1 C = 6.24 x 10 18 el ectro ns Charge has the unit coulomb (C). Q and q are both used when discussing charge. Generally, Q is used for a large or total charge, while q is used if discussing small charges such as electrons that contribute to the total charge. Type of Particle Charge on the Particle Electron - 1.6 x 10-19 C Proton + 1.6 x 10-19 C As well as charging by gaining or losing of electrons, objects can also become charged by emitting charged particles, or by having charged particles collide with them. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS The Cathode Ray Tube A cathode ray tube (CRT) is a vacuum tube that contains one or more electron guns (a source of electrons) and a fluorescent screen. They create images when the electrons strike the screen. It has a means to accelerate and deflect the electron beam(s) onto the screen to create the images. Electron beam Cathode Focussing anodes y-plates x-plates High voltage supply Phosphor screen The electron gun uses a heater to provide energy to the electrons on the cathode. This allows the electrons to overcome the forces which are holding them to that metal. A high voltage supply is attached to the cathode and the anode, making the cathode negatively charged and the anode positively charged. The free electrons are now repelled by the negative cathode and attracted to the positive anode, creating the electron beam. When the beam of electrons reach the anode they encounter a gap in the anode, pass through the anode and travel along the cathode tube. Once the electron beam has passed the anode it travels through vertical and horizontal deflecting plates. These are designed to attract/repel the electron beam, so it can be directed into the desired position. Millikan began designing and performing an experiment to accurately calculate the charge on an electron. At that time there were no accurate measurements for either their mass or charge. Using the ‘falling drop method’, Millikan was able to accurately calculate the charge of an electron. This was a breakthrough in the world of physics, and in 1923 Robert Millikan was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the electron as well as other work on the 'Photoelectric Effect'. Millikan’s falling drop method works by placing oil droplets between two parallel plates, then adjusting the electric field strength so that the gravitational and electrostatic forces on the droplets are equal and opposite. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: DC ELECTRICITY Understanding Voltage Voltage (or potential difference) is a measure of the amount of electrical energy changed (∆E) to other forms of energy by one unit of charge (coulomb) as it moves between two positions. 10 V 10 V The voltage source (battery/power-pack) raises the electrical potential energy of the electrons (that are distributed evenly and everywhere within the circuit). However, no work can be done to the electrons (i.e. they can't be moved) unless there is a difference in electrical potential energy. 10 V 5V Kinetic energy + Heat There is now a difference in voltage in the wire. Because of this, all the electrons move at the same time from an area of high electrical potential energy to an area of lower electrical potential energy. This potential difference is measured in volts (V) using a voltmeter. The voltmeter measures the electric potential energy of electrons before and after a component. For example, in a light bulb, voltmeters measure the electrical energy (per coulomb) changed to heat and light. Therefore, voltmeters must be connected in parallel to the component to be able to record the difference. The total resistance is very useful and often necessary when wanting to find out the total current flowing around a circuit. However, solving combination circuits requires that all the voltage, current and resistance rules are known and can be applied. Series Circuits Parallel Circuits Current Constant Each branch's current adds up to total current entering the parallel block. Voltage Each component shares voltage that adds to the total. Each branch uses identical voltage to other branches. Resistance Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 + .... 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 + .... When asked to find a quantity in one section of a combination circuit, it is a useful strategy to use the following steps: Step 1: Check if all the information needed to find that quantity is provided in that particular section. • If yes, then find the quantity. • If no, then move to step 2. Step 2: Check if the other sections of the circuit can be used to find the information required for the section in question. • If yes, then use it to find the required information, then find the quantity. • If no, then move to step 3. Therefore, to determine if one lamp will be brighter than another, you must calculate which lamp has the greatest power. Shorting Lamps: Placing a wire in parallel with a lamp shorts it (i.e. it creates a short circuit). This means that all the current flows along the wire, bypassing the lamp. Since no current flows through the lamp, it uses no voltage, draws no power and does not glow. Blowing Bulbs: Lamps are designed to operate at a certain voltage. They can handle a small percentage more voltage (20% more will generally work), but once that margin is exceeded the bulb will burn out. With most bulbs this means the filament has melted. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM The Simple DC Motor The simple DC motor is a basic version of the modern electric motors that are used in many different applications. Both forms utilise the concept of an electromagnet force on a wire carrying a current to create motion. The simple motor has a number of key components that are vital to ensure that the motor spins as expected. Coil Current flows around a wire coil in between a permanent magnet. This creates an electromagnetic force as it interacts with the magnet. The coil can be made of multiple loops of wire which increases the length of wire inside the magnetic field while minimising the amount of space used. Coil Carbon brush Split-ring commutator Gorilla Plutonium Split Ring Commutator To ensure that current always flows in the same direction around the coil, a splitring commutator is used. It reverses the connection to the power supply as the coil rotates 180°. In the diagram the current will always flow anti-clockwise, even though the coil rotates. Carbon Brushes Brushes connect the stationary parts of the motor to the moving components. In a motor the brushes are normally made out of carbon. Carbon is a material which can conduct electricity and also self-lubricate which reduces the friction when the commutators move against it. 1. The diagram below represents a simple DC motor. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Electromagnetic Induction During the motor effect, a length of wire that has a current flowing through it will experience a force when moved perpendicular to a magnetic field. Electromagnetic induction is the opposite effect. If a force is used to move a length of wire through a magnetic field, a voltage will be induced in the wire. It is important to note that it is a voltage being created, not a current. A current will flow provided certain conditions are met. If a current does not flow, electromagnetic induction will still happen, and a voltage will always be induced. Conducting Rod Induced voltage can be explained by the Lorentz Force (F=Bqv) on electrons (in this example they are moving down the page). The electrons are the “free electrons” in the conducting rod, also moving down the page and crossing the magnetic field lines that are into the page. Using the right-hand slap rule (negative charge version): • Fingers = magnetic field into page. • Thumb = upwards (against negative particle motion). • Palm to the left = force on electrons inside the moving conducting rod. We can see the free electrons will be pulled to the left side of the rod. This will leave the right side of the rod with a net positive charge. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Simple Generator Generators are used to convert kinetic energy to electrical energy. A simple generator is very similar to the DC motor. Just like the DC motor the basis of the generator is a coil (with multiple loops) that is placed inside a permanent magnetic field. Carbon brushes are used to provide a self-lubricating contact. The main component difference between the DC motor and the simple generator is the slip rings. Axle Coil B C A D Carbon brush Slip rings Slip Rings: The simple generator has two slip rings, one being attached to the side A-B, and the other attached to the side C-D. This means that the side A-B will always be attached to the right-hand side carbon brush, and the side C-D will always be attached to the left-hand side. As the coil spins inside the magnetic field a voltage is induced across each side (A-B and C-D). Since the coil is spinning either clockwise or anti-clockwise, one side of the coil will be moving upwards through the magnetic field on one part of the rotation, and downwards on the other. The result of this changing direction is that the induced voltage (and subsequent current) will reverse, meaning that the simple generator will produce an alternating voltage and current (AC electricity). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Force Against Motion Whenever a voltage is induced by the motion of a conductor, a force that opposes the motion is produced. The right-hand slap rule (negative charge version) can be used to show that the top of the rod will have an excess of positive charge, and the bottom an excess of negative charge. By considering the current flowing through the conducting rod the force against motion is found. The induced voltage has created its own force which opposes its motion. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Calculating Total Charge Objects become charged because they have gained or lost electrons. Gaining or losing electrons creates an imbalance of charge and results in the object gaining an overall charge. If electrons are gained, the object will become negatively charged and positively charged if electrons are lost. The size of an object’s overall charge depends on the number of electrons that have been gained or lost. An object that has gained 4 x 106 electrons will be twice as negatively charged as an object that has gained only 2 x 106 electrons. The following equation can be used to calculate the total charge on an object: Q = nq Q = total charge n = number of charged particles q = charge on the particle 1 C = 6.24 x 10 18 el ectro ns Charge has the unit coulomb (C). Q and q are both used when discussing charge. Generally, Q is used for a large or total charge, while q is used if discussing small charges such as electrons that contribute to the total charge. Type of Particle Charge on the Particle Electron - 1.6 x 10-19 C Proton + 1.6 x 10-19 C As well as charging by gaining or losing of electrons, objects can also become charged by emitting charged particles, or by having charged particles collide with them. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS The Cathode Ray Tube A cathode ray tube (CRT) is a vacuum tube that contains one or more electron guns (a source of electrons) and a fluorescent screen. They create images when the electrons strike the screen. It has a means to accelerate and deflect the electron beam(s) onto the screen to create the images. Electron beam Cathode Focussing anodes y-plates x-plates High voltage supply Phosphor screen The electron gun uses a heater to provide energy to the electrons on the cathode. This allows the electrons to overcome the forces which are holding them to that metal. A high voltage supply is attached to the cathode and the anode, making the cathode negatively charged and the anode positively charged. The free electrons are now repelled by the negative cathode and attracted to the positive anode, creating the electron beam. When the beam of electrons reach the anode they encounter a gap in the anode, pass through the anode and travel along the cathode tube. Once the electron beam has passed the anode it travels through vertical and horizontal deflecting plates. These are designed to attract/repel the electron beam, so it can be directed into the desired position.
