uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: DC ELECTRICITY Understanding Current When a closed circuit is formed, an electrical field (E) is created in the conductor. The charges (+ve and -ve) within the conductor experience a force (F). The direction of the electrical field is the same as the direction of the force on a positive charge. Electrons move in the opposite direction to the direction of the electrical field (i.e. towards the positive terminal). This flow of electrons is called electrical current. Negative charges move in the opposite direction to the electrical field. Electrical field F E F Positive charges move in the same direction as the electrical field. Each electron that flows around the circuit has a very small amount of charge, however there are huge numbers of electrons available in electrical circuits. The amount of charge that passes a certain point per second is defined as current. Scientists express the relationship between charge and current with the following formula. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Energy Transfer Energy cannot be created or destroyed. Therefore, when a charged particle’s electrostatic potential energy changes, the change must be accounted for by different forms of energy. A common example of this is when a positively charged particle is placed beside a positive parallel plate. The particle will accelerate away from the positive plate and lose electrostatic potential energy. This ‘lost’ energy is being converted into kinetic energy, and is the reason why the particle speeds up. Using the principle of Conservation of Energy and the equation for kinetic energy, the speed that the particle reaches can be calculated. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Floating Charges - Millikan's Experiment In the early 1900s an American physicist called Robert A. Millikan began designing and performing an experiment to accurately calculate the charge on an electron. At that time there were no accurate measurements for either their mass or charge. Using the ‘falling drop method’, Millikan was able to accurately calculate the charge of an electron. This was a breakthrough in the world of physics, and in 1923 Robert Millikan was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the electron as well as other work on the 'Photoelectric Effect'. Millikan’s falling drop method works by placing oil droplets between two parallel plates, then adjusting the electric field strength so that the gravitational and electrostatic forces on the droplets are equal and opposite. This causes the droplets to have zero net force on them, and they float motionless between the parallel plates. The diagram below is an simplified model of Robert A. Millikan’s experiment. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: DC ELECTRICITY Understanding Voltage Voltage (or potential difference) is a measure of the amount of electrical energy changed (∆E) to other forms of energy by one unit of charge (coulomb) as it moves between two positions. 10 V 10 V The voltage source (battery/power-pack) raises the electrical potential energy of the electrons (that are distributed evenly and everywhere within the circuit). However, no work can be done to the electrons (i.e. they can't be moved) unless there is a difference in electrical potential energy. 10 V 5V Kinetic energy + Heat There is now a difference in voltage in the wire. Because of this, all the electrons move at the same time from an area of high electrical potential energy to an area of lower electrical potential energy. This potential difference is measured in volts (V) using a voltmeter. The voltmeter measures the electric potential energy of electrons before and after a component. For example, in a light bulb, voltmeters measure the electrical energy (per coulomb) changed to heat and light. Therefore, voltmeters must be connected in parallel to the component to be able to record the difference. Scientists express this relationship with the following formula: V = ∆E / q V = Voltage (volts , V) ∆E = Change in Potential Energy (joules , J) q = Charge (coulombs, C) 1. Shorting Lamps: Placing a wire in parallel with a lamp shorts it (i.e. it creates a short circuit). This means that all the current flows along the wire, bypassing the lamp. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM The Simple DC Motor The simple DC motor is a basic version of the modern electric motors that are used in many different applications. Both forms utilise the concept of an electromagnet force on a wire carrying a current to create motion. The simple motor has a number of key components that are vital to ensure that the motor spins as expected. Coil Current flows around a wire coil in between a permanent magnet. This creates an electromagnetic force as it interacts with the magnet. The coil can be made of multiple loops of wire which increases the length of wire inside the magnetic field while minimising the amount of space used. Coil Carbon brush Split-ring commutator Gorilla Plutonium Split Ring Commutator To ensure that current always flows in the same direction around the coil, a splitring commutator is used. It reverses the connection to the power supply as the coil rotates 180°. In the diagram the current will always flow anti-clockwise, even though the coil rotates. Carbon Brushes Brushes connect the stationary parts of the motor to the moving components. In a motor the brushes are normally made out of carbon. Carbon is a material which can conduct electricity and also self-lubricate which reduces the friction when the commutators move against it. 1. The diagram below represents a simple DC motor. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Charged Particles In Magnetic Fields When a charged particle moves through a magnetic field it experiences a force. Conventional current is described as the flow of positive charges, therefore a single positive charge moving can be thought of as a small conventional current. By using the right-hand slap rule the electromagnetic force can be found, but this time it is acting on a single charge rather than a length of wire. If the charged particle is negative, use the rig ht-hand slap rule as if the charg e is positive, then reverse the dir ection of the answer. Alternativel y, you could just turn your th umb against the negative particle’s velocity to get the correct dir ection of the Lorentz Force. This will minimise the need to remembe r extra rules. Fingers point in the direction of the magnetic field. Palm points in the direction of the force. Thumb points in the direction of the positive particle’s velocity. The electromagnetic force on a charged particle acts perpendicular to the particle’s velocity, and causes the particle to move in a circular path (it undergoes centripetal acceleration). If the magnetic field is not in a particularly large region the charged particle may leave the magnetic field before completing a full circle. Solenoids are used in electrical circuits due to their electromagnetic properties. The strength of the magnetic field produced by a solenoid can be increased by using more coils of wire, increasing the current or placing a soft iron rod through the middle of the coils of wire. Before turning the power supply on, note the direction the compasses are pointing. 4. Turn the power supply on and observe. 5. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Electromagnetic Induction During the motor effect, a length of wire that has a current flowing through it will experience a force when moved perpendicular to a magnetic field. Electromagnetic induction is the opposite effect. If a force is used to move a length of wire through a magnetic field, a voltage will be induced in the wire. It is important to note that it is a voltage being created, not a current. A current will flow provided certain conditions are met. If a current does not flow, electromagnetic induction will still happen, and a voltage will always be induced. Conducting Rod Induced voltage can be explained by the Lorentz Force (F=Bqv) on electrons (in this example they are moving down the page). The electrons are the “free electrons” in the conducting rod, also moving down the page and crossing the magnetic field lines that are into the page. Using the right-hand slap rule (negative charge version): • Fingers = magnetic field into page. • Thumb = upwards (against negative particle motion). • Palm to the left = force on electrons inside the moving conducting rod. We can see the free electrons will be pulled to the left side of the rod. This will leave the right side of the rod with a net positive charge. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 2.6 Elect.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Simple Generator Generators are used to convert kinetic energy to electrical energy. A simple generator is very similar to the DC motor. Just like the DC motor the basis of the generator is a coil (with multiple loops) that is placed inside a permanent magnetic field. Carbon brushes are used to provide a self-lubricating contact. The main component difference between the DC motor and the simple generator is the slip rings. Axle B Coil C A D Carbon brush Slip rings Slip Rings: The simple generator has two slip rings, one being attached to the side A-B, and the other attached to the side C-D. This means that the side A-B will always be attached to the right-hand side carbon brush, and the side C-D will always be attached to the left-hand side. As the coil spins inside the magnetic field a voltage is induced across each side (A-B and C-D). Since the coil is spinning either clockwise or anti-clockwise, one side of the coil will be moving upwards through the magnetic field on one part of the rotation, and downwards on the other. The result of this changing direction is that the induced voltage (and subsequent current) will reverse, meaning that the simple generator will produce an alternating voltage and current (AC electricity). 1. The focal point lies on the primary axis - an imaginary line that passes through the centre of the mirror. The position of the mirror that the principal axis passes through is called the pole (P). At the pole, the mirror can be thought of as a plane/flat mirror. The distance between the pole and focal point is called the focal length (f). If the curved mirror was extended it would eventually form a circle. At the centre of this circle is the centre of curvature (C). The radius of curvature (r) is measured from the centre of curvature to the pole. Halfway between the centre of curvature (C) and the mirror is the focal point, therefore C = 2f or alternatively r = 2f. A concave mirror has a real focal point (i.e. the rays of light actually pass through it). Convex Mirrors In order to determine the focal point and length, centre and radius of curvature, dotted lines (without arrows) are drawn inside the mirror to show the path of light. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: LIGHT Refraction Ever noticed how a drinking straw appears to bend in two when it's viewed in a glass filled with water? This is because of refraction. Refraction occurs because light changes speed when it moves from one medium into another. Medium is the word used by scientists to describe any region that allows waves to travel through it. Air, water and glass are all different mediums. Each allows waves to travel through them, but with varying amounts of ease. How easily light can travel through a medium depends on its optical density. If the medium is more optically dense the light travels slower, and vice versa. The straw appears bent because the light travels faster through air than through water. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: LIGHT What is Light? Light is a form of energy called electromagnetic radiation. Electromagnetic radiation occurs as waves and includes visible light, invisible light (such as infrared and ultraviolet), x-rays, microwaves and radio waves. The components of visible light can be memorised by using the mnemonic ROYGBIV: an abbreviation of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. ROYGBIV also helps you to remember the wavelength of the different colours. Red has the longest wavelength and these decrease in order through to violet which has the smallest wavelength. Light has properties that are responsible for the phenomena that will be studied in this course. These properties are: • Light travels in straight lines. • Light travels at 300 000 000 m s-1 (c = 3 x 108 m s-1) in a vacuum. • Light can travel through a vacuum (empty space). Speed of Light Light travels at approximately 300 000 000 m s-1 (metres per second) or 300 000 km s-1 (kilometres per second). This speed is almost unimaginable to us. If you were travelling by road at the speed of light it would take 0.0067 seconds to get from Cape Reinga (the top of the North Island) to Bluff (the bottom of the South Island). uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: LIGHT Magnification With Refraction As well as appearing shallower than they really are, images of submerged objects often appear larger. This can be explained by using the ‘apparent depth backtracking method’ from both ends of the submerged object. If the observer is looking at the object from an angle, the rays from the front and the back of the submerged object must travel at different angles to reach the observer's eye. Rays from the back of the object travel a 'flatter' path than those from the front. When the brain 'backtracks' these rays, the back rays must travel a further horizontal distance. This increased distance results in the image appearing larger, as well as shallower, than the actual object. 1. Sarah is fishing with her friends when she hooks a snapper. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES What is a Wave? Waves are a regular pattern of disturbance. They transfer energy from one position to another. The difference between waves and other forms of energy transfer is that the energy moves from one place to another without any transfer of matter. An example of this is a singer at a concert. The singer’s voice creates sound waves that the concert-goers hear. However, when hearing the music, they do not receive the original particles that were in contact with the singer’s voice box. The sound energy has been transferred without the particles travelling to the listeners’ ears. 1. Light Waves Mechanical Waves Light waves are a special type of wave called electromagnetic radiation. They are special because they are able to travel through a vacuum. Not all light waves are visible and include things such as infrared light and x-rays. Mechanical waves include sound, water and seismic waves, and are the waves that people are most familiar with. Mechanical waves require a medium to travel through such as water, air, glass or the earth. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Transverse Waves The word ‘trans’ means across. Transverse waves oscillate particles at 90° to the direction the waves are travelling. An easy way to visualise a transverse wave is to think of it as a piece of string. Without a wave travelling along it, the string lies in a straight line. This is called the equilibrium position. When a wave travels along the string it oscillates (moves back and forth at a regular speed). The highest point of the wave is called the crest or peak. The lowest point of the wave is called the trough. When interference happens, positions where the wave is at the equilibrium position are called nodes, while troughs and peaks are known as antinodes. The wavelength (symbol = l) of the wave is the distance it takes for the wave to repeat itself. This can be found either by measuring the distance between successive peaks or the distance between successive troughs. Wavelength is measured in metres (m). The amplitude (symbol = A) is the maximum distance moved from the equilibrium position. It can be measured above (crest) or below (trough) the equilibrium position. Amplitude is measured in metres (m). 1. Label the diagram below using the following words. Some words may be used more than once. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Longitudinal Waves The particles in longitudinal waves vibrate/oscillate parallel to the direction the wave is moving. As the oscillations are parallel to the wave direction, the particles can be moving in the same direction as the wave, as well as in the opposite direction. Since longitudinal waves have particles that oscillate backwards and forwards, the wave has regions where the particles are squashed up and other regions where the particles are spread out. The squashed-up regions are called compressions and the spread regions are called rarefactions. The distance between successive compressions or successive rarefactions is the wavelength (symbol = l) of a longitudinal wave. Sound waves and the primary waves created by earthquakes (seismic waves) are longitudinal. 1. Label the diagram below using the following words. Some words may be used more than once. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: LIGHT What is Refraction? When light/waves move from one medium to another it changes speed and a change of direction can be observed. However, only the change of speed is refraction. The change in direction is an observable effect due to the light changing direction. Consider a lawnmower that is moving from a concrete surface (fast medium - equivalent to small index of refraction) to a grassy surface (slow medium - equivalent to a large index of refraction). Concrete (n1) • Fast medium. • Smaller index of refraction. d ray Refracte θ2 NORMAL θ1 nt e cid ray In Grass (n2) • Slow medium. • Larger index of refraction. Since the lawnmower is at an angle, the wheels closest to the normal (the right-hand side wheels) encounter the grass first and slow down. Since the wheels on the outside are still on the concrete they keep moving ‘fast’. The difference between the wheels on each side causes the lawnmower to change direction and move towards the normal. Similarly, refraction is a change of speed as waves move from one medium to another. This change of speed can create a change in direction. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Standing Waves Standing waves (also known as ‘stationary waves’) are produced when two waves with the same amplitude and frequency are travelling in opposite directions. The waves are moving, but some places have a very large amplitude oscillation (called antinodes) while others have zero amplitude and completely destructive interference (called nodes). The resultant wave does not appear to be travelling forward, hence the terms ‘standing wave’ or ‘stationary wave’. Most stringed instruments are designed to produce a standing wave pattern. 1 2 Antinodes Nodes A wave approaches a fixed, reflective end. The wave is reflected and inverted. The two waves interfere with each other to produce a new wave form. There is no displacement at the nodes. The antinodes move up and down but in opposite directions to each other. The result is a standing wave. 1. Nodes Distinguish between a ‘node’ and an ‘antinode’.   are locations in the  string (or medium) where there is no motion in the standing wave. Nodes are  made by the two waves destructively interfering. Antinodes are locations  in the medium where there is maximum vibration. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MOTION Horizontal Projectile Motion Horizontal projectile motion is a form of motion in which an object is projected at an angle to the Earth’s surface. The object will move along a curved path due to the force of gravity alone. The path followed by the projectile is called its trajectory. If we ignore the air friction or drag, we can assume that the curved trajectory is caused by the object moving at a constant horizontal velocity, while accelerating downwards due to gravity. The object’s vertical velocity decreases as it moves upwards, and increases as it moves downwards. At the top of the path, the vertical instantaneous velocity is zero, but the ball still has its constant horizontal velocity. The horizontal velocity of a projectile does not change with time. The vertical component decreases in magnitude as the ball rises, then increases as it falls. To solve projectile motion problems it is necessary to separate the initial motion into horizontal and vertical components. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Temperature and Heat Most people use the terms ‘heat’ and ‘temperature’ in interchangeable ways, without realising that they are talking about two different quantities. Temperature (symbol T) describes how hot an object is. This is related to energy, but it is not energy. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in an object. A hot object simply has particles that are moving faster than those of a cold object. Heat energy (symbol Q) is the total kinetic and potential energies of the particles that make up the object. Heat is a form of energy that can be transferred, and is sometimes called thermal energy. It is measured in Joules (J). The addition or removal of heat from an object can cause the object to experience a change of temperature, as well as a change of state. The temp erature o f an object ca n be meas ured. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ENERGY AND MOMENTUM Conservation of Momentum The principle of conservation of momentum states that "the total momentum before a collision (or explosion) is equal to the total momentum after the collision, unless acted upon by an external net force". It is important to remember that momentum is a vector. When finding the total momentum the direction of the vector components must be taken into account. An external net force is a force from something that is not initially considered to be part of the system. If two trolleys collide they should rebound away so that the sum of their initial momentums is equal to the sum of their final momentums. It is important to realise that this does not mean that the principle of the conservation of momentum has been broken. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Calculating Total Charge Objects become charged because they have gained or lost electrons. Gaining or losing electrons creates an imbalance of charge and results in the object gaining an overall charge. If electrons are gained, the object will become negatively charged and positively charged if electrons are lost. The size of an object’s overall charge depends on the number of electrons that have been gained or lost. An object that has gained 4 x 106 electrons will be twice as negatively charged as an object that has gained only 2 x 106 electrons. The following equation can be used to calculate the total charge on an object: Q = nq Q = total charge n = number of charged particles q = charge on the particle 1 C = 6.24 x 10 18 el ectro ns Charge has the unit coulomb (C). Q and q are both used when discussing charge. Generally, Q is used for a large or total charge, while q is used if discussing small charges such as electrons that contribute to the total charge. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS The Cathode Ray Tube A cathode ray tube (CRT) is a vacuum tube that contains one or more electron guns (a source of electrons) and a fluorescent screen. They create images when the electrons strike the screen. It has a means to accelerate and deflect the electron beam(s) onto the screen to create the images. Electron beam Cathode Focussing anodes y-plates x-plates High voltage supply Phosphor screen The electron gun uses a heater to provide energy to the electrons on the cathode. This allows the electrons to overcome the forces which are holding them to that metal. A high voltage supply is attached to the cathode and the anode, making the cathode negatively charged and the anode positively charged. The free electrons are now repelled by the negative cathode and attracted to the positive anode, creating the electron beam. When the beam of electrons reach the anode they encounter a gap in the anode, pass through the anode and travel along the cathode tube. Once the electron beam has passed the anode it travels through vertical and horizontal deflecting plates. These are designed to attract/repel the electron beam, so it can be directed into the desired position. Therefore, when a charged particle’s electrostatic potential energy changes, the change must be accounted for by different forms of energy. A common example of this is when a positively charged particle is placed beside a positive parallel plate. The particle will accelerate away from the positive plate and lose electrostatic potential energy. This ‘lost’ energy is being converted into kinetic energy, and is the reason why the particle speeds up. Using the principle of Conservation of Energy and the equation for kinetic energy, the speed that the particle reaches can be calculated. The charges (+ve and -ve) within the conductor experience a force (F). The direction of the electrical field is the same as the direction of the force on a positive charge. Electrons move in the opposite direction to the direction of the electrical field (i.e. towards the positive terminal). This flow of electrons is called electrical current. Negative charges move in the opposite direction to the electrical field. Electrical field F E F Positive charges move in the same direction as the electrical field. Each electron that flows around the circuit has a very small amount of charge, however there are huge numbers of electrons available in electrical circuits. The amount of charge that passes a certain point per second is defined as current. Scientists express the relationship between charge and current with the following formula. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Floating Charges - Millikan's Experiment In the early 1900s an American physicist called Robert A. Millikan began designing and performing an experiment to accurately calculate the charge on an electron. At that time there were no accurate measurements for either their mass or charge. Using the ‘falling drop method’, Millikan was able to accurately calculate the charge of an electron. This was a breakthrough in the world of physics, and in 1923 Robert Millikan was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the electron as well as other work on the 'Photoelectric Effect'. Millikan’s falling drop method works by placing oil droplets between two parallel plates, then adjusting the electric field strength so that the gravitational and electrostatic forces on the droplets are equal and opposite. This causes the droplets to have zero net force on them, and they float motionless between the parallel plates. The diagram below is an simplified model of Robert A. Millikan’s experiment. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: DC ELECTRICITY Understanding Voltage Voltage (or potential difference) is a measure of the amount of electrical energy changed (∆E) to other forms of energy by one unit of charge (coulomb) as it moves between two positions. 10 V 10 V The voltage source (battery/power-pack) raises the electrical potential energy of the electrons (that are distributed evenly and everywhere within the circuit). However, no work can be done to the electrons (i.e. they can't be moved) unless there is a difference in electrical potential energy. 10 V 5V Kinetic energy + Heat There is now a difference in voltage in the wire. Because of this, all the electrons move at the same time from an area of high electrical potential energy to an area of lower electrical potential energy. This potential difference is measured in volts (V) using a voltmeter. The voltmeter measures the electric potential energy of electrons before and after a component. For example, in a light bulb, voltmeters measure the electrical energy (per coulomb) changed to heat and light. Therefore, voltmeters must be connected in parallel to the component to be able to record the difference. Scientists express this relationship with the following formula: V = ∆E / q V = Voltage (volts , V) ∆E = Change in Potential Energy (joules , J) q = Charge (coulombs, C) 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: DC ELECTRICITY The Voltage Divider Sometimes a power supply will provide more voltage than an appliance is designed to operate with. To overcome this issue a device called a voltage divider (also called a 'potential divider') can be used. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: DC ELECTRICITY Properties of Lamps Brightness: Lamps convert electrical energy to light and heat energy. Shorting Lamps: Placing a wire in parallel with a lamp shorts it (i.e. it creates a short circuit). This means that all the current flows along the wire, bypassing the lamp. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Electromagnetic Induction During the motor effect, a length of wire that has a current flowing through it will experience a force when moved perpendicular to a magnetic field. Electromagnetic induction is the opposite effect. If a force is used to move a length of wire through a magnetic field, a voltage will be induced in the wire. It is important to note that it is a voltage being created, not a current. A current will flow provided certain conditions are met. If a current does not flow, electromagnetic induction will still happen, and a voltage will always be induced. Conducting Rod Induced voltage can be explained by the Lorentz Force (F=Bqv) on electrons (in this example they are moving down the page). We can see the free electrons will be pulled to the left side of the rod. This will leave the right side of the rod with a net positive charge. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Simple Generator Generators are used to convert kinetic energy to electrical energy. A simple generator is very similar to the DC motor. Just like the DC motor the basis of the generator is a coil (with multiple loops) that is placed inside a permanent magnetic field. Carbon brushes are used to provide a self-lubricating contact. The main component difference between the DC motor and the simple generator is the slip rings. Axle Coil B C A D Carbon brush Slip rings Slip Rings: The simple generator has two slip rings, one being attached to the side A-B, and the other attached to the side C-D. This means that the side A-B will always be attached to the right-hand side carbon brush, and the side C-D will always be attached to the left-hand side. As the coil spins inside the magnetic field a voltage is induced across each side (A-B and C-D). Since the coil is spinning either clockwise or anti-clockwise, one side of the coil will be moving upwards through the magnetic field on one part of the rotation, and downwards on the other. The result of this changing direction is that the induced voltage (and subsequent current) will reverse, meaning that the simple generator will produce an alternating voltage and current (AC electricity). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: LIGHT Components of Curved Mirror Reflection Concave Mirrors r Radius of curvature Focal point Pole P C F Principal axis Centre of curvature Focal length f When rays of light parallel to the principal axis hit a concave mirror, all rays of light are reflected into a single spot called the focal point (F). The focal point lies on the primary axis - an imaginary line that passes through the centre of the mirror. The position of the mirror that the principal axis passes through is called the pole (P). At the pole, the mirror can be thought of as a plane/flat mirror. The distance between the pole and focal point is called the focal length (f). If the curved mirror was extended it would eventually form a circle. At the centre of this circle is the centre of curvature (C). The radius of curvature (r) is measured from the centre of curvature to the pole. Halfway between the centre of curvature (C) and the mirror is the focal point, therefore C = 2f or alternatively r = 2f. A concave mirror has a real focal point (i.e. the rays of light actually pass through it). Convex Mirrors In order to determine the focal point and length, centre and radius of curvature, dotted lines (without arrows) are drawn inside the mirror to show the path of light. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: LIGHT Refraction Ever noticed how a drinking straw appears to bend in two when it's viewed in a glass filled with water? This is because of refraction. Refraction occurs because light changes speed when it moves from one medium into another. Medium is the word used by scientists to describe any region that allows waves to travel through it. Air, water and glass are all different mediums. Each allows waves to travel through them, but with varying amounts of ease. How easily light can travel through a medium depends on its optical density. If the medium is more optically dense the light travels slower, and vice versa. The straw appears bent because the light travels faster through air than through water. Because it slows down as it enters the liquid, the light bends towards the normal. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: LIGHT What is Light? Light is a form of energy called electromagnetic radiation. Electromagnetic radiation occurs as waves and includes visible light, invisible light (such as infrared and ultraviolet), x-rays, microwaves and radio waves. The components of visible light can be memorised by using the mnemonic ROYGBIV: an abbreviation of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. ROYGBIV also helps you to remember the wavelength of the different colours. Red has the longest wavelength and these decrease in order through to violet which has the smallest wavelength. Light has properties that are responsible for the phenomena that will be studied in this course. These properties are: • Light travels in straight lines. • Light travels at 300 000 000 m s-1 (c = 3 x 108 m s-1) in a vacuum. • Light can travel through a vacuum (empty space). Speed of Light Light travels at approximately 300 000 000 m s-1 (metres per second) or 300 000 km s-1 (kilometres per second). This speed is almost unimaginable to us. If you were travelling by road at the speed of light it would take 0.0067 seconds to get from Cape Reinga (the top of the North Island) to Bluff (the bottom of the South Island). Or, to put it more simply, you could drive the entire length of New Zealand 150 times in one second! The speed of light can be calculated using the following formula: v=d/t v d t 1. = = = Light speed

uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: LIGHT Magnification With Refraction As well as appearing shallower than they really are, images of submerged objects often appear larger. This can be explained by using the ‘apparent depth backtracking method’ from both ends of the submerged object. If the observer is looking at the object from an angle, the rays from the front and the back of the submerged object must travel at different angles to reach the observer's eye. Rays from the back of the object travel a 'flatter' path than those from the front. When the brain 'backtracks' these rays, the back rays must travel a further horizontal distance. This increased distance results in the image appearing larger, as well as shallower, than the actual object. 1. Sarah is fishing with her friends when she hooks a snapper. The difference between waves and other forms of energy transfer is that the energy moves from one place to another without any transfer of matter. An example of this is a singer at a concert. The singer’s voice creates sound waves that the concert-goers hear. However, when hearing the music, they do not receive the original particles that were in contact with the singer’s voice box. The sound energy has been transferred without the particles travelling to the listeners’ ears. 1. 2. Light Waves Mechanical Waves Light waves are a special type of wave called electromagnetic radiation. They are special because they are able to travel through a vacuum. Not all light waves are visible and include things such as infrared light and x-rays. Mechanical waves include sound, water and seismic waves, and are the waves that people are most familiar with. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Longitudinal Waves The particles in longitudinal waves vibrate/oscillate parallel to the direction the wave is moving. As the oscillations are parallel to the wave direction, the particles can be moving in the same direction as the wave, as well as in the opposite direction. Since longitudinal waves have particles that oscillate backwards and forwards, the wave has regions where the particles are squashed up and other regions where the particles are spread out. The squashed-up regions are called compressions and the spread regions are called rarefactions. The distance between successive compressions or successive rarefactions is the wavelength (symbol = l) of a longitudinal wave. Sound waves and the primary waves created by earthquakes (seismic waves) are longitudinal. 1. Label the diagram below using the following words. Some words may be used more than once. Amplitude 2. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Transverse Waves The word ‘trans’ means across. Transverse waves oscillate particles at 90° to the direction the waves are travelling. An easy way to visualise a transverse wave is to think of it as a piece of string. Without a wave travelling along it, the string lies in a straight line. This is called the equilibrium position. When a wave travels along the string it oscillates (moves back and forth at a regular speed). The highest point of the wave is called the crest or peak. The lowest point of the wave is called the trough. When interference happens, positions where the wave is at the equilibrium position are called nodes, while troughs and peaks are known as antinodes. The wavelength (symbol = l) of the wave is the distance it takes for the wave to repeat itself. MP 80:4 G3 3G DAPICS 4:08 PM SCIPAD © © kcolnu ot edils slide to unlock HO (Height of Object) People see objects because light travels from the object into the person’s eye. Since light is given off in all directions, and the pupil is not an infinitely small dot, more than one ray from any point of the object can enter the person’s eye. These rays are diverging (spreading out) and by tracing the rays back to where they come from, the person can locate the position of the object. di (Image distance) When the rays of light have reflected off a mirror before entering the eye, they have changed direction. However, the person’s brain is unaware of this change of direction and the person traces the rays back as if they have always been travelling in that direction. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Pulses Pulses are waves (i.e. disturbances that travel through a medium). Pulses reflect with different characteristics depending on whether the boundary is fixed or free. Fixed End When a pulse collides with a fixed end the pulse exerts a force on the end. The fixed end will exert an equal and opposite force on the pulse (Newton’s Law). This causes an inverted (upside down) pulse to be reflected back. Crest Crest Crest Free End When a pulse collides with a free end it is reflected without a phase change. The reflected pulse is the same way up as the incident pulse. Crest 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Reflection and Transmission of Pulses When a pulse travels from one medium to another, both reflection and transmission can occur. Transmission can also be thought of as refraction since the transmitted wave experiences a change in speed. Moving from a Less Dense to a More Dense Medium When the pulse moves from a less dense to a more dense medium, the boundary will act in a similar manner to a fixed boundary - the reflected pulse will experience a phase change. The amplitude of the reflected portion is less than the amplitude of the incident wave as some of the energy from the pulse has been taken by the transmitted/refracted pulse. Less Dense Medium More Dense Medium BEFORE Boundary AFTER The pulse will move slower in the more dense medium. Therefore, the refracted pulse will not have travelled as far from the boundary, and will have a smaller wavelength than the reflected pulse. Moving from a More Dense to a Less Dense Medium The boundary between the two mediums acts as a free end, meaning that the reflected pulse will be in phase with the incident pulse. Note the longer wave in the thin rope compared to the thick rope. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Standing Waves Standing waves (also known as ‘stationary waves’) are produced when two waves with the same amplitude and frequency are travelling in opposite directions. The waves are moving, but some places have a very large amplitude oscillation (called antinodes) while others have zero amplitude and completely destructive interference (called nodes). The resultant wave does not appear to be travelling forward, hence the terms ‘standing wave’ or ‘stationary wave’. Most stringed instruments are designed to produce a standing wave pattern. 1 2 Antinodes Nodes A wave approaches a fixed, reflective end. The wave is reflected and inverted. The two waves interfere with each other to produce a new wave form. There is no displacement at the nodes. The antinodes move up and down but in opposite directions to each other. The result is a standing wave. 1. Distinguish between a ‘node’ and an ‘antinode’.             2. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Two Point Source Interference Point sources produce curved wavefronts. When two point sources create waves near to each other the following situation can arise: • Constructive interference occurs where troughs meet troughs and crests meet crests. • Destructive interference occurs where troughs meet crests. In this region no displacement will occur. This can also occur in sound waves (compressions/rarefactions instead of peak/trough). Two point sources can be created in different ways: • Two gaps in a barrier causing diffracted wavefronts. • Two sound sources emitting circular wavefronts. • Two point sources in water (refer to the image above). All of these contexts rely on the wavefronts having the same wavelengths and being in phase with each other. They can be represented by the following type of diagram: A C D E B Point Source (S1) Point Source (S2) The lines are wavefronts. They illustrate the crests or ‘peaks’ of the waves. In the middle, between successive crests, are the troughs. Where two lines (crests) intersect there will be constructive interference. Two troughs meeting will also create constructive interference. Where a line (crest) is mid-way between lines from the other source (a trough) destructive interference will occur. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: LIGHT What is Refraction? When light/waves move from one medium to another it changes speed and a change of direction can be observed. However, only the change of speed is refraction. The change in direction is an observable effect due to the light changing direction. Consider a lawnmower that is moving from a concrete surface (fast medium - equivalent to small index of refraction) to a grassy surface (slow medium - equivalent to a large index of refraction). Concrete (n1) • Fast medium. • Smaller index of refraction. d ray Refracte θ2 NORMAL θ1 nt e cid ray In Grass (n2) • Slow medium. • Larger index of refraction. Since the lawnmower is at an angle, the wheels closest to the normal (the right-hand side wheels) encounter the grass first and slow down. Since the wheels on the outside are still on the concrete they keep moving ‘fast’. The difference between the wheels on each side causes the lawnmower to change direction and move towards the normal. Similarly, refraction is a change of speed as waves move from one medium to another. This change of speed can create a change in direction. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MOTION Vectors and Scalars Physical quantities can be separated into two categories: vectors, that show a size and a direction, and scalars that only show a size. The difference between vectors and scalars can be demonstrated by considering the quantities speed and velocity. Speed is a scalar; it indicates how fast an object is travelling. Velocity is a vector; it indicates how quickly an object is moving and the direction that the object is moving. Think about a car travelling north at 28 m s-1. It has a speed of 28 m s-1, and a velocity of 28 m s-1 north. There are vector and scalar quantities that represent similar concepts, such as speed and velocity. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MOTION If a change in distance or displacement, and the amount of time required to cover that distance, is known then the following equation can used to used to calculate the average speed or velocity. vav = ∆d/∆t vav = average speed/velocity (m s-1) ∆d = change in distance/displacement (m) ∆t = change in time (s) This equation is useful if the object is travelling at a constant speed or velocity, or if an average value is sufficient. However, instantaneous speeds or velocities cannot be calculated from this equation. For example, if a sprinter runs 100 m in 10 s, his average speed is 10 m s-1. However, the sprinter starts from rest and accelerates to his maximum speed and may even begin to slow down over the last section of the race. The sprinter will reach speeds in excess of 10 m s-1. The average speed/velocity equation cannot be used to calculate any of these instantaneous speeds. If scalar quantities are used in this equation, the answer will be a scalar, and vector quantities will give a vector answer. For example, using displacement and time will give a velocity (a vector quantity), as displacement is also a vector quantity. 1. Use the average speed/velocity equation to find the unknown variables. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MOTION Horizontal Projectile Motion Horizontal projectile motion is a form of motion in which an object is projected at an angle to the Earth’s surface. The object will move along a curved path due to the force of gravity alone. The path followed by the projectile is called its trajectory. If we ignore the air friction or drag, we can assume that the curved trajectory is caused by the object moving at a constant horizontal velocity, while accelerating downwards due to gravity. The object’s vertical velocity decreases as it moves upwards, and increases as it moves downwards. At the top of the path, the vertical instantaneous velocity is zero, but the ball still has its constant horizontal velocity. The horizontal velocity of a projectile does not change with time. The vertical component decreases in magnitude as the ball rises, then increases as it falls. To solve projectile motion problems it is necessary to separate the initial motion into horizontal and vertical components. Weight Forces can speed things up, slow things down, change the direction that the object is travelling or change the object’s shape. When forces on an object are balanced there is no net force. If the object is moving, it will be moving at a constant speed. If it is not moving, it will remain stationary. When forces on an object are unbalanced there is a net force and the object will accelerate or decelerate. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: MECHANICAL WAVES Refraction of Wavefronts The speed of a wave is dependent upon the properties of the medium through which the waves travel. If the medium (and its properties) is changed, the speed of the waves also changes. The most significant property of water that affects the speed of waves travelling on its surface is the depth of the water. Water waves travel fastest when the medium is the deepest. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ENERGY AND MOMENTUM Conservation of Momentum The principle of conservation of momentum states that "the total momentum before a collision (or explosion) is equal to the total momentum after the collision, unless acted upon by an external net force". It is important to remember that momentum is a vector. When finding the total momentum the direction of the vector components must be taken into account. An external net force is a force from something that is not initially considered to be part of the system. If two trolleys collide they should rebound away so that the sum of their initial momentums is equal to the sum of their final momentums. It is important to realise that this does not mean that the principle of the conservation of momentum has been broken. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Calculating Total Charge Objects become charged because they have gained or lost electrons. Gaining or losing electrons creates an imbalance of charge and results in the object gaining an overall charge. If electrons are gained, the object will become negatively charged and positively charged if electrons are lost. The size of an object’s overall charge depends on the number of electrons that have been gained or lost. An object that has gained 4 x 106 electrons will be twice as negatively charged as an object that has gained only 2 x 106 electrons. The following equation can be used to calculate the total charge on an object: Q = nq Q = total charge n = number of charged particles q = charge on the particle 1 C = 6.24 x 10 18 el ectro ns Charge has the unit coulomb (C). Q and q are both used when discussing charge. Generally, Q is used for a large or total charge, while q is used if discussing small charges such as electrons that contribute to the total charge. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Energy Transfer Energy cannot be created or destroyed. Therefore, when a charged particle’s electrostatic potential energy changes, the change must be accounted for by different forms of energy. A common example of this is when a positively charged particle is placed beside a positive parallel plate. The particle will accelerate away from the positive plate and lose electrostatic potential energy. This ‘lost’ energy is being converted into kinetic energy, and is the reason why the particle speeds up. Using the principle of Conservation of Energy and the equation for kinetic energy, the speed that the particle reaches can be calculated. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS The Cathode Ray Tube A cathode ray tube (CRT) is a vacuum tube that contains one or more electron guns (a source of electrons) and a fluorescent screen. They create images when the electrons strike the screen. It has a means to accelerate and deflect the electron beam(s) onto the screen to create the images. Electron beam Cathode Focussing anodes y-plates x-plates High voltage supply Phosphor screen The electron gun uses a heater to provide energy to the electrons on the cathode. This allows the electrons to overcome the forces which are holding them to that metal. A high voltage supply is attached to the cathode and the anode, making the cathode negatively charged and the anode positively charged. The free electrons are now repelled by the negative cathode and attracted to the positive anode, creating the electron beam. When the beam of electrons reach the anode they encounter a gap in the anode, pass through the anode and travel along the cathode tube. Once the electron beam has passed the anode it travels through vertical and horizontal deflecting plates. These are designed to attract/repel the electron beam, so it can be directed into the desired position. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: DC ELECTRICITY Understanding Current When a closed circuit is formed, an electrical field (E) is created in the conductor. The charges (+ve and -ve) within the conductor experience a force (F). The direction of the electrical field is the same as the direction of the force on a positive charge. Electrons move in the opposite direction to the direction of the electrical field (i.e. towards the positive terminal). This flow of electrons is called electrical current. Negative charges move in the opposite direction to the electrical field. Electrical field F E F Positive charges move in the same direction as the electrical field. Each electron that flows around the circuit has a very small amount of charge, however there are huge numbers of electrons available in electrical circuits. The amount of charge that passes a certain point per second is defined as current. Scientists express the relationship between charge and current with the following formula. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROSTATICS Floating Charges - Millikan's Experiment In the early 1900s an American physicist called Robert A. Millikan began designing and performing an experiment to accurately calculate the charge on an electron. At that time there were no accurate measurements for either their mass or charge. Using the ‘falling drop method’, Millikan was able to accurately calculate the charge of an electron. This was a breakthrough in the world of physics, and in 1923 Robert Millikan was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the electron as well as other work on the 'Photoelectric Effect'. Millikan’s falling drop method works by placing oil droplets between two parallel plates, then adjusting the electric field strength so that the gravitational and electrostatic forces on the droplets are equal and opposite. This causes the droplets to have zero net force on them, and they float motionless between the parallel plates. The diagram below is an simplified model of Robert A. Millikan’s experiment. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: DC ELECTRICITY Understanding Voltage Voltage (or potential difference) is a measure of the amount of electrical energy changed (∆E) to other forms of energy by one unit of charge (coulomb) as it moves between two positions. 10 V 10 V The voltage source (battery/power-pack) raises the electrical potential energy of the electrons (that are distributed evenly and everywhere within the circuit). However, no work can be done to the electrons (i.e. they can't be moved) unless there is a difference in electrical potential energy. 10 V 5V Kinetic energy + Heat There is now a difference in voltage in the wire. Because of this, all the electrons move at the same time from an area of high electrical potential energy to an area of lower electrical potential energy. This potential difference is measured in volts (V) using a voltmeter. The voltmeter measures the electric potential energy of electrons before and after a component. For example, in a light bulb, voltmeters measure the electrical energy (per coulomb) changed to heat and light. Therefore, voltmeters must be connected in parallel to the component to be able to record the difference. Scientists express this relationship with the following formula: V = ∆E / q V = Voltage (volts , V) ∆E = Change in Potential Energy (joules , J) q = Charge (coulombs, C) 1. To overcome this issue a device called a voltage divider (also called a 'potential divider') can be used. A voltage divider is made by placing two resistors in series that have connections to the appliance so that it can be placed in parallel with the second resistor. The total resistance is very useful and often necessary when wanting to find out the total current flowing around a circuit. However, solving combination circuits requires that all the voltage, current and resistance rules are known and can be applied. Series Circuits Parallel Circuits Current Constant Each branch's current adds up to total current entering the parallel block. Voltage Each component shares voltage that adds to the total. Each branch uses identical voltage to other branches. Resistance Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 + .... 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 + .... Step 2: Check if the other sections of the circuit can be used to find the information required for the section in question. • If yes, then use it to find the required information, then find the quantity. • If no, then move to step 3. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: DC ELECTRICITY Properties of Lamps Brightness: Lamps convert electrical energy to light and heat energy. A bright lamp is converting more energy than a dim lamp. The rate that a component transforms energy is called power. Therefore, to determine if one lamp will be brighter than another, you must calculate which lamp has the greatest power. Shorting Lamps: Placing a wire in parallel with a lamp shorts it (i.e. it creates a short circuit). This means that all the current flows along the wire, bypassing the lamp. Since no current flows through the lamp, it uses no voltage, draws no power and does not glow. Blowing Bulbs: Lamps are designed to operate at a certain voltage. They can handle a small percentage more voltage (20% more will generally work), but once that margin is exceeded the bulb will burn out. With most bulbs this means the filament has melted. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM What is a Magnet? Materials that can be magnetised, which are also the ones that are attracted to magnets, are called ferromagnetic. They include iron, nickel, cobalt, some alloys of rare earth metals and some naturally occurring minerals such as lodestone. All materials that have the ability to be magnetised contain regions called ‘magnetic domains’. These are regions that have a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other. S S N N N S N N S S N N N S S S In non-magnetised objects magnetic domains are arranged randomly. The north and south poles cancel out and the object will not be a magnet. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Electromagnetic Induction During the motor effect, a length of wire that has a current flowing through it will experience a force when moved perpendicular to a magnetic field. Electromagnetic induction is the opposite effect. If a force is used to move a length of wire through a magnetic field, a voltage will be induced in the wire. It is important to note that it is a voltage being created, not a current. A current will flow provided certain conditions are met. If a current does not flow, electromagnetic induction will still happen, and a voltage will always be induced. Conducting Rod Induced voltage can be explained by the Lorentz Force (F=Bqv) on electrons (in this example they are moving down the page). The electrons are the “free electrons” in the conducting rod, also moving down the page and crossing the magnetic field lines that are into the page. Using the right-hand slap rule (negative charge version): • Fingers = magnetic field into page. • Thumb = upwards (against negative particle motion). • Palm to the left = force on electrons inside the moving conducting rod. We can see the free electrons will be pulled to the left side of the rod. This will leave the right side of the rod with a net positive charge. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Loops Moving Through Magnetic Fields When a conducting wire or rod is moved through a magnetic field a voltage is induced across it, meaning that one end of the conductor becomes positively charged and the other end negatively charged. If the conductor is formed into a loop and moved into a magnetic field a current may be induced to flow around the loop. 1 Initially no part of the loop is inside the magnetic field, therefore no voltage is induced in any part of the loop. A B +A B D C D C +A B - A B D C D C + - 3 When the entire loop is inside the magnetic field both sides AB and C-D have induced voltages. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics External/.searchText: ELECTROMAGNETISM Simple Generator Generators are used to convert kinetic energy to electrical energy. A simple generator is very similar to the DC motor. Just like the DC motor the basis of the generator is a coil (with multiple loops) that is placed inside a permanent magnetic field. Carbon brushes are used to provide a self-lubricating contact. The main component difference between the DC motor and the simple generator is the slip rings. Axle B Coil C A D Carbon brush Slip rings Slip Rings: The simple generator has two slip rings, one being attached to the side A-B, and the other attached to the side C-D. This means that the side A-B will always be attached to the right-hand side carbon brush, and the side C-D will always be attached to the left-hand side. As the coil spins inside the magnetic field a voltage is induced across each side (A-B and C-D). Since the coil is spinning either clockwise or anti-clockwise, one side of the coil will be moving upwards through the magnetic field on one part of the rotation, and downwards on the other. The result of this changing direction is that the induced voltage (and subsequent current) will reverse, meaning that the simple generator will produce an alternating voltage and current (AC electricity). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Physics 1.5 Heat/.searchText: HEAT TRANSFER Temperature and Heat Most people use the terms ‘heat’ and ‘temperature’ in interchangeable ways, without realising that they are talking about two different quantities. Temperature (symbol T) describes how hot an object is. This is related to energy, but it is not energy. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in an object. A hot object simply has particles that are moving faster than those of a cold object. Heat energy (symbol Q) is the total kinetic and potential energies of the particles that make up the object. Heat is a form of energy that can be transferred, and is sometimes called thermal energy. It is measured in Joules (J). The addition or removal of heat from an object can cause the object to experience a change of temperature, as well as a change of state. The temp erature o f an object ca n be meas ured. NCEA Examiner’s report : “Many candidates could not calculate weight when given mass”. In science, mass is a measure of the amount of matter in an object. It is measured in kilograms (kg). The mass of an object does not change if the object changes its location. Weight is a measure of the force on an object and is caused by the effect of gravity on that object. Like all forces, weight is measured in newtons (N). If you drop an object, it will accelerate towards the centre of Earth at approximately 10 metres per second for every second it is falling. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.1 Mecha.searchText: FORCES Air Resistance When an object falls there are two main forces acting on it: • The weight of the object is the force acting downwards. Weight force is caused by the effect of Earth’s gravity on the object’s mass. • Friction caused by air resistance is the force acting in an upwards direction. This force opposes the movement of the object. Air resistance is the result of collisions of the object’s leading surface with air molecules. The more air molecules that an object collides with, the greater the air resistance force. Subsequently, the amount of air resistance is dependent upon the speed of the falling object and the surface area of the falling object. 4:08 PM slide to unlock As the object moves faster, the air resistance increases. As a result the net force gets smaller. It is still accelerating as the forces are unbalanced. Eventually the downwards force is balanced by the upwards force of the air resistance and the object falls at a constant rate (no acceleration) called its terminal velocity. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.1 Mecha.searchText: POWER, WORK AND ENERGY Introduction to Energy Energy lets us do work and is required to make anything happen. Energy is not a substance that you can see or touch but we can often observe its effects. Energy is measured in joules (J). Energy exists in many forms and it can be transformed from one form to another. However, it cannot be created or destroyed. This means whenever there is an energy transformation no extra energy is created and no energy disappears, it just changes into a new form. 1. Match the forms of energy with the correct description. Heat Energy • Energy of an object due to its motion. • Examples include moving cars, running and swimming. Light Energy • The movement of electrically charged • particles. Found in wires, generators and lightning. Sound Energy • The energy of electromagnetic • waves. Found in microwaves, X-rays, and visible light. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.1 Mecha.searchText: POWER, WORK AND ENERGY Calculating Gravitational Potential Energy When an object is lifted up against the force of gravity it gains gravitational potential energy. For example, if you place a cup on a shelf you have to do work against the force of gravity. The cup has gained gravitational potential energy. The amount of gravitational potential energy depends on its height above Earth and its mass. The cup and glasses on the two shelves have gravitational potential energy. The cup and glass on the top shelf have more gravitational potential energy than the glasses on the bottom because they are higher. The cup on the top shelf has more gravitational potential energy than the glass on the same shelf because it has more mass. The glasses on the bottom shelf have the same amount of gravitational potential energy because they have the same mass and are the same height above the Earth. Gravitational Potential Energy can be calculated using the following formula: ∆EP = m g ∆h = = = ∆EP= mg∆h Because m x g is the calculation for weight force, the formula can also be expressed as : ∆EP= force x ∆height. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.1 Mecha.searchText: POWER, WORK AND ENERGY Energy Transformations Energy is most important to us when it is transformed from one form to another. These energy transformations cause all of the change that occurs around you. For example, when you turn on your phone chemical potential energy in the battery is transformed into electrical energy. The electrical energy is then transformed into light energy by the screen and sound energy by the speaker. These changes can be summarised in an energy transformation diagram. A light bulb (a) converts electrical energy to light energy. A car engine (b) converts chemical potential energy to kinetic energy. A microphone (c) converts sound energy to electrical energy. A candle (d) converts chemical potential energy to heat energy. A stereo speaker (e) converts electrical energy to sound energy. An electric heater (f) converts electrical energy to heat energy. An electric motor (g) converts electrical energy to kinetic energy. Flinging a rubber band (h) converts elastic potential energy to kinetic energy. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.1 Mecha.searchText: FORCES Friction Friction is a force that occurs when an object moves, or tries to move, against another object or fluid. Friction often acts to oppose (prevent or stop) the movement of an object. Friction can generate heat, causes wear and tear, and slow moving objects down. The effects of friction can be reduced if the surfaces of the two materials are lubricated (with water or oil, etc). Friction can be increased by making one or more of the surfaces rougher or by pressing them together more strongly. 1. 2. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.1 Mecha.searchText: FORCES Mass and Weight In everyday language, we often confuse the terms mass and weight. NCEA Examiner’s report : “Many candidates could not calculate weight when given mass”. In science, mass is a measure of the amount of matter in an object. It is measured in kilograms (kg). The mass of an object does not change if the object changes its location. Weight is a measure of the force on an object and is caused by the effect of gravity on that object. Like all forces, weight is measured in newtons (N). If you drop an object, it will accelerate towards the centre of Earth at approximately 10 metres per second for every second it is falling. Because weight is a force, we can use the formula: Fnet = m = a = Fnet = ma net force (N) mass (kg) acceleration (m s-2) When calculating the weight of an object on Earth, acceleration (a) is due to gravity (g). Acceleration due to gravity is constant (10 m s-2 or alternatively 10 N kg-1 - either way, use the number 10 in your calculations). uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.1 Mecha.searchText: FORCES Air Resistance When an object falls there are two main forces acting on it: • The weight of the object is the force acting downwards. Weight force is caused by the effect of Earth’s gravity on the object’s mass. • Friction caused by air resistance is the force acting in an upwards direction. This force opposes the movement of the object. Air resistance is the result of collisions of the object’s leading surface with air molecules. The more air molecules that an object collides with, the greater the air resistance force. Subsequently, the amount of air resistance is dependent upon the speed of the falling object and the surface area of the falling object. 4:08 PM slide to unlock As the object moves faster, the air resistance increases. As a result the net force gets smaller. It is still accelerating as the forces are unbalanced. Eventually the downwards force is balanced by the upwards force of the air resistance and the object falls at a constant rate (no acceleration) called its terminal velocity. Energy is not a substance that you can see or touch but we can often observe its effects. Energy is measured in joules (J). Energy exists in many forms and it can be transformed from one form to another. However, it cannot be created or destroyed. This means whenever there is an energy transformation no extra energy is created and no energy disappears, it just changes into a new form. 1. Match the forms of energy with the correct description. Heat Energy • Energy of an object due to its motion. • Examples include moving cars, running and swimming. Light Energy • The movement of electrically charged • particles. Found in wires, generators and lightning. Sound Energy • The energy of electromagnetic • waves. Found in microwaves, X-rays, and visible light. For example, if you place a cup on a shelf you have to do work against the force of gravity. The cup has gained gravitational potential energy. The amount of gravitational potential energy depends on its height above Earth and its mass. The cup and glasses on the two shelves have gravitational potential energy. The cup and glass on the top shelf have more gravitational potential energy than the glasses on the bottom because they are higher. The cup on the top shelf has more gravitational potential energy than the glass on the same shelf because it has more mass. The glasses on the bottom shelf have the same amount of gravitational potential energy because they have the same mass and are the same height above the Earth. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.5 Acids.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Getting To Know The Periodic Table If you look at the NCEA Periodic Table, you will notice that each element has a number associated with it. The number is called the atomic number and represents the number of protons found in the nucleus of a single atom of that element. Since the number of protons is equal to the number of electrons, the atomic number also tells you how many electrons there are in the energy levels around the nucleus. Another important number you will not find on the NCEA Periodic Table is called the mass number. This tells you the total number of particles, protons plus neutrons, found in the nucleus of an atom. So, if you know the mass number and the atomic number of an element, it is possible to work out the number of neutrons in the nucleus. By subtracting the number of protons from the mass number, you can calculate the total number of neutrons. Worked Example 1. A lithium atom has a mass number of 7. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.5 Acids.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Naming Ions When naming ions, you must adhere to the following rules: • Positive ions (i.e. the metals and hydrogen) are usually named after the element they are formed from. For example, the ion formed when calcium loses two electrons is also called the calcium ion (Ca2+). • Negative monatomic ions (‘mono’ means one, so monatomic means ‘ions made of only one atom’) are usually named using the suffix - ide. For example, chlorine (Cl) forms the negative ion chloride (Cl-), and oxygen (O) forms the oxide ion (O2-) • Polyatomic ions (‘poly’ means many, so polyatomic means ‘ions made of many atoms’) are usually named using the suffix -ate. For example, SO42- is the sulfate ion and CO32- is called the carbonate ion. Exceptions to this rule include the hydroxide ion (OH-) and the ammonium ion ( NH4+). • Some ions can have more than one charge. For example, iron can be Fe2+ or Fe3+. Chemists use roman numerals to distinguish (tell the difference) between them. Therefore, Fe2+ is written as Iron(II) and Fe3+ is written as iron(III). 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.5 Acids.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY A Closer Look at Electrons Chemical reactions are occurring all around us. Metals are corroding, food is cooking, plants are photosynthesising, etc. But how can we tell if two chemicals are going to react? The answer depends on their electrons. Electrons surround the nucleus of an atom in various energy levels (often referred to as ‘shells’ or ‘layers’). Each energy level can only contain a certain number of electrons. The first level (closest to the nucleus) can hold 2 electrons. The second level can hold 8 electrons. The third level can hold 8 electrons. 1. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.5 Acids.searchText: FOUNDATION CHEMISTRY Balancing Chemical Equations Nearly 2 500 years ago, Greek philosophers (early scientists) came up with the theory that “nothing comes from nothing”. Over time many scientists have further refined this theory to suggest that “matter can not be created or destroyed” - a statement that scientists refer to as the “Law of Conservation of Mass”. In simple terms, this means if you weighed the ingredients of a cake, then baked it in a closed system, the mass of the cake at the end would equal the mass of the ingredients. The same is true for chemical reactions. The number of atoms in the reactants will always equal the number of atoms in the products. Scientists show this by writing balanced equations. For example, consider hydrogen gas reacting with oxygen gas to create water. Graphically this reaction would look like this: H H + O O O H As a chemical equation is would look like this: H2 + 2 atoms of hydrogen H H2O O2 2 atoms of oxygen 2 atoms of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen The equation is unbalanced. There are 4 atoms in total on the left-hand side of the equation and only 3 atoms on the right hand side - an oxygen atom is missing! In order to balance an equation there are a couple of rules you must stick to: • You can never add small numbers to a compound (e.g. H2O cannot become H2O2) • You can only add numbers to the front of a compound. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.5 Acids.searchText: RATES OF REACTION Factors Affecting the Rate of a Reaction Temperature The rate of a chemical reaction can be increased by raising the temperature of the reaction. Low Temperature High Temperature Low Concentration High Concentration Small Surface Area Larger Surface Area Raising the temperature causes the reactant particles to move more quickly. This means they have more energy (specifically kinetic energy). Particles that are moving more quickly, with more energy, have a higher chance of colliding successfully and will collide more often. Concentration The rate of a chemical reaction can be increased by increasing the concentration of one or all of the reactants. Increasing the concentration means particles are more numerous and closer together, so there is an increased chance of collisions. Surface area Increasing the surface area of a reactant leads to an increase in reaction rate. If a solid reactant is broken into small pieces, or ground into a powder, then its surface area has increased. This means more particles are exposed, meaning more particles are able to collide. Catalysts Catalysts are special chemicals that speed up the rate of reaction but are not used up in that reaction. uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.5 Acids.searchText: RATES OF REACTION Investigating the Effect of Concentration on Reaction Rate Concentration is defined as the number of many particles are in a given volume. Concentration is measured in moles per litre (mol L-1). A concentrated acid contains more acid particles and less water particles than a more dilute acid. Increasing the concentration of a solution leads to more collisions (greater frequency of collisions), because the particles are closer together, so the rate of the reaction goes up. In other words, with a more concentrated acid, the number of acid particles is greater, so the number of collisions is greater and the rate of the reaction is higher (faster). In a less concentrated acid, the number of collisions is lower, so the rate of the reaction is slower. Changing the concentration of a reactant does not change how quickly the particles are moving (i.e. it doesn’t increase the amount of kinetic energy they have). uploads/science/Scipad/Science 1.5 Acids.searchText: ACIDS AND BASES Acids Acids are substances composed of one or more hydrogen atoms chemically bonded to one, or a group of, non-metal atoms. For example, sulfuric acid (H2SO4) is composed of two hydrogen atoms (H) bonded to a sulfate group (SO42-). When an acid molecule is added to water, it will dissociate (break apart) into its ions. For example, hydrochloric acid is a solution of hydrogen chloride (HCl) in water. The HCl molecule dissociates into hydrogen ions (H+) and chloride ions (Cl-). Strong acids completely dissociate, releasing all of their hydrogen ions when they come into contact with water. The common laboratory acids (hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric acids) are all strong acids. Weak acids, on the other hand, do not completely dissociate and only release some of their hydrogen ions when they come into contact with water. Organic acids (acetic, citric and other carboxylic acids) are weak acids. 1. Acids share a number of common properties.
